00:09.160 --> 00:12.880
to connect to the database and interact with it, play around with it.

00:13.240 --> 00:17.890
And the cool thing about that is once this is installed, we're actually going to be able to start writing

00:17.890 --> 00:21.340
code, which I think is the reason we're all here, or at least I hope so.

00:21.460 --> 00:24.490
Let's, let's go ahead and click install SSmS.

00:25.490 --> 00:30.500
And you'll be taken to a Microsoft website that will have another link we'll need to click to download

00:30.590 --> 00:31.550
SSmS.

00:32.560 --> 00:37.810
So if we click this link, we should see an executable file appear in the bottom left hand corner of

00:37.810 --> 00:38.560
the screen.

00:39.450 --> 00:41.580
And that's going to take a few minutes to download.

00:41.580 --> 00:43.830
So I'm going to go ahead and fast forward a little bit here.

00:54.320 --> 00:57.590
So now the executable file has finally finished downloading.

00:57.920 --> 01:06.410
And if I can stop clicking the wrong button, I actually need to go ahead and click open file and that

01:06.410 --> 01:09.230
should kick off the installation wizard.

01:09.350 --> 01:14.780
Now, at this point, you may see a dialog box pop up asking you if you want to allow this application

01:14.780 --> 01:16.430
to make changes on your computer.

01:16.460 --> 01:20.780
If so, just click yes and we should be able to proceed with installation.

01:21.590 --> 01:26.030
Now, at this point, we just need to wait for the first screen of the installation wizard to appear.

01:26.060 --> 01:32.690
Once it does, we'll click install and then we'll need to wait a few minutes for the installation process

01:32.690 --> 01:33.260
to complete.

01:33.260 --> 01:35.840
So I'll fast forward here for your viewing pleasure.

01:45.880 --> 01:48.670
So it looks like our installation completed successfully.

01:48.700 --> 01:54.040
So first we'll click close to Exit the Installation Wizard and then we'll click the start button at

01:54.040 --> 01:55.630
the bottom left corner of the screen.

01:56.320 --> 02:01.360
And then look up under recently added at the top and click SQL Server Management Studio.

02:02.360 --> 02:07.760
Now, it's possible that on your machine, SQL Server Management Studio won't appear under recently

02:07.760 --> 02:11.050
added applications, but if not, that's no big deal.

02:11.060 --> 02:16.280
Just type the name of the application SQL Server Management Studio in the search bar at the bottom left

02:16.280 --> 02:17.330
and it should appear.

02:17.940 --> 02:20.400
Now, this is a pretty big application.

02:20.400 --> 02:25.650
So the very first time you open it, it's possible it will take a couple minutes to to open.

02:25.650 --> 02:27.810
So I'm actually going to fast forward a little bit here.

02:33.820 --> 02:39.520
Now that management studio has finally opened, we should see this connect to server dialog box appear.

02:39.640 --> 02:43.840
Now we're ultimately going to stick with all the defaults you see in this dialog box, but I want to

02:43.840 --> 02:46.990
offer a brief explanation of them before we move on.

02:47.260 --> 02:49.360
The server type is a database engine.

02:49.360 --> 02:52.210
That's what you're pretty much always going to choose there.

02:52.240 --> 02:58.750
The server name is just the computer name, so to speak, of the database that we just installed, the

02:58.750 --> 03:05.410
database server we just installed, and the authentication method is Windows authentication.

03:05.440 --> 03:09.390
What that really means is the database is authenticating you.

03:09.400 --> 03:14.460
It is verifying that you are you with the same credentials that you use to log into your computer,

03:14.470 --> 03:16.450
your login and your password.

03:16.480 --> 03:23.170
Alternatively, you can set up a login and a username and a password for this database.

03:23.170 --> 03:23.890
This is different.

03:23.890 --> 03:27.100
That is different than the one you used on your Windows machine to log in.

03:27.100 --> 03:30.250
But for now we'll just stick with Windows authentication.

03:30.250 --> 03:32.380
It works the same and it's a little simpler.

03:32.470 --> 03:37.400
So now we'll go ahead and click Connect to actually Connect Management Studio to the database.

03:38.060 --> 03:42.740
And after a few seconds we should see some stuff appear in the left hand side of the screen.

03:43.280 --> 03:50.570
And that stuff is what's going to allow us to explore our data once we get a sample database installed.

03:50.750 --> 03:55.700
But obviously, first things first, we have to install that sample database and that's what we'll do

03:55.700 --> 03:56.790
in the next video.

03:56.810 --> 03:57.800
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.650 --> 00:01.850
Hey, welcome back.

00:02.060 --> 00:07.760
So we've gotten through two of the three big downloads and installations that we have to get through

00:07.760 --> 00:11.950
in order to get to the fun stuff where we're writing code and getting our hands dirty.

00:11.960 --> 00:18.110
So the last one is to download the Adventureworks sample database that is provided by Microsoft.

00:18.260 --> 00:25.580
So what we need to know about this is that is an example database pertaining to a fictitious company

00:25.580 --> 00:31.430
called Adventureworks that's meant to simulate the types of data that you're going to see in the wild

00:31.430 --> 00:37.220
that you would see working as a data analyst for for a large company, even a smaller company.

00:37.250 --> 00:45.080
So while the data may not be real, the patterns and the data structures that you see are very similar

00:45.080 --> 00:47.300
to things that you'll see in the real world.

00:47.910 --> 00:54.240
So to get to that sample database, I just googled download Adventureworks sample database, and the

00:54.240 --> 00:56.070
first link that comes up is from Microsoft.

00:56.070 --> 00:57.870
So I click that.

00:59.060 --> 01:05.120
And if you scroll down, you'll see that there are a number of files available to download with this

01:05.120 --> 01:07.460
funny little extension back.

01:08.130 --> 01:17.600
Now back means that the file is a backup file so that can be used to restore a database.

01:17.630 --> 01:21.230
A backup essentially of a database to a database server.

01:21.230 --> 01:28.610
So what we're going to do is take that file and use it to restore that adventureworks database on our

01:28.610 --> 01:29.600
database server.

01:30.190 --> 01:38.470
So you'll see that these back files are organized under three different column headings and one is OLTP

01:38.710 --> 01:40.240
and the second is data warehouse.

01:40.240 --> 01:44.920
So these represent different ways of structuring data within a database.

01:45.340 --> 01:48.760
They're both somewhat common, but OLTP is the most common.

01:48.760 --> 01:54.220
It's probably what you're going to be working with most of the time on on the job.

01:54.220 --> 01:58.080
So we're going to stick with the the database that's formatted that way.

01:58.090 --> 02:02.480
And since we've already installed the most recent version of SQL Server Express.

02:02.500 --> 02:07.420
SQL Server Express 2019, we're going to use the most recent version of Adventureworks.

02:07.840 --> 02:11.530
So I'll click that download link to begin.

02:18.730 --> 02:19.120
All right.

02:19.120 --> 02:24.970
It looks like our file has downloaded, but instead of clicking open file like we did previously.

02:25.090 --> 02:31.480
Instead, we're going to click these three dots to the right of the file name, and we're going to click

02:31.510 --> 02:39.190
show in folder, and that will show us the the location where that file was downloaded because we actually

02:39.190 --> 02:45.250
want to move it to a special folder where our database server is stored on our file system.

02:47.310 --> 02:52.290
So here is where the back file landed on my computer.

02:52.650 --> 02:55.500
It looks like I've downloaded it twice, but that's fine.

02:55.510 --> 02:57.270
We'll just use the first one here.

02:58.190 --> 03:00.530
And that's the file I want.

03:00.530 --> 03:08.420
But again, I want to move it to this special folder on the location on my computer where our database

03:08.420 --> 03:08.960
server is.

03:08.960 --> 03:12.560
So first I'm going to right click and copy.

03:13.280 --> 03:17.660
And then I'm going to navigate to the folder where the database server is stored on my computer.

03:18.480 --> 03:21.450
Now, typically that's going to be first under your C drive.

03:22.280 --> 03:24.800
And then under program files.

03:25.820 --> 03:31.040
Once you're under program files, you're going to want to find the the folder for Microsoft SQL Server.

03:33.290 --> 03:35.130
And then SQL Express.

03:35.150 --> 03:40.490
Now, if by some chance you have multiple versions of SQL Server on your computer, you would probably

03:40.490 --> 03:46.520
see multiple folders for the different types of of SQL Server on your computer, but most likely you've

03:46.520 --> 03:48.950
just installed SQL Express, so that'll be the only one.

03:49.560 --> 03:50.790
So we'll click that one.

03:51.390 --> 03:53.880
And then got to go through one more folder.

03:53.880 --> 03:58.620
And finally we see within that last folder there is a folder called backup.

03:59.180 --> 04:02.210
And remember, the extension of that file is back.

04:02.240 --> 04:03.640
It's a backup file.

04:03.650 --> 04:07.040
So we're going to finally go into the backup folder.

04:07.630 --> 04:09.790
Right click and paste.

04:09.790 --> 04:16.000
So now we've got our backup file in the designated backup folder for our database server.

04:16.880 --> 04:20.960
So now the next step is to open SQL Server Management Studio.

04:21.630 --> 04:24.330
Which I'm going to do by clicking the start menu.

04:24.330 --> 04:28.590
And this time, instead of opening under recently added, although it is there, I'm actually going

04:28.590 --> 04:36.090
to type in the search box SQL and as soon as I type in SQL, there's SQL Server Management Studio and

04:36.090 --> 04:41.760
while it's pulled up there just to make things more convenient going forward, I'm going to right click

04:41.760 --> 04:45.080
that and say PIN to Taskbar.

04:45.090 --> 04:51.330
So from now on when we want to open it, we can just hover our mouse over the icon down here, click

04:51.330 --> 04:52.950
it and it'll pop right up.

04:53.850 --> 04:56.400
So let's go ahead and open SQL Management Studio.

04:58.900 --> 05:01.450
And we will connect to the database server as before.

05:06.870 --> 05:07.230
All right.

05:07.260 --> 05:10.740
Now that we're connected to the database, we want to.

05:11.550 --> 05:18.480
Locate that backup file that we saved in the backup folder and actually use that to restore the Adventureworks

05:18.480 --> 05:20.970
database to our database server.

05:21.360 --> 05:28.020
So to do that, you want to click over here on the left under the Object Explorer where it says databases

05:28.350 --> 05:30.030
and then right click.

05:30.910 --> 05:33.310
And choose restore database.

05:36.110 --> 05:42.720
Now, then a dialog box will pop up and it will prompt you to choose a source, database or device.

05:42.740 --> 05:45.530
In this case, we're going to choose device.

05:45.560 --> 05:50.570
Now, after you've selected device, you're going to want to go over to this little button with three

05:50.570 --> 05:52.730
dots on it and left click that.

05:53.750 --> 05:59.720
And we'll have yet another dialogue box pop up that asks you to select the backup media type.

05:59.900 --> 06:01.550
The choices are file and URL.

06:01.580 --> 06:07.250
Well, we have a backup file, so we'll leave file selected and then you'll want to click Add.

06:08.250 --> 06:09.690
And this is pretty cool.

06:09.690 --> 06:17.070
So SQL Management Studio is smart enough to look in that backup folder that we saved the backup file

06:17.070 --> 06:18.270
to by default.

06:18.270 --> 06:20.520
So we'll go ahead and select that click.

06:20.520 --> 06:21.120
Okay.

06:24.370 --> 06:26.140
And then we'll click okay one more time.

06:28.530 --> 06:36.180
And before we click okay a third time, you want to make sure that the box under restore here is checked.

06:36.540 --> 06:39.120
So finally we'll click okay again.

06:39.700 --> 06:44.500
And we see some green progress bars, which is generally a good sign and it says Database Adventureworks

06:44.500 --> 06:46.630
2019 restored successfully.

06:47.110 --> 06:47.850
That is great news.

06:47.860 --> 06:48.850
We'll click okay.

06:49.640 --> 06:51.290
And now the moment of truth.

06:51.530 --> 06:57.920
We'll click the plus sign to the left of databases which will expand all the databases that are available

06:57.920 --> 07:00.770
for us to view on this database server.

07:01.880 --> 07:04.130
And there's Adventureworks 2019.

07:04.870 --> 07:10.480
Now that we've confirmed that the Adventureworks 2019 sample database has been restored successfully,

07:10.510 --> 07:16.300
we have everything in place that we'll need to begin writing code to interact with that database in

07:16.300 --> 07:21.250
the same way that you'll be writing code to interact with your company's database in your role as a

07:21.250 --> 07:23.280
data analyst or a data scientist.

07:23.290 --> 07:28.360
So congratulations on making it through all of the installations because the fun stuff begins now.

07:28.360 --> 07:29.770
I'll see you in the next video.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.170 --> 00:01.130
Welcome back.

00:01.880 --> 00:08.690
Now that we've got our Adventureworks sample database installed, I want to take a few minutes to familiarize

00:08.690 --> 00:12.840
you with that database and also with SQL Server Management Studio.

00:12.860 --> 00:15.080
If you haven't already used it.

00:15.260 --> 00:20.750
Now, if you're taking this course, I assume that you have a solid background in SQL.

00:20.780 --> 00:27.080
But I do not assume that you necessarily have a background in SQL Server or have used some of the SQL

00:27.080 --> 00:29.840
Server specific tools like Management Studio here.

00:29.840 --> 00:34.790
So if you came from an Oracle background, it's probably going to be pretty easy and intuitive for you

00:34.790 --> 00:36.840
to learn how to use management studio.

00:36.860 --> 00:41.240
But that said, I'll walk you through a couple of the features that we'll use the most.

00:41.930 --> 00:49.430
So first over here on the left is Object Explorer, which is sort of a catalog of the objects in our

00:49.430 --> 00:50.360
database.

00:50.600 --> 00:55.580
For the purposes of this course, we're mostly going to be hanging out under this databases section.

00:55.580 --> 00:58.310
In fact, I think we'll entirely be hanging out under there.

00:58.760 --> 01:05.840
The other sections are more for database administration type tasks, and specifically we'll be under

01:05.840 --> 01:08.300
the Adventureworks 2019 database.

01:08.330 --> 01:15.830
As you can see, Object Explorer is basically just a kind of tree like structure that has headings that

01:15.830 --> 01:20.960
when you click the plus sign to the left of the heading, you see a series of subcategories and then

01:20.960 --> 01:26.540
you click the plus signs next to those and you get even more subcategories all the way down.

01:27.190 --> 01:30.970
So the sub category I just clicked was tables.

01:30.970 --> 01:36.430
And as you might imagine, that's probably where we're going to spend most of our time in this course.

01:36.760 --> 01:44.760
So under Adventureworks 2019 here, the tables section lists out all the tables in our database.

01:44.770 --> 01:51.400
And as you can see, it's quite a few, probably not many compared to production or commercial database,

01:51.400 --> 01:53.500
but enough to give us something to chew on.

01:54.660 --> 02:01.470
Now digging a little deeper, if we click the plus sign to the left of an individual table, let's say,

02:01.470 --> 02:05.940
for example, our sales order header table, which is one that we're going to be querying against a

02:05.940 --> 02:06.540
lot.

02:06.810 --> 02:14.670
You now see different categories pertaining to metadata about the table, the columns, the keys constraints,

02:14.670 --> 02:16.050
indexes, etcetera.

02:16.410 --> 02:23.070
And then if you click the plus sign in front of, say, columns, now you get a list of all the columns

02:23.070 --> 02:30.420
in that table, their respective data types and other information, like whether that column is a primary

02:30.420 --> 02:33.510
key, a foreign key or what have you.

02:34.040 --> 02:39.830
Now, one cool trick you can do in management studio is if you want to just preview the data in a table

02:39.830 --> 02:46.520
without having to write out the SQL by hand, you can right click the table over here in Object Explorer

02:46.520 --> 02:54.860
and just choose select top 1000 rows and SQL will automatically write a select top 1000 query for you.

02:54.890 --> 02:58.730
So it's just a nice, convenient way to get a little preview of a table.

02:58.730 --> 03:03.110
If you're curious about what's in it, about what the data looks like without you having to write the

03:03.110 --> 03:04.040
SQL by hand.

03:04.070 --> 03:05.780
I personally use this a lot.

03:05.780 --> 03:10.910
A lot of times I'll use select top 1000 to generate the code and then I'll go in and modify it however

03:10.910 --> 03:15.260
I need to so it can kind of function as almost a starter or a template.

03:16.230 --> 03:20.610
Now, let's say we wanted to select the top 2000 rows instead.

03:21.990 --> 03:29.820
To run this query again, you would click the execute button here or alternatively, just hit F5 on

03:29.820 --> 03:30.690
your keyboard.

03:31.140 --> 03:38.280
Now, if we wanted to write our own query brand new from scratch, you would click the new query button

03:38.280 --> 03:38.850
here.

03:39.450 --> 03:46.710
And once you do that, the first thing you probably want to do is check this box here that currently

03:46.710 --> 03:52.920
says Adventureworks 2019 Just to make sure the database that you're interested in querying against is

03:52.920 --> 03:53.620
selected.

03:53.640 --> 03:58.950
Sometimes the master database will be selected by default, which is not the one that has our sample

03:58.950 --> 03:59.470
data.

03:59.490 --> 04:06.330
So when you're creating a new query with that new query button, just make sure Adventureworks 2019

04:06.360 --> 04:07.140
is selected.

04:07.140 --> 04:11.430
Or if you're at work and you're using SQL Server, make sure whatever database that you're trying to

04:11.430 --> 04:14.710
query is selected in that window when you're writing a new query.

04:14.730 --> 04:19.900
If it's not, sometimes you'll you'll run up against a nasty surprise when the code that you've written

04:19.900 --> 04:22.840
doesn't run because it's pointing to the wrong database.

04:23.290 --> 04:29.080
So then if we write a query and we want to save it, so let's just write something super simple like

04:29.290 --> 04:34.240
select Hello world.

04:34.240 --> 04:35.530
Just for old time's sake.

04:35.530 --> 04:37.360
For tradition sake.

04:37.840 --> 04:41.290
Then you would click file save as.

04:41.960 --> 04:44.690
And just choose the name of your query.

04:44.690 --> 04:48.560
We'll just call it hello and Save.

04:49.400 --> 04:54.510
And then if we want to open a query that we have closed, that's just as intuitive.

04:54.530 --> 04:57.560
So let's go ahead and close our Hello dot SQL file here.

04:58.120 --> 04:59.600
And then open it back up.

04:59.620 --> 05:02.230
You just go to file Open.

05:03.610 --> 05:04.360
File.

05:04.960 --> 05:10.900
And then we just browse to wherever our file is located in the file system, select it and click open.

05:11.580 --> 05:17.280
Now there are lots of other menus and toolbars and management studio that I'm not going to waste your

05:17.280 --> 05:22.530
time going through because what we have already covered is what you're going to use 90% of the time

05:22.530 --> 05:24.690
in this course and on the job.

05:25.140 --> 05:30.690
So the last thing I want to go over is just a brief review of a couple of the tables in our database

05:30.690 --> 05:32.880
that we're going to be using most of the time.

05:33.510 --> 05:41.220
Probably the biggest thing to understand is the difference between our sales order header table here.

05:41.780 --> 05:44.480
And our sales order detail table.

05:44.690 --> 05:51.260
So we've already taken a brief look at our sales order header table via the top 1000 query we did against

05:51.260 --> 05:51.650
it.

05:52.310 --> 05:58.760
And just looking at the data rows in the table are unique by sales order ID.

05:59.090 --> 06:05.180
Basically, what's going on with this table is that there is one row per sales order.

06:05.700 --> 06:12.810
Now, by contrast, if we go look at our sales order detail table, this table is not unique by sales

06:12.810 --> 06:18.780
order ID right off the bat, you see that certain sales order IDs are repeated multiple times.

06:19.050 --> 06:25.580
That's because this table has a row for every line item in a sales order.

06:25.590 --> 06:34.590
So say somebody orders, for example, two bicycles and five bicycle helmets, all as part of one order.

06:34.680 --> 06:41.280
That order is going to get one row in our sales order header table, but it's going to get as many rows

06:41.280 --> 06:45.870
in our sales order detail table as there were items in the order.

06:46.050 --> 06:51.750
So in other words, there is a one to many relationship between our sales order header table and our

06:51.750 --> 06:53.490
sales order detail table.

06:53.580 --> 06:59.490
And I'm going to be leveraging that relationship and a lot of examples that will work through throughout

06:59.490 --> 07:00.240
the course.

07:00.660 --> 07:07.450
Similarly, there is a purchase order header table and a purchase order detail table.

07:07.570 --> 07:10.990
They work very similarly to their sales counterparts.

07:10.990 --> 07:15.460
There's a similar one to many relationship between the purchase order header table and the purchase

07:15.460 --> 07:16.360
order detail table.

07:16.360 --> 07:21.610
And sometimes we'll use this pair of tables instead of the sales tables or in addition to the sales

07:21.610 --> 07:24.490
tables for other types of examples.

07:25.120 --> 07:31.840
Another table that we'll use quite a bit is the human resources dot employee table, which.

07:32.370 --> 07:39.000
Has a variety of information about all the employees in our fictional company, their titles, their

07:39.030 --> 07:42.420
their birth dates, hire dates, the amount of vacation time they have.

07:42.420 --> 07:43.230
ET cetera.

07:43.260 --> 07:50.760
Useful data points for some of the types of calculations that we're going to practice doing as part

07:50.760 --> 07:51.600
of the course.

07:52.560 --> 07:59.280
A couple of other tables that we'll see from time to time are the person person table, which just has

07:59.280 --> 08:06.270
a row for every person associated with our fictional company, whether in a capacity as a customer or

08:06.270 --> 08:07.320
as an employee.

08:08.260 --> 08:14.290
And then we will also occasionally be using our production dot product table.

08:15.190 --> 08:19.540
Which has information about all the products that our company sells.

08:19.990 --> 08:26.050
Again, a lot of kind of juicy text and numerical data in here that we can creatively apply criteria

08:26.050 --> 08:30.370
for that will be useful for demonstrating certain types of examples.

08:31.030 --> 08:31.660
All right.

08:31.690 --> 08:37.240
My goal at this point is not for you to be an expert in SQL Server Management studio by any means.

08:37.270 --> 08:43.060
I really just want you to have enough knowledge to work through the code examples that I'll be presenting

08:43.060 --> 08:49.450
as we go, because it's that hands on experience that's really going to get you comfortable and familiar

08:49.450 --> 08:53.650
with the application to the point where you can be dangerous with it in the real world.

08:54.490 --> 08:59.370
And don't worry about having an encyclopedic knowledge of our sample database.

08:59.380 --> 09:04.720
We will be working through plenty of examples that will get you more familiar with all the with the

09:04.720 --> 09:06.610
tables that we're using the most.

09:06.610 --> 09:12.250
And now that you know how to use Object Explorer over here in our left, you essentially know how to

09:12.250 --> 09:12.730
fish.

09:12.730 --> 09:17.770
So if you want more information about a table, you can always just click the plus sign to the left

09:17.770 --> 09:23.980
and dig in to see more about the columns and their data types and any keys that are on the table and

09:23.980 --> 09:25.060
so on and so forth.

09:26.110 --> 09:26.530
All right.

09:26.530 --> 09:32.530
So at this point, we should have everything we need in place to actually start coding, which is I

09:32.530 --> 09:33.730
know why you're here.

09:33.730 --> 09:36.640
So without further ado, let's get started with that.

09:36.640 --> 09:38.020
I'll see you in the next video.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.290 --> 00:01.340
Welcome back.

00:02.010 --> 00:07.110
Assuming you've worked with aggregate queries in SQL, you know how useful they can be in performing

00:07.110 --> 00:14.820
calculations like sum Count or Max, just for example, across the rows of our data while optionally

00:14.820 --> 00:18.420
grouping the results of these calculations by other values in the data.

00:19.120 --> 00:24.970
However, these functions also force us to compromise the level of detail available to us in our query

00:24.970 --> 00:25.720
output.

00:25.840 --> 00:31.690
For example, if you want to see a count of all the rows in your table not broken up into groups, you

00:31.690 --> 00:34.030
won't actually be able to see these rows.

00:34.060 --> 00:38.290
Instead, your output will simply consist of the count and nothing else.

00:38.590 --> 00:43.450
So if we look at the records from our sales order header table.

00:45.580 --> 00:52.900
And then contrast that with a query that takes the sum of the total do column from that same table.

00:54.040 --> 01:01.500
You'll see that we lose all the detail, we lose all the columns and all the rows in that table.

01:01.510 --> 01:04.330
Everything is boiled down to this one single number.

01:04.980 --> 01:09.720
And then if you want to add new fields, you'll have to group by them, meaning the grand total will

01:09.720 --> 01:14.010
now be divided up across multiple groups based on the values in the fields you added.

01:14.340 --> 01:17.160
So we can look at this query here.

01:17.910 --> 01:26.040
So now we've added salesperson ID, which is fine, but if we're really trying to get to the amount,

01:26.040 --> 01:31.260
the total amount of sales, we're not seeing that in any one of these rows because that total amount

01:31.260 --> 01:34.290
is being broken up by salesperson ID.

01:34.290 --> 01:37.980
And then if we added another field to group by, it would be broken up even further.

01:38.010 --> 01:44.250
Now, this may be fine in many cases, but what if you need to see aggregate totals like dollar totals

01:44.250 --> 01:48.630
or row counts alongside the individual rows of your data?

01:48.840 --> 01:54.390
For example, let's say you wanted to compare an individual salesperson's year to date sales to the

01:54.390 --> 01:57.570
total of all year to date sales in our table.

01:57.960 --> 02:01.200
Traditional aggregate functions won't be able to help us here.

02:01.980 --> 02:05.910
Well, that's where window functions come in like.

02:05.940 --> 02:06.990
Aggregate functions.

02:06.990 --> 02:12.990
Window functions allow you to perform calculations like sum and count across groups of rows within your

02:12.990 --> 02:16.920
data, or alternately, all the rows in your data set.

02:17.590 --> 02:23.430
Whereas aggregate functions collapse the rows of your data into groups based on the unique values and

02:23.430 --> 02:25.590
the columns you include in your select statement.

02:25.920 --> 02:32.010
So you can see that the two records for Brandon in our detail data example here.

02:32.870 --> 02:39.050
Have collapsed down into one single record where those two sales amounts have been added up to.

02:39.080 --> 02:40.130
To one number.

02:40.160 --> 02:46.100
Now, by contrast, window functions allow you to retain row level detail while performing the same

02:46.100 --> 02:47.540
types of calculations.

02:48.620 --> 02:53.330
The aggregate calculation simply becomes another column in your query output.

02:54.280 --> 02:59.740
Now, again, you see that we've got two records for Brandon here in our detailed data, one with a

02:59.740 --> 03:02.980
$100 sales amount, one with a $200 sales amount.

03:03.220 --> 03:11.290
But in our window function version, we have this new column, Total Sales, where both records for

03:11.290 --> 03:15.140
Brandon reflect that total sales amount for Brandon.

03:15.160 --> 03:22.150
So we get the same result that we got with the aggregate query in terms of calculating Brandon's total

03:22.150 --> 03:22.660
sales.

03:22.660 --> 03:28.240
But we don't have to collapse our data down based on including that aggregate calculation.

03:28.240 --> 03:31.660
We can just tack it on as a new column in our query output.

03:32.310 --> 03:37.650
Now that we know when we might want to use a window function, let's take a quick look at the syntax

03:37.650 --> 03:39.300
before we dive into an example.

03:40.770 --> 03:42.870
Now, the first piece is just a function.

03:42.900 --> 03:51.210
It could be some count Max or any other aggregate function or one of a number of ranking functions specifically

03:51.210 --> 03:55.170
used alongside window functions, which we'll dig into a lot more later.

03:55.350 --> 03:59.550
But for now, we'll just stick with aggregate functions and sum in this example.

04:00.240 --> 04:04.110
Now, the second piece of the syntax is what makes this a window function.

04:04.200 --> 04:05.850
The over keyword.

04:06.560 --> 04:13.280
That when no arguments are passed over, as in this case, it simply applies our sum function here across

04:13.280 --> 04:18.350
the entire dataset, returning the result for each record in the dataset.

04:19.280 --> 04:24.350
Now, arguments can also be passed over, as you might have guessed, because of the parentheses after

04:24.350 --> 04:24.710
it.

04:24.710 --> 04:27.500
And rest assured, we'll get into that a lot more later.

04:28.000 --> 04:33.280
But for now, let's take a look at how a window function can help us with our year to date sales example.

04:33.550 --> 04:37.960
So here we have commented out a total year to date sales column.

04:38.050 --> 04:42.940
So let's go ahead and code this up really quick with a window function.

04:43.180 --> 04:50.800
So what we'll want to do is first type A sum because window functions will start with some kind of just

04:50.800 --> 04:55.570
a function that you're applying across your whole dataset or or groups within your dataset.

04:55.750 --> 04:59.590
And we'll plug sales year to date into that.

05:01.540 --> 05:07.060
And then we'll simply add over with parentheses after it.

05:07.870 --> 05:09.370
Now let's try running that.

05:11.690 --> 05:16.820
And you'll see that we get the same number for each record in our data set.

05:16.820 --> 05:22.310
And that number reflects the total year to date sales across all salespeople.

05:22.310 --> 05:23.750
And just to confirm that.

05:25.230 --> 05:31.140
Let's run an aggregate query that just pulls that and you'll see it's the same number.

05:31.680 --> 05:38.790
So as you can see, we were able to perform this aggregate calculation and include it in our query output

05:38.820 --> 05:41.550
without otherwise modifying our query in any way.

05:41.550 --> 05:46.590
We have all these other columns and if you want to wanted to add a new column like let's say we want

05:46.590 --> 05:52.590
to tack on sales last year, we can do that, no problem.

05:52.890 --> 05:59.490
Unlike an aggregate query where now you have to include that new field in your group by and it adds

05:59.490 --> 06:07.080
one more layer of grouping that breaks your your number that you're summing or doing a max of or averaging

06:07.080 --> 06:09.090
out over more and more groups here.

06:09.090 --> 06:15.090
You can keep that sum calculation over the entire data set no matter how many columns you choose to

06:15.090 --> 06:15.540
add.

06:16.180 --> 06:21.700
And we can just as easily add more columns with new and different aggregate calculations.

06:21.730 --> 06:25.240
Again, without impacting the rest of our query output in any way.

06:25.360 --> 06:32.020
For example, we can also add the maximum individual year to date sales amount for any salesperson as

06:32.020 --> 06:35.200
another data point to compare to our individual sales numbers.

06:35.440 --> 06:41.260
So this is going to work almost exactly like the total year to date sales, so much so that we're just

06:41.260 --> 06:43.150
going to copy the code.

06:44.380 --> 06:51.700
The only difference is we'll just type a max and let's see how that works.

06:53.140 --> 07:00.280
So now what you see for each row is the maximum sales year to date for any of our sales people.

07:00.280 --> 07:02.680
And again, just to confirm that this is working.

07:04.290 --> 07:07.650
Let's pull that as an aggregate query.

07:12.580 --> 07:13.870
And it's the same number.

07:14.290 --> 07:20.620
Now, even better, we can actually use these aggregate totals in row level formulas and calculations.

07:20.800 --> 07:26.860
If, for instance, we wanted to compute each salesperson's year to date sales as a percentage of the

07:26.860 --> 07:30.130
highest performers sales, which is the number we're looking at right here.

07:30.610 --> 07:32.810
Window functions make it really easy.

07:32.830 --> 07:41.290
So to do that, all we have to do is divide our sales year to date field, which is a.

07:42.060 --> 07:45.810
Row level field that's specific to each salesperson.

07:47.820 --> 07:51.540
And we divide that by our.

07:52.280 --> 07:59.720
Window function here that calculates the max sales year to date over all of our sales people.

07:59.720 --> 08:08.060
So what we should get is any given sales persons, percentage of the very best sales persons performance.

08:09.010 --> 08:14.740
And what we should also see is whoever got the best performance should have a one in this column because

08:14.740 --> 08:19.780
their sales are 100% of the best salesperson sales.

08:23.920 --> 08:24.370
All right.

08:24.370 --> 08:27.340
So if we scroll down here, we see.

08:27.960 --> 08:29.890
It looks like it's working as it should.

08:29.910 --> 08:36.000
We see one record where the percentage of best performer is 100%, and this is in fact the person who

08:36.000 --> 08:38.130
had the best sales year to date.

08:38.130 --> 08:44.100
So this is just an example of how you can code a pretty useful metric, one that lets you compare an

08:44.100 --> 08:49.320
individual salesperson's performance against some kind of benchmark pretty easily using window functions.

08:49.500 --> 08:55.230
In short, window functions give you the power to include aggregate calculations in your queries without

08:55.230 --> 08:57.810
changing the rest of your query output in any way.

08:58.690 --> 09:04.060
The calculation is simply added to your data set as another column with no impact on the rest of the

09:04.060 --> 09:04.570
data.

09:05.370 --> 09:11.160
But you may be asking since window functions can perform aggregate calculations on the rows of our data

09:11.160 --> 09:17.070
similar to aggregate functions, is there a way to break these calculations out based on groups within

09:17.070 --> 09:20.400
our data like we accomplished previously with Group by.

09:21.030 --> 09:23.610
There sure is its partition.

09:23.610 --> 09:27.000
And we'll look at how to plug it into our window functions in the next video.

09:27.180 --> 09:28.230
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.230 --> 00:01.310
Welcome back.

00:01.950 --> 00:08.220
We've seen how to perform aggregate calculations across our entire dataset without losing row level

00:08.220 --> 00:09.900
visibility into our data.

00:09.930 --> 00:11.280
Using over.

00:11.550 --> 00:16.820
But what if we wanted to roll those aggregate totals up into groups the same way we do with group by

00:16.830 --> 00:18.360
using aggregate functions?

00:18.390 --> 00:20.100
How would that work with over?

00:20.850 --> 00:22.800
The answer is partition by.

00:24.050 --> 00:30.320
When we combine our over function with partition by, we now have the power to compute aggregate totals

00:30.320 --> 00:37.670
for groups within our data while still retaining that row level detail that distinguishes window functions

00:37.670 --> 00:39.080
from aggregate functions.

00:39.110 --> 00:45.890
The first step partition by takes is to assign each row of your query output to a group, but it does

00:45.890 --> 00:51.080
this behind the scenes without collapsing your data into fewer rows as with group by.

00:51.170 --> 00:52.970
So how does it do this?

00:53.540 --> 00:56.690
Kind of like group B, but not exactly.

00:57.650 --> 01:03.680
Instead of groups being assigned based on the distinct values of all the non-aggregated columns of our

01:03.680 --> 01:07.610
data, we have to specify the columns these groups will be based on.

01:08.090 --> 01:11.270
Let's dive into some code to see what this looks like in action.

01:11.840 --> 01:19.580
First, we'll try grouping our sales order detail data by product ID and order quantity using a traditional

01:19.580 --> 01:20.690
aggregate query.

01:21.110 --> 01:28.280
As you recall, this operation works by creating a group for each unique combination of values from

01:28.280 --> 01:32.900
all the fields listed in our group by product ID and order quantity.

01:32.900 --> 01:40.190
In our case, the aggregate calculation or calculations of our choosing sum count et cetera will then

01:40.220 --> 01:42.470
be performed over each of these groups.

01:42.650 --> 01:46.430
So how does this kind of grouping translate to our window functions?

01:47.150 --> 01:53.270
Here we have another query against the sales order detail data, this time with an over function that

01:53.270 --> 01:59.380
calculates the sum of line totals for the entire dataset and returns this value to each row.

01:59.390 --> 02:02.510
So let's run this really quick and see what the output looks like.

02:03.760 --> 02:05.890
Should be fairly familiar to us by now.

02:06.190 --> 02:12.460
Now, if we want this sum broken out into subtotals similar to our aggregate query above, we will still

02:12.460 --> 02:17.550
need to spell out the columns that define our groupings, product ID and order quantity.

02:17.590 --> 02:21.730
And that is done in the partition by clause of the over function.

02:21.910 --> 02:24.040
So here's what that looks like in code.

02:24.690 --> 02:28.230
So what we'll do is within our over function.

02:28.230 --> 02:29.790
So partition by goes.

02:29.820 --> 02:38.880
Goes inside of the over function within those parentheses we'll type partition by and we are partitioning

02:38.880 --> 02:40.770
by product ID.

02:45.270 --> 02:46.800
An order quantity.

02:51.040 --> 02:53.020
So now let's run that.

02:53.410 --> 02:58.340
Okay, So we have obviously retained the row level detail of our query output.

02:58.360 --> 03:00.370
Unlike with aggregate functions.

03:00.610 --> 03:04.060
But how do these groupings work, exactly?

03:05.030 --> 03:10.970
Behind the scenes sequel is creating the same groups we saw in our aggregate query based on the same

03:10.970 --> 03:17.720
unique combinations of the fields we listed in our partition by, in this case, product ID and order

03:17.720 --> 03:18.470
quantity.

03:19.090 --> 03:27.190
Then SQL assigns each row of our data to one of these groups returning the associated aggregate total.

03:27.760 --> 03:35.650
Now let's take, for example, the combination of product ID 707 and order Quantity 24 and compare what

03:35.650 --> 03:37.120
we see in our two queries.

03:37.450 --> 03:41.540
So to do that, I'm going to run both of our queries simultaneously.

03:41.560 --> 03:45.100
So I'll just highlight both queries.

03:46.540 --> 03:50.410
And run them now in our aggregate query.

03:50.440 --> 03:56.590
This combination gets exactly one row in our output, as do all other combinations.

03:56.950 --> 04:04.000
And you can see that the the aggregate line total for all orders with product ID 707 and order quantity

04:04.030 --> 04:06.790
24 is 743.

04:07.510 --> 04:14.860
But in our window function example, every row in our query output with this combination of values is

04:14.860 --> 04:17.370
simply considered a member of the same group.

04:17.380 --> 04:25.150
And you can see in this case it's two records, but both records that have product ID 707 and Order

04:25.150 --> 04:31.260
Quantity 24 are assigned this number 743 point.

04:31.360 --> 04:32.890
A lot of decimal places.

04:33.250 --> 04:39.970
That is the exact same number as the total for those two product for that product ID and that order

04:39.970 --> 04:42.910
quantity that was returned by our aggregate query.

04:43.540 --> 04:51.310
So the window function is basically returning the sum of line total for each of these rows, as our

04:51.310 --> 04:54.190
aggregate function did for the entire group.

04:54.370 --> 04:59.830
So in this way we are able to perform aggregate calculations on groups within our data.

05:00.430 --> 05:05.920
Without losing any row level detail or the flexibility to include any columns we want.

05:06.070 --> 05:12.130
And if we want to add more layers to our groups, it's as easy as tacking on an extra field onto our

05:12.130 --> 05:13.450
partition by clause.

05:13.660 --> 05:18.940
But unlike traditional aggregate functions, we don't have to worry about adding or removing fields

05:18.940 --> 05:20.720
from our select or group by statements.

05:20.740 --> 05:24.580
It just works without affecting the rest of our query output in any way.

05:25.690 --> 05:31.180
So now that we've learned how to leverage window functions as a more flexible alternative to traditional

05:31.180 --> 05:34.990
aggregate functions, it's time to dig into some entirely new things.

05:34.990 --> 05:38.230
They allow us to accomplish that no other technique can.

05:38.410 --> 05:40.460
We'll kick that off in the next video.

05:40.480 --> 05:41.500
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.000 --> 00:00.870
Welcome back.

00:01.780 --> 00:08.020
Up to this point, we've basically used window functions as a more sophisticated alternative to traditional

00:08.020 --> 00:09.220
aggregate queries.

00:09.550 --> 00:15.670
And while aggregate calculations like sum or count are a perfectly good application of window functions,

00:15.670 --> 00:18.550
they also give us something entirely new.

00:18.550 --> 00:25.750
The ability to assign a ranking either within partition groups or overall throughout our query output

00:25.990 --> 00:28.030
to the records within our data set.

00:28.610 --> 00:33.680
Let's go back to our sales order detail dataset for an example of what this can look like.

00:33.890 --> 00:40.550
So here we have a query against our sales order detail data with a window function giving us the sum

00:40.580 --> 00:43.160
of line totals for each sales order ID.

00:44.210 --> 00:46.190
As you remember from the last video.

00:46.220 --> 00:52.010
Each record in the dataset is assigned a group based on the field we have listed in our partition by

00:52.010 --> 00:54.650
clause, and that's sales order ID right here.

00:55.040 --> 01:02.060
And then the sum for the group, which we can also see in this aggregate query down here.

01:03.140 --> 01:04.820
Is assigned to that record.

01:06.970 --> 01:12.310
So at this point, we're hopefully pretty confident in our ability to assign the individual records

01:12.310 --> 01:19.660
in our data to various groups behind the scenes and then return an associated aggregate total to each

01:19.660 --> 01:20.350
record.

01:20.590 --> 01:25.930
But what if we instead wanted to somehow rank the records within each group?

01:25.960 --> 01:32.290
For example, we could assign a ranking to the records within each cluster of identical sales order

01:32.290 --> 01:37.660
IDs instead of simply returning a sum of the line totals for that particular ID.

01:38.580 --> 01:40.650
So what would this look like in code?

01:41.180 --> 01:48.110
The most straightforward way to implement this kind of ranking is the row number function which we use

01:48.110 --> 01:49.820
alongside the over function.

01:49.820 --> 01:54.020
In the same way we used aggregate functions like sum and count previously.

01:54.700 --> 02:01.450
Row number will assign a unique ranking, beginning with one to every record within a group.

02:01.960 --> 02:07.480
Our groups are defined by unique combinations of values from all the fields listed in the partition

02:07.480 --> 02:08.110
by clause.

02:08.140 --> 02:11.470
Just like before, assuming we have a partition by at all.

02:12.100 --> 02:14.500
So let's try that here and see what happens.

02:14.800 --> 02:21.820
So we'll start out basically by just mimicking what we've already done to calculate product line ID

02:21.850 --> 02:29.830
total by sales order ID, and we'll just change the name of the field to ranking.

02:32.350 --> 02:37.600
And instead of doing a sum of line total, we'll just do.

02:38.600 --> 02:47.620
The function row underscore number and then an open and closed parentheses without any arguments passed.

02:47.630 --> 02:53.150
It's still a function, so you need those parentheses, but you don't pass any arguments to row number.

02:53.360 --> 02:58.370
Finally, we'll get rid of this comma and run the query and see what happens.

03:00.640 --> 03:01.540
Yikes.

03:01.570 --> 03:02.440
An error.

03:02.710 --> 03:09.550
So management studio is telling us we need to have an over clause with order by.

03:09.850 --> 03:11.770
So what the heck does that mean?

03:12.630 --> 03:15.510
Well, if you think about it, it kind of makes sense.

03:15.780 --> 03:21.840
We're asking SQL to rank records within a group, but we're not telling it how to rank them.

03:22.080 --> 03:24.240
And that's where order by comes in.

03:24.930 --> 03:30.660
So as you've seen, we already use order by to sort the data in our overall query output.

03:30.870 --> 03:37.980
But it turns out it can also be used to sort data within our partition groups to determine how records

03:37.980 --> 03:40.140
within those groups will be ranked.

03:40.410 --> 03:46.260
So in this example, let's try sorting the records within our partition groups by line amount.

03:46.530 --> 03:57.360
So syntax wise, how that looks is that we'll take our line amount field here and within our over function.

03:57.360 --> 04:05.400
But after partition by we'll type order by and then we'll drop in that line total.

04:05.670 --> 04:10.380
Now note here there are no commas separating partition by and order by.

04:10.410 --> 04:13.890
This is a little confusing to most people who are first learning these functions.

04:13.890 --> 04:21.270
You're kind of used to arguments within a function being separated by commas, but in this case within

04:21.270 --> 04:27.910
over your partition by piece and your order by piece are not separated by commas.

04:27.940 --> 04:29.080
It's just a space.

04:29.080 --> 04:34.240
And if you were to have if you were to be partitioning by more than one field, those fields would need

04:34.240 --> 04:40.150
to be separated by commas, but then you would not have a comma like this after the last field.

04:40.210 --> 04:46.030
There is no comma between the last field in partition by and then the order by keyword.

04:46.030 --> 04:51.340
And likewise, if you ordered by more than one field, you would have commas in between those fields

04:51.340 --> 04:52.390
after order by.

04:52.720 --> 04:56.200
So let's run this and see how that changes our output.

04:58.840 --> 05:00.250
All right, now we're talking.

05:00.400 --> 05:07.330
Our code ran successfully, and we appear to have an actual rank right here in our ranking field.

05:07.600 --> 05:09.640
But what does the rank mean?

05:09.940 --> 05:13.600
So I've gone ahead and sorted our query output by sales order ID.

05:13.930 --> 05:21.490
Just to clarify how this works and please note that sorting in your overall query is not in any way

05:21.520 --> 05:25.810
necessary for a window function like row number to work.

05:25.810 --> 05:31.750
It works regardless of whether you sort your overall query output with order by.

05:31.780 --> 05:39.100
But in this case it's just useful to group the like sales order IDs so we can see how the rankings within

05:39.100 --> 05:41.200
that group over here work.

05:41.230 --> 05:45.700
So basically within each group of like sales order IDs.

05:45.700 --> 05:51.940
So we could start, for example, with 45043659.

05:52.570 --> 05:57.640
The ranking is determined by the amount of the line total right here.

05:58.160 --> 06:00.800
The lowest total gets ranked number one.

06:00.920 --> 06:02.480
That's $10 here.

06:02.480 --> 06:09.380
And you can see that is in fact, the lowest total among all the identical sales order IDs over here

06:09.380 --> 06:10.400
in the first column.

06:11.160 --> 06:14.460
The second lowest gets ranked number two and so on.

06:14.790 --> 06:21.030
Now, this is because we have the order by within our over function sorting in ascending order, if

06:21.030 --> 06:24.390
you recall, order by sorts and ascending order by default.

06:24.390 --> 06:29.120
So ascending order will put the smallest number first.

06:29.130 --> 06:37.470
So because the smallest number is sorted first, the smallest line total gets the first ranking.

06:38.070 --> 06:44.700
