And then with a couple of quick modifications, we can get it to do what we want.

05:24.510 --> 05:29.640
So as my first step, of course, I'll change the name of this column to Highest Total.

05:33.640 --> 05:39.610
Next, I'll swap in our new first value function for row number right here.

05:43.370 --> 05:44.000
Uh oh.

05:44.360 --> 05:48.760
Now we see a red squiggly line under our code that we didn't see a moment ago.

05:48.770 --> 05:50.570
So what's going on with that?

05:51.530 --> 05:56.720
Well, that's appearing because we actually need to pass an argument to the first value function.

05:57.050 --> 06:02.030
Unlike with row number, but kind of like with the lead and lag functions we saw earlier.

06:02.900 --> 06:09.530
And that argument is the field that you actually want to see the first value from.

06:10.440 --> 06:17.580
Now, in our case, we want to see the first line total for a given sales order ID within our query

06:17.580 --> 06:18.150
output.

06:18.150 --> 06:20.430
So I'll just pass line total in here.

06:23.310 --> 06:28.830
And just like that, our squiggly line has gone away and we actually have everything we need to get

06:28.830 --> 06:29.610
this working.

06:30.160 --> 06:32.260
So if we go ahead and run this code.

06:33.810 --> 06:37.500
Scanning the results in our new highest total column.

06:37.860 --> 06:46.380
It looks like the the value in that column always represents the highest line total for any given partition

06:46.380 --> 06:48.780
group window in our query.

06:49.540 --> 06:55.570
So for our very first sales order ID, the highest line total is 6074.

06:56.120 --> 07:03.050
And sure enough, our highest total column reflects that number for every row in that group.

07:03.410 --> 07:09.080
But as soon as we switch to a new sales order ID, which means a new window, since that's what we're

07:09.080 --> 07:16.730
partitioning by, that highest total value changes to reflect the highest line total of the two records

07:16.730 --> 07:18.590
we have for that sales order ID.

07:20.210 --> 07:26.720
Now, you might be wondering what if for some reason I wanted to see the lowest line total for each

07:26.720 --> 07:28.730
order and not the highest?

07:29.430 --> 07:31.950
Or window function expert that you are.

07:31.980 --> 07:33.990
You might have already figured that one out.

07:34.730 --> 07:39.410
So all I have to do and I'll go ahead and copy and paste our new code here

07:42.380 --> 07:45.260
and I'll name our new column, Lowest total.

07:48.010 --> 07:56.860
Now all we need to do is simply change the sort order inside of our over function from descending to

07:56.860 --> 07:58.870
its default of ascending.

07:59.260 --> 08:04.990
Meaning that within each partition group, the lowest value comes first.

08:05.500 --> 08:07.600
So now running this query again.

08:11.790 --> 08:17.550
And then looking at the value that was returned in our lowest total column for that very first window,

08:17.850 --> 08:26.880
it looks like it's the same value, basically $10.37 as the lowest line total for that particular partition

08:26.880 --> 08:27.450
group.

08:27.930 --> 08:33.810
So by removing that descending keyword, we were able to get a completely different window, if you

08:33.810 --> 08:35.190
will, into our data.

08:36.660 --> 08:37.380
Okay.

08:37.590 --> 08:45.150
So because another very common application of this sort of operation is to identify a value based on

08:45.150 --> 08:50.070
the oldest or most recent date within a group.

08:50.250 --> 08:53.760
Let's look at one more example that does just that.

08:55.520 --> 08:57.410
So running this query.

08:58.800 --> 09:06.210
You can see that it fetches customer ID, order date and total amount due from the sales order header

09:06.210 --> 09:06.780
table.

09:07.610 --> 09:14.330
Also note that the output is sorted first by customer ID, then by order date.

09:15.000 --> 09:20.730
That way we can compare a given customer's orders to each other in chronological order.

09:21.500 --> 09:28.190
So now let's say we want to create another column that for a given customer displays the amount of the

09:28.190 --> 09:31.040
very first order that customer placed.

09:31.690 --> 09:35.470
So let's first create a new column called First Order Amount.

09:40.780 --> 09:47.530
And then we'll use, of course, the first value function to bring our new derived column to life.

09:50.410 --> 09:57.850
So now, since the actual value we want, our new derived column to return is the total due amount.

09:57.880 --> 10:01.300
We'll pass that in as the argument to first value.

10:04.050 --> 10:08.370
Then of course we'll add an over function since we're dealing with a window function.

10:09.150 --> 10:16.230
Then since we're basing which total value we want to fetch on the order in which customers made their

10:16.230 --> 10:17.160
purchases.

10:17.400 --> 10:22.110
In particular, we want to grab the amount of their first or oldest purchase.

10:22.290 --> 10:27.720
We'll order by order date in ascending order within the over function.

10:31.290 --> 10:38.940
Finally, because we want first value to give us the amount of the first order per customer as opposed

10:38.940 --> 10:40.680
to for the dataset as a whole.

10:40.680 --> 10:43.050
We'll partition by customer ID.

10:48.540 --> 10:50.670
And that should do it.

10:50.820 --> 10:53.070
So now running our code.

10:55.910 --> 11:02.990
Zooming in on the first grouping of like customer IDs in our query or the first window, if you will.

11:03.830 --> 11:10.370
Note that this customer's very first order was placed on June 21st, 2011, and that the amount of that

11:10.370 --> 11:13.370
order was $3,756.

11:14.120 --> 11:21.650
So now looking over at our first order amount column, we see that that same number is reflected in

11:21.650 --> 11:27.050
every row of that column for this particular window of our query output.

11:27.080 --> 11:34.010
In other words, for that particular customer ID, But as soon as we switch to a new customer ID, that

11:34.010 --> 11:36.500
is to say a new window within our query output.

11:37.310 --> 11:39.320
Because we're dealing with a new customer.

11:39.350 --> 11:46.280
There is, of course, a new first order amount, this time for $3,729.

11:46.580 --> 11:54.230
And sure enough, that is the exact amount reflected in every row of our new column for that particular

11:54.230 --> 11:54.950
customer.

11:56.040 --> 12:01.950
Now, of course, if for some reason you wanted to return the amount of the most recent order per customer,

12:01.950 --> 12:08.160
instead it would simply be a matter of tweaking the way we sort order date in the over function.

12:08.900 --> 12:14.870
So if I just add the descending keyword here and then run our query once more.

12:17.740 --> 12:24.790
Now, that first order amount coincides with the most recent order placed by a given customer.

12:26.000 --> 12:31.670
Now, one thing that's worth noting about the first value function is that there's also a corresponding

12:31.670 --> 12:38.360
last value function that, as you would expect based on its name, works in a similar way, but in the

12:38.360 --> 12:39.860
exact opposite direction.

12:40.770 --> 12:48.150
However, because it's so easy to change the behavior of the first value function by simply ordering

12:48.150 --> 12:52.740
by whatever field you pass into the over function in a different way.

12:52.770 --> 12:54.660
Ascending versus descending.

12:54.870 --> 12:59.250
I really don't find a lot of utility in even using the last value function at all.

13:00.400 --> 13:07.810
That combined with the fact that last value actually forces us to include some additional kind of wonky

13:07.840 --> 13:13.990
syntax to get it to behave in the way we might expect is a good reason to just stick to the first value

13:13.990 --> 13:14.620
function.

13:17.190 --> 13:17.880
All right.

13:18.000 --> 13:24.300
So with that, we're pretty much done with first value, but we're not done with window functions just

13:24.300 --> 13:24.900
yet.

13:25.500 --> 13:32.430
In the next video, we'll get our first taste of an extremely powerful technique in SQL that can help

13:32.430 --> 13:35.190
us get even more value out of window functions.

13:35.550 --> 13:37.230
Among many other things.

13:37.590 --> 13:38.610
See you there.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.320 --> 00:01.430
Welcome back.

00:02.330 --> 00:08.990
Thus far, all the queries we've written have consisted of a single step, a single select query.

00:09.320 --> 00:16.520
But in the real world, complicated data analysis often requires multiple and sometimes many steps.

00:17.150 --> 00:18.680
For those situations.

00:18.680 --> 00:23.870
We need some way to break these problems into smaller, more manageable pieces.

00:24.540 --> 00:29.460
Now, there are actually several techniques for doing this in SQL, all of which have their place.

00:29.460 --> 00:33.030
But we'll start by looking at the simplest type, which is subqueries.

00:33.180 --> 00:38.700
As a motivating example, let's take a look at one of the queries we created earlier on when we covered

00:38.700 --> 00:39.930
the row number function.

00:40.470 --> 00:46.230
If you recall, this query ranks the items within each sales order by their line total.

00:46.790 --> 00:52.010
But what if we weren't interested in seeing all the records in the table, but rather the single record

00:52.010 --> 00:54.860
with the highest line total per each order?

00:55.040 --> 00:57.200
How could we accomplish this in SQL?

00:58.100 --> 01:03.710
The most obvious approach is to take the window function from our select and simply drop it into the

01:03.710 --> 01:05.930
where clause where we can apply our criteria.

01:06.230 --> 01:08.540
So let's try that and see what happens.

01:09.620 --> 01:19.520
So I'll just copy our window function right out of the select and add a where clause and we'll just

01:19.520 --> 01:21.200
try to set this equal to one.

01:21.230 --> 01:29.990
Basically, the goal is to pluck this record and this record and so on and so forth out of our data.

01:30.020 --> 01:35.600
We're basically trying to identify out of each group of like sales order IDs.

01:35.600 --> 01:39.380
We only want to see the one record that had the highest line total.

01:39.470 --> 01:42.230
So let's run this and see what happens.

01:43.820 --> 01:44.670
Ouch.

01:44.690 --> 01:47.390
So SQL is now giving us an error message.

01:47.420 --> 01:53.480
We're apparently only allowed to use window functions in the select and order by clauses, which leaves

01:53.480 --> 01:54.290
where out.

01:54.860 --> 01:59.990
So how the heck are we supposed to apply criteria to the fields that we generate with our window functions?

02:00.700 --> 02:03.520
The most straightforward answer is subqueries.

02:04.660 --> 02:07.360
Subqueries work pretty much like they sound.

02:07.600 --> 02:16.000
There is an inner or sub query that is nested within and then referred to by an outer query.

02:16.700 --> 02:23.360
We are essentially defining a kind of virtual table in one select query and then referring to that table

02:23.360 --> 02:27.470
in our outer query as though it was any other table in our database.

02:27.680 --> 02:30.070
But enough talk about subqueries.

02:30.080 --> 02:33.680
Let's take a look at how we can apply them to solve our problem here.

02:34.840 --> 02:41.230
The first step should typically be to build and test the query that we will need to refer to as a table

02:41.230 --> 02:41.890
later.

02:42.100 --> 02:45.340
This initial query will ultimately be our sub query.

02:46.020 --> 02:50.400
In our case, we've already written the subquery, which is our query with the window function right

02:50.400 --> 02:50.940
here.

02:51.810 --> 02:57.420
Now we need to be able to refer to the output of this query as though it is again simply another table

02:57.420 --> 03:02.460
in our database so we can apply criteria to this ranking field here that we created.

03:03.440 --> 03:06.200
The syntax for doing all this is pretty straightforward.

03:07.120 --> 03:11.080
First, we'll simply wrap our entire subquery in parentheses.

03:11.950 --> 03:20.230
So I'll start by entering down one and adding an open parentheses before and then a closing parentheses

03:20.230 --> 03:21.640
after our inner query.

03:21.640 --> 03:28.210
And note that I'm not going to be keeping this where clause from our original query because and we'll

03:28.220 --> 03:30.130
we'll see this more in a later step.

03:30.160 --> 03:35.730
I'll be applying the logic from our where clause in the outer query.

03:35.740 --> 03:37.270
So we'll get rid of that.

03:37.510 --> 03:43.630
But before we write any more code, I want you to try and visualize this query wrapped in parentheses

03:43.630 --> 03:48.000
that we see here as simply a reference to a table in our database.

03:48.010 --> 03:52.390
Except the table, as it were, is just the output of the query.

03:52.660 --> 03:56.350
So if I run this query just as a visual aid.

03:57.200 --> 04:03.830
Try to imagine that this query output you see down here is just another table and you can select fields

04:03.830 --> 04:05.780
from it like you can with any other table.

04:05.780 --> 04:11.360
And just as importantly, if not more, you can also apply criteria to it, just like you could in other

04:11.360 --> 04:11.870
table.

04:11.870 --> 04:16.730
And those criteria could include something like setting line total ranking equal to one.

04:17.290 --> 04:23.860
Looking at subqueries this way will go a really long way towards helping you understand them, especially

04:23.860 --> 04:29.650
when you're trying to read and interpret someone else's code that makes heavy use of subqueries.

04:30.270 --> 04:31.980
But back to our code.

04:32.250 --> 04:37.380
Now that we have our virtual table defined here, it's simply a matter of selecting fields from it,

04:37.380 --> 04:42.210
like we would with any other table and then applying criteria to the appropriate fields in the Where

04:42.240 --> 04:42.730
clause.

04:42.750 --> 04:44.100
So let's give that a shot.

04:45.190 --> 04:48.520
First, I'll add my select up here.

04:49.540 --> 04:55.810
And just to keep things simple, I'll do a select star and we'll also need the from keyword, just like

04:55.810 --> 04:57.850
you would with any normal query.

04:58.870 --> 05:05.500
And as I mentioned previously, I'm going to add a where clause below our subquery, below this closing

05:05.500 --> 05:08.770
parenthesis that marks the end of our inner query.

05:09.510 --> 05:18.840
And I'm going to apply that criteria we tried to use earlier to our line total ranking field by just

05:19.200 --> 05:24.030
asking SQL to return us any records where that line total ranking is equal to one.

05:24.700 --> 05:28.960
So you probably see these little squiggly red lines here and you probably know that means this is going

05:28.960 --> 05:29.440
to error out.

05:29.440 --> 05:31.930
But let's go ahead and run it just to make sure.

05:34.160 --> 05:35.150
And it did.

05:35.630 --> 05:42.350
So it turns out we're getting this error because we actually need to name or alias our subquery in the

05:42.350 --> 05:46.160
same way that we might alias any other table we bring into a query.

05:46.700 --> 05:50.420
So let's alias it A and try to run it again.

05:51.680 --> 05:53.630
So I'll just add that A afterwards.

05:54.500 --> 05:56.360
Highlight and run again.

05:57.620 --> 05:58.730
And there we go.

05:58.850 --> 06:00.060
Just like that.

06:00.080 --> 06:01.370
Our problem is solved.

06:02.420 --> 06:07.640
Now, in the real world, you will encounter plenty of different situations that require a multi step

06:07.640 --> 06:08.990
analysis in SQL.

06:09.080 --> 06:12.590
The scenario we just covered is a common one, but there are many more.

06:13.180 --> 06:17.860
For that reason, we're going to be revisiting the concept of multi-step queries throughout the rest

06:17.860 --> 06:20.410
of the course and not just subqueries.

06:21.170 --> 06:28.280
In fact, aside from a few specialized use cases that will expound on in the next few lessons, subqueries

06:28.280 --> 06:32.570
are best utilized for simple two step analysis like we saw in this video.

06:33.250 --> 06:39.220
While it's certainly possible to nest subqueries within other subqueries many layers down, this kind

06:39.220 --> 06:42.460
of code gets confusing and unwieldy fast.

06:43.260 --> 06:48.500
SQL gives us other approaches that are better suited to queries that require three or more steps.

06:48.510 --> 06:51.300
And rest assured, we're going to be covering those soon as well.

06:52.220 --> 06:59.180
But first we're going to go over a few incredibly powerful and often poorly understood applications

06:59.180 --> 07:00.200
of subqueries.

07:00.390 --> 07:02.100
That'll start in the next video.

07:02.120 --> 07:03.080
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.170 --> 00:01.310
Welcome back.

00:02.270 --> 00:09.800
So you know how lead and lag let you target individual rows in your data relative to the position of

00:09.800 --> 00:17.510
the current row, say the next row or perhaps two rows previous based on some specified ordering of

00:17.510 --> 00:18.170
the data.

00:18.840 --> 00:25.890
Well, now I want to introduce you to another spin on window functions called Rose between that lets

00:25.890 --> 00:28.710
you target whole groups of rows in your data.

00:28.800 --> 00:31.800
Again, relative to a given row in your data set.

00:32.640 --> 00:34.360
So how does that work?

00:34.380 --> 00:38.280
And more importantly, why the heck would we even want to go to the trouble?

00:39.820 --> 00:43.630
So say you have a query output that looks something like this.

00:44.330 --> 00:51.680
Now using rows between, you can actually generate a new column that for each row in an existing column

00:51.710 --> 00:59.060
of data does something with the data in any number of rows surrounding that row.

01:00.030 --> 01:06.660
Now, it's worth noting that this set of rows surrounding the current row also called a window.

01:06.690 --> 01:11.610
Hence, window functions will include the current row by default.

01:12.300 --> 01:19.830
So just as an example, you could target the current row, which for our purposes here is row five with

01:19.830 --> 01:25.770
an order amount of $555.55 and the two rows prior.

01:26.790 --> 01:32.550
Alternatively, you could target the current row and three rows after that.

01:33.840 --> 01:36.030
Or even everything in between.

01:36.840 --> 01:38.760
But now the question remains.

01:38.940 --> 01:43.980
Once we've captured these rows with SQL, what the heck do we do with them?

01:45.050 --> 01:47.660
In short, we aggregate them.

01:47.930 --> 01:52.940
Now, typically this means using an aggregate function like sum or average.

01:54.090 --> 02:01.170
So using some on our previous example that showed the preceding two rows plus the current row, as you

02:01.170 --> 02:08.790
may have already recognized, what we see here in row five of our new rolling Sum column is basically

02:08.790 --> 02:10.110
a rolling total.

02:10.720 --> 02:16.570
And in case you don't believe me, feel free to pause the video, whip out the calculator on your smartphone

02:16.570 --> 02:18.310
and add these three numbers up.

02:19.000 --> 02:22.120
Or if you really love math, just do it in your head.

02:23.230 --> 02:23.680
Now.

02:23.680 --> 02:29.080
Alternatively, if we take an average of this same window of rows.

02:29.770 --> 02:37.780
Now, instead of a rolling total, we have a rolling average, also commonly known as a moving average.

02:38.470 --> 02:44.770
Now, in case you're wondering why it's useful to calculate this kind of moving average in which the

02:44.770 --> 02:49.450
window over which we calculate that average changes for each row in our data.

02:50.380 --> 02:56.950
Moving averages are used so frequently because they're good at smoothing out short term fluctuations

02:56.950 --> 03:04.300
in the overall trending of our data, making it easier to identify patterns and longer term trends.

03:05.380 --> 03:12.130
Now it's important to note that we can also incorporate future rows into these windows, so to speak,

03:12.130 --> 03:15.220
just as easily as past rows.

03:15.340 --> 03:18.550
And we can also omit the current row if we like.

03:19.140 --> 03:24.480
But that's getting a little too far into the weeds without having some actual code in front of us.

03:24.870 --> 03:26.790
So speaking of that.

03:27.940 --> 03:31.510
Let's go ahead and look at a concrete example of this in code.

03:32.310 --> 03:39.510
So here we have a simple query that aggregates the total do column in our sales order header table by

03:39.510 --> 03:40.370
order date.

03:40.380 --> 03:48.000
So each row of our output will represent one distinct order date and then the sum of all the totals

03:48.000 --> 03:49.470
due for that date.

03:50.090 --> 03:55.640
And I've also filtered our output to only look at orders that occurred in 2014.

03:56.600 --> 04:03.920
Also note that I have sorted or ordered the output of our query by order date in ascending order.

04:04.190 --> 04:10.880
So the very first date in our dataset, chronologically speaking, comes first and so on and so forth.

04:12.030 --> 04:19.320
So let's say our goal here is to add a new column to this query that returns a running total of the

04:19.320 --> 04:21.570
last three days worth of sales.

04:22.470 --> 04:28.260
Now, since we can't use a window function in the same query as an aggregate function, we're actually

04:28.260 --> 04:30.780
going to have to accomplish this in two steps.

04:30.990 --> 04:38.130
Now, to do that, we'll turn this query into a sub query just like we saw in the last video, and then

04:38.130 --> 04:42.540
do our work with rows between in the outer layer of that query.

04:43.290 --> 04:52.170
So to turn this into a sub query above our current query, I'll type select, and then I'll just copy

04:52.410 --> 04:56.610
the two columns that we'll be displaying in our query output.

04:57.690 --> 05:02.970
And since we're not calculating the sum in the outer query that's being done in the inner query, I'll

05:02.970 --> 05:03.810
delete that.

05:04.520 --> 05:06.170
And then I'll say from.

05:07.410 --> 05:14.340
And then an open parenthesis and then a closing parenthesis after our inner query and an alias.

05:15.060 --> 05:23.280
And now running this again, we have a query that is functionally the same as what we had before, but

05:23.280 --> 05:27.660
now gives us the flexibility to work with window functions in the outer query.

05:28.170 --> 05:33.630
Now before we move on, I'll go ahead and indent this inner subquery just to visually offset it from

05:33.630 --> 05:34.530
everything else.

05:35.820 --> 05:43.380
Okay, so back to the task at hand, generating a running total of the last three days worth of sales.

05:44.330 --> 05:47.660
So I'll start by simply aliasing our new column.

05:47.810 --> 05:50.630
I'll call it sales last three days.

05:53.420 --> 06:00.140
And then since we're going to be summing total, do the first part of this will just be sum of total

06:00.140 --> 06:00.620
due.

06:03.560 --> 06:10.010
And I now realize I need to put a comma after total due in our select since SQL is making it very clear

06:10.010 --> 06:13.130
to me that it's quite upset that I'm not separating these columns with commas.

06:14.820 --> 06:20.580
So now, after our sum, as is usually the case when we're playing with window functions, I'll type

06:20.580 --> 06:22.320
out the over function.

06:23.530 --> 06:30.550
Now, thus far, this probably looks a lot like a standard window function to you where we're aggregating

06:30.550 --> 06:35.230
some column in this case total Du over some window.

06:36.540 --> 06:44.040
Now our next step, very similar to when we worked with lead and lag, will be to add an order by clause

06:44.040 --> 06:52.290
with which we'll define a sort order that gives our query a definition of which rows come before and

06:52.290 --> 06:54.090
after which other rows.

06:54.990 --> 07:00.720
Now, in this case, the obvious candidate to apply that sort order would be order date.

07:00.720 --> 07:03.360
So I'll just say order by order date.

07:07.610 --> 07:12.890
Now the importance that this field that we order by cannot be overstated.

07:13.490 --> 07:21.500
The sorting of our data set by this field determines the actual meaning of next three rows or previous

07:21.500 --> 07:24.410
two rows relative to the current row.

07:24.830 --> 07:29.090
Again, much like with lead lag and many other window functions.

07:30.160 --> 07:36.280
So with order by in place, we're now ready to add the two little words that this whole video is about.

07:36.990 --> 07:38.430
Rose between.

07:41.220 --> 07:49.560
So now after rose between is the part where we'll specify the boundaries of the window that our code

07:49.560 --> 07:52.560
will be evaluating relative to each row.

07:53.230 --> 08:00.940
Now, again, the window in our case will be the current row, plus the previous two rows for a total

08:00.940 --> 08:02.890
of a rolling three rows.

08:03.780 --> 08:10.230
Now to define this window, we'll use more special keywords in concert with rows between.

08:10.800 --> 08:13.710
And those key words are preceding.

08:14.250 --> 08:16.890
Following and current row.

08:18.040 --> 08:25.300
Now, in this case, we want to summarize all rows between two rows preceding the current row and the

08:25.300 --> 08:26.530
current row itself.

08:27.510 --> 08:37.260
Now with preceding and its counterpart following, you need to well precede the keyword with the exact

08:37.290 --> 08:44.190
number of rows you want the window to span in that direction relative to the current row.

08:44.850 --> 08:48.480
So in our case, we'll say two preceding.

08:50.660 --> 08:56.660
Now from here, this works a lot like between in the where clause of a query.

08:57.240 --> 09:02.700
We specify the start of our window, that being two preceding in this case.

09:02.940 --> 09:10.780
Then the keyword and and then the end of our window, which in this case is.

09:10.800 --> 09:12.030
Current row.

09:15.060 --> 09:21.090
Now, it's worth noting here that just like when you've used plain old between in the where clause of

09:21.090 --> 09:27.120
your SQL queries between in this context is also inclusive by default.

09:27.300 --> 09:36.270
So when we say we want to sum total due across a window between two rows preceding and the current row,

09:36.390 --> 09:39.690
we're including that current row in the calculation.

09:40.910 --> 09:44.870
Okay, so that's entirely enough talk and entirely enough syntax.

09:44.870 --> 09:47.720
So let's go ahead and run this and see what happens.

09:50.910 --> 09:58.800
And now if we look at this total for sales last three days in our third row, it should equal the sum

09:58.830 --> 10:02.400
of the total due values in the first three rows.

10:02.670 --> 10:05.250
So let's go ahead and copy those into Excel.

10:07.890 --> 10:17.190
And then looking at the sum, which is 1,715,596, and then going back to SQL.

10:18.150 --> 10:23.910
Sure enough, that's exactly what our rows between window function generated as well.

10:25.150 --> 10:31.660
So now that we have the basics down, let's play around with the boundaries of that window to see if

10:31.660 --> 10:36.250
we can get it to span different time frames relative to the current row.

10:37.060 --> 10:44.530
For example, what if we want to look at a rolling sum of the three days prior to the current row,

10:44.530 --> 10:46.600
not including the current row?

10:47.350 --> 10:54.850
So to do that, I'll just copy this query and oh, by the way, if I haven't pointed it out before,

10:54.850 --> 11:01.030
my apologies for the incredibly confusing rolling seven day total comment that I left at the top.

11:01.330 --> 11:05.560
By no means is our code attempting to calculate a rolling seven day total.

11:05.590 --> 11:10.690
We're instead calculating a rolling three day total, so you should expect the comment to reflect that

11:10.690 --> 11:14.140
in the downloadable SQL file you'll find in the course resources.

11:14.230 --> 11:15.550
But I digress.

11:16.180 --> 11:19.780
So rolling down our SQL file, I'll paste this code.

11:20.920 --> 11:28.820
And again, our goal here is to redefine our window to look at the three rows prior to the current row.

11:29.450 --> 11:39.080
So I can do that by simply saying rows between three preceding and then I'll replace current row with

11:39.080 --> 11:40.670
one preceding.

11:42.420 --> 11:45.810
In other words, the row prior to the current row.

11:46.770 --> 11:49.350
So now if I highlight this code and run it.

11:52.140 --> 11:59.220
And then compare the total in my third column here to the sum of the previous three total2 values,

11:59.250 --> 12:01.320
not including that current row.

12:01.890 --> 12:06.330
And then hop over to excel once again and paste those in.

12:07.260 --> 12:09.480
Sure enough, the sum matches.

12:11.420 --> 12:18.160
Now, while it's again not as common for the windows you defined to encompass future rows, so to speak,

12:18.170 --> 12:20.600
that's definitely something you can do.

12:21.240 --> 12:28.410
So, for example, what if we want our window to span the current row and include the row prior and

12:28.410 --> 12:29.730
the row after?

12:30.330 --> 12:33.030
So once again, I'll copy and paste our code.

12:34.020 --> 12:38.100
Then roll down our SQL file and paste that in.

12:39.330 --> 12:48.330
And here I'll just need to change our code to say between one preceding and one following.

12:50.760 --> 12:56.640
So while we don't even mention current row here, it's implied because the current row is going to be

12:56.640 --> 13:00.390
between the row preceding it and the row following it.

13:01.020 --> 13:03.390
So now I'll highlight this code and run it.

13:06.660 --> 13:14.580
And here we would expect this value in the second row of our new column to equal the sum of the totals

13:14.580 --> 13:16.950
due in the previous row.

13:16.980 --> 13:19.440
The current row and the following row.

13:19.680 --> 13:21.450
So let's sum those.

13:23.100 --> 13:26.220
And sure enough, the total we see in Excel.

13:27.130 --> 13:30.520
Matches what we see in that second row of our new column.

13:31.690 --> 13:36.820
Now, finally, we've saved arguably our most useful example for last.

13:37.030 --> 13:42.040
And that's that rolling or moving average we talked about at the beginning of the video.

13:42.490 --> 13:45.910
So to get to that, I'll once again copy our code here.

13:46.950 --> 13:48.780
And then roll down a little bit further.

13:49.410 --> 13:50.640
Paste that in.

13:51.870 --> 13:58.380
And here I'll first reset the boundaries of our window to once again look at the two days prior to the

13:58.380 --> 14:02.270
current row and then include the current row as well in that window.

14:02.280 --> 14:07.200
So I'll say between two preceding and current row.

14:09.330 --> 14:16.890
And now to change this rolling sum to a rolling average, literally all I have to do is change our aggregate

14:16.890 --> 14:18.720
function from sum.

14:20.240 --> 14:21.080
The average.

14:21.530 --> 14:23.510
So now if I run this.

14:26.780 --> 14:33.770
Now, if I look at another row in our new column, let's say the value here in row four, we would expect

14:33.770 --> 14:41.300
this number to equal the average of the totals due from that row and the previous two rows.

14:41.750 --> 14:43.850
So let's paste these into Excel.

14:45.970 --> 14:50.170
And here we see the average of these is 59,201.

14:50.440 --> 14:52.270
And then if we go back to SQL.

14:53.810 --> 14:57.620
Sure enough, that's the value in the fourth row of our new column.

14:57.980 --> 14:59.060
Pretty cool.

15:00.580 --> 15:01.030
Whew.

15:01.630 --> 15:04.990
So that was a lot to bite off for one video.

15:05.290 --> 15:12.850
But rose between is so much fun, at least for data nerds like me and hopefully you too, that I think

15:12.850 --> 15:13.690
it was worth it.

15:14.370 --> 15:18.120
With that said, though, I think we've earned ourselves a little break.

15:18.270 --> 15:23.580
So go fetch some coffee or tea or Red Bull, if that's your thing.

15:23.670 --> 15:26.040
And we'll reconvene in the next video.

15:26.460 --> 15:27.450
See you there.

00:00.230 --> 00:01.310
Welcome back.

00:01.760 --> 00:08.540
In this one, we're going to look at a specific type of subquery called a scalar subquery, as well

00:08.540 --> 00:10.610
as some use cases we can apply them to.

00:11.420 --> 00:17.120
Before we get into any code, let's get to the bottom of what the heck scalar even means.

00:17.830 --> 00:22.930
It turns out scalar really just means a single value in SQL terms.

00:22.930 --> 00:26.080
That means a single row with a single column.

00:26.080 --> 00:27.880
Basically one cell.

00:28.810 --> 00:34.150
Let's take a look at a couple of examples of scalar queries, which in SQL typically mean aggregate

00:34.150 --> 00:36.850
queries against a single field in our data.

00:37.690 --> 00:44.620
Now, if you look at these queries, you'll see we have taken the maximum of all the list prices from

00:44.620 --> 00:52.000
the production dot product table and also the average of the list prices as well from the same table.

00:52.300 --> 00:58.480
And since we're applying an aggregate function to a single field, our output in both cases is a single

00:58.480 --> 01:02.890
column and a single row of data, essentially a scalar value.

01:02.920 --> 01:09.220
But how can we use these sub queries to do anything besides reducing a single column to a single number?

01:09.400 --> 01:15.680
Well, one application is to include such a number alongside other fields in our select clause.

01:15.700 --> 01:17.800
Kind of like we did with window functions.

01:18.010 --> 01:20.140
So let's see what that would look like in code.

01:21.340 --> 01:27.670
Now over here I have a simple select query against our production product table, and I've commented

01:27.670 --> 01:30.090
out a field called Average List Price.

01:30.100 --> 01:37.510
So what I'm going to plug into this field is the average list price for all of the products in the table.

01:37.720 --> 01:43.540
And that average list price will appear on every single row of our output and the average list price

01:43.540 --> 01:44.170
column.

01:44.410 --> 01:46.600
So let's see what the syntax would look like.

01:47.320 --> 01:53.500
First of all, uncomment this out and since we're dealing with a subquery, we'll need parentheses to

01:53.500 --> 01:54.270
wrap it in.

01:54.280 --> 01:56.590
So let me go ahead and type those.

01:56.830 --> 02:01.360
And now what we're going to do is simply type select

02:03.730 --> 02:05.170
the average

02:08.800 --> 02:12.640
list price from.

02:14.190 --> 02:18.690
Our same table that we're querying against in our main query.

02:20.220 --> 02:21.930
And it's really just that simple.

02:21.960 --> 02:23.970
We'll highlight this and run it.

02:24.270 --> 02:31.290
And as you can see, we have the average list price for the overall table in every single row of our

02:31.290 --> 02:34.590
output in the average list price column.

02:34.590 --> 02:40.500
So what this is basically doing what the sub query select average list price is basically doing is just

02:40.500 --> 02:45.540
executing for every row of our data and returning that same value for every row.

02:45.540 --> 02:52.830
And just to verify, let's go back to our first couple of examples where we just selected the average

02:52.860 --> 02:58.620
on its own and you'll see it's the same number that is appearing in every row of our query here.

02:59.410 --> 03:05.440
Now, even more usefully, you can do calculations against these scalar subqueries in our select as

03:05.440 --> 03:06.050
well.

03:06.070 --> 03:11.860
So let's say, for example, I wanted to create another derived field, which is the difference between

03:11.860 --> 03:18.120
the list price for a given product and the overall average list price for all products.

03:18.130 --> 03:23.800
You can see how that might be a useful calculation, like how much more or how much less expensive is

03:23.800 --> 03:25.420
this than the average product.

03:25.750 --> 03:33.700
So to do that, we'll use our current scalar subquery as a starting point and we'll call our new field

03:33.700 --> 03:44.860
average list price diff, and we'll simply take the list price for the given row and then subtract the

03:44.860 --> 03:46.780
average overall list price from it.

03:47.290 --> 03:49.810
So let's run this and see what happens.

03:50.950 --> 03:53.100
And it looks like it's doing what we expect.

03:53.110 --> 04:00.370
So for products with a list price of zero, the difference is -438 since that's the overall average

04:00.370 --> 04:00.880
list price.

04:00.880 --> 04:08.710
But if we scroll down to more expensive list prices, now we suddenly see the average list price diff

04:08.740 --> 04:10.630
updating just as we'd expect.

04:11.290 --> 04:17.050
Now if you've got sharp eyes, you might have noticed that we are not including an alias after our subqueries

04:17.050 --> 04:20.980
here like we had to after the subqueries in our last video.

04:21.740 --> 04:27.680
Sequel is actually somewhat inconsistent in terms of when it does and does not require an alias after

04:27.680 --> 04:28.550
a subquery.

04:29.520 --> 04:35.070
Instead of trying to list out all the scenarios in which SQL does and does not require that alias and

04:35.070 --> 04:40.830
then expecting you to remember it, I would instead encourage you to simply remember that subqueries

04:40.830 --> 04:45.090
in the from clause need to be aliased and most other subqueries do not.

04:45.390 --> 04:50.130
There are exceptions, but when they arise you should be able to infer what happened from the error

04:50.130 --> 04:52.680
message and add an alias as needed.

04:53.910 --> 04:58.230
Now, you might be wondering why are we going to the trouble of learning yet another way to include

04:58.230 --> 05:02.640
aggregate calculations in our select clause when we've seen that window functions are more than up to

05:02.640 --> 05:03.450
the task?

05:03.810 --> 05:05.550
And you would have a valid point.

05:05.730 --> 05:11.130
I typically like to find the single best, most idiomatic way of doing something and just stick with

05:11.130 --> 05:11.670
that.

05:12.390 --> 05:17.670
But I really just showed you this example to build your understanding of scalar subqueries so we can

05:17.670 --> 05:19.890
begin to use them where they really come in handy.

05:19.890 --> 05:21.420
And that's the where clause.

05:21.660 --> 05:28.440
So as an example, let's add criteria to our query here that will filter out any records whose list

05:28.440 --> 05:33.080
price is less than or equal to the average list price of all products.

05:33.090 --> 05:38.910
That is to say, we only want to see a product if its list price is greater than the average list price

05:38.910 --> 05:39.990
of all products.

05:40.810 --> 05:47.620
If you recall, we cannot include window functions in the where clause, but we can include scalar subqueries.

05:47.620 --> 05:49.420
So this is where they really shine.

05:49.450 --> 05:54.730
So without further ado, let's plug our average list price scalar subquery into the where clause and

05:54.730 --> 05:55.690
see what happens.

05:56.500 --> 05:56.890
All right.

05:56.890 --> 05:58.900
So I'll start by adding a where clause.

05:59.920 --> 06:09.520
And what we want is records where the list price for that product is greater than the average overall

06:09.520 --> 06:10.030
list price.

06:10.030 --> 06:12.670
And we're getting that from this subquery right here.

06:12.970 --> 06:15.610
So we'll just copy and paste that down into our where.

06:16.600 --> 06:22.300
And just to help make clear how this is all working, I'll sort our final output by list price.

06:26.760 --> 06:28.470
And then we'll go ahead and run it.

06:31.940 --> 06:32.300
All right.

06:32.300 --> 06:39.380
And as you can see, our list prices start at 539.99, which is greater than the average list price.

06:39.380 --> 06:44.780
And as we scroll down to higher and higher list prices, those are obviously included as well.

06:44.780 --> 06:51.200
But we do not see any list prices lower than that 438 number that we know is the average list price

06:51.200 --> 06:52.220
of all products.

06:53.150 --> 06:59.390
So the bottom line to keep in mind is any time you want to include aggregate calculations directly in

06:59.390 --> 07:02.330
your where clause, scalar subqueries are the way to go.

07:03.130 --> 07:03.820
All right.

07:03.850 --> 07:09.130
Up next, we're going to start our exploration of correlated subqueries, which take the concepts we've

07:09.130 --> 07:12.730
learned thus far in an exciting but challenging new direction.

07:12.760 --> 07:13.690
See you then.

00:00.260 --> 00:01.400
Welcome back.

00:01.610 --> 00:07.220
Now that we've covered the basics, there are a few advanced applications of subqueries that are worth

00:07.220 --> 00:13.250
diving into which allow us to do things that can be quite difficult using other techniques.

00:14.130 --> 00:16.980
First up is correlated subqueries.

00:17.560 --> 00:17.920
Now.

00:17.920 --> 00:25.780
In short, correlated subqueries are subqueries that run once for each record in the main or outer query

00:25.900 --> 00:29.380
and then return a single value for that record.

00:29.950 --> 00:34.390
They are typically connected to the outer query by some common field.

00:34.390 --> 00:35.590
Kind of like a join.

00:36.760 --> 00:42.550
Correlated subqueries can be included in either the select clause or the where clause and have different

00:42.550 --> 00:44.020
applications in each.

00:44.200 --> 00:50.200
But we'll start by seeing how correlated subqueries can be useful in creating derived fields based on

00:50.200 --> 00:52.870
some pretty complex logic in our select.

00:52.990 --> 00:56.110
So we're turning to the example of our sales order data.

00:56.140 --> 01:02.290
Let's say that for each sales order we would like to see a count of the items within that order which

01:02.290 --> 01:03.970
had a quantity greater than one.

01:04.000 --> 01:07.000
That is to say, more than one of that item was ordered.

01:07.890 --> 01:13.620
If we try to accomplish this by joining directly to the sales order detail data, now we're going to

01:13.620 --> 01:19.290
have multiple records in our output per sales order depending on how many line items were in that order.

01:19.590 --> 01:21.420
If that's not what we want.

01:21.540 --> 01:29.130
If instead we simply want one row per sales order with a column that tells us how many items within

01:29.130 --> 01:35.340
that order had a quantity greater than one, a correlated subquery is probably the fastest way to achieve

01:35.340 --> 01:36.690
the output we're looking for.

01:37.390 --> 01:39.670
So let's see what this would look like in code.

01:40.440 --> 01:45.960
So right in front of us here we have a basic select query against our sales order header table.

01:46.290 --> 01:53.190
So what we'll try to do is add that derived field that shows us the number of line items per order that

01:53.190 --> 01:54.840
have a quantity greater than one.

01:55.750 --> 02:02.860
Now, as usual, it's probably easiest to understand how the subquery works by first coding it independently,

02:02.860 --> 02:06.490
then seeing how it fits into the bigger picture of the outer query.

02:06.790 --> 02:14.110
The point of the subquery is ultimately to answer the question for a given sales order ID How many line

02:14.110 --> 02:18.340
items in the sales order detail table had a quantity greater than one?

02:18.700 --> 02:24.250
So let's just take one sales order ID from the output of our query right here and use it as a jumping

02:24.250 --> 02:26.260
off point for writing our subquery.

02:26.440 --> 02:30.970
So I've got a bit of a starter query already written here that I'll remove the comments from.

02:31.870 --> 02:38.680
And as you can see, it basically just selects the sales order ID and the order quantity from the sales

02:38.680 --> 02:44.590
order detail table, and it's waiting for us to plug in a particular sales order ID.

02:44.980 --> 02:51.550
So what I'll do is just I'll choose the very first sales order ID from our query against the sales order

02:51.550 --> 02:56.960
header table from our first query and run this and see what we get.

02:58.000 --> 02:58.420
All right.

02:58.420 --> 03:02.860
So it looks like there were 12 line items in the order overall.

03:02.950 --> 03:11.380
And of those one, two, three, four, five, six had an order quantity greater than one.

03:11.530 --> 03:19.720
So what we would want to see in our outer query for the record with sales order ID 43659 is the number

03:19.720 --> 03:20.440
six.

03:20.470 --> 03:21.580
Makes sense.

03:21.910 --> 03:28.060
To accomplish this, the sub query has to run once for each record in our outer query.

03:28.060 --> 03:34.300
And just to remind you, I'll rerun our query against the sales order header table because this ultimately

03:34.300 --> 03:35.470
will be the outer query.

03:35.500 --> 03:44.080
So for each record in this output, our sub query will need to run with the sales order ID unique to

03:44.110 --> 03:45.190
that record.

03:45.190 --> 03:47.350
In this case, it's four three, 659.

03:47.350 --> 03:53.980
But for the next record it would be 43660 and so on and so forth being passed into the Where clause.

03:54.010 --> 04:00.740
Right now we're hard coding it, but what we ultimately need to do is run this query for each and every

04:00.740 --> 04:01.430
record.

04:01.460 --> 04:05.510
This guy, this guy, this guy, so on and so forth in the outer query.

04:05.510 --> 04:11.720
And instead of hard coding the sales order ID we need to pass in the sales order ID for each record

04:11.720 --> 04:12.890
in that outer query.

04:13.010 --> 04:20.300
So how do we pass in the sales order ID to the sub query and how do we get the query to run for every

04:20.300 --> 04:20.960
record?

04:21.140 --> 04:23.720
Well, let's just take it one step at a time.

04:24.080 --> 04:28.430
The first thing we'll do is just write the name of our field in our select.

04:28.430 --> 04:30.590
And in this case, I actually already have it here.

04:30.590 --> 04:31.730
Just comment it out.

04:32.060 --> 04:37.790
And then since we're dealing with a sub query, we'll put a pair of parentheses after the field name.

04:37.940 --> 04:41.870
Remember, sub queries are always wrapped in parentheses.

04:42.080 --> 04:45.050
So let's go ahead and uncomment the field.

04:45.050 --> 04:51.830
I've called multi order account and we're going to just create an opening and closing set of parentheses

04:51.950 --> 04:53.960
to enclose our sub query.

04:54.320 --> 04:59.780
Now, since we've already written the kind of template for our sub query, let's just drop that in between

04:59.780 --> 05:02.270
these parentheses so we can use it as a starting point.

05:02.270 --> 05:03.950
So we'll just go down here.

05:04.710 --> 05:05.850
Copy this guy.

05:07.220 --> 05:13.700
And drop him right in here and we'll tab over a couple times to get everything neatly aligned.

05:14.610 --> 05:19.290
Now, obviously, this isn't going to work because we're still hard coding our sales order ID here,

05:19.290 --> 05:24.570
but there are actually a couple of other reasons why we'll need to change this subquery.

05:24.840 --> 05:29.070
First is that we are selecting multiple fields.

05:29.310 --> 05:33.240
And second is that we are potentially selecting multiple rows.

05:33.750 --> 05:39.510
So a correlated subquery in our select statement must return a scalar value.

05:39.510 --> 05:40.920
Essentially a single value.

05:40.950 --> 05:42.810
One row, one column.

05:43.140 --> 05:48.600
Now, since the correlated subquery is going to run for each row of data in our outer query, it needs

05:48.600 --> 05:54.210
to return one single value to that row, which is what's going to populate our derived field.

05:54.390 --> 06:00.060
This means we can only have one column in the select statement of our subquery, and that one column

06:00.060 --> 06:02.070
can only return a single row.

06:02.790 --> 06:09.360
This usually means we need to apply some sort of aggregate function like count sum or max to ensure

06:09.360 --> 06:10.860
that we return a single value.

06:11.840 --> 06:15.290
In this case, we are, in fact, looking for a count of records.

06:15.410 --> 06:19.220
So we'll replace the fields in our select with a simple count star.

06:19.250 --> 06:20.990
So let's go ahead and do that.

06:26.240 --> 06:30.680
So now the missing piece is what to do about that hard coded sales order ID?

06:31.600 --> 06:37.900
What we really need to do is pass in a different sales order ID for each record in our outer query so

06:37.900 --> 06:42.880
that the correlated subquery is going to run based on the appropriate sales order ID for that record.

06:43.520 --> 06:44.840
But how to do this?

06:45.600 --> 06:50.670
While this technically is not a join, the way it works is actually pretty similar.

06:51.190 --> 06:56.860
We basically just need to tie the sales order ID from the table in our subquery to the table in our

06:56.860 --> 07:00.850
outer query, which we can do in our where clause as follows.

07:01.090 --> 07:07.690
So instead of saying where sales order ID equals four three, 659, I'm going to go ahead and alias

07:07.810 --> 07:19.360
my table in my subquery and then I'm going to set sales order ID from this inner table to sales order

07:19.360 --> 07:23.170
ID from the outer table.

07:25.410 --> 07:29.590
This is where the correlated part of the correlated subquery comes in.

07:29.610 --> 07:38.550
We are correlating this inner query to the table in the outer query by this relationship between the

07:38.550 --> 07:44.670
sales order header table and the sales order detail table specifically on like sales order IDs.

07:45.790 --> 07:48.340
So let's run this and see what happens.

07:49.720 --> 07:56.890
So the query ran and we are getting numbers at our multi order count field, but it's not the number

07:56.890 --> 08:01.560
we expected for sales order ID 43659.

08:01.570 --> 08:07.450
If you recall, there were actually six line items within that order that had a quantity greater than

08:07.450 --> 08:08.090
one.

08:08.110 --> 08:10.540
So what's going on here?

08:10.870 --> 08:14.860
Actually, there's nothing wrong with the way we coded our correlated subquery.

08:14.890 --> 08:18.310
We just neglected to include one additional piece of logic.

08:18.310 --> 08:24.280
And this kind of illustrates the point that correlated subqueries have a tremendous amount of flexibility

08:24.280 --> 08:31.270
in that you can include all the logic you want in this where clause to refine the results that you get.

08:31.570 --> 08:39.580
So right now we're just pulling a count of all of the line items with within each sales order.

08:39.580 --> 08:44.350
But what we really want is a count of those line items where the quantity is greater than one.

08:44.590 --> 08:50.630
So all we have to do is just add that to the where logic in our correlated subquery.

08:50.630 --> 08:53.120
So we'll just say and.

08:58.430 --> 09:03.170
B dot order quantity is greater than one.

09:04.550 --> 09:08.780
Let's run that again and boom!

09:08.810 --> 09:14.780
Now our sales order ID 43659 has the correct multi order count that we were looking for.

09:15.140 --> 09:20.540
Now just to take one more pass that reinforcing how this works, let's look at one more sales order

09:20.540 --> 09:21.740
ID from our query.

09:21.770 --> 09:25.760
This time one that returned a zero in our derived field.

09:26.180 --> 09:30.320
This very next record, 43660 is just such an example.

09:30.350 --> 09:35.540
So let's try running our original subquery template with this ID and see what happens.

09:35.900 --> 09:44.450
So I'll just copy this guy and go down here to our original subquery template and just swap out the

09:44.450 --> 09:46.430
sales order ID and run this.

09:47.800 --> 09:53.800
So now you see that this order only had two line items, both of which had an order quantity of one.

09:53.800 --> 09:58.360
So there were in fact zero line items that had an order quantity greater than one.

09:58.360 --> 10:01.930
So it looks like our correlated subquery is working like we expect.

10:02.640 --> 10:09.480
Now, it's worth noting here that in this case we technically could have achieved the same result as

10:09.480 --> 10:13.920
our correlated subquery with a combination of joins and aggregate queries.

10:14.760 --> 10:16.530
But for certain types of problems.

10:16.530 --> 10:23.310
And I would argue that this is one a correlated subquery is just a more straightforward and less cumbersome

10:23.310 --> 10:25.050
approach than any alternative.

10:25.930 --> 10:30.140
We'll cover another powerful application of correlated subqueries in the next video.

10:30.160 --> 10:32.530
This time in the where clause.

10:32.560 --> 10:33.580
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.320 --> 00:01.340
Welcome back.

00:01.960 --> 00:07.930
Up to this point, you've most likely used joins to add fields from other tables to your select queries.

00:08.470 --> 00:13.600
Even when applying criteria to these fields, using where we still typically display the results in

00:13.600 --> 00:14.440
our output.

00:14.740 --> 00:20.290
But in situations where we don't need to see those fields in our output and instead only need to apply

00:20.320 --> 00:24.460
criteria to them to limit our data set, there's an alternative to joins.

00:24.790 --> 00:30.910
And that's the exists operator, which allows us to make use of correlated subqueries in the where clause

00:30.940 --> 00:31.960
of our queries.

00:32.290 --> 00:37.930
But the question is why would we ever use exists when a join can accomplish the same thing?

00:38.170 --> 00:43.210
I don't know about you, but I personally find it pretty annoying to be presented with 37 different

00:43.210 --> 00:44.950
ways of accomplishing the same thing.

00:44.950 --> 00:46.930
Just show me the best, easiest way.

00:46.960 --> 00:47.560
Dang it.

00:47.950 --> 00:53.470
Well, as long as we're connecting tables that have a 1 to 1 relationship, that is to say, each row

00:53.470 --> 00:58.930
in one table has no more than one match in the other table, there really is very little functional

00:58.930 --> 01:03.250
difference between applying criteria via joins versus exists.

01:03.980 --> 01:08.210
However, things get more interesting when dealing with one to many joins.

01:08.600 --> 01:11.540
Let's take a look at some examples to see why.

01:12.370 --> 01:18.730
So our Adventureworks database has a sales order header table with one record for each customer order

01:18.730 --> 01:24.850
and also a sales order detail table with a record for each item within a customer order.

01:25.150 --> 01:29.080
Now here are the records from each table for a particular sales order.

01:29.080 --> 01:31.660
ID 43683.

01:32.230 --> 01:36.400
And as you can see, there's a single record from our sales order header table.

01:36.520 --> 01:42.280
But 13 records from our sales order detail table looks like a one to many situation, right?

01:43.310 --> 01:50.210
So let's say we want to see all customer orders that have at least one item with a line total of more

01:50.210 --> 01:51.680
than $10,000.

01:52.040 --> 01:55.490
Now, here's an example of how we might try to accomplish that with a join.

01:56.120 --> 02:03.410
So as you can see here, we used sales order header as our primary table and then we joined in sales

02:03.410 --> 02:04.460
order detail.

02:05.220 --> 02:08.970
On the sales order ID field in each table, the field they have in common.

02:09.120 --> 02:14.180
And then we applied our criteria where line total is greater than $10,000.

02:14.190 --> 02:17.160
So let's run this and see what the output looks like.

02:18.960 --> 02:21.270
So this works kind of.

02:21.600 --> 02:23.610
We are indeed getting all the records.

02:23.610 --> 02:28.690
We're interested in orders that have at least one item with a value over $10,000.

02:28.710 --> 02:29.970
As we can see here.

02:31.310 --> 02:35.720
But we are also getting a record for every item over $10,000.

02:35.900 --> 02:41.810
Meaning the information specific to the overall order as opposed to the items within the order is being

02:41.810 --> 02:42.680
duplicated.

02:43.520 --> 02:48.650
So what if we don't care about the specifics of the items within the order and just want to see a single

02:48.650 --> 02:51.770
record for each order that meets our criteria?

02:52.520 --> 02:54.410
That's where exists comes in.

02:54.650 --> 02:59.600
Let's take a look at how we can rewrite our example here with exists to accomplish this.

03:00.460 --> 03:06.190
So the first thing to remember with exists is, as is so often the case with SQL, it does exactly what

03:06.190 --> 03:07.120
it sounds like.

03:07.150 --> 03:14.140
It checks to see if a match according to whatever criteria we've set exists in another table, but it

03:14.140 --> 03:19.330
doesn't particularly care which record matches or how many matches there are exists.

03:19.330 --> 03:23.890
Typically does this with a correlated subquery, much like the ones we've seen previously.

03:24.410 --> 03:28.940
The main difference here, other than the correlated subquery being in the where clause rather than

03:28.940 --> 03:33.620
select is that the exists subquery doesn't actually return any data.

03:33.650 --> 03:35.930
Know counts, sums or maxes.

03:35.960 --> 03:39.890
It is simply checking for the existence of a record in another table.

03:39.920 --> 03:45.440
As such, it actually doesn't matter what you put in the select clause of the exist subquery as long

03:45.440 --> 03:46.490
as you put something.

03:46.670 --> 03:51.050
Now I know all this probably sounds a little weird, so let's just go ahead and see what it looks like

03:51.050 --> 03:51.770
in code.

03:52.100 --> 03:58.790
So I've got a starter query here that consists of just a simple select of the sales order ID order date

03:58.790 --> 04:01.760
and total due fields from the sales order header table.

04:01.760 --> 04:04.430
And I'll go ahead and run this just so we can see the output.

04:05.560 --> 04:14.290
And what we're going to try to do is add criteria to this query such that we only include records where

04:14.290 --> 04:21.820
at least one line item per each order has a line total greater than $10,000.

04:21.820 --> 04:28.810
But we're going to try to do that without a join and more importantly, without expanding the number

04:28.810 --> 04:29.990
of rows in our output.

04:30.010 --> 04:36.970
Remember, if we join a table on the one side of a one to many relationship with a with the table on

04:36.970 --> 04:39.460
the many side, suddenly our output is going to blow up.

04:39.460 --> 04:45.130
If we have five matches in the on the many side for one record on the one side.

04:45.160 --> 04:49.060
Now we're going to have five records in our output, which in this case isn't what we want.

04:49.300 --> 04:55.840
So we'll start by adding a where clause and then we'll add that exists keyword.

04:57.190 --> 05:05.690
And then because this is a subquery, we'll add our opening and closing parentheses and a select.

05:05.900 --> 05:07.910
And here's where things get a little weird.

05:08.390 --> 05:11.840
Now again exists isn't returning any data.

05:11.840 --> 05:17.260
It's just checking for the existence of at least one matching record in a secondary table.

05:17.270 --> 05:19.940
So it actually doesn't matter what we put here.

05:19.940 --> 05:26.780
We could put a text string or we could put a number.

05:26.810 --> 05:32.630
What you'll see most often is just the number one, but it could be two, five, whatever you like.

05:33.020 --> 05:38.270
It's one of the few areas in SQL coding or coding otherwise where it truly doesn't matter what you type

05:38.270 --> 05:39.620
as long as you type something.

05:40.220 --> 05:42.290
So now I'll go ahead and add my from.

05:43.280 --> 05:49.820
And the table we're referencing is the sales order detail table, which I'll alias as B and finally

05:49.820 --> 05:58.100
I'll add a where clause to my subselect where I will first apply the criteria that we're interested

05:58.100 --> 06:04.400
in, which is the line total being greater than $10,000.

06:04.760 --> 06:10.070
Now, if you recall how correlated subqueries work, you might anticipate the next step, which is to

06:10.070 --> 06:17.630
tie each record in my subquery with the record in the outer query and our common field is sales order

06:17.630 --> 06:22.520
ID, So all I have to do is add that to our where clause.

06:29.680 --> 06:32.200
And now this should be our complete query.

06:32.530 --> 06:34.810
So just to reiterate what's going on here.

06:35.050 --> 06:42.700
For every record in our outer query for each of these 31,465 records here, SQL is going to take that

06:42.700 --> 06:50.350
sales order ID for the record and scan the sales order detail table via our little sub query here and

06:50.350 --> 06:57.490
see if there is at least one match such that the line total is greater than $10,000.

06:57.640 --> 07:01.630
If there is, we get to keep that record with the sales order ID.

07:02.560 --> 07:03.750
In the outer query.

07:03.760 --> 07:06.730
If there is no match, the record gets clipped out.

07:07.120 --> 07:08.800
So let's run this.

07:11.420 --> 07:18.380
And I've sorted by sales order ID to clarify which order IDs were included and which ones weren't.

07:18.740 --> 07:22.120
So just to verify, this is working the way we expect.

07:22.130 --> 07:24.230
Let's look at a couple of example.

07:24.230 --> 07:25.700
Sales order IDs.

07:26.690 --> 07:32.480
So we see that four three, six, eight three is being included and that is actually the sales order

07:32.480 --> 07:36.170
ID that we used in our detail queries earlier.

07:36.170 --> 07:44.180
So let's run this query against the sales order detail table for that sales order ID And looking down

07:44.180 --> 07:51.100
at the line totals, we see that in fact there is one record greater than $10,000.

07:51.110 --> 07:53.720
So that record was correctly included.

07:53.960 --> 08:01.160
But now let's look at another example of a sales order ID that did not have at least one line total

08:01.160 --> 08:02.360
greater than 10,000.

08:03.990 --> 08:09.200
So if you look at the line totals for this guy, there is not a single one greater than 10,000.

08:09.210 --> 08:13.830
So this record should not have been included in our exists output.

08:14.730 --> 08:16.940
So let's verify that that's the case.

08:16.950 --> 08:27.960
So I'll just add a criteria to our overall query that says sales order ID equals this guy and we'll

08:27.960 --> 08:28.800
rerun our query.

08:28.800 --> 08:32.760
And what we expect is no records, and that's exactly what we get.

08:33.360 --> 08:39.120
So you've probably learned by now that when it comes to SQL, anything you can do, you can also do

08:39.120 --> 08:44.250
the opposite of not equal to not in not like et cetera.

08:44.740 --> 08:51.450
While exists is no different and as you might have guessed, its opposite number is not exists.

08:51.780 --> 08:54.450
To see a case where not exists can help us.

08:54.450 --> 08:57.330
We'll modify the requirements of our previous example.

08:57.780 --> 09:04.390
Let's say that instead of wanting to see any orders that have an item over $10,000, we want the opposite

09:04.510 --> 09:07.750
orders that don't have any items over $10,000.

09:08.310 --> 09:08.670
Now.

09:08.670 --> 09:12.540
We could try coding this with a join as follows.

09:12.870 --> 09:17.640
So here we're again joining the sales order detail table to the sales order header table on sales order

09:17.640 --> 09:17.910
ID.

09:18.890 --> 09:24.200
And we're saying we only want to see records where the line total is less than $10,000.

09:24.230 --> 09:29.930
And I'm just going to show you this for a particular sales order ID, but this really doesn't even do

09:29.960 --> 09:30.740
what we want.

09:31.270 --> 09:35.140
As long as our sales order ID has at least one item.

09:35.940 --> 09:38.130
Less than or equal to $10,000.

09:38.160 --> 09:40.980
Our query will return the order and the item.

09:41.250 --> 09:46.590
So as you see here, we're returning a record for every single line item associated with the sales order

09:46.590 --> 09:50.160
ID that has a line total less than $10,000.

09:50.430 --> 09:56.880
The problem is we only want to see orders where none of the items exceed $10,000.

09:57.440 --> 10:04.310
And if we go back to our detail queries where we just look at all the line items for a given sales order

10:04.310 --> 10:09.290
ID, and we look at that for this particular sales order ID.

10:13.340 --> 10:17.330
We'll see that we do, in fact, have a line total greater than $10,000.

10:17.480 --> 10:24.050
So all our query here is really doing is just showing us all the individual line items that have a line

10:24.050 --> 10:31.100
total, less than 10,000, but it's not kicking out a sales order ID if it has any line totals greater

10:31.100 --> 10:32.750
than or equal to $10,000.

10:32.960 --> 10:36.550
So the bottom line is our join is clearly not getting the job done.

10:36.560 --> 10:40.310
So let's see if we can solve our problem here with not exists.

10:40.640 --> 10:46.910
So I'll actually roll back up to our previous exists example because all we're really going to require

10:46.910 --> 10:48.650
is a slight tweak to this code.

10:49.060 --> 10:53.450
Now, first of all, I'll comment out the hard coded sales order ID criteria for now.

10:54.130 --> 10:58.870
And then I'll simply add not in front of exists with a space.

10:59.590 --> 11:02.380
Now, before we run this, I'll just clarify again what it's doing.

11:02.590 --> 11:10.000
It's saying for every sales order ID in our outer query, SQL is going to scan the sales order detail

11:10.000 --> 11:18.040
table and see if there are any line totals associated with that sales order ID greater than $10,000.

11:18.430 --> 11:24.550
If there is one, it's going to kick our record out because we're saying not exists.

11:24.580 --> 11:31.510
We don't want to see the sales order ID if there are any matches in the sales order detail table such

11:31.510 --> 11:33.850
that the line total is greater than $10,000.

11:34.380 --> 11:35.790
So let's run this.

11:37.760 --> 11:42.140
And we see that it is returning a record for four, three, six, five, nine.

11:42.290 --> 11:50.030
And just to refresh our memories, if we roll back up and look at the detail for that particular sales

11:50.030 --> 11:56.420
order ID, we'll see that there's not a single record with a line total greater than $10,000.

11:56.420 --> 11:58.580
So it looks like the query is doing what we want.

11:58.610 --> 12:08.060
If, on the other hand, we look at a different sales order ID that does have a line total greater than

12:08.060 --> 12:09.200
$10,000.

12:09.920 --> 12:17.960
And we plug that same sales order ID as a criteria into our not exists.

12:22.550 --> 12:23.780
And run it again.

12:27.010 --> 12:32.230
We'll see that we do not get a record for that sales order ID, So it looks like this is giving us what

12:32.230 --> 12:32.830
we want.

12:34.130 --> 12:39.920
To conclude this section, let's summarize when I would recommend using and not using exists.

12:41.130 --> 12:46.950
Use exists when you want to apply criteria to fields from a secondary table but don't need to include

12:46.950 --> 12:48.330
those fields in your output.

12:49.450 --> 12:54.550
As long as the tables you're connecting have a 1 to 1 relationship you could pretty much use exists

12:54.550 --> 12:55.960
or joins interchangeably.

12:55.960 --> 13:01.480
But I prefer exists because this use is consistent with its purpose and may come with a slight performance

13:01.480 --> 13:02.440
benefit as well.

13:04.230 --> 13:06.510
When your tables have a one to many relationship.

13:06.510 --> 13:09.840
On the other hand, you'll have to make a more strategic decision.

13:10.490 --> 13:15.410
If you need to see all matches from the mini side of the relationship, you should probably stick with

13:15.410 --> 13:16.100
a join.

13:16.430 --> 13:21.950
If, on the other hand, you only want one record in your output per each match from the one side of

13:21.950 --> 13:24.380
the relationship stick with exists.

13:25.790 --> 13:31.550
Finally, if you need to check a secondary table to make sure a match of some type does not exist,

13:31.580 --> 13:34.650
well, the solution is practically spelled out for you.

13:34.670 --> 13:41.360
As we saw in our last example, not exists is just a superior option to a join in this scenario.

13:42.290 --> 13:42.680
All right.

13:42.680 --> 13:43.070
That's it.

13:43.070 --> 13:44.030
On exist for now.

13:44.060 --> 13:45.530
I'll see you in the next video.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.260 --> 00:01.280
Welcome back.

00:01.800 --> 00:08.280
So now that we've got correlated subqueries down, I'd like to present an advanced and okay, I'll admit

00:08.280 --> 00:12.150
it, somewhat confusing application of correlated subqueries.

00:12.360 --> 00:18.960
I apologize in advance as the syntax and overall concepts can be pretty gnarly, but I really wanted

00:18.960 --> 00:24.420
to include this topic because there are just certain scenarios that no other technique in SQL can handle.

00:25.250 --> 00:31.910
In a previous video we saw that we can return an output based on multiple rows in some secondary table

00:31.940 --> 00:34.400
to a single row in our main query.

00:35.000 --> 00:40.610
So if the table we're querying has a one to many relationship with some other table, we can aggregate

00:40.610 --> 00:46.370
matches from the many side of the relationship into a single number and then return that to the output

00:46.370 --> 00:47.510
of our main query.

00:47.810 --> 00:52.820
But what if instead of aggregating the matches on the many side of the relationship, we instead want

00:52.820 --> 00:55.400
to actually see some detail about those matches.

00:55.430 --> 00:57.090
A number, some texts.

00:57.140 --> 00:57.980
ET cetera.

00:58.190 --> 01:02.390
That gives us real visibility into what was in those individual records.

01:03.640 --> 01:06.510
Take our sales order detail table, for example.

01:06.520 --> 01:07.150
Again.

01:08.030 --> 01:13.580
In a previous video, we simply counted matches from that table for a given order in our sales order

01:13.580 --> 01:14.330
header table.

01:14.870 --> 01:20.330
But it's also quite possible that we might want the information about those individual line items and

01:20.330 --> 01:25.610
the sales order detail table flattened out into a single row of our main query output.

01:26.350 --> 01:33.820
So if you look at this graphic here, you'll see that the line totals for sales order ID one have been

01:33.820 --> 01:37.810
flattened out into a single cell, separated by commas.

01:37.840 --> 01:43.720
And similarly, we have three records for sales order ID, two with different line totals.

01:43.720 --> 01:49.660
And in the flattened version of this, there's only one record for that sales order ID, and the three

01:49.660 --> 01:53.010
line totals are now in a single cell separated by commas.

01:53.020 --> 01:58.840
So this is actually a fairly common scenario in data analysis, but one that does not have an abundance

01:58.840 --> 01:59.860
of solutions.

02:00.580 --> 02:07.570
Fortunately we do have one in SQL, but unfortunately the syntax is honestly kind of frightening.

02:08.140 --> 02:09.610
But it is worth learning.

02:09.610 --> 02:12.550
So we'll get through it together one step at a time.

02:13.180 --> 02:19.180
As usual, the subqueries will start from the basics with the subquery isolated from the outer query

02:19.180 --> 02:20.860
that we will ultimately plug it into.

02:21.600 --> 02:27.540
Here we have a simple count star from the sales order detail table for one given sales order ID.

02:28.260 --> 02:33.150
This is similar to the basis of our correlated subquery example from a previous video.

02:34.340 --> 02:39.980
But if we're going to include actual detail about records within the table aggregating these records

02:39.980 --> 02:43.910
down to a scalar value with a count average or Max won't cut it.

02:44.550 --> 02:48.350
So let's start by changing this query to a simple select star.

02:48.360 --> 02:55.260
So we just need to get rid of the Prince and the Count, and then we'll run this.

02:56.820 --> 02:57.360
All right.

02:57.390 --> 03:02.820
Now we can see all the records and all the fields in the sales order detail table where the sales order

03:02.820 --> 03:05.310
ID equals four, three, six, five, nine.

03:05.640 --> 03:12.000
Let's say what we're really interested in is seeing all of the line totals for a given sales order ID

03:12.270 --> 03:18.570
from the sales order detail table flattened out into a single row in our outer query against the sales

03:18.570 --> 03:19.560
order header table.

03:20.150 --> 03:25.130
The real challenge then, is how to flatten these six rows out into a single row.

03:25.840 --> 03:31.090
Let's move in that direction by simply selecting the line totals for this particular sales order ID.

03:31.570 --> 03:39.460
So instead of doing a select star, I'll just select line total and then we'll run that again.

03:41.970 --> 03:42.630
Okay.

03:42.630 --> 03:45.270
This is where things start to get a little bit weird.

03:46.240 --> 03:46.720
All right.

03:46.750 --> 03:47.680
A lot weird.

03:48.160 --> 03:53.530
We're going to add some syntax below our where clause that is going to look strange because it is.

03:54.110 --> 04:01.190
We'll add the keywords for XML path and then we'll follow path with a pair of parentheses since it's

04:01.190 --> 04:07.490
a function and then put an empty string denoted by a pair of single quotes inside the parentheses.

04:07.670 --> 04:09.470
All right, so let's go ahead and add all that.

04:09.470 --> 04:17.150
So we'll type for XML path and then because path is a function, we'll give it the parentheses and then

04:17.150 --> 04:19.280
the argument will just be an empty string.

04:19.790 --> 04:23.180
So what in the wide world of sports is going on here?

04:24.000 --> 04:28.080
Let's take a first step towards figuring it out by actually running the query.

04:31.020 --> 04:36.150
So unfortunately, it looks like the output is even more bizarre than the syntax unless you happen to

04:36.150 --> 04:37.860
be familiar with XML.

04:38.220 --> 04:42.720
And I don't expect you to be, nor do you need to be in order to use this code.

04:42.870 --> 04:49.440
All you really need to know is that XML is a kind of markup language similar to the HTML used to code

04:49.440 --> 04:50.430
websites.

04:50.430 --> 04:54.030
That is just another way of programmatically structuring data.

04:54.750 --> 04:59.430
But just for Funsies, let's click the XML in the query output to see what it looks like.

05:00.450 --> 05:06.090
So even without knowing XML, it's probably somewhat clear that this function we have applied in our

05:06.090 --> 05:12.660
query is surrounding each value in our output with some kind of tag whose name is based on the name

05:12.660 --> 05:13.980
of the field we selected.

05:14.680 --> 05:16.210
More useful to us.

05:16.240 --> 05:22.660
This XML is actually just a big text string, so if we could find a way to get rid of those XML tags

05:22.660 --> 05:28.390
and replace them with some kind of text delimiter like a comma or a semicolon, we'd be well on our

05:28.390 --> 05:30.220
way to getting the output we're looking for.

05:31.010 --> 05:36.260
And that leads us to the next trick, which is to concatenate the line total number with a comma.

05:36.350 --> 05:37.940
So let's try that.

05:38.270 --> 05:46.550
So instead of just saying line total, we're going to concatenate a comma with line total with the plus

05:46.550 --> 05:49.100
operator and try to run that.

05:50.960 --> 05:56.480
Okay, now we're getting an error because we're trying to concatenate a string, the comma with a number,

05:56.480 --> 05:57.620
which is the line total.

05:57.620 --> 06:00.830
So we'll need to cast that line total as a varchar.

06:01.400 --> 06:03.140
So we'll do that real quick.

06:06.200 --> 06:10.130
And I probably need to include a space between as and varchar.

06:10.890 --> 06:12.270
And then we'll run that again.

06:12.840 --> 06:15.420
Okay, So it looks like we're getting a little bit warmer.

06:15.660 --> 06:22.470
Of course we've still got an XML output, but if we click that XML, we now see a comma separated list

06:22.470 --> 06:28.560
of all the line totals for sales order ID 43659, which is pretty close to what we want.

06:28.920 --> 06:35.100
One issue I can see here is that we have lots of unnecessary trailing zeros after the decimal place

06:35.190 --> 06:36.210
for these numbers.

06:36.210 --> 06:42.570
So I'm going to employ one more trick before we move on, which is to cast this line total as money

06:42.570 --> 06:44.320
before casting it as varchar.

06:44.340 --> 06:49.860
That'll make sure that we have a nice neatly formatted decimal that will look good on our output.

06:50.190 --> 06:54.330
So we'll just cast the line total.

06:56.760 --> 07:02.460
As money and then that will be cast as a varchar.

07:02.850 --> 07:05.520
So let's run that again and again.

07:05.520 --> 07:10.200
Click our XML output and now our output is looking pretty dang good.

07:10.410 --> 07:16.210
Now we just need to convert this XML to a plain old string that we can drop into our query output.

07:16.620 --> 07:22.140
And while we're at it, we also need to get rid of that first comma before the first item in the series

07:22.140 --> 07:23.070
of line totals.

07:23.310 --> 07:27.840
Fortunately, Sql's stuff function can help us with all of these things.

07:28.350 --> 07:34.650
Now stuff takes a string that we supply it and then stuffs it into another string at a position that

07:34.650 --> 07:35.640
we specify.
