07:36.000 --> 07:41.910
It also allows us to trim off characters from the text that we are stuffing into another string.

07:42.240 --> 07:46.200
So let's take a look at the syntax for stuff before we move on.

07:46.930 --> 07:51.790
So we're actually going to feed this the output of this entire subquery, which is this XML string we

07:51.790 --> 07:55.960
just saw into the stuff function as one of its arguments.

07:55.960 --> 08:02.410
So that means that this query we just wrote is now going to be a subquery.

08:02.530 --> 08:09.100
So we'll have to write another select for our outer query and then I'll type stuff.

08:11.110 --> 08:14.620
Which is our function followed by an open parentheses.

08:14.950 --> 08:21.550
And the first argument for stuff is going to be the text value that we'll stuff into some other string.

08:21.790 --> 08:24.100
And in this case that's the XML.

08:24.100 --> 08:25.780
That was our previous query output.

08:25.780 --> 08:32.050
So this query, or rather the output of this query will be the first argument for stuff.

08:32.050 --> 08:35.470
But since it's a subquery, we'll need to wrap it in parentheses.

08:37.980 --> 08:39.210
So we'll do that.

08:39.600 --> 08:41.550
So that is our very first argument.

08:42.150 --> 08:47.730
Now, not to skip around, but it actually makes the most sense to consider the fourth and last argument

08:47.760 --> 08:48.480
next.

08:48.570 --> 08:51.960
That's the string that we are stuffing our text into.

08:51.990 --> 08:57.540
So I'll just type a couple of extra commas as placeholders where our second and third arguments will

08:57.540 --> 08:58.050
go.

08:58.170 --> 09:04.530
And then I'll type our fourth argument, which is actually just an empty string, since all we really

09:04.530 --> 09:08.880
want as our final output is just the text from our XML and nothing more.

09:08.910 --> 09:09.990
This makes sense.

09:10.020 --> 09:15.090
We're basically taking the entire output of that XML and just stuffing it into an empty string.

09:15.240 --> 09:22.920
Now the second argument, which we'll go right here is the position within the string in argument four

09:22.920 --> 09:27.450
at which we want to stuff the text from argument one into.

09:28.210 --> 09:29.980
Since argument four is an empty string.

09:29.980 --> 09:34.660
Anyway, we really just want to stuff our XML text starting in position one.

09:34.660 --> 09:36.820
So the second argument will just be a one.

09:37.360 --> 09:42.640
Now finally, the third argument tells SQL how many characters, if any.

09:42.670 --> 09:45.790
We want to clip off the text from our first argument.

09:45.790 --> 09:52.960
And remember our first argument is that XML text before we stuff it into the string in argument for

09:52.990 --> 09:54.010
our empty string.

09:54.570 --> 09:57.360
So remember that leading comma we wanted to get rid of?

09:57.480 --> 09:59.880
That's what this argument will help us with.

10:00.000 --> 10:06.450
By specifying a one in this position, we are going to clip off the character in the first position,

10:06.450 --> 10:08.130
which was that unwanted comma.

10:09.090 --> 10:15.540
And then the last step is just going to be to close out stuff with a closing parenthesis and then to

10:15.540 --> 10:17.520
run it to see what we get.

10:18.660 --> 10:19.580
Wow.

10:19.590 --> 10:22.950
It looks like we finally have the output we were shooting for.

10:23.160 --> 10:28.440
If you look at the one cell that was returned, you see all of the line totals neatly formatted and

10:28.440 --> 10:32.160
separated by commas and a flattened out into a single row.

10:32.610 --> 10:39.840
The last step then, is simply to plug this code into an outer query as a correlated subquery, which

10:39.840 --> 10:43.110
will work just like the correlated subqueries we've already been dealing with.

10:43.350 --> 10:50.100
So let me paste in an example query against the sales order header table which will function as our

10:50.100 --> 10:50.730
outer query.

10:50.760 --> 10:51.960
Our main query.

10:52.050 --> 10:59.610
And then look at how we can plug in our stuff function with the correlated subquery within it in such

10:59.610 --> 11:02.640
a way that will get this output that we're seeing here.

11:02.640 --> 11:07.920
For every sales order ID, for every row of that sales order header table.

11:08.050 --> 11:14.200
So first I'll just copy this stuff function and add it to the select down here.

11:17.000 --> 11:20.750
And then I'll tab over to get everything lined up.

11:22.350 --> 11:24.870
And I'll also need to alias this.

11:24.870 --> 11:35.850
And since we're dealing with line totals plural, I think a logical name would just be line totals.

11:37.700 --> 11:44.270
And then the only change we really have to make is to tie the sales order detail table in our subquery

11:44.510 --> 11:49.790
to the sales order header table in our outer query on sales order ID just like before.

11:50.440 --> 11:52.120
So we'll go ahead and do that.

11:52.270 --> 12:00.610
Basically by swapping out this hardcoded sales order ID with the sales order ID from our sales order

12:00.610 --> 12:02.580
detail table in our subquery.

12:02.590 --> 12:08.440
But because we've already got the sales order header table from our outer query aliased as a we'll just

12:08.440 --> 12:16.210
re alias our sales order detail table as B and then we'll say where sales order ID from.

12:16.210 --> 12:24.100
The sales order header table equals the sales order ID from the sales order detail table.

12:25.570 --> 12:29.200
So we've got the correlated part of our correlated subquery working.

12:29.200 --> 12:35.740
We've got our four XML path converting multiple rows of data into a single XML string and then we've

12:35.740 --> 12:42.160
got our stuff function subsequently converting that into a single piece of text that we can jam into

12:42.160 --> 12:44.290
one cell of our query output.

12:44.800 --> 12:49.030
I've got a good feeling about this one, but I think I'm going to squint and look away from my monitor

12:49.030 --> 12:49.600
as I run it.

12:49.600 --> 12:50.990
Just in case.

12:51.980 --> 12:54.560
Well, it looks like we can congratulate ourselves.

12:54.560 --> 12:55.400
We did it.

12:55.670 --> 13:02.420
Looking at the output and our line totals field for each row of our query, it appears that all of the

13:02.420 --> 13:08.900
associated line totals for each sales order ID are jammed together in a single row, separated by commas.

13:09.770 --> 13:16.160
And keep in mind that other than the funky XML path syntax, this is just a correlated subquery like

13:16.160 --> 13:17.390
all the others we've seen.

13:17.480 --> 13:22.610
This means you can apply additional criteria in the where clause as the situation calls for.

13:23.280 --> 13:28.350
I hope you can see what a powerful technique this can be and imagine how many applications it can have.

13:28.880 --> 13:33.470
While the syntax is pretty funky, you don't need to fully understand it to use it.

13:33.920 --> 13:39.980
I've used it many times and each time I simply take a previous example, copy and paste the code and

13:39.980 --> 13:42.890
adapt it to whatever new scenario I'm trying to apply it to.

13:43.540 --> 13:48.610
I guarantee you the first time you solve a problem that was previously considered unsolvable.

13:48.610 --> 13:51.490
With this technique, your teammates will be blown away.

13:52.250 --> 13:55.040
Okay that's it on correlated subqueries for now.

13:55.040 --> 13:56.930
And I'll bet you're pretty relieved.

13:57.200 --> 14:02.000
For what it's worth, this was definitely one of the toughest concepts in the entire course, and there

14:02.000 --> 14:04.010
were certainly plenty of candidates to choose from.

14:04.580 --> 14:09.620
If you found it a little tough to understand, I highly encourage you to rewatch the video and play

14:09.620 --> 14:14.540
around with the example code and definitely do your best to complete the exercises after the video as

14:14.540 --> 14:15.020
well.

14:16.090 --> 14:16.750
All right.

14:16.750 --> 14:22.030
Up next, we're going to dive into an all new application of subqueries and a new approach to flattening

14:22.030 --> 14:22.630
data.

14:22.810 --> 14:29.200
That's the pivot operator, which lets us transpose and aggregate our data and all sorts of useful ways.

14:29.230 --> 14:30.220
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.140 --> 00:01.190
Welcome back.

00:01.520 --> 00:07.820
So in this one, we're going to look at another way that you can flatten your data, so to speak, in

00:07.820 --> 00:08.540
SQL.

00:08.540 --> 00:12.080
And this time we'll be doing it with an operator called Pivot.

00:12.710 --> 00:19.210
Now, if you've ever used pivot tables in Excel, you'll see that Sql's flavor of Pivot is quite similar,

00:19.220 --> 00:21.170
although a little clunkier to use.

00:21.830 --> 00:24.770
So how does it look when Pivot flattens your data?

00:25.070 --> 00:26.690
Well, let's take an example.

00:26.690 --> 00:32.510
With multiple records, with the same sales order ID and various line totals.

00:32.660 --> 00:40.460
How Pivot would flatten that out is to give us a column for each unique sales order ID and our sales

00:40.460 --> 00:41.480
order ID column.

00:41.480 --> 00:46.040
And then it would apply some type of aggregation to the line totals.

00:46.040 --> 00:48.320
In this case, we're doing a sum.

00:49.360 --> 00:50.380
So again.

00:50.950 --> 00:59.140
If you look at the two records with sales order ID one, those become a single column in our pivoted

00:59.170 --> 00:59.990
output.

01:00.010 --> 01:03.820
And the same is true for the three records with sales order ID two.

01:03.970 --> 01:13.450
Basically, for each unique value in our sales order ID column, we're getting a column in our pivoted

01:13.450 --> 01:14.170
output.

01:14.530 --> 01:21.190
You can think of this kind of like the data being transposed and the sales order ID column being sort

01:21.190 --> 01:27.070
of on a hinge and swinging from a vertical orientation up to a horizontal orientation.

01:27.250 --> 01:33.070
But now, instead of five records translating to five columns, we only have as many columns as there

01:33.070 --> 01:36.370
are unique values in that sales order ID field.

01:36.580 --> 01:42.130
And then again, if you look at what happened to the line totals, they basically got added together.

01:42.160 --> 01:45.550
Now you can apply different types of aggregate functions within Pivot.

01:45.580 --> 01:47.800
We could have done an average, we could have done a max.

01:47.800 --> 01:50.260
But in this case, we just applied a sum.

01:50.260 --> 01:57.200
So so the $50 and the 541 totaled up to 591 for sales order ID one.

01:57.200 --> 01:59.960
And the same thing happened with sales order ID two.

02:00.860 --> 02:01.270
All right.

02:01.280 --> 02:05.360
Before we get into any syntax, I'm actually going to do something a little unconventional.

02:05.390 --> 02:12.530
I'm going to take us out of the SQL Development environment and over into Microsoft Excel, the spreadsheet

02:12.530 --> 02:13.430
application.

02:13.580 --> 02:19.550
I'm going to do this because pivot tables in spreadsheets and this could be Google Sheets or your spreadsheet

02:19.550 --> 02:26.240
application of choice demonstrate the concept of pivoting, I think, more intuitively than any other

02:26.240 --> 02:26.810
way.

02:27.080 --> 02:30.470
So I've got a starter query here that's pretty basic.

02:30.470 --> 02:38.750
It just ties together our product category names from the production dot product category table here.

02:39.980 --> 02:47.390
With the line totals of any items within those categories that were ordered from the sales order detail

02:47.390 --> 02:48.220
table here.

02:48.230 --> 02:54.530
Now, I have to include these intermediate joins because there is no direct relation between the sales

02:54.530 --> 02:56.390
order detail table here.

02:56.960 --> 03:00.050
And the production product category table.

03:00.050 --> 03:06.830
Here we have to join in a couple of intermediate tables to tie our individual line items and our sales

03:06.830 --> 03:09.080
orders all the way back to a product category.

03:09.080 --> 03:15.920
But the bottom line is this query output has for every line item that has been ordered, the category

03:15.920 --> 03:19.640
of that line item and the line total of that line item.

03:19.640 --> 03:25.550
So what we're going to do is take this output and drop it into an Excel spreadsheet and build a pivot

03:25.580 --> 03:31.190
table on it to see what pivoting looks like in an intuitive way before we dive into trying to do the

03:31.190 --> 03:32.540
same thing in SQL.

03:32.540 --> 03:40.670
So let's go ahead and copy this data out of SQL and then I will drop it right into our Waiting Excel

03:40.670 --> 03:41.480
spreadsheet.

03:42.110 --> 03:44.630
So then I'll just select all the data.

03:45.820 --> 03:47.260
And insert a pivot table.

03:49.210 --> 03:57.100
And now what I'm going to do is drag our product category name into the columns area down here and the

03:57.100 --> 03:59.470
line total into the values.

04:00.700 --> 04:06.730
So by default, Excel assumes that I want to sum the line totals, which is what it did.

04:06.970 --> 04:12.280
And if you look at the layout of the pivot table that Excel has generated for us, you'll see that there

04:12.280 --> 04:18.150
is a column for each of the unique values in that product category column.

04:18.160 --> 04:25.520
And now all of the line totals have been reduced to a single sum for each of these product categories.

04:25.540 --> 04:28.630
So in that way, our data has now been flattened out.

04:28.660 --> 04:33.280
What were once values in our product category column?

04:33.580 --> 04:42.100
These guys right here bikes, clothing, accessories, components have now become columns in our pivot

04:42.130 --> 04:50.890
table, and all of the individual line totals have been rolled up into four sums, one for each of our

04:50.890 --> 04:52.030
product categories.

04:52.300 --> 04:58.630
So I hope the whole concept of pivoting and how it transforms your data makes sense at this point because

04:58.630 --> 05:01.070
now we're going to dive into the syntax which is.

05:01.700 --> 05:06.560
A little hairy, to be honest with you, but just like we've done previously, we'll take it one step

05:06.560 --> 05:07.250
at a time.

05:07.550 --> 05:12.020
So the first step is to think carefully about what we want our output to look like.

05:12.320 --> 05:14.000
Now, we've already done that in this case.

05:14.000 --> 05:19.820
We know that we want a column for each unique value in our product category name.

05:19.970 --> 05:26.090
And under those columns, we want a single number for each product category that represents the sum

05:26.120 --> 05:31.100
total of all of the line totals for all the products within that category.

05:31.280 --> 05:37.950
Essentially, we're going to transform this data in the exact same way that we just did it in Excel.

05:37.970 --> 05:40.390
I wish it was as easy as it is in Excel.

05:40.400 --> 05:41.240
It's not.

05:41.240 --> 05:47.090
But when you're dealing with huge amounts of data that Excel may struggle with, or you just need your

05:47.090 --> 05:54.650
data transformed in this way as some kind of intermediate step in a larger data transformation process,

05:54.650 --> 05:58.090
Pivot can still be an essential tool in SQL.

05:58.850 --> 05:59.270
All right.

05:59.270 --> 06:05.720
So the first step is to actually wrap our query here in parentheses, because ultimately it is going

06:05.720 --> 06:07.100
to be a sub query.

06:07.490 --> 06:14.600
The sub query will be the base table essentially, because as far as SQL is concerned, a sub query

06:14.600 --> 06:18.610
is treated like a table that the pivot operator is going to reference.

06:18.620 --> 06:23.480
And because this is a sub query that will be used in the from clause, we will be aliasing it.

06:23.480 --> 06:24.920
So we'll just alias it a.

06:25.100 --> 06:31.910
Now the next step is to add our pivot keyword which will go directly below our sub query.

06:32.840 --> 06:37.760
And after pivot we'll have an opening and closing parentheses.

06:38.180 --> 06:45.980
And now is where we want to think about which column in our data has the categorical output.

06:46.010 --> 06:52.580
Think the type of values that would help us slice and dice and filter our data as opposed to some kind

06:52.580 --> 06:55.920
of numerical field that we're trying to perform calculations on.

06:55.940 --> 07:05.690
That field is what we're typically going to pivot to translate the unique values in that field to columns.

07:05.700 --> 07:09.240
So in that case, that is our product category name.

07:09.540 --> 07:15.930
And then we also need to think about which column in our data we're going to perform some sort of calculation

07:15.930 --> 07:19.740
on some kind of aggregation, a sum, an average, a max.

07:19.740 --> 07:20.490
ET cetera.

07:20.490 --> 07:22.530
In this case, that is line total.

07:23.570 --> 07:26.780
So first we'll actually apply the aggregation.

07:26.780 --> 07:34.940
So we'll type sum of line total and now we account for our product category name.

07:35.740 --> 07:40.150
The syntax is a little funky, but follow closely and it'll ultimately make sense.

07:40.820 --> 07:53.390
So next we type for product category name N, and then after the end keyword, we're going to have opening

07:53.390 --> 07:54.760
and closing parentheses.

07:54.770 --> 08:02.030
And now we actually need to list out every product category name that we want to see as a column in

08:02.030 --> 08:02.840
our output.

08:03.470 --> 08:09.860
Unlike Excel pivot tables, our pivot here is not going to automatically detect all the unique values

08:09.860 --> 08:14.240
in the product category, name field and transpose them over into columns.

08:14.270 --> 08:19.430
We actually have to spell out which values we want to see in our output.

08:19.520 --> 08:25.220
So, for example, if we only include bikes and clothing, we're only going to have columns for bikes

08:25.220 --> 08:26.450
and clothing in our output.

08:26.450 --> 08:28.500
But in this case, we want to see all four.

08:28.520 --> 08:30.260
So let's go ahead and add those.

08:31.100 --> 08:36.320
And to save you the tedium of watching me type, I'm just going to paste these guys in here.

08:36.560 --> 08:44.390
Now, it's worth noting that in examples of pivot code, typically these items in the in list will be

08:44.390 --> 08:47.840
surrounded by brackets like this.

08:48.110 --> 08:53.630
Now, it's actually not necessary for our code to run, but I'm going to add them anyway just because

08:53.630 --> 09:00.020
it may be confusing if you see other examples of code with pivot that do have these brackets, because

09:00.050 --> 09:03.150
again, that is the the most common approach.

09:03.600 --> 09:11.790
Now, the last piece is to actually select these four items that we are pivoting out into columns.

09:11.790 --> 09:14.370
And remember, these are going to be columns in our data set.

09:14.370 --> 09:18.660
So we're going to select them just like we would any other columns in our outer query.

09:18.900 --> 09:26.070
Up to this point, we've just defined a subquery here and then our pivot statement here.

09:26.190 --> 09:31.230
But ultimately we need a select statement at the very beginning that's going to select these four columns.

09:31.650 --> 09:31.980
All right.

09:31.980 --> 09:35.910
So we'll just type select and then we'll.

09:36.540 --> 09:41.040
Paste in our four items that are now becoming columns.

09:41.760 --> 09:45.300
And lastly, we'll add the from keyword and let's expand this out.

09:45.300 --> 09:45.870
So.

09:47.330 --> 09:48.860
You can see the code more clearly.

09:49.220 --> 09:51.710
And at this point, I think we've got something that might work.

09:51.710 --> 09:54.290
So let's go ahead and run it and see what happens.

09:54.530 --> 09:55.100
All right.

09:55.100 --> 09:59.620
It looks like we have successfully replicated the output of our Excel pivot table.

09:59.630 --> 10:06.830
We have a column for each of our product categories, and under that column is the total of all the

10:06.830 --> 10:10.910
line totals of all the products that were sold within those categories.

10:11.090 --> 10:14.960
Now, up next, I'm going to throw a slightly more complicated example at you.

10:14.970 --> 10:15.980
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.230 --> 00:01.310
Welcome back.

00:01.460 --> 00:07.280
Now that we've got our basic syntax working, I'm going to introduce a few more quirks that show you

00:07.400 --> 00:13.580
different ways to manipulate or enhance your pivot output or to just make it a little bit easier to

00:13.580 --> 00:15.080
use pivot in the first place.

00:15.110 --> 00:21.650
First up, I'm actually going to replace these four column references with Select Star.

00:22.020 --> 00:27.170
Turns out that will actually work just fine and it will save you a lot of typing and copying and pasting

00:27.170 --> 00:34.340
if all you want to see are columns whose names are exactly the same as the values in the column that

00:34.340 --> 00:34.940
we're pivoting.

00:34.940 --> 00:37.190
So let's run that just to make sure it works.

00:37.550 --> 00:38.510
And it does.

00:39.210 --> 00:39.550
Now?

00:39.570 --> 00:39.750
No.

00:39.750 --> 00:48.540
Earlier I said that we have to explicitly tell SQL exactly what values in our column that we're pivoting,

00:48.660 --> 00:53.580
our column that we're transposing, that we want to see as column headers in our final output.

00:53.580 --> 00:55.980
And that's the values in this list here.

00:55.980 --> 01:00.720
So what would happen if I removed accessories and components?

01:00.900 --> 01:02.160
Let's try that.

01:02.430 --> 01:06.090
And as you can see now, we only have two columns in our output.

01:06.090 --> 01:11.490
So again, pivot is not as smart as a pivot table in Excel or another spreadsheet application.

01:11.490 --> 01:16.350
We have to kind of hold its hand and tell it, okay, these are the values in my product category name.

01:16.350 --> 01:19.770
These are the product categories that I want to see as columns in my output.

01:20.580 --> 01:26.760
So now let's look at the effect of adding another field to our our sub query.

01:26.790 --> 01:32.010
Our sub select here that is ultimately providing us the data that we're then pivoting.

01:32.130 --> 01:38.580
So right now we've got one field product category name that is being pivoted and transposed into column

01:38.580 --> 01:39.180
headers.

01:39.180 --> 01:43.670
And we've got another field line total that's being aggregated with a sum function.

01:43.680 --> 01:50.190
But what happens if we add a third field that isn't being pivoted or transposed and isn't being aggregated?

01:51.010 --> 01:52.810
Well, kind of like I did before.

01:53.140 --> 01:59.530
I'll start by pulling this off in Excel where it's a little more intuitive, a little more visual,

01:59.530 --> 02:01.660
and then we'll translate it to SQL.

02:02.320 --> 02:07.330
So first let me add order quantity to this inner query and I'll just run it and then drop that output

02:07.330 --> 02:08.410
right into Excel.

02:10.900 --> 02:12.850
So I'll go ahead and run this.

02:15.280 --> 02:21.130
And you can see all we did was just add the order quantity to each line item from the sales order detail

02:21.130 --> 02:21.600
table.

02:21.610 --> 02:24.130
So let's copy this output.

02:31.310 --> 02:33.620
And drop it right into an Excel spreadsheet.

02:35.640 --> 02:37.890
And now we'll create another pivot table.

02:41.770 --> 02:44.830
We'll still have our product category names as the columns.

02:45.380 --> 02:52.370
We'll still have our line total being summed in the value section, but now we're going to take our

02:52.370 --> 02:55.630
order quantity over here and drop it into the rows section.

02:55.640 --> 03:04.820
So now you can see that each unique order quantity gets its own row in our pivot table, and our subtotals

03:04.820 --> 03:11.510
under each product category are now being broken out not just by product category, but also by order

03:11.510 --> 03:12.230
quantity.

03:12.230 --> 03:19.430
So if we drill into this number here, we're now seeing all the individual line items that had an order

03:19.430 --> 03:23.240
quantity of one under the accessories category.

03:24.090 --> 03:24.480
All right.

03:24.480 --> 03:30.270
So now that we've seen how to make our pivoted data a little more granular by adding an additional layer

03:30.270 --> 03:34.140
of grouping, let's go back and see what this looks like in SQL.

03:34.350 --> 03:40.260
So we've actually already added order quantity to our inner query and we actually don't need to do anything

03:40.260 --> 03:41.340
else in our pivot.

03:42.100 --> 03:48.040
Pivot only cares about the field that we're transposing, which is product category name and the field

03:48.040 --> 03:50.680
that we're applying aggregation to, which is line total.

03:50.860 --> 03:56.950
Any additional fields we can just include in our subquery here and they will also be included in the

03:56.950 --> 03:57.590
output.

03:57.610 --> 03:59.080
So let's run this.

03:59.950 --> 04:00.250
All right.

04:00.250 --> 04:03.430
We see the output looks a lot like what we had in Excel.

04:03.760 --> 04:10.870
But just to clarify things, let's go ahead and sort by order, quantity and rerun.

04:11.710 --> 04:12.100
All right.

04:12.100 --> 04:15.520
And it looks like we have replicated our Excel pivot table.

04:16.060 --> 04:22.930
So just to clarify what's going on here, any column you include in your subquery here that is providing

04:22.930 --> 04:28.690
the base data that you're ultimately pivoting that is not being aggregated.

04:29.520 --> 04:33.240
Or transpose like we're transposing product category name.

04:33.930 --> 04:36.480
Becomes a new column in our output.

04:37.070 --> 04:45.350
And our aggregated totals under each column we specified at our enlist are now broken out by all of

04:45.350 --> 04:51.380
the unique values in that additional column we have in our subquery.

04:51.680 --> 04:53.390
And we could continue with this.

04:53.420 --> 04:56.060
We could add more columns to our subquery.

04:56.060 --> 05:03.920
And now our totals under bikes and clothing would be broken out by all of the unique combinations of

05:03.920 --> 05:08.000
values from all the additional columns we include in that subquery.

05:08.180 --> 05:10.760
And that can be good to a point.

05:10.940 --> 05:14.310
And past that point, it makes our output pretty much useless.

05:14.330 --> 05:23.390
For example, if I just select all columns from our sales order detail table, now Pivot is going to

05:23.390 --> 05:30.800
have to give us a record for every unique combination of values from all of those columns, which means

05:30.800 --> 05:36.440
we're probably just going to end up with the same amount of records that exist in the sales order detail

05:36.440 --> 05:37.330
table at all.

05:37.350 --> 05:39.150
But let's run that to confirm.

05:39.420 --> 05:43.310
And sure enough, we end up with the same number of records that are in the table overall.

05:43.320 --> 05:48.540
So at this point, our pivoting, our the aggregation that our pivoting gives us isn't really helping

05:48.540 --> 05:52.860
us at all because we're not rolling any records up into groups.

05:53.040 --> 05:59.610
So the bottom line is think carefully about the fields you include in your subquery that are not part

05:59.610 --> 06:04.080
of your pivot syntax down here because they will have a big impact on your output.

06:04.680 --> 06:05.040
All right.

06:05.040 --> 06:08.910
Let me go ahead and restore our query to its original state.

06:09.150 --> 06:16.260
And now the last thing I want to show you is how to alias columns in your main query.

06:16.500 --> 06:23.100
For example, what if we don't want order quantity to be abbreviated like it currently is in our output?

06:23.130 --> 06:27.390
What if we want to alias it in some more business friendly way?

06:27.660 --> 06:30.390
Well, at this point we won't be able to get away with Select Star anymore.

06:30.390 --> 06:33.750
We'll actually have to spell out the columns we're selecting, but that's fine.

06:34.020 --> 06:43.110
So first we'll add our transposed values from the product category name column, and now I will simply

06:43.110 --> 06:48.930
alias Order quantity order qty as order quantity.

06:49.470 --> 06:51.780
So I'll just type order.

06:56.940 --> 06:58.260
And now we'll run that.

06:58.980 --> 07:03.960
So now we have a nice, clean, business friendly alias for the order quantity field.

07:04.380 --> 07:09.720
And again, you can alias the fields in your outer select, your main select however you like.

07:10.680 --> 07:11.040
All right.

07:11.040 --> 07:12.580
So that's pretty much it on Pivot.

07:12.600 --> 07:19.380
I know that syntax was pretty rough, but as I have encouraged with some prior code examples that are

07:19.380 --> 07:24.300
a little bit more challenging, where the syntax is a little bit counter-intuitive, I would encourage

07:24.300 --> 07:31.620
you to keep a snippet of working pivot code around as an example, and then every time you encounter

07:31.620 --> 07:39.210
a scenario where you need to flatten data like this, just take that code and modify it to fit the situation

07:39.210 --> 07:40.560
that you're facing.

07:41.080 --> 07:46.150
Generally speaking with techniques that involve harder to remember syntax.

07:46.150 --> 07:49.720
I like to just keep a little library of code examples around that.

07:49.720 --> 07:52.360
I can copy and paste and adapt as I need to.

07:53.160 --> 07:53.520
All right.

07:53.520 --> 07:57.750
At this point, we have pretty much covered the bases on subqueries.

07:57.750 --> 08:05.130
So up next, we're going to explore a whole new approach to breaking our data transformation problems

08:05.130 --> 08:06.180
into steps.

08:06.510 --> 08:10.320
And that is common table Expressions or CTEs.

08:10.650 --> 08:12.000
That's coming up next.

08:12.000 --> 08:12.930
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.200 --> 00:01.220
Welcome back.

00:01.640 --> 00:08.150
So far, we've looked at Subqueries as a way of breaking up complicated data analysis into manageable

00:08.150 --> 00:08.930
steps.

00:09.260 --> 00:14.000
But sometimes even subqueries aren't enough to keep things from getting confusing.

00:14.390 --> 00:20.240
Subqueries are fine as long as we only need to reference one inner query in an outer query.

00:20.360 --> 00:24.110
But what about when our analysis requires three or more steps?

00:24.500 --> 00:32.750
Fortunately, SQL offers a construct called a common table expression or CTE for short that helps make

00:32.750 --> 00:36.710
these kinds of complex, multi-stage problems more manageable.

00:37.350 --> 00:42.840
So this graphic shows the difference between how a subquery would handle a multi step analysis versus

00:42.870 --> 00:43.470
a CTE.

00:44.660 --> 00:46.400
What the subquery approach.

00:46.430 --> 00:52.370
Each subquery is referenced by some outer query, which in turn can be a subquery that is referenced

00:52.370 --> 00:57.770
again by some other outer query and so on and so forth until we finally reach our main query.

00:58.620 --> 01:04.080
As messy as this might seem, it gets even worse when you plug real code into all of these layers of

01:04.080 --> 01:04.950
subqueries.

01:05.550 --> 01:10.590
With this approach, your queries can be difficult to interpret and reason about, which is a problem

01:10.590 --> 01:14.790
not just for you, but for anyone who might need to understand your code.

01:15.740 --> 01:22.160
Seats, on the other hand, allow us to express multi-stage data transformations in a linear, step

01:22.160 --> 01:25.280
by step way that is easy to follow and reason about.

01:25.760 --> 01:31.340
But instead of jumping right into coding seats, let's try and tackle a complex query that requires

01:31.340 --> 01:34.220
multiple steps using only subqueries.

01:34.640 --> 01:37.040
The goal of the query will be as follows.

01:37.190 --> 01:43.820
We need to identify the ten biggest sales orders per month and then sum those up so that we have a single

01:43.820 --> 01:45.140
total per month.

01:45.410 --> 01:50.570
Then we need to compare the sum of the ten biggest sales orders per month against the same total for

01:50.570 --> 01:51.530
the previous month.

01:52.170 --> 01:55.050
The output of our query should look something like this.

01:55.680 --> 02:00.750
Now that we know what we're trying to accomplish, let's take a crack at getting this done with subqueries.

02:01.420 --> 02:07.300
So our starter query here simply consists of the order, date and total due columns from our sales order

02:07.300 --> 02:08.140
header table.

02:08.440 --> 02:14.380
Obviously these are the two foundational pieces of information we're going to need for all of our calculations.

02:14.930 --> 02:21.200
First up, since we're going to be not only grouping the data by month, but also tying records by current

02:21.200 --> 02:27.470
month versus previous month, we'll need a field in our data that identifies the month of a given sales

02:27.470 --> 02:28.220
order date.

02:28.460 --> 02:34.610
To do this, we'll use the date from parts function to parse out the first date of the month for any

02:34.610 --> 02:36.080
given sales order date.

02:36.110 --> 02:37.910
So let's go ahead and type that out.

02:38.330 --> 02:49.310
So we'll type order month, which is the name of our field, and then we'll use the date from parts

02:49.310 --> 02:50.120
function.

02:50.120 --> 02:55.340
And this takes three arguments, which are the year we're interested in.

02:55.580 --> 03:00.740
So to extract the year for our order date, we'll just use the year function.

03:05.610 --> 03:10.500
And then the month and this will work exactly like year just with the month function.

03:12.480 --> 03:17.460
And then lastly, to get the first day of the month, we'll simply type the number one.

03:17.940 --> 03:24.630
And now this date time from parts function here is going to extract the first day of the month that

03:24.630 --> 03:26.550
corresponds to any given order date.

03:26.550 --> 03:32.700
So if the order date is May 12th, the order month field is going to return May 1st.

03:32.970 --> 03:35.280
And let's just run this to see what that looks like.

03:36.430 --> 03:36.670
All right.

03:36.670 --> 03:41.290
And there you see an order month of May 1st for all of our May 31st orders.

03:41.290 --> 03:46.380
But if we scroll down, you'll see we have orders on October 5th or sixth.

03:46.390 --> 03:49.450
The order month is still October 1st.

03:49.930 --> 03:50.530
Okay.

03:50.530 --> 03:56.980
Next up, we're going to need to rank all of our sales orders by the total amount due, but do this

03:56.980 --> 03:59.620
within groups defined by like months.

03:59.890 --> 04:05.950
So in this way, sales orders that took place within a given month will be ranked sequentially based

04:05.950 --> 04:07.210
on the total amount due.

04:07.780 --> 04:10.450
That will let us grab the top ten orders per month.

04:11.150 --> 04:15.380
So if you're thinking that sounds like a window function type of problem, you're right on.

04:15.380 --> 04:17.090
So let's go ahead and code that up.

04:17.240 --> 04:19.940
So we'll create another field called Order Rank

04:23.030 --> 04:28.550
and we'll set it equal to a window function in this case row number,

04:31.970 --> 04:34.220
and we'll partition by

04:37.460 --> 04:40.730
the calculation that we dropped into our order month field.

04:40.730 --> 04:48.470
So I'll just copy and paste that because we're going to create groups based on the months that individual

04:48.470 --> 04:49.730
orders belong to.

04:50.690 --> 05:00.350
And then lastly, I will order by our total due field, but because we want the top ten biggest, we'll

05:00.350 --> 05:02.120
order in descending order.

05:02.930 --> 05:05.120
All right, let's run that and see what it looks like.

05:05.870 --> 05:13.320
And you can see just for example, for the month of May 2011, we have all of our total amounts due

05:13.320 --> 05:19.680
ranked from one all the way through 43 for the 43 orders that took place that month.

05:19.680 --> 05:21.630
So it looks like this is doing what we want.

05:22.080 --> 05:22.500
All right.

05:22.530 --> 05:27.570
We're finally at the point where we need to make use of a subquery to actually get our top ten sales

05:27.570 --> 05:28.470
orders per month.

05:28.470 --> 05:33.660
So now we'll just nest this query within an outer query.

05:34.050 --> 05:36.360
And for now, we'll just do a select star.

05:39.120 --> 05:46.560
And we just need to apply criteria saying that that order rank is less than or equal to ten.

05:53.390 --> 05:54.710
Now let's run that.

05:55.970 --> 05:58.100
So it's the same output as before.

05:58.100 --> 06:02.300
But now we only have our top ten sales orders per month.

06:02.720 --> 06:08.750
Now, if you recall, we also need to compute the sum total of the top ten orders per month and then

06:08.750 --> 06:10.250
group those totals by month.

06:11.210 --> 06:17.150
So to do that, we'll change our select star here to an aggregate query that groups our output by order

06:17.150 --> 06:21.380
month and sums the top ten sales order amounts by these months.

06:21.500 --> 06:32.360
So I'll replace my star here with order month, which is the field we'll group by and also the output

06:32.360 --> 06:37.280
of an aggregate function and I'll call that top ten total.

06:37.730 --> 06:44.120
And that will just be the sum of our total due amounts.

06:44.330 --> 06:50.690
And then because this is going to be an aggregate query, I'll need to group by our order month field.

06:55.010 --> 06:56.300
And now let's run that.

06:57.440 --> 07:04.490
Okay, so now we have one record per month with the sum total of the top ten orders for that month.

07:04.730 --> 07:08.240
So at this point, we've gotten fairly close to the output we want.

07:08.840 --> 07:13.340
However, we now need to compare this output essentially to itself.

07:13.550 --> 07:18.650
We have the month level roll ups we are looking for, but we still need to tie them to the equivalent

07:18.680 --> 07:20.330
totals from the previous month.

07:21.170 --> 07:26.660
To do this, we're going to need a whole new subquery identical to the one we just coded so we can join

07:26.660 --> 07:27.290
the two together.

07:27.320 --> 07:28.270
On order month.

07:28.280 --> 07:35.690
So now let's copy and paste our subquery code here to create two basically identical subqueries so we

07:35.690 --> 07:37.840
can join them together on order month.

07:37.850 --> 07:42.320
And since we don't want to join equivalent order months, we want to join current month to previous

07:42.320 --> 07:42.770
month.

07:42.770 --> 07:45.160
That's also going to require a little bit of date math.

07:45.170 --> 07:52.790
So first I'll enter down a couple times to give some room and then I'll nest this subquery in parentheses

07:52.790 --> 07:59.330
and I'll just name it A and then I'll copy.

08:02.410 --> 08:14.710
The entire subquery and I'll name the second copy B and we're going to join this second subquery on

08:15.490 --> 08:20.800
a dot order month equals.

08:20.980 --> 08:23.260
And here's where the date math comes in.

08:23.530 --> 08:31.510
We want our top ten total from the second subquery that we've alias B here to represent the previous

08:31.510 --> 08:32.230
months.

08:32.260 --> 08:33.430
Top ten total.

08:33.790 --> 08:42.610
So how do we take a given month from our a subquery and latch it on to the previous month from B?

08:42.760 --> 08:51.460
So what we want to do is say date ad and then we'll be adding a month to the date and it'll be a single

08:51.460 --> 08:57.940
month and we'll add that to B dot order month.

08:58.780 --> 09:05.360
So what this is basically doing is saying join my A subquery and my B subquery such that the order month

09:05.360 --> 09:11.670
in my a subquery is equal to the order month in my B subquery plus an additional month.

09:11.690 --> 09:16.790
So if you take May 1st and add a month to it, you get June 1st.

09:16.910 --> 09:24.140
So in that way, our June 1st total in our a subquery is going to be tied to our May 1st total in our

09:24.170 --> 09:25.190
B subquery.

09:26.120 --> 09:26.360
All right.

09:26.360 --> 09:32.240
So the last thing we have to do here is just add an actual select to pull data from the two subqueries

09:32.240 --> 09:33.290
we've joined together.

09:33.680 --> 09:35.840
So we'll type select.

09:37.610 --> 09:38.690
A quarter month,

09:43.220 --> 09:52.850
a dot top ten total, and then we'll have our previous top ten total, which will be the top ten total

09:52.850 --> 09:56.480
field from our B subquery, the one that has previous month data.

09:56.480 --> 10:00.080
So we'll just call this previous top ten total

10:02.930 --> 10:10.340
and we'll set that equal to our top ten total field from our B subquery.

10:16.150 --> 10:18.790
And obviously we need to throw in the from keyword.

10:20.110 --> 10:20.650
All right.

10:20.650 --> 10:22.300
This looks like it should work.

10:22.300 --> 10:23.740
So let's run it and see.

10:24.340 --> 10:24.730
All right.

10:24.730 --> 10:25.870
It does look like it's working.

10:25.870 --> 10:30.520
But just to clarify the output, I'll go ahead and order by order month.

10:32.260 --> 10:36.130
And one more thing I'll do is actually make this join a left.

10:36.130 --> 10:36.790
Join.

10:37.270 --> 10:43.960
That way, if there is no previous month, instead of no record returning at all, we'll simply have

10:43.960 --> 10:46.510
a null in that previous top ten total field.

10:46.510 --> 10:50.140
So after converting that join to a left outer join, we'll run again.

10:50.560 --> 10:54.550
And now this is exactly what I would expect for our very first order month.

10:54.550 --> 10:59.890
There is a null value in our previous top ten total because there is no month before that.

10:59.890 --> 11:06.040
But then if you look at the previous top ten total for June, it is the top ten total for May.

11:06.070 --> 11:08.230
So it looks like this is doing what we want.

11:08.380 --> 11:15.010
That said, I hope you can see how the nested subqueries we've set up here and nested subqueries like

11:15.010 --> 11:21.740
these can be confusing to interpret and difficult to maintain and potentially redundant considering

11:21.740 --> 11:26.180
that we essentially had to duplicate our code to get the month over month comparison we were looking

11:26.180 --> 11:26.690
for.

11:27.050 --> 11:33.890
Up next, we'll take a look at refactoring some of the messiness out of our code here using cte's.

11:33.920 --> 11:34.910
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.460 --> 00:07.150
So now let's take a look at how CTS can help us solve this problem in a much cleaner, more linear way

00:07.150 --> 00:08.860
and with less repetitive code.

00:09.520 --> 00:13.960
So the first step when coding a CTE is the width keyword.

00:13.960 --> 00:16.000
That's w i t h.

00:16.210 --> 00:20.840
All cte's begin with width.

00:21.310 --> 00:21.580
Okay.

00:21.580 --> 00:26.260
That's a little awkward to say, but we'll go ahead and type it just to get started.

00:26.950 --> 00:31.150
So then we have to specify a name for the first virtual table.

00:31.150 --> 00:34.030
We will be coding followed by the as keyword.

00:34.690 --> 00:40.180
This virtual table is similar to a subquery in that we can reference it in other queries as though it

00:40.180 --> 00:41.020
is a table.

00:41.200 --> 00:48.040
However, these virtual tables in a CTE offer us a lot more flexibility than subqueries do, as you'll

00:48.040 --> 00:48.580
see.

00:49.360 --> 00:54.430
So first we'll plug in our innermost subquery as the first virtual table.

00:54.760 --> 01:02.400
So let's just grab this query here, which is at the innermost level of nesting in our subqueries,

01:02.410 --> 01:07.540
and we'll just call our virtual table step one for now.

01:07.840 --> 01:12.160
So we'll say with step one as and then a pair of parentheses.

01:12.940 --> 01:20.110
And then there's our query that represented the output of our innermost nested subquery.

01:20.620 --> 01:30.520
Now that this virtual table has been defined, all we have to do is just say, select star from step

01:30.520 --> 01:31.030
one.

01:31.630 --> 01:33.130
So let's run this.

01:34.230 --> 01:37.830
So now you can see the basic format of the CTE.

01:38.010 --> 01:44.220
It starts with a width keyword and then you have a name of a virtual table, whatever you want to name

01:44.220 --> 01:50.070
it, followed by the as keyword, followed by whatever query defines that virtual table.

01:50.070 --> 01:51.870
And that's nested in parentheses.

01:51.870 --> 01:55.440
And as you'll see in a minute, you can have as many virtual tables as you want.

01:55.740 --> 02:02.820
So we'll use this as a starting point to begin rewriting our messy subquery code down here as a CTE.

02:02.940 --> 02:09.690
But before we move on, I would like to take the opportunity to name my first virtual table in a slightly

02:09.690 --> 02:10.440
more descriptive way.

02:10.440 --> 02:11.730
I'll call it sales.

02:14.880 --> 02:18.810
Now let's start adding in the other subqueries from our previous example.

02:19.170 --> 02:25.560
Now keep in mind that whereas subqueries work inside out with the most foundational step being buried

02:25.560 --> 02:32.130
deep within other subqueries, cte's work more sequentially with the foundational step coming first

02:32.130 --> 02:35.240
and subsequent steps following in a logical fashion.

02:35.260 --> 02:43.330
That's why we took the subquery that was nested most deeply in our code and use that as the very first

02:43.330 --> 02:44.770
virtual table in our CTE.

02:45.520 --> 02:52.510
So to add more virtual tables to your CTE, you simply need a comma after your previous virtual table,

02:52.840 --> 02:58.120
and then you name your next virtual table, which we'll just call top ten.

02:58.630 --> 03:03.790
And you again include the as keyword and again a pair of parentheses.

03:04.030 --> 03:09.740
And inside those parentheses you'll include the definition of your second virtual table.

03:09.760 --> 03:17.110
So going back to our subquery code, you see that the next layer out from our innermost subquery is

03:17.110 --> 03:21.490
this query that computes the sum of the top ten orders.

03:21.490 --> 03:28.660
So that seems like a logical next virtual table for us to define because that's the next step that referenced

03:28.660 --> 03:30.350
that innermost subquery.

03:30.370 --> 03:32.320
So we'll just grab this code.

03:33.940 --> 03:39.190
And drop it into our definition of our top ten virtual table.

03:39.370 --> 03:44.380
And this is already going to demonstrate how much more readable CTEs are than subqueries.

03:44.410 --> 03:52.570
So instead of selecting these data points from this mess of embedded code here, we're instead going

03:52.570 --> 03:56.500
to reference our sales virtual table, which we've already defined previously.

03:57.370 --> 04:02.860
So we'll just say select Order month and top ten total from sales.

04:03.100 --> 04:09.550
And now instead of our final query being select Star from sales, let's make it select star from top

04:09.550 --> 04:10.120
ten.

04:10.540 --> 04:12.040
And now we can run that.

04:13.120 --> 04:13.690
Beautiful.

04:13.690 --> 04:15.850
It looks like we're making great progress so far.

04:16.030 --> 04:19.390
And even though we're only using two virtual tables here.

04:19.510 --> 04:24.460
Keep in mind that you can define as many as you need to as many as your analysis requires.

04:24.610 --> 04:29.740
And they give you a tremendous amount of flexibility because once you've defined one of those virtual

04:29.740 --> 04:34.960
tables, you can reference it in any of the virtual tables that follow.

04:34.960 --> 04:40.210
So if I have ten virtual tables defined here instead of just the two that you see, my eighth virtual

04:40.210 --> 04:43.480
table can reference my second, my third and my fourth.

04:43.510 --> 04:49.420
Whereas with subqueries, each layer can only access the layer immediately beneath it.

04:49.420 --> 04:53.590
It can't reference the subquery buried 2 or 3 layers below.

04:54.790 --> 05:00.190
Okay, so now that we have our virtual table set up, we can put together our final select query.

05:00.370 --> 05:04.240
CTS can have as many steps or virtual tables as you need.

05:04.270 --> 05:09.820
As I've mentioned before, but they must end with a single query that will give us our final output.

05:10.570 --> 05:16.150
Now, if you recall, we essentially had to create two duplicate subqueries in our previous example

05:16.150 --> 05:18.460
so we could tie them together month over month.

05:19.090 --> 05:25.810
But in our CTE, we can simply reference our second virtual table here, the top ten virtual table twice

05:25.840 --> 05:28.750
without having to actually copy and paste code.

05:29.430 --> 05:35.100
This makes our query not only much easier to read and follow, but also easier to maintain since we

05:35.100 --> 05:38.970
don't have to potentially update to subqueries that do the same thing.

05:39.570 --> 05:41.460
So let's go ahead and code this up.

05:42.240 --> 05:50.430
First of all, I'll use the outermost select from our subquery example here as sort of a jumping off

05:50.430 --> 05:55.590
point for our select statement at the end of our CTE because we're going to need the same fields.

05:56.070 --> 06:02.370
But then for our from, we'll actually just reference our top ten virtual table here.

06:04.050 --> 06:13.950
And since we're joining it to itself, I'll just alias the first copy A and the second copy B and now

06:13.950 --> 06:19.110
for my join, I'm actually going to go down and steal some more code from our previous example, that

06:19.110 --> 06:24.180
being where I joined current order month to previous order month.

06:24.990 --> 06:31.260
So now I'll go back up here and it looks like I didn't actually type the join keyword before my top

06:31.260 --> 06:32.370
ten virtual table.

06:32.370 --> 06:33.150
That would help.

06:33.910 --> 06:35.250
Now I'll type on.

06:35.850 --> 06:36.240
All right.

06:36.240 --> 06:40.140
I know that was a bit of a whirlwind of copying and pasting, so let's walk through it really quick.

06:40.840 --> 06:48.280
We are selecting our order month and top ten total fields from one copy of our top ten virtual table

06:48.280 --> 06:48.820
here.

06:48.970 --> 06:51.640
The output of which we see here below.

06:51.640 --> 06:58.150
And then we're also pulling in the previous top ten total from a second copy of that top ten virtual

06:58.150 --> 07:03.250
table that we're joining in on current month from copy A.

07:04.110 --> 07:06.360
Two previous month.

07:07.040 --> 07:08.630
From copy B.

07:09.020 --> 07:15.470
So in theory, this little bit of code right here should do the exact same thing as all of this messy

07:15.500 --> 07:17.030
subquery code down here.

07:17.240 --> 07:18.890
But let's see if it does.

07:19.530 --> 07:23.850
So we'll highlight and run and it looks like it's working.

07:23.850 --> 07:32.130
But just to make sure, let me go ahead and order by our order month to get kind of an apples to apples

07:32.130 --> 07:34.650
comparison with the subquery code we ran before.

07:35.160 --> 07:36.090
And there we are.

07:36.120 --> 07:42.000
There's our same first order month with I believe the same number for our top ten total and a null value

07:42.000 --> 07:44.940
as we would expect for the previous top ten total.

07:45.630 --> 07:52.590
So I hope I have convinced you at this point that CTEs are usually a superior tool versus subqueries

07:52.590 --> 07:58.320
for any kind of analysis or data transformation process that requires more than two steps.

07:58.680 --> 08:05.400
They're easy to read, easy to maintain, and also confer some truly unique benefits that go beyond

08:05.400 --> 08:08.400
simply breaking complicated problems into linear steps.

08:09.030 --> 08:15.750
One of those is Cte's ability to refer to themselves recursively, which makes things like generating

08:15.750 --> 08:18.030
series of numbers and dates a breeze.

08:18.300 --> 08:20.260
We'll explore that in the next video.

08:20.280 --> 08:21.240
I'll see you then.

transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.340 --> 00:01.360
Welcome back.

00:01.980 --> 00:07.620
Now that we've got the hang of seats, let's explore one of their special superpowers that no other

00:07.620 --> 00:09.360
technique in SQL can match.

00:09.660 --> 00:15.540
That's the ability to apply recursion, which, if you're not familiar with the term, is a technique

00:15.540 --> 00:21.540
in which a programming construct like a function, is able to refer to itself to a number of problems

00:21.540 --> 00:25.440
which would otherwise require substantial amounts of engineering and overhead.

00:26.330 --> 00:31.820
For the sake of keeping the focus on SQL and not digging too deep into recursion itself, which would

00:31.820 --> 00:34.370
need a lot more than one video to thoroughly explore.

00:34.370 --> 00:41.000
Anyway, I'm going to stick with one use case that is a relatively simple but extremely powerful application

00:41.000 --> 00:42.530
of recursion in SQL.

00:43.160 --> 00:45.380
And that is generating series.

00:45.530 --> 00:48.980
Series of numbers, series of dates and so on.

00:49.650 --> 00:53.070
It sounds like an easy enough thing to do, but think about it.

00:53.100 --> 01:00.000
What if you needed to create a column with 365 rows, one for each date in the current year to use as

01:00.000 --> 01:04.380
a kind of calendar table that other tables with date values could be tied into.

01:04.980 --> 01:07.740
Unless you want to manually type and union together.

01:07.740 --> 01:09.850
365 different queries.

01:09.870 --> 01:15.900
This task isn't quite as straightforward as it seems, but with recursion and in particular recursive

01:15.900 --> 01:20.370
CTEs, we can accomplish this sort of thing with just a few lines of code.

01:20.490 --> 01:21.660
Let's see how.

01:22.440 --> 01:28.450
For our first example, we'll simply try to generate a series of numbers from 1 to 100.

01:28.470 --> 01:34.470
So our final output will be a single column with 100 rows, one for each number in the series.

01:35.380 --> 01:41.080
Then when working with recursive CTEs, it's useful to think of the CTE as being divided into three

01:41.080 --> 01:42.130
components.

01:42.710 --> 01:44.870
The first is the anchor member.

01:45.230 --> 01:50.570
You can think of this as the first item in the series that the rest of the series builds upon.

01:51.380 --> 01:53.810
In our case, that's simply the number one.

01:54.470 --> 01:57.830
This anchor member needs to be expressed as a select query.

01:57.830 --> 02:03.400
So we'll start here by simply selecting the number one and aliasing it as my number.

02:03.410 --> 02:04.760
So we'll just type.

02:05.930 --> 02:11.600
Select one as my number.

02:13.070 --> 02:14.270
Simple enough.

02:15.050 --> 02:21.020
Now, the next component of the recursive CTE is what's called the recursive member.

02:21.230 --> 02:24.230
This is where the actual recursion happens.

02:24.260 --> 02:28.430
In other words, it's where things will eventually get kind of weird.

02:29.210 --> 02:35.450
But first, let's focus on the fact that all we're really trying to do is build on our anchor member

02:35.450 --> 02:40.910
in such a way that we generate our series or sequence in whatever way we want.

02:41.600 --> 02:48.500
So to start, let's plug our anchor member query inside of a CTE and then simply select from it below

02:48.500 --> 02:51.620
the CTE, adding one to our anchor member.

02:51.830 --> 03:01.310
So first we'll just create our CTE with the with keyword and we'll call our CTE number series.

03:07.750 --> 03:20.410
And then we'll select my number plus one from our number series, Virtual table.

03:20.680 --> 03:27.650
So this is the first step in the series of steps that will build out our entire sequence.

03:27.670 --> 03:29.230
My number plus one.

03:29.230 --> 03:33.460
As you'll see if we run this simply outputs two, just like you'd expect.

03:34.240 --> 03:38.310
In order to count from 1 to 100, you first got to count from 1 to 2.

03:38.320 --> 03:44.050
But to continue the series without writing some really repetitive code is where we'll need help from

03:44.050 --> 03:44.830
recursion.

03:45.310 --> 03:51.790
Recursion will allow us to repeat this process of adding one, which could also be any other number

03:51.790 --> 03:52.420
of our choosing.

03:52.420 --> 03:58.810
If we wanted to sequence by two or 3 or 4, that would be fine to the previous number in the series

03:58.810 --> 04:01.900
until we finally get to our 100 number output.

04:02.460 --> 04:04.440
So let's see what that looks like in code.

04:04.710 --> 04:14.190
So the recursive part of the recursive subquery is basically where code inside of our virtual table

04:14.190 --> 04:17.800
code inside of our definition of number series.

04:17.820 --> 04:18.810
References.

04:18.840 --> 04:20.340
Number series itself.

04:20.370 --> 04:26.940
So what we're going to do is actually cut this code that's outside of our virtual table definition,

04:27.840 --> 04:33.930
and we're going to union it right below our anchor member.

04:34.110 --> 04:40.590
So I don't expect you to be able to fully visualize exactly how that's this is working, which is instead

04:40.590 --> 04:46.530
why I want to present this as more of a kind of pattern or a recipe, so that if you need to generate

04:46.530 --> 04:54.930
a sequence of something, numbers or dates in SQL, you can take this code and just tweak the particulars

04:54.930 --> 04:56.670
to get it to do whatever you want.

04:57.420 --> 05:04.230
So again, we have our anchor member here, which is sort of the the seed, the starting point of our

05:04.230 --> 05:05.190
series.

05:05.280 --> 05:08.190
And then below that, we union all.

05:08.190 --> 05:12.060
And this is how any recursive CTE that you code is going to look.

05:12.090 --> 05:15.690
You're first going to have your anchor member, then you're going to have a union all.

05:15.960 --> 05:22.200
And then you will have your recursive member here which references.

05:22.910 --> 05:26.030
The definition of the virtual table itself.

05:26.840 --> 05:32.870
And then increments that field in the anchor member by some amount.

05:33.080 --> 05:36.530
Now, in this case, we want to increment it by one.

05:36.530 --> 05:39.770
So we're just saying my number plus one.

05:40.290 --> 05:47.520
And since we're unioning all, we're basically stacking this incremented number below the current value

05:47.520 --> 05:48.360
of my number.

05:49.020 --> 05:53.430
And because of how recursion works, this process is just going to continue.

05:53.430 --> 05:57.990
It's just going to repeat and repeat and repeat, which is what we want to appoint.

05:57.990 --> 06:01.020
But in a second we're going to see how that can also be a problem.

06:01.560 --> 06:08.340
So the last step here, as with any other CTE, will be to write the select statement that will generate

06:08.340 --> 06:12.390
our final output below our virtual table definition.

06:12.690 --> 06:21.840
So I'll just type select my number from.

06:24.390 --> 06:25.680
Number series.

06:27.900 --> 06:30.930
So let's see what happens if we run this.

06:32.370 --> 06:34.260
And we're getting an error.

06:35.040 --> 06:41.220
Siegel says the maximum recursion 100 has been exhausted before statement completion.

06:41.550 --> 06:43.530
So what do we make of that?

06:43.950 --> 06:51.750
Well, remember, I said that this recursive member in the definition of our virtual table because it

06:51.750 --> 06:53.250
is referring.

06:53.810 --> 06:55.730
To the virtual table itself.

06:56.390 --> 07:04.910
Is going to simply repeat that process of unioning an incremented number over and over again within

07:04.910 --> 07:06.140
that virtual table.

07:06.500 --> 07:12.820
And by over and over again, I basically mean forever until SQL finally says enough is enough.

07:12.830 --> 07:14.240
I'm not going to let you do this.

07:14.240 --> 07:15.080
Infinitely.

07:15.350 --> 07:22.940
Recursion gives us the power to repeat some action, some process, many, and possibly infinitely many

07:22.940 --> 07:23.660
times.

07:23.810 --> 07:30.260
So to protect itself from being overloaded by some code, running on an infinite loop by default, the

07:30.260 --> 07:35.180
database limits your recursive CTE to calling itself only 100 times.

07:36.250 --> 07:38.690
But this actually aligns with our goal anyway.

07:38.710 --> 07:43.800
We're not trying to generate an infinite series of numbers, but rather a list of the numbers from 1

07:43.800 --> 07:44.500
to 100.

07:44.590 --> 07:50.920
So what we need here is a way to make our recursion stop or terminate once we've hit that threshold.

07:51.710 --> 07:57.230
And that leads us to the third component of recursive CTEs, which is the termination condition.

07:57.860 --> 07:59.660
This is a logical condition.

07:59.660 --> 08:05.570
We include in our recursive member that ensures it will stop executing after a certain point.

08:06.300 --> 08:12.330
In our case, since we're just trying to count to 100, we'll just add the criteria where my number

08:12.330 --> 08:14.010
is less than or equal to 100.

08:14.490 --> 08:23.370
So in our recursive member here, we'll just add a where clause and we'll say where my number is less

08:23.370 --> 08:25.320
than or equal to 100.

08:26.650 --> 08:35.320
So what this should do is cause this series of recursive calls to stop once my number is finally 100.

08:35.350 --> 08:37.060
So now let's run that.

08:37.960 --> 08:39.880
And that appears to have worked.

08:40.490 --> 08:47.030
But if we scroll down to the bottom, it looks like we're actually counting to 101 instead of 100.

08:47.530 --> 08:48.730
So why is that?

08:49.700 --> 08:56.090
Well, if you think about what's happening in the recursive member, it's adding one to each previous

08:56.090 --> 09:02.060
number in the series to generate the current number, and we're telling it to stop once the value of

09:02.060 --> 09:04.400
my number is greater than 100.

09:04.430 --> 09:10.730
In other words, where it's not less than or equal to 100, what that means is when my number equals

09:10.730 --> 09:13.430
100, I'm still going to add one to it.

09:13.520 --> 09:18.290
Then the query will terminate in the next cycle now that my number is greater than 100.

09:18.320 --> 09:23.750
So all we need to do is change our termination condition to simply be less than 100.

09:23.930 --> 09:26.420
So let's update that and rerun.

09:28.070 --> 09:30.950
And now if we scroll down to the bottom of our output.

09:31.450 --> 09:33.340
It looks like we've got what we want.

09:34.090 --> 09:39.910
And there we have it, a few lines of code that generate a series of 100 numbers, but could just as

09:39.910 --> 09:42.400
easily have been 1000 or 10,000.

09:42.950 --> 09:48.560
So before we move on, let's take a look at how this same technique can be applied to generate series

09:48.560 --> 09:49.490
of dates.

09:50.130 --> 09:56.160
Let's say, for example, we want to generate a series of all dates in the year 2021.

09:56.820 --> 10:03.840
Basically, our query output should consist of 365 rows, one for each date in 2021.

10:04.650 --> 10:07.470
This works almost exactly like our previous example.

10:07.470 --> 10:09.900
So we should be able to fly through this with no problem.

10:10.800 --> 10:14.670
Instead of writing a new query from scratch, I'm actually just going to modify the one we've already

10:14.670 --> 10:15.180
got.

10:15.860 --> 10:21.140
So we'll call our virtual table date series instead of number series.

10:21.650 --> 10:26.510
And then our anchor member is just going to be the first date in 2021.

10:26.810 --> 10:43.490
So I'll do a cast 0101 2021 as date and I'll alias that field my date and we can actually just run this

10:43.490 --> 10:44.450
as a select.

10:45.590 --> 10:52.400
So you see the value that is returned by the anchor member, the, the seed, the starting point of

10:52.400 --> 10:57.230
our recursion will be the first day of 2021.

10:57.530 --> 11:03.590
Now, next, we're going to add the recursive member, which is going to add one day to the previous

11:03.590 --> 11:06.260
day in the series for each cycle of recursion.

11:06.680 --> 11:16.140
So instead of doing my number plus one, we'll take advantage of the date add function in SQL to add

11:16.140 --> 11:21.740
one day to increment my date by one day for each cycle of recursion.

11:21.750 --> 11:28.380
So we'll say day one and then we'll refer to my date.

11:29.070 --> 11:35.430
And because we are using recursion, we're actually referencing the virtual table inside the virtual

11:35.430 --> 11:36.060
table.

11:36.210 --> 11:39.660
And then lastly, we're going to add the termination condition.

11:39.960 --> 11:46.800
Now, in this case, that should be that my date is less than December 31st, 2021.

11:47.640 --> 11:52.050
Once the last date in our series is December 30th, 2021.

11:52.170 --> 11:57.840
Adding one to that date will finish off our series, so we won't need to take any more action once the

11:57.840 --> 12:00.480
last date in the series is December 31st.

12:00.810 --> 12:03.150
So let's go ahead and add that.

12:03.420 --> 12:13.980
So I'll say in our where clause here where my date is less than and I just copied and pasted that cast

12:14.010 --> 12:15.810
to save a little bit of typing.

12:16.140 --> 12:21.420
Is less than 1231 2021.

12:21.570 --> 12:28.410
And then lastly, I'll just update the references, the field and table referenced in our final select

12:28.710 --> 12:31.380
to reference our my date field.

12:33.110 --> 12:37.370
And our date series Virtual Table.

12:40.900 --> 12:43.270
And now I think we're ready to go ahead and run.

12:44.320 --> 12:45.070
Oops.

12:45.070 --> 12:47.050
I thought this was going to be easy.

12:47.230 --> 12:51.970
So now SQL is giving us this same max recursion error we saw before.

12:52.520 --> 12:55.120
But we have a termination condition in place.

12:55.130 --> 12:56.540
So how is this happening?

12:57.280 --> 13:05.320
While we do have a termination condition, that condition allows recursion to occur 365 times, which

13:05.350 --> 13:10.060
exceeds the max recursion limit of 100 that SQL has in place by default.

13:10.830 --> 13:16.900
Now, fortunately, we can override that limit with a special keyword after our final select query.

13:16.920 --> 13:18.510
So let's see what that looks like.

13:19.400 --> 13:25.580
Basically below our final select that produces our output, we'll just type option.

13:25.910 --> 13:33.740
And then in parentheses after option Max recursion 365.

13:34.940 --> 13:36.380
So let's run that again.

13:37.760 --> 13:39.290
And it looks like it worked.

13:39.290 --> 13:41.300
So if we scroll all the way down.

13:42.250 --> 13:48.580
We'll see that we have 365 records and our last date is, in fact, December 31st, 2021.

13:49.690 --> 13:50.110
All right.

13:50.110 --> 13:57.040
So there we have it, A quick, if not easy way to generate series of numbers and dates in SQL.

13:57.070 --> 14:00.490
A problem that is far from trivial to solve with any other technique.

14:00.820 --> 14:04.480
Now, I know this recursion stuff can be pretty hard to wrap your head around.

14:04.510 --> 14:10.810
That's why I would encourage you to focus more on the pattern of the problems we work through, namely

14:10.810 --> 14:16.150
generating series so that when you recognize a problem with a similar pattern in the wild, you'll be

14:16.150 --> 14:21.130
able to adapt this code to it without necessarily needing a deep understanding of recursion.

14:21.660 --> 14:27.720
In other words, as I mentioned before, you can look at this code as a kind of recipe for generating

14:27.720 --> 14:29.370
series of values in SQL.

14:29.760 --> 14:30.270
Okay.

14:30.270 --> 14:32.220
That's it on Cte's for now.

14:32.610 --> 14:38.460
Up next, we'll look at temp tables, which are an even more powerful technique for breaking large,

14:38.460 --> 14:41.100
complicated problems into manageable steps.

14:41.280 --> 14:42.300
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.230 --> 00:01.220
Welcome back.

00:01.930 --> 00:08.770
Now that we've got our arms around seats, I want to discuss an alternative to seats called temp tables

00:08.770 --> 00:12.130
that can be more flexible and more powerful.

00:12.310 --> 00:17.200
But what are some limitations of seats that would cause us to reach for another solution in the first

00:17.200 --> 00:17.860
place?

00:18.220 --> 00:22.850
Well, first seats can only be used in the current query scope.

00:22.870 --> 00:24.190
Now, what's that mean?

00:24.520 --> 00:31.660
Basically, it means you can't reference those virtual tables you're you're creating after the select

00:31.660 --> 00:33.670
statement that produces our output.

00:33.700 --> 00:39.280
Now, for smaller, less complex queries, this may not be a problem, but it can be a problem If you

00:39.280 --> 00:43.540
need to reuse your virtual tables multiple times for different purposes.

00:43.840 --> 00:50.350
Also, your virtual tables can't be referenced individually, that is to say, outside of the context

00:50.350 --> 00:55.060
of running them together with all of the other virtual tables that are part of your statement.

00:55.060 --> 00:57.220
And that makes debugging more difficult.

00:57.720 --> 01:00.360
So imagine you have a really complex CTE.

01:00.930 --> 01:06.390
Maybe you have ten virtual tables, each of which depends on the previous one.

01:06.540 --> 01:12.180
And your final query is either erroring out or the output isn't what you expect.

01:12.180 --> 01:18.210
And maybe you think there's an issue with your fifth virtual table and your fifth virtual table is pulling

01:18.210 --> 01:19.810
from your fourth virtual table.

01:19.830 --> 01:24.330
So what you'd really like to be able to do is dig into that fourth virtual table and see what's going

01:24.330 --> 01:25.260
on with the data.

01:25.440 --> 01:27.420
But with Cte's, you can't do that.

01:27.420 --> 01:32.270
All of those virtual tables combine with that select statement at the end are kind of part of a whole,

01:32.280 --> 01:34.350
so you have to run the whole thing together.

01:34.860 --> 01:39.880
Now, finally, there are certain optimization techniques that aren't available to Cte's.

01:39.930 --> 01:44.070
We haven't really dug into optimization yet and we will a little bit later on.

01:44.630 --> 01:49.880
But for now, it's enough to know that temp tables and regular tables just offer us some optimization

01:49.880 --> 01:52.130
techniques that you don't have with CTEs.

01:52.820 --> 01:58.970
Now let's take a look at an example of what some of these limitations look like with a real life code

01:58.970 --> 01:59.690
example.

02:00.290 --> 02:05.690
So here we have our code example from the last video where we actually accomplished something pretty

02:05.690 --> 02:07.000
cool, the CTE.

02:07.720 --> 02:14.080
We basically pulled out the top ten sales orders by month, aggregated them by month, and then join

02:14.080 --> 02:18.400
that data to itself to create a nice month over month view.

02:19.050 --> 02:21.420
But what if we wanted to take this a step further?

02:21.970 --> 02:26.470
Right now we are just aggregating all of this data in our last select statement.

02:26.740 --> 02:31.800
But what if we wanted a second select statement that shows us order level detail?

02:31.810 --> 02:37.510
So instead of seeing the top ten orders rolled up by month, we actually see those individual top ten

02:37.510 --> 02:38.140
orders.

02:38.530 --> 02:45.640
Now, if we roll up here, we'll see that that's basically the data we're pulling when we create this

02:45.640 --> 02:48.070
very first virtual table sales.

02:48.160 --> 02:53.800
If I run the select statement that creates the sales virtual table, you'll see that we have our order

02:53.800 --> 02:56.740
level detail and that those orders are ranked.

02:57.330 --> 03:04.890
So all we really need to do is select from this sales virtual table where this order rank field here.

03:05.710 --> 03:07.180
Is less than or equal to ten.

03:07.210 --> 03:09.190
That will give us the top ten per month.

03:09.460 --> 03:17.110
So you'd think this might be as simple as just taking our sales virtual table and typing another select

03:17.110 --> 03:18.340
statement down here

03:21.250 --> 03:29.470
and applying that criteria where order rank is less than or equal to ten.

03:29.830 --> 03:31.390
So let's try that.

03:33.010 --> 03:36.730
And SQL is telling us that sales is an invalid object name.

03:37.580 --> 03:43.580
But that doesn't make any sense because if we scroll up, we see that sales is being referenced right

03:43.580 --> 03:48.560
here on line 16 to create the top ten sales virtual table.

03:49.530 --> 03:55.410
So how is it available here on line 16 but not available here on line 33?

03:55.740 --> 04:01.470
Well, that's what I meant earlier when I said that CTS are limited to query level scope.

04:01.590 --> 04:03.690
The scope of the current query.

04:03.930 --> 04:10.650
So CTS are typically going to have the select statement at the very end following all of your virtual

04:10.650 --> 04:11.340
tables.

04:12.170 --> 04:17.020
After the select statement and the output it produces, those virtual tables are gone.

04:17.030 --> 04:18.230
They vanish into thin air.

04:18.230 --> 04:20.870
They are no longer available for you to do anything with.

04:21.050 --> 04:29.360
So if we want to reuse that sales virtual table after our final select, we'll need some other technique

04:29.360 --> 04:30.320
besides the CTE.

04:30.740 --> 04:33.080
And that's where temp tables can help us.

04:33.630 --> 04:39.630
So temp tables, instead of being limited by the scope of the current query, are only limited by the

04:39.630 --> 04:40.920
current session.

04:41.310 --> 04:43.530
So what do I mean by session?

04:43.830 --> 04:47.760
Session basically is defined by this code editor window.

04:47.790 --> 04:49.950
This entire window that we're looking at here.

04:50.190 --> 04:55.500
And to kill your session, you would click this X here to close out your window.

04:55.500 --> 04:59.010
But until you do that, your session is still open.

04:59.750 --> 05:07.250
Which means that if you create a temp table all the way at the top of your editor window here, that

05:07.250 --> 05:14.870
temp table is available to you anywhere below that point throughout the rest of your code as long as

05:14.870 --> 05:16.130
this window is open.

05:16.160 --> 05:22.760
So that means if we recode this example with temp tables, I should be able to reference sales as a

05:22.760 --> 05:26.870
temp table here or as many other times as I need to.

05:27.480 --> 05:35.190
Now that we know why we might want to use temp tables, how do we go about converting a CTE to a temp

05:35.220 --> 05:35.700
table?

05:36.420 --> 05:38.310
Well, fortunately, it's actually pretty simple.

05:38.550 --> 05:44.550
So the first step will be to take our very first virtual table here and just convert that to a temp

05:44.550 --> 05:45.090
table.

05:45.840 --> 05:51.090
Now, there are actually a couple of different ways of creating temp tables, but for now, we're going

05:51.090 --> 05:54.580
to stick with the simplest way, which is called select into.

05:55.030 --> 06:02.130
To use that, we'll simply get rid of our opening and closing parentheses around the select statement

06:02.820 --> 06:12.150
and then after all of the items in the select, but before the from, we'll type in the keyword into

06:12.990 --> 06:16.770
and then the name that we want to assign to our temp table.

06:18.330 --> 06:21.410
But there's one additional thing to remember.

06:21.420 --> 06:28.470
We need to precede the name of that temp table with the pound sign that tells SQL that this is a temp

06:28.500 --> 06:31.050
table and is to be handled as such.

06:31.080 --> 06:36.700
SQL actually has a special place in memory just for temp tables, and that's what causes them to be

06:36.730 --> 06:39.280
handled a little differently than other objects.

06:39.280 --> 06:44.680
For example, explicitly defining something as a temp table by including this pound sign before the

06:44.680 --> 06:50.290
name causes that object to disappear as soon as you close out of your query window, as soon as you

06:50.290 --> 06:51.640
close out your session.

06:52.030 --> 06:52.420
All right.

06:52.420 --> 06:55.720
So converting this to a temp table was literally that simple.

06:55.720 --> 07:00.070
If we just run this, we'll see that.

07:00.070 --> 07:03.250
Now, 31,465 rows were created.

07:03.280 --> 07:10.090
Basically, what was the output of this query has now just been dropped into a temporary table called

07:10.090 --> 07:11.140
pound sales.

07:11.560 --> 07:17.410
And just to prove that to you, let me actually select everything from that table real quick.

07:23.360 --> 07:25.220
And you can see all of our data is there.

07:26.240 --> 07:28.940
So now we'll just continue the pattern with our.

07:29.830 --> 07:31.400
Second virtual table.

07:31.420 --> 07:37.840
So I'll copy this name and then just get rid of the parentheses and the as keyword.

07:39.490 --> 07:43.630
And now I'll type the into keyword after.

07:44.360 --> 07:50.960
All the atoms in our select, but before our from and then the name of our new temp table.

07:50.990 --> 07:56.030
But again, I have to precede that with the pound sign and then I'll try to run this.

07:58.080 --> 07:59.190
But it's erroring out.

07:59.190 --> 08:01.830
It says invalid object name sales.

08:02.050 --> 08:07.560
Ah, that's because I did not include that pound sign before the name of the sales table.
