08:07.710 --> 08:14.790
So if I add that suddenly it looks like all of our red squigglies have gone away, so we should be able

08:14.790 --> 08:16.170
to run this without an error.

08:17.160 --> 08:18.240
And we were.

08:18.270 --> 08:24.170
So now we have another table called pound top ten sales with 38 records.

08:24.180 --> 08:28.290
That is, for all intents and purposes equivalent to the virtual table we had before.

08:28.710 --> 08:35.400
Now, finally, we just need to convert what had been our last query to use the pound top ten sales

08:35.400 --> 08:39.870
temp table instead of the top ten sales virtual table from our CTE.

08:41.640 --> 08:45.720
So let's convert that and run this query again.

08:47.790 --> 08:50.280
And lo and behold, we get the exact same result.

08:51.060 --> 08:55.420
And now we can even solve the problem that started us down this path in the first place.

08:55.440 --> 09:00.480
So if I just put that pound sign in front of our reference to the sales table.

09:01.260 --> 09:04.260
I can actually run both of these select statements.

09:05.430 --> 09:07.560
And now we have the output we were looking for.

09:07.560 --> 09:11.580
We have an aggregated view and a detail view side by side.

09:12.830 --> 09:19.340
And again, that's because since we're using temp tables now, that sales temp table is available to

09:19.340 --> 09:23.900
me anywhere throughout the script, as long as it's below where I defined it.

09:24.650 --> 09:30.590
And as I alluded to earlier, this can really help us with debugging as well because we can now select

09:30.590 --> 09:36.620
against sales or our top ten sales temp tables anytime we want, wherever we want.

09:36.950 --> 09:43.790
If one part of our overall chain of processes is breaking down, we can inspect that individually.

09:44.120 --> 09:49.010
We can query each of these temporary tables individually without having to run all of them at once,

09:49.010 --> 09:55.250
which really, really helps when you've got a process with many steps all chained together and only

09:55.250 --> 09:56.510
one of them is breaking.

09:56.600 --> 10:03.290
Again, with a CTE, everything has to be run as one giant statement, which is fine for smaller queries

10:03.290 --> 10:05.090
and less complex analysis.

10:05.090 --> 10:10.940
But when you start to get into hundreds or even thousands of lines of code and only one link in the

10:10.940 --> 10:16.470
chain is breaking, it's really nice to just be able to inspect that link and not the entire chain.

10:17.120 --> 10:23.480
Now, up next, we're going to take a look at just how temporary temp tables are and why this is something

10:23.480 --> 10:26.210
we need to consider when we're using them in our code.

10:26.360 --> 10:27.320
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.450 --> 00:01.560
Welcome back.

00:01.920 --> 00:06.870
Now, we've seen some advantages of temp tables, but I also want to point out a potential pitfall before

00:06.870 --> 00:13.530
we move on, and that is the flip side to their biggest advantage, and that is that they don't disappear

00:13.530 --> 00:15.430
after they're used in a select statement.

00:15.450 --> 00:16.530
They hang around.

00:16.740 --> 00:23.130
So what would happen if I just tried to say, rerun all of our code here, except instead of saying

00:23.130 --> 00:27.180
where order rank is less than or equal to ten, perhaps I just want to look at the top five.

00:27.600 --> 00:29.400
So let's rerun this code.

00:30.630 --> 00:31.400
Oh no.

00:31.410 --> 00:37.380
Now I've got an error message saying there is already an object named sales in the database.

00:37.860 --> 00:38.100
Huh?

00:39.290 --> 00:46.070
So what's basically happening here is that we are trying to create a table called pound sales, just

00:46.070 --> 00:47.140
like we did before.

00:47.150 --> 00:52.760
But because that pound sales temporary table is still in our database, SQL gets confused.

00:52.760 --> 00:58.430
We're trying to create something with a name that is owned by some other thing that's already there.

00:58.460 --> 01:02.840
There's already a pound sales temp table in our session and we're trying to create another one.

01:03.140 --> 01:13.370
So the answer is to actually explicitly tell SQL to get rid of or drop that sales table so we can recreate

01:13.370 --> 01:14.960
it once more.

01:15.290 --> 01:17.170
Fortunately, doing that's very easy.

01:17.180 --> 01:23.600
So all I have to do is take the name of our table and typically you'll do this at the bottom of your

01:23.600 --> 01:30.620
script and I'll just type drop table pound sales.

01:30.980 --> 01:37.550
So if I run that, it basically deletes that pound sales temp table from our session.

01:37.820 --> 01:45.690
So now if I run this statement that creates the sales temp table, it works.

01:46.290 --> 01:53.130
But then if I try to create the top ten sales temp table, we run into the same issue because we haven't

01:53.130 --> 01:54.960
explicitly dropped that one yet.

01:55.110 --> 02:04.380
So once again, I'll need to throw a drop table statement at the end of our SQL script here, and this

02:04.380 --> 02:06.480
time we'll drop top ten sales.

02:09.220 --> 02:15.400
And now if I rerun the code that generates that table, it runs.

02:15.790 --> 02:19.870
And now we're able to run both of our queries as before.

02:20.350 --> 02:25.360
Now, the best part about including these drop table statements at the end of your code is that as long

02:25.360 --> 02:30.820
as you run all of this code in sequence, your temporary tables will automatically be dropped after

02:30.820 --> 02:36.310
they're needed so that if you want to rerun the code, they won't be sitting out there in your session

02:36.310 --> 02:38.620
getting in the way of you trying to recreate them.

02:39.210 --> 02:39.990
Also.

02:39.990 --> 02:44.970
And this becomes a bigger concern as you deal with larger and larger data sets.

02:45.120 --> 02:51.720
It's just good practice to drop your temporary tables at the end of your code because they do take up

02:51.720 --> 02:54.120
memory in SQL servers.

02:54.150 --> 02:55.800
Temporary data storage.

02:55.800 --> 03:00.450
So if you've got a temporary table with hundreds of millions of records in it, it's just sitting there

03:00.450 --> 03:03.990
hogging up a lot of memory when it may not even be needed.

03:04.290 --> 03:10.560
So as a best practice, I would say after the point in your code where you're definitely done using

03:10.560 --> 03:12.510
a temp table, just drop it.

03:12.540 --> 03:18.030
It saves SQL Server memory and it keeps you from potentially trying to overwrite a table that's already

03:18.030 --> 03:18.480
there.

03:19.490 --> 03:24.200
So in the big picture, when would we use temp tables versus CTS?

03:24.620 --> 03:29.960
I would recommend using temp tables when you need to reference one of your virtual tables in multiple

03:29.960 --> 03:31.850
outputs, as we just saw.

03:32.860 --> 03:38.320
Would also recommend temp tables when you need to join massive data sets in your virtual tables.

03:38.680 --> 03:43.780
So if you have a step one and a step two, both of which have hundreds of millions of records, temp

03:43.810 --> 03:50.980
tables are going to give you some options for optimizing joins between those tables that cte's just

03:50.980 --> 03:51.250
can't.

03:51.250 --> 03:53.200
And we'll get into those a little bit more later.

03:53.590 --> 03:59.320
And lastly, I would say use temp tables when you need a script instead of a query.

03:59.320 --> 04:05.020
And what I mean by a script is a bundle of SQL statements that might be doing many different things.

04:05.020 --> 04:10.920
They might be producing query outputs, they might be manipulating tables in your database in some way.

04:10.930 --> 04:14.860
Basically something more complicated than just returning a single output.

04:15.700 --> 04:17.860
So when would we use CTEs?

04:18.600 --> 04:26.070
Use seats when you just need a single query output and you're querying small to medium sized datasets.

04:26.610 --> 04:29.610
So what do I mean by small to medium sized?

04:30.300 --> 04:34.080
The bottom line is if you can get the job done with a CTE.

04:34.440 --> 04:35.430
Use a CTE.

04:35.790 --> 04:41.730
But if it starts running slow, try rewriting it with temp tables and using some of the optimization

04:41.730 --> 04:43.530
techniques we'll talk about later on.

04:43.740 --> 04:49.050
And that's probably a good principle to apply to SQL in general or even programming in general.

04:49.140 --> 04:55.440
Use the simplest technique you can get away with that does the job and then when that technique is no

04:55.440 --> 05:00.300
longer working or is no longer optimal, maybe graduate to the next more advanced technique.

05:00.990 --> 05:01.380
All right.

05:01.380 --> 05:05.010
So now we've looked at the simplest way to create temp tables.

05:05.100 --> 05:10.560
Up next, we're going to look at a more explicit way of creating temp tables that gives you more control

05:10.560 --> 05:11.760
over how they're defined.

05:11.790 --> 05:12.780
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.140 --> 00:01.160
Welcome back.

00:01.460 --> 00:10.360
So in the last video, we talked about how to convert CCTVs to temporary tables using select into.

00:10.370 --> 00:13.940
And as you saw, that technique is quite simple and convenient.

00:14.060 --> 00:20.450
But now I'm going to do something counterintuitive and show you a somewhat more elaborate way of doing

00:20.450 --> 00:21.410
the same thing.

00:21.710 --> 00:27.590
And at first you're going to think I'm crazy because at face value, the two approaches pretty much

00:27.620 --> 00:28.970
accomplish the same thing.

00:28.970 --> 00:36.140
But whereas select into leaves defining the structure of your table to SQL based on whatever data you're

00:36.140 --> 00:43.850
selecting, the technique I'm about to show you gives you much more fine tuned control over the table

00:43.850 --> 00:46.340
you're creating and the data within it.

00:46.460 --> 00:51.950
Now, the benefits of this additional control won't be obvious at first, and I'm not going to cover

00:51.950 --> 00:54.020
an explicit example in this video.

00:54.020 --> 01:01.440
But later on, we will take a look at an example of how creating your own data structure and then inserting

01:01.440 --> 01:08.430
data into it can have some advantages in more complex scenarios versus simply dumping the output of

01:08.430 --> 01:13.680
a select query into a table and letting SQL define the structure of that table for you.

01:13.680 --> 01:16.350
So let's dive in and see what this looks like in code.

01:17.680 --> 01:23.470
So we'll pick up where we left off in the last video where we had converted our CTE process into a series

01:23.470 --> 01:25.350
of temp tables using Select into.

01:25.360 --> 01:30.910
But now we're going to use that new method I referenced to accomplish the same thing.

01:31.450 --> 01:38.380
So the basis of our new approach is we actually create the temporary table in advance with no data in

01:38.380 --> 01:44.380
it, and then we insert the data from our select query into the temporary table.

01:44.380 --> 01:47.890
So now it's two steps per temp table instead of one.

01:48.010 --> 01:53.980
Again, I know this sounds much more convoluted and difficult than necessary, but you'll see the benefits

01:53.980 --> 01:54.700
later on.

01:55.410 --> 02:01.830
So obviously the first step will be and we'll take our sales temp table here as the first example.

02:02.530 --> 02:09.370
To create a table that has these four fields that we've included in our select query.

02:09.730 --> 02:15.760
Now, just as a quick review, let's take a look at the sales order header table over here in Object

02:15.760 --> 02:16.510
Explorer.

02:17.160 --> 02:21.390
To remind you of how table structures work in SQL.

02:21.630 --> 02:26.410
Now, each of these fields in the sales order header table has a data type.

02:26.430 --> 02:33.240
And when we define our sales temporary table, we too will have to define data types for each field.

02:34.180 --> 02:40.420
Now, since the fields that we're dropping into our sales temp table are coming from the sales order

02:40.420 --> 02:46.480
header table, we should probably reference the data types in those fields in the source table when

02:46.480 --> 02:53.170
we're creating our temporary table and just looking at the fields in our select, we have order date,

02:53.620 --> 02:57.010
which in the sales order header table is a date time data type.

02:57.340 --> 03:05.440
We have order month, which is actually a derived field we're creating that essentially returns a date.

03:05.440 --> 03:07.480
So that would be a date data type.

03:08.290 --> 03:15.580
We have total do, which if we look at that in the sales order header table, it's actually a money

03:15.580 --> 03:16.390
data type.

03:16.390 --> 03:22.360
And then finally we have order rank, which is again a derived field which returns the numerical rank

03:22.360 --> 03:25.390
of a given sales order, and that's just an integer.

03:25.780 --> 03:29.650
So now we have all the data type information we need to proceed.

03:29.680 --> 03:31.750
So let's go ahead and start coding.

03:32.560 --> 03:35.830
How to do that, we'll need the create table statement.

03:36.070 --> 03:43.540
So we'll just type create table and we'll follow that with a pair of parentheses.

03:44.170 --> 03:50.200
And now we just need to list out the fields that are going to be in our table and to save a lot of repetitive

03:50.200 --> 03:57.790
typing, I'm just going to copy our select list here and get rid of any code I'm using to derive fields.

03:58.180 --> 04:00.940
And after the name of each field here.

04:01.540 --> 04:04.390
I'm going to need to specify its data type.

04:05.260 --> 04:11.260
So we remember order date was a date time data type in our SQL table.

04:11.260 --> 04:14.020
So we'll just say date time.

04:16.470 --> 04:21.600
Border month, which we're deriving is a date total.

04:21.630 --> 04:25.200
Du is a money data type.

04:25.230 --> 04:30.240
If I can spell money and order, rank is an int.

04:30.870 --> 04:34.680
Now one thing I've forgotten to do is actually name our table.

04:34.770 --> 04:39.480
We actually have to include the name of the table we're creating after create table.

04:40.160 --> 04:41.960
We're going to call it the same as before.

04:42.770 --> 04:44.120
Pound sales.

04:45.390 --> 04:46.830
So let me run this.

04:48.580 --> 04:48.970
All right.

04:48.970 --> 04:54.580
So we have created a temporary table called sales that shouldn't have any data in it.

04:54.580 --> 04:56.680
But let's just go ahead and see what that looks like.

04:56.680 --> 04:58.540
So I'll just do a quick select star.

05:05.430 --> 05:12.510
And just like you'd expect, we have four columns with no data, no rows because we haven't inserted

05:12.510 --> 05:13.880
anything into this table yet.

05:13.890 --> 05:18.500
It's basically just a blank shell with the data types that we specified.

05:18.510 --> 05:25.530
So now the next step is to actually insert the output of this select statement into our new temp table.

05:25.740 --> 05:31.500
First, we'll need to get rid of this N2 statement because we're no longer selecting the output into

05:31.500 --> 05:32.430
a brand new table.

05:32.430 --> 05:38.970
That's what N2 does into both, creates the table and drops the data into it at the same time.

05:38.970 --> 05:46.590
Because we've already created a table, we'll need a new technique and that is intuitively enough insert.

05:47.190 --> 05:56.190
So all we'll need to do is type insert into and then the name of the table we're inserting into, and

05:56.190 --> 05:58.290
then we'll add a pair of parentheses.

05:58.830 --> 06:03.210
And then within these parentheses we'll specify the fields.

06:03.210 --> 06:08.040
We're inserting data into and the order in which we're inserting those fields.

06:08.050 --> 06:13.090
Now, remember, I said this technique gives you a lot more flexibility than just select into.

06:13.330 --> 06:17.650
So we wouldn't necessarily have to insert into all four columns.

06:17.650 --> 06:23.020
Every time we do an insert, we could actually simply insert data into one of the columns.

06:23.020 --> 06:29.230
And then for all the rows that we inserted into that table, there would be nulls in the other three

06:29.230 --> 06:31.150
columns we didn't insert data into.

06:31.180 --> 06:36.130
And as weird as that might seem, that's something we're actually going to take advantage of in an example

06:36.130 --> 06:37.480
in a later video.

06:37.570 --> 06:42.460
But for now, we're just going to insert into all the columns that are already in that table in the

06:42.460 --> 06:44.860
same order that they exist in that table.

06:45.130 --> 06:49.420
So again, we'll just copy and paste to make life a little bit easier.

06:49.420 --> 06:54.940
We'll copy and paste the names of our fields and we don't need to specify data types in the insert.

06:54.970 --> 06:57.760
We only need to do that when we're defining the table with Create.

06:59.320 --> 07:07.480
So now we're specifying these are the four fields we are inserting to, and this is the order in which

07:07.480 --> 07:11.380
you can expect them to appear in the select statement below.

07:12.280 --> 07:15.010
And that's really all we need to get this to work.

07:15.130 --> 07:17.650
So now if I highlight this and run it.

07:19.570 --> 07:23.140
You'll see that 31,465 rows were affected.

07:23.140 --> 07:28.360
And if you recall, that's the same number of rows that this query returns.

07:28.480 --> 07:32.860
And if we, again, do a select star from our sales table.

07:37.960 --> 07:39.820
There's our output, same as before.

07:40.420 --> 07:47.530
Now, one thing I want to point out before we move on is that our order date values are formatted as

07:47.530 --> 07:55.690
a date time, but we don't seem to have any actual time information after the dates in any of the rows.

07:56.050 --> 08:01.510
So really we just have a date without a time value that's being stored as a date time.

08:01.630 --> 08:08.080
I could even go so far as to say I don't really agree with the data type that was chosen for the table

08:08.080 --> 08:11.170
in our source data in our adventureworks database.

08:11.820 --> 08:16.470
So what if I wanted to actually change that data type in our temp table?

08:16.890 --> 08:18.180
Actually, I can.

08:18.630 --> 08:23.730
All I have to do is change the data type for our order date field from a date time to a date.

08:24.240 --> 08:30.960
Now, in order for me to cement this change, I'm going to need to recreate the sales temporary table.

08:30.960 --> 08:32.640
Which means I need to drop it first.

08:32.640 --> 08:33.960
So I'll just roll down.

08:34.610 --> 08:39.200
To the bottom of our code and drop the sales temp table.

08:39.620 --> 08:44.720
And now let me recreate it and then rerun our insert.

08:47.690 --> 08:49.010
And that looks like it worked.

08:49.010 --> 08:52.820
But we'll run our query against our sales temp table one more time just to confirm.

08:53.420 --> 08:54.640
And there we have it.

08:54.650 --> 09:00.380
It looks like our data is still accurate, but instead of those unnecessary time stamps that all basically

09:00.380 --> 09:06.980
just said midnight after each of the order dates, we now just have a nicely formatted clean date.

09:07.100 --> 09:13.940
So that's one small example of how us having control over how these temp tables are defined can help

09:13.940 --> 09:14.450
us.

09:15.080 --> 09:15.500
All right.

09:15.530 --> 09:23.600
Next, we'll follow the same process to create an insert to a top ten sales temporary table.

09:23.690 --> 09:27.200
So first, let me wipe out this query against our sales temp table.

09:27.950 --> 09:30.980
And then I'm just going to recreate the process that we saw above.

09:31.010 --> 09:38.000
We'll type create table, then we'll copy the name of our current temp table.

09:39.290 --> 09:41.690
Follow that with a pair of parentheses.

09:42.690 --> 09:45.810
And this time we only have two fields to worry about.

09:46.800 --> 09:53.700
Order Month, which we know is a date and top ten total, which looks like it's summing the total due

09:53.730 --> 09:54.000
field.

09:54.000 --> 09:57.150
So it should be a money data type just like total do was.

09:57.840 --> 10:02.430
And obviously I need to separate these with commas and since I didn't mention this before and it could

10:02.430 --> 10:09.270
be a point of confusion, note that you do not include a comma between the name of the field and the

10:09.270 --> 10:10.410
data type you specify.

10:10.410 --> 10:12.210
The comma comes afterwards.

10:13.130 --> 10:17.540
So let's run this create table statement to create our top ten sales table.

10:19.130 --> 10:22.070
And now we can get to work on our insert statement.

10:22.970 --> 10:28.670
So I'll type insert into and then our top ten sales table.

10:29.270 --> 10:34.010
But this time, instead of following the table name with a pair of parentheses and then listing out

10:34.010 --> 10:35.810
the fields we're going to insert into.

10:35.840 --> 10:37.610
I'm going to use a little bit of shorthand.

10:37.640 --> 10:40.730
I'm actually not going to include those parentheses at all.

10:41.090 --> 10:48.260
I'm just going to knock out our into statement here and run our insert and assuming this works, which

10:48.260 --> 10:50.720
I hope it does, I'll explain why after.

10:51.500 --> 10:51.860
All right.

10:51.890 --> 10:53.000
38 rows affected.

10:53.000 --> 10:54.170
It looks like it worked.

10:54.170 --> 10:58.460
But let's run a quick select star against our top ten sales table just to confirm.

11:04.060 --> 11:06.460
And it looks like our outputs just what we expect.

11:06.580 --> 11:13.270
So how was I able to get away with not listing out the field names we're inserting to after my insert

11:13.270 --> 11:16.730
statement like I did up here for our sales table?

11:16.750 --> 11:24.130
Well, if you don't include those parentheses, SQL assumes that the fields in your select are in the

11:24.130 --> 11:27.110
same order as the fields in the table.

11:27.130 --> 11:32.290
So if order month is the first field in our table definition, which it is, and top ten total is the

11:32.290 --> 11:37.510
second field which it is, as long as we include those fields in that order.

11:37.510 --> 11:43.120
In our select statement, we don't even have to spell out to SQL which fields we're inserting to and

11:43.120 --> 11:43.960
in what order.

11:44.170 --> 11:46.660
So this will save you quite a bit of typing.

11:46.690 --> 11:52.300
I personally tend to avoid it just because I like my code to be very explicit and I feel like an approach

11:52.300 --> 11:57.220
such as this can allow insidious little errors to creep into your code.

11:57.880 --> 12:03.470
Imagine if you had another date field after order month and your top ten sales table, and then in your

12:03.470 --> 12:08.480
select you swapped the order of your order month field and this other date field.

12:08.840 --> 12:14.690
The insert would still run successfully because you're still inserting to date values into two date

12:14.690 --> 12:16.940
fields in the top ten sales table.

12:16.970 --> 12:20.430
But they would be the wrong dates going into the wrong fields.

12:20.450 --> 12:25.730
So I tend to spell out my fields after my insert into.

12:25.760 --> 12:30.290
But feel free to use this technique if you want to save on some typing and you're pretty confident you're

12:30.290 --> 12:31.400
not going to make that error.

12:31.760 --> 12:32.120
All right.

12:32.120 --> 12:33.500
So enough preaching for me.

12:33.860 --> 12:35.660
I'll wipe out this select star.

12:35.660 --> 12:42.800
And at this point we can just run our final couple of queries to make sure everything else is doing

12:42.800 --> 12:43.640
what we want.

12:44.900 --> 12:49.490
And if we scroll down to see our second output, it looks like we've got the same output we had last

12:49.490 --> 12:50.030
time.

12:50.600 --> 12:51.110
All right.

12:51.110 --> 12:57.440
I know that was more painful than using select into, but hopefully it wasn't that painful because creating

12:57.470 --> 13:02.700
tables explicitly with create table and then inserting our data to them definitely has some advantages.

13:02.720 --> 13:08.720
We saw a minor one in that we were able to change the data type of a field to one that made more logical

13:08.720 --> 13:09.550
sense.

13:09.560 --> 13:15.710
But an even bigger advantage can come into play when we include fields in our temporary tables that

13:15.710 --> 13:17.690
don't even exist in our source data.

13:17.780 --> 13:21.290
Now we'll look at an example of that in the next video.

13:21.320 --> 13:22.280
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.000 --> 00:00.810
Welcome back.

00:01.080 --> 00:07.680
So in this one, we're going to introduce the Truncate command, which allows us to clear out the data

00:07.680 --> 00:10.800
in tables while keeping their structure intact.

00:11.070 --> 00:14.970
And this comes in especially handy when we want to reuse tables.

00:14.970 --> 00:20.940
So imagine you've created a temp table with a certain structure and inserted data into it, and maybe

00:20.940 --> 00:25.260
at some point down the line you would like to reuse that table with different data.

00:25.380 --> 00:31.890
Well, Truncate allows you to basically clear all the data out of the table while retaining the structure

00:31.890 --> 00:33.030
of the table itself.

00:33.300 --> 00:35.250
In short, it basically empties it.

00:35.250 --> 00:39.970
So now you can insert new data into the table and use that for a different purpose.

00:40.050 --> 00:47.610
So to get a better idea of how this can come in handy in the wild, I'm going to apply truncate to streamlining

00:47.610 --> 00:50.500
a pretty complicated script that we'll put together.

00:50.520 --> 00:51.900
So let's jump right in.

00:52.290 --> 00:57.840
First up, we'll take a look at our example query from the previous video, which will be our jumping

00:57.840 --> 00:59.020
off point for this one.

00:59.040 --> 01:07.020
If you recall in this script, we basically pulled out the top ten orders by month, aggregated them

01:07.020 --> 01:11.730
by month, and then join that data to itself on current month to previous month.

01:11.730 --> 01:13.740
So we have a month over month view.

01:13.830 --> 01:19.260
So what we're going to try to do in this video is actually layer in purchase data.

01:19.530 --> 01:21.120
So what would that look like?

01:21.690 --> 01:28.290
Well, if we go over to this other code example and zoom into the data, you'll see that the output

01:28.290 --> 01:31.110
is quite similar to what we've already produced.

01:31.110 --> 01:38.010
But now instead of one record per month, we have two records per month, one for purchases and one

01:38.010 --> 01:38.910
for sales.

01:39.060 --> 01:45.150
So we can take a couple of approaches to layering the purchase data into our script alongside the sales

01:45.150 --> 01:45.720
data.

01:45.810 --> 01:52.170
Now the first one, which I've already coded up here, is a more repetitive approach that we're ultimately

01:52.170 --> 01:54.090
going to streamline using Truncate.

01:54.090 --> 02:01.080
But I want to briefly review it just so you'll better understand how the ability to reuse temp tables

02:01.080 --> 02:02.970
with Truncate can help us out.

02:03.300 --> 02:08.820
So first up, we create the sales temp table just like we did in our previous example.

02:08.820 --> 02:12.210
But then we also have to create a purchases temp table.

02:12.360 --> 02:17.520
Now the structure of this purchases temp table is basically identical to our sales temp table because

02:17.520 --> 02:21.700
the purchases data is very similar in structure to the sales data.

02:21.880 --> 02:28.710
Then we have to insert sales data from our sales order header table into the sales temp table.

02:28.720 --> 02:34.270
And then we have to do the same thing with our purchases table from the purchase purchase order header

02:34.270 --> 02:34.840
table.

02:35.230 --> 02:42.940
At this point, I'm sure you can already see the repetitiveness sneaking into our code and in SQL or

02:42.940 --> 02:50.590
really any other kind of coding you can undertake when you start seeing very similar code being repeated

02:50.590 --> 02:56.140
throughout your program or throughout your script that's normally assigned, something is has gone wrong

02:56.140 --> 02:59.200
and that there's an opportunity for some optimization.

03:00.070 --> 03:06.700
And then if we scroll further down, you'll see that we have to create the top ten table for sales and

03:06.700 --> 03:12.100
also the top ten table for purchases and then do separate inserts for the sales and the purchases.

03:12.100 --> 03:16.270
And then finally, at the very end of it all, we union together.

03:16.630 --> 03:23.920
Our sort of was is current month, previous month queries for sales and for purchases.

03:23.920 --> 03:28.720
And then finally we have to drop four tables instead of the original two.

03:29.140 --> 03:32.940
Now, this does work, but it's definitely not optimal.

03:32.980 --> 03:35.050
So how can truncate help us here?

03:35.320 --> 03:40.900
Well, let's start from the top and work our way down and see just how much we can streamline this code.

03:41.640 --> 03:46.260
Now, first up, instead of having a sales and a purchases table, we're just going to have an orders

03:46.260 --> 03:46.850
table.

03:46.860 --> 03:52.560
Considering that the structure of the sales and purchases table is identical, the fields are the same,

03:52.560 --> 03:56.940
the data types are the same, and they both involve orders just of a different type.

03:56.970 --> 04:04.290
We're just going to create one orders table and then we're just going to wipe out this purchases table

04:04.290 --> 04:08.040
altogether so our sales table no longer exists.

04:08.040 --> 04:11.580
So we'll change this insert into to insert to the orders table.

04:12.540 --> 04:13.860
If I can spell orders.

04:15.510 --> 04:23.250
And how this is generally going to work is we're going to handle the sales data and the purchase data

04:23.580 --> 04:24.810
one at a time.

04:24.810 --> 04:32.880
So we'll process the sales data in our sort of generic orders table that's going to ultimately handle

04:32.910 --> 04:35.190
both data sets first.

04:35.190 --> 04:40.410
And then once we've processed our sales data, we'll move on to processing our purchase data.

04:40.620 --> 04:43.540
So we've inserted our sales data into orders.

04:43.540 --> 04:49.000
So the next step is to actually insert the sales data into our top ten table.

04:49.000 --> 04:51.490
But right now we have two top ten tables.

04:51.490 --> 04:55.090
We have a top ten sales table and a top ten purchases table.

04:55.240 --> 04:57.190
Again, we're not going to need both.

04:57.190 --> 05:03.520
We're just going to need one top ten table because we're not trying to create duplicate tables when

05:03.520 --> 05:04.780
they're really not needed.

05:04.780 --> 05:12.670
So I'll go ahead and get rid of our top ten purchases table and I'll grab our insert into the top ten

05:12.670 --> 05:18.220
sales table and the create table for top ten sales and cut those out.

05:19.420 --> 05:24.190
And move them up here under our insert into the orders table.

05:26.600 --> 05:34.670
And now, as you might have guessed, I'm going to rename this top ten sales table, just top ten orders.

05:36.110 --> 05:38.330
But the fields and the data types are the same.

05:38.660 --> 05:44.480
And then I'm going to insert into top ten orders.

05:46.520 --> 05:50.450
And we're still getting this error message because we're still trying to select from the sales table,

05:50.600 --> 05:54.260
but we actually just need to select from orders table.

05:54.770 --> 06:02.570
So just to clarify what's going on so far, we are creating a generic orders table that can just as

06:02.570 --> 06:06.830
easily hold our sales data as our purchase data.

06:06.920 --> 06:12.170
And then we're inserting just our sales data into that order table.

06:12.170 --> 06:18.590
And this is the stage in our process where the data is very granular and we actually have the individual

06:18.590 --> 06:20.240
sales orders ranked.

06:20.420 --> 06:27.560
Then we're creating a generic top ten table for just orders which could be either sales or purchase

06:27.560 --> 06:28.250
orders.

06:28.250 --> 06:35.220
And then we're inserting just our sales orders at this point into that top ten orders table.

06:35.240 --> 06:37.520
So how do we know they're just sales orders?

06:37.520 --> 06:43.880
Because the only data we've inserted into this orders table thus far is from the sales order header

06:43.880 --> 06:44.330
table.

06:45.010 --> 06:50.890
But there's one more thing to keep in mind before we actually try to run this series of statements.

06:51.600 --> 06:53.070
In our top ten orders table.

06:53.070 --> 06:58.530
We're going to need some way to distinguish our sales data from our purchase data.

06:58.650 --> 07:04.140
So what we'll actually do is add an order type field to our top ten orders table.

07:06.870 --> 07:10.470
And just to be safe, we'll give it a pretty big text data type.

07:10.500 --> 07:14.010
Do a VarChar 32.

07:15.240 --> 07:25.050
And now when we do our insert into the top ten orders table with sales data, we'll just include a hardcoded

07:25.050 --> 07:33.540
field in our select that sets the value of that order type field to sales.

07:38.740 --> 07:45.190
So now when the output of this aggregated select query is loaded into our top ten table, there will

07:45.190 --> 07:49.000
be a way to distinguish these records as pertaining to sales.

07:49.000 --> 07:55.150
So later on when we insert purchase records, our order type for those records will be purchase.

07:55.150 --> 07:59.950
So now at the very end of our process, we'll have a way to distinguish between these two.

08:00.620 --> 08:06.980
So just to make sure I'm not crazy, I'm going to go ahead and run what just what we have done so far

08:07.220 --> 08:10.730
and select from the temp tables as we go.

08:11.150 --> 08:13.640
So first we created the orders table.

08:15.840 --> 08:23.880
Then we inserted our sales order header data into the orders table and let's just go ahead and select

08:23.880 --> 08:25.470
from the orders table real quick.

08:32.710 --> 08:35.020
And that looks just like what we'd expect.

08:35.850 --> 08:38.620
Now we're going to create our top ten orders table.

08:40.330 --> 08:46.180
And now we're going to insert just from our sales data, because that's all we've loaded into the orders

08:46.180 --> 08:48.730
table, into the top ten orders table.

08:50.260 --> 08:52.000
And now let's select from that.

09:02.350 --> 09:04.480
And that also looks just like what we'd expect.

09:04.480 --> 09:11.560
And you see, we have this order type field which will later on allow us to distinguish these aggregated

09:11.560 --> 09:15.220
records from the purchase data that we'll insert later.

09:15.850 --> 09:17.470
Okay, So far so good.

09:17.800 --> 09:19.570
But what about Truncate?

09:19.870 --> 09:25.990
Well, up next, we're going to take a look at using Truncate to clean up some of the repetitiveness

09:25.990 --> 09:26.920
in this code.

09:26.950 --> 09:27.970
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.530 --> 00:01.700
Welcome back.

00:01.940 --> 00:06.710
Now is where things get interesting and now is where we're going to introduce Truncate.

00:07.040 --> 00:15.230
So the whole point of this exercise was to not create unnecessary redundant temp tables.

00:15.440 --> 00:19.910
So the alternative to that is to reuse a table we already have.

00:20.090 --> 00:24.290
The first example of that is going to be the orders table.

00:24.590 --> 00:32.660
Now, that's where we inserted all of our granular order level sales data and the first step in our

00:32.660 --> 00:39.590
very first insert, what we're going to do is truncate this table, empty it out so we can now insert

00:39.590 --> 00:42.050
our purchase data into the same table.

00:42.050 --> 00:47.030
And from there we'll pretty much repeat the same steps with the purchase data that we did with our sales

00:47.030 --> 00:47.540
data.

00:47.960 --> 00:57.890
So down here below our last insert that we wrote, I'll write truncate table

01:01.190 --> 01:05.780
orders and the statement really is that simple.

01:05.780 --> 01:08.120
This is pretty much the, the syntax and the format.

01:08.120 --> 01:12.050
You just write truncate table followed by the name of the table you're trying to truncate.

01:12.200 --> 01:19.130
And to reiterate what it does is just clear out all of the data from the table without affecting the

01:19.130 --> 01:20.840
actual structure of the table.

01:21.540 --> 01:23.190
So let's run this.

01:25.450 --> 01:28.750
And then run another select against orders to see what happened.

01:34.810 --> 01:38.740
And just like I said before, we have the same columns that we had before.

01:38.770 --> 01:41.610
The data types are the same, but there's no more data.

01:41.620 --> 01:47.740
So now we essentially have a fresh, clean table that we can insert all new data to, and that data

01:47.740 --> 01:49.510
will be our purchase data.

01:51.640 --> 01:58.960
So right below our truncate is where we had previously inserted our purchase order data into the purchases

01:58.960 --> 01:59.840
temp table.

01:59.860 --> 02:05.290
Well, we no longer have a purchase temp table, but we don't need one because now we've got this generic

02:05.290 --> 02:08.520
orders table that can handle sales and purchases.

02:08.530 --> 02:15.820
So let me just insert into that and we'll run this insert and then we'll do one more select against

02:15.820 --> 02:16.780
the orders table.

02:24.270 --> 02:28.500
And now you can see it's repopulated, but now with purchase order data.

02:28.890 --> 02:32.510
And now at this point, we're basically just repeating the steps we followed for sales.

02:32.520 --> 02:37.720
So we've got our insert to the top ten purchases table that we had done formerly.

02:37.740 --> 02:41.460
Well, now it's just top ten orders.

02:42.630 --> 02:48.750
And remember, we have that additional field that we added to the top ten orders table to allow us to

02:48.750 --> 02:51.330
distinguish sales from purchases.

02:51.360 --> 02:54.150
And that was called order type.

02:54.300 --> 02:56.670
So we'll need to include that in our insert.

03:00.640 --> 03:04.660
And then in our select we'll just set order type equal to

03:08.260 --> 03:09.220
purchase.

03:13.450 --> 03:18.970
And then the last piece is to change this reference to the purchases table, which no longer exists

03:18.970 --> 03:20.350
to the orders table.

03:21.340 --> 03:28.000
And now it looks like we should be able to run this now instead of truncating the top ten orders table

03:28.000 --> 03:29.750
like we did the orders table.

03:29.770 --> 03:32.380
We just executed a second insert to it.

03:32.380 --> 03:33.970
So what did that do?

03:34.150 --> 03:35.710
Well, let's go ahead and see.

03:40.380 --> 03:45.060
So the first few records of the table all appear to be sales data.

03:45.060 --> 03:49.500
But if we keep scrolling, suddenly we see all of the purchase records.

03:49.830 --> 03:55.830
So if you insert data to a table that already has data, it just appends that data below the data that's

03:55.830 --> 04:00.000
already there, kind of like a union or a union all if you have used those before.

04:00.550 --> 04:07.660
So now we've got our purchase data just kind of stacked below our sales data and we have a convenient

04:07.690 --> 04:12.390
way to identify the records that pertain to sales versus purchases.

04:12.400 --> 04:15.130
So we should be ready for our final query.

04:15.280 --> 04:17.620
So let's dive right into refactoring that.

04:19.250 --> 04:22.870
So our current final query does the unioning itself.

04:22.880 --> 04:25.960
It basically has two different select statements.

04:25.970 --> 04:32.420
One against what were our purchase specific tables and one against what were our sales specific tables.

04:32.420 --> 04:34.640
And then IT unions those outputs together.

04:34.820 --> 04:39.110
But now we've got all of our data in one place in this top ten orders table.

04:39.260 --> 04:42.770
So we aren't even going to need this union all or a second query.

04:42.800 --> 04:45.470
We're actually just going to be able to get away with one query.

04:45.590 --> 04:47.000
So how does that work?

04:47.420 --> 04:55.070
Well, first, let's just change the reference from top ten sales to top ten orders in both cases,

04:55.070 --> 04:57.620
because we don't have a top ten sales table anymore.

05:02.080 --> 05:07.240
Okay, so SQL is not showing us any red squiggly lines to indicate that we might have some kind of a

05:07.240 --> 05:08.350
syntax error.

05:08.350 --> 05:11.110
But I can tell you this is not going to do what we want.

05:11.260 --> 05:14.740
So right now we're doing what's called a self join.

05:14.740 --> 05:20.860
If you're not familiar, that basically just means you're joining a table to itself, which, as it

05:20.860 --> 05:23.650
turns out, is really no different than any other join.

05:23.680 --> 05:30.730
Behind the scenes SQL basically just makes a copy of the table and joins it to itself as though they

05:30.730 --> 05:32.230
were two separate tables.

05:32.500 --> 05:40.030
And in this case, we're joining copy B to copy A on order month, namely current month to previous

05:40.030 --> 05:40.540
month.

05:40.780 --> 05:46.630
But that's not quite enough because now we have sales records and purchase records all mixed together

05:46.630 --> 05:47.530
in that table.

05:48.210 --> 05:53.760
But what we really want to do is tie like records together across different months.

05:53.790 --> 06:00.930
In other words, we want to compare sales orders month over month and purchase orders month over month.

06:01.200 --> 06:06.390
So all we're actually going to need to do is just add another criteria to our left.

06:06.390 --> 06:16.110
Join where we'll say, and a dot order type equals B dot order type.

06:16.620 --> 06:23.910
So this is going to ensure that we're connecting the same types of orders across current month to previous

06:23.910 --> 06:29.130
month instead of inadvertently tying sales orders to purchase orders and vice versa.

06:31.050 --> 06:38.100
And a related change is to go from hard coding order type up here and here in our select to actually

06:38.100 --> 06:42.450
pulling that directly from our top ten orders table.

06:42.690 --> 06:45.030
So we'll just say a order type.

06:45.360 --> 06:47.650
And at this point, I think we should be ready to run.

06:47.670 --> 06:49.050
So let's do that.

06:49.650 --> 06:55.800
And if we scroll down, we'll see that it appears we're getting the exact output we were looking for

06:55.830 --> 06:59.150
for each month that actually had purchases and sales.

06:59.160 --> 07:05.880
We're getting one aggregated record for purchases and one aggregated record for sales, comparing the

07:05.880 --> 07:10.590
total of the top ten orders for that month versus the previous month.

07:10.740 --> 07:16.610
Now the last little bit of refactoring we can do is to get rid of some of these drop table statements.

07:16.620 --> 07:20.010
So now we're only working with two temp tables and not four.

07:20.340 --> 07:27.210
So we'll first of all, just get rid of two of our drop tables and then we'll just need to change the

07:27.210 --> 07:29.730
names of the temp tables we're dropping.

07:31.210 --> 07:35.230
To top two orders and then top ten orders.

07:35.710 --> 07:37.660
And at this point, we're basically done.

07:38.230 --> 07:46.000
So I hope you see the value here of using Truncate to clear out and reuse temp tables, especially in

07:46.000 --> 07:52.870
cases where you have data coming from different sources that nonetheless is structured quite similarly.

07:52.870 --> 07:57.110
That allows us to take advantage of the same temp tables in our code.

07:57.130 --> 08:00.340
In the real world, this is a lot more common than you might think.

08:00.610 --> 08:05.950
And with the sheer volumes of data you're working with in the real world, you really want to take any

08:05.950 --> 08:09.550
opportunity you can to streamline and optimize your code.

08:10.610 --> 08:11.000
All right.

08:11.000 --> 08:12.440
That is it on Truncate.

08:12.440 --> 08:19.310
So up next, we're going to take a look at the update statement, which actually allows you to modify

08:19.310 --> 08:23.840
a table in place without having to select any data from it at all.

08:24.110 --> 08:25.010
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.260 --> 00:01.370
Welcome back.

00:02.090 --> 00:06.920
Now we're briefly going to delve into another way to manipulate tables in SQL.

00:07.630 --> 00:14.290
This time, instead of adding brand new data to a table, as we did with insert or removing all of a

00:14.290 --> 00:20.260
table's data as we did with Truncate, we're actually going to change the data in an existing table

00:20.260 --> 00:23.440
in place without needing to select from that table.

00:24.550 --> 00:27.220
So what advantages does this approach offer us?

00:28.120 --> 00:33.910
One is a potential opportunity for optimizing queries, which we're going to get into a little bit later.

00:34.460 --> 00:40.610
But in this video, we're going to focus on how modifying the fields of a table in place can allow us

00:40.610 --> 00:47.480
to build layers of logic upon each other without having to resort to multiple selects and subselects

00:47.480 --> 00:49.910
or complex nested logic.

00:50.270 --> 00:53.600
To see what I mean, let's dive right into a code example.

00:54.360 --> 01:00.240
Our starter code here is simply a create table statement that creates a temporary table called sales

01:00.240 --> 01:02.700
orders with a number of different fields.

01:03.450 --> 01:08.610
You may recognize some of these fields from the sales order header table in our Adventureworks database,

01:08.610 --> 01:15.690
but several others which you see down here about the last five of our fields, don't actually exist

01:15.690 --> 01:16.860
in our source data.

01:17.130 --> 01:19.080
So how will these be populated?

01:19.900 --> 01:25.660
Before getting into that, I'm going to populate some of the fields with an insert statement that will

01:25.660 --> 01:31.690
pull all orders from our sales order header table with an order date in 2013.

01:32.460 --> 01:36.810
I've already written that code to keep you from having to watch me type, so let's go ahead and run

01:36.810 --> 01:37.140
it.

01:37.440 --> 01:42.450
So first I'll just run this create table statement to create our sales orders temp table.

01:43.560 --> 01:48.450
And then I'll roll down to my insert statement, which you can see is pretty straightforward.

01:48.450 --> 01:55.380
I'm just pulling fields from our sales order header table where the order date is 2013 and dropping

01:55.380 --> 01:58.890
those into our sales orders temp table.

01:59.460 --> 02:05.670
Now, the one wrinkle you might notice is that I am also inserting a field called order category that

02:05.670 --> 02:08.360
is not being sourced from our sales order header table.

02:08.370 --> 02:12.300
It's just a hard coded value called non-holiday order.

02:12.720 --> 02:16.800
So how useful is a category field with only one category?

02:17.490 --> 02:22.920
Well, it turns out we're actually going to add more categories to this field later using update.

02:23.130 --> 02:25.530
But we've got a little other work to do first.

02:25.800 --> 02:30.990
So let me go ahead and run this insert and then do a quick select star from our table as it currently

02:30.990 --> 02:36.180
stands, just to get a good picture in our heads of what we'll ultimately need to update.

02:36.420 --> 02:40.530
So I'll just highlight this guy, run the insert.

02:41.340 --> 02:45.030
And then I'll run a quick select star against our table.

02:52.820 --> 02:58.370
So as you can see from this output, several of the fields in our table are completely empty.

02:58.550 --> 03:01.400
That is to say, populated with null values.

03:02.150 --> 03:08.360
The empty fields are the ones that we defined in our create table statement but did not insert data

03:08.360 --> 03:08.760
to.

03:08.780 --> 03:10.280
With our insert statement.

03:10.820 --> 03:15.650
Now it's these fields that we're going to populate with a series of update statements.

03:16.790 --> 03:18.610
Just to get the syntax down.

03:18.620 --> 03:25.130
Let's start with the tax freight percent field, which will be a calculation based on the percentage

03:25.130 --> 03:30.170
of the total amount due that the tax amount plus freight represents.

03:31.100 --> 03:36.170
To clarify what this calculation looks like, I'm actually going to write it out in a select query so

03:36.170 --> 03:40.210
we can see what the data output will look like before I plug it into an update.

03:40.220 --> 03:42.740
So let me write this query really quick.

03:43.040 --> 03:56.930
I'll say select tax freight percent equals and the formula is basically going to be our tax amount plus

03:56.930 --> 03:59.030
freight amount divided by total due.

03:59.330 --> 04:07.940
So I'll just copy our tax amount, drop that in and then I'll add in our freight amount.

04:10.280 --> 04:14.180
And then I'll divide that by total due.

04:17.750 --> 04:20.960
And then let's run that to see what the output looks like.

04:21.290 --> 04:26.210
And as you can see, we just get a decimal that represents the percentage of the total due.

04:26.840 --> 04:29.960
Comprised by the freight plus the tax amount.

04:30.650 --> 04:36.920
Okay, now that we've got our logic button down, let's actually populate our tax rate percent field

04:36.920 --> 04:40.460
in our table with update using this logic.

04:41.280 --> 04:43.980
So the syntax for update is straightforward.

04:44.490 --> 04:51.990
First the keyword update followed by the name of the table we're updating, which is just our sales

04:51.990 --> 05:00.920
order table, followed by the set keyword and then the name of the field or fields we're updating,

05:00.930 --> 05:03.960
followed by the values we are updating them to.

05:04.170 --> 05:10.470
Now, in this case, that's the tax rate percent field that we're updating and we're updating it to

05:10.470 --> 05:13.440
just this calculation that we saw from our previous select query.

05:13.440 --> 05:19.050
So I can actually just copy all of this code and drop it right after our set keyword.

05:19.890 --> 05:26.220
Now, keep in mind in this example, we're just updating a single field, but it's perfectly acceptable

05:26.220 --> 05:30.030
to update more than one field at a time, as we'll see in a moment.

05:30.240 --> 05:33.780
So this update is actually a complete update statement.

05:33.780 --> 05:38.430
So let's run it and then do another select from our sales order table to see what happened.

05:38.640 --> 05:40.680
So we'll just highlight this to run.

05:41.760 --> 05:49.270
It ran successfully and now we'll just do a quick select star again from our sales orders table.

05:55.790 --> 05:56.150
All right.

05:56.150 --> 06:02.450
We've still got some null fields, but our tax rate percent field is now populated with those same values

06:02.450 --> 06:08.090
that we saw when we used our logic in a select query against the sales orders temp table.

06:08.210 --> 06:14.720
And if we scroll all the way down through our temp table, it looks like every row in our tax freight

06:14.720 --> 06:19.550
percent field was populated based on the calculation we applied in our update statement.

06:19.790 --> 06:21.320
And that's how update works.

06:21.320 --> 06:28.460
By default, it operates over every single row in whatever table you specify after the update keyword,

06:28.490 --> 06:32.360
updating whatever fields you specify after the set keyword.

06:33.140 --> 06:37.970
But as I mentioned previously, we're not limited to updating one field at a time.

06:38.270 --> 06:44.780
We can actually update as many fields as we want as long as all of the data that our logic depends on

06:44.810 --> 06:45.770
is available.

06:46.850 --> 06:53.420
So let's tack on another update this time to the order amount bucket field in this very same update

06:53.420 --> 06:54.110
statement.

06:55.000 --> 07:01.480
Our logic for the update is going to rely on our old friend the case statement to bucket total due amounts

07:01.480 --> 07:04.600
into small, medium and large buckets.

07:05.250 --> 07:11.490
Adding this logic to our update statement is as simple as just placing a comma after our tax rate percent

07:11.490 --> 07:16.980
field definition and then adding a similar definition for our order amount Bucket field.

07:17.850 --> 07:21.240
All right, So we're updating our order amount bucket field.

07:21.630 --> 07:29.760
So first I'll just type out the name of our field and then we're going to set that equal to a case statement.

07:31.620 --> 07:40.590
And we'll say case when total due is less than 100.

07:40.860 --> 07:45.540
We'll say that's a small order.

07:47.970 --> 08:01.140
And then when total due is less than 1000, but greater than or equal to 100, we'll say it's a medium

08:01.140 --> 08:01.800
order.

08:02.340 --> 08:04.920
And then otherwise, oops.

08:04.950 --> 08:08.370
If I can spell else, we'll just say it's a large order.

08:11.040 --> 08:13.110
Nothing terribly groundbreaking here.

08:13.410 --> 08:18.880
So now let's run this and take another look at our sales order temp table to see what the effect was.

08:19.150 --> 08:21.190
So we'll just run this update.

08:21.610 --> 08:26.140
And again, we'll run a quick select star against our sales orders temp table.

08:26.710 --> 08:32.170
And now we'll see that our order amount bucket field was populated and we see some larges, some medium,

08:32.170 --> 08:33.140
some smalls.

08:33.160 --> 08:35.980
So it looks like our logic is working correctly.

08:36.100 --> 08:42.340
So with one update statement, our tax rate percent field and our order amount bucket fields have been

08:42.340 --> 08:44.560
populated for every row of our table.

08:44.590 --> 08:45.610
Pretty cool.

08:46.220 --> 08:53.630
So up next, we're going to take a look at updating our two remaining null fields based on values in

08:53.630 --> 08:55.580
the fields we just updated.

08:55.760 --> 08:56.810
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.480 --> 00:01.590
Welcome back.

00:02.150 --> 00:04.070
Now comes the interesting part.

00:04.460 --> 00:11.300
What if we need to update one field based on the value in another field that we also populated with

00:11.300 --> 00:12.080
an update?

00:12.900 --> 00:17.100
In this case, the order in which we apply our updates is very important.

00:17.490 --> 00:22.890
While it's technically possible to update a field that is full of null values, as you might imagine,

00:22.890 --> 00:24.960
there's not a lot of benefit to doing so.

00:25.790 --> 00:33.020
So if we want to update, for example, our tax rate bucket field based on the output of our tax rate

00:33.020 --> 00:37.640
percent field, we would need to update our tax rate percent field first.

00:38.380 --> 00:40.180
Fortunately, we've already done that.

00:40.300 --> 00:46.630
So now we can write another update statement against our tax rate bucket field that will reference the

00:46.630 --> 00:50.800
values that we just populated in our tax rate percent field.

00:51.040 --> 00:52.930
So let's see what that would look like.

00:53.200 --> 00:55.780
So now we're going to write another update statement.

00:57.610 --> 01:04.060
And again, we're obviously updating our sales orders, temp table, and then we'll type out the set

01:04.090 --> 01:04.870
keyword.

01:05.260 --> 01:10.960
And this time we're just updating a single field, and that is our tax rate bucket field.

01:11.380 --> 01:13.990
And we're going to set that equal to another case statement.

01:15.850 --> 01:23.320
But in this case, our case statement is going to reference the output of that tax rate percent field

01:23.320 --> 01:26.050
that we populated with the previous update.

01:26.350 --> 01:35.170
So we'll just copy and paste that field name and say when the value of that field is less than 0.1,

01:35.380 --> 01:39.050
we'll say that the tax rate bucket is small.

01:42.140 --> 01:49.730
And then when it's less than 0.2, we'll say it's medium.

01:55.030 --> 01:57.670
And then otherwise we'll just say it's large.

02:03.850 --> 02:07.090
So this pretty much works like our previous update statements.

02:07.120 --> 02:14.140
The only difference is we're now referencing a field that was originally null based on our first insert

02:14.170 --> 02:15.490
to our temp table.

02:15.520 --> 02:18.040
So again, we'll run the update.

02:19.190 --> 02:21.740
And we'll run another select against our temp table.

02:22.100 --> 02:24.560
And now we've got yet another field populated.

02:24.590 --> 02:27.890
If you look at our tax freight bucket, we'll see.

02:27.890 --> 02:30.110
It's now populated for all the rows in our data.

02:30.110 --> 02:32.420
We've got some smalls, we've got some mediums.

02:32.630 --> 02:34.340
I think there are some larges mixed in there.

02:34.340 --> 02:35.960
If I would scroll slowly enough.

02:36.200 --> 02:40.070
So now we're down to just one field in our table that is not populated.

02:40.640 --> 02:46.850
So I hope at this point you can see how update statements can be extremely useful in cases where you

02:46.850 --> 02:52.100
need to build derived fields and logic based on other derived fields in logic.

02:52.130 --> 02:54.200
Potentially several layers down.

02:55.070 --> 03:00.770
While it is certainly possible to do this with a series of subqueries or temp tables in which every

03:00.770 --> 03:03.680
step builds a new layer of logic on the previous one.

03:03.860 --> 03:10.700
In that scenario, you're now selecting the entire contents of a table just to update a few fields using

03:10.700 --> 03:11.030
update.

03:11.030 --> 03:16.310
On the other hand, we are only updating the data we want to update without touching anything else.

03:17.140 --> 03:22.360
So whenever you encounter a situation which requires you to build several layers of derived logic in

03:22.360 --> 03:29.110
your data analysis in which each layer references the previous layer, consider using a series of updates

03:29.110 --> 03:31.390
in the fashion that we've discussed in this video.

03:32.600 --> 03:33.140
All right.

03:33.140 --> 03:38.990
Before we go on, I'd like to dive into just one more example that explores how we can apply criteria

03:38.990 --> 03:42.860
to our update statements to limit the records we're applying them to.

03:43.910 --> 03:50.780
Now, if you'll recall, we previously inserted a hard coded value of non-holiday to our order category

03:50.780 --> 03:55.040
field, which didn't seem like a terribly practical use of a category field.

03:55.280 --> 04:01.640
If you look at our order category field here and we scroll all the way down, every single value is

04:01.640 --> 04:03.340
non-holiday order.

04:03.350 --> 04:08.750
And then if I scroll up to my insert statement here, you'll see that I just inserted that hard coded

04:08.750 --> 04:14.090
value non-holiday order to that field, which is why we're seeing what we're seeing in the table.

04:14.600 --> 04:20.420
Well, it turns out that there actually are some records in our table that qualify as holiday orders.

04:20.420 --> 04:28.160
And what we'll now do is target just those records with an update statement to update their order category

04:28.160 --> 04:29.030
to holiday.

04:29.730 --> 04:35.640
Now, thus far, all the updates we've seen have affected every single record in our sales order temp

04:35.670 --> 04:36.240
table.

04:36.730 --> 04:42.970
But by adding a where clause to our update, we can target individual records in much the same way as

04:42.970 --> 04:44.680
we would with a select query.

04:45.070 --> 04:46.690
So let's see what that looks like.

04:47.540 --> 04:47.840
All right.

04:47.840 --> 04:50.870
So I'll go back down to where we've been writing our updates.

04:51.200 --> 04:57.560
And now I'm going to again update our sales orders table.

04:58.760 --> 05:04.370
And I'm going to apply the update to our order category field.

05:06.350 --> 05:08.990
And I'm going to set it equal to

05:12.020 --> 05:12.900
holiday.

05:13.700 --> 05:20.330
But the thing is, we don't want to update all the records to holiday because some are legitimately

05:20.330 --> 05:21.470
non holiday.

05:21.800 --> 05:27.200
Instead, we want to target those records which qualify as holiday records per some logic, we're about

05:27.200 --> 05:31.550
to define and update only those records with the value holiday.

05:32.530 --> 05:38.890
To do that, we'll add a where clause right below our set statement, and then we're going to apply

05:38.890 --> 05:51.220
the criteria where date part and then we'll use the date part of quarter of our order date.

05:52.330 --> 05:53.770
If I can spell order date

05:56.080 --> 05:57.700
equals four.

05:57.820 --> 06:04.330
So what this date part function is doing, if you're not familiar with it, is saying if we look at

06:04.330 --> 06:12.340
the quarter of the year corresponding to a given order date is that quarter four.

06:12.370 --> 06:19.420
If the quarter of that particular date is four, that means it's the fourth quarter of the year, meaning

06:19.450 --> 06:25.750
October, November and or December, which in many places is considered the holidays, quote, unquote.

06:25.870 --> 06:29.380
So let's go ahead and run this to see how it changed our temp table.

06:32.800 --> 06:37.390
Now take note that while all of our other update statements have been updating all of the records in

06:37.390 --> 06:44.410
the temp table, which is about 14,000, this guy only updated around 6000, and that is the targeting

06:44.410 --> 06:46.630
action of this where clause at work.

06:46.870 --> 06:51.100
And if we select from our sales orders table again.

06:51.800 --> 06:57.590
So if we roll down to the records of our sales order temp table, we'll see that we now have some holiday

06:57.590 --> 07:00.020
values mixed into our order category field.

07:00.020 --> 07:03.530
So it looks like our targeted update worked just like we intended.

07:03.650 --> 07:04.400
Awesome.

07:05.500 --> 07:12.010
So I'm hopeful that this video helped to illustrate the value of creating predefined temp table structures

07:12.010 --> 07:17.620
versus simply selecting data into a temp table via select into, as we saw before.

07:18.560 --> 07:24.500
The additional fields that we defined in our Create Table statement were later able to be updated in

07:24.500 --> 07:28.460
a series of short readable steps via update statements.

07:28.640 --> 07:35.000
And these update statements were able to build on each other sequentially again in a linear, easy to

07:35.000 --> 07:36.020
follow fashion.

07:36.790 --> 07:42.370
As is always the case with SQL, there are multiple perfectly valid ways of solving this problem.

07:42.370 --> 07:48.460
But in situations where you need to build layers of derived logic upon each other, using update statements

07:48.460 --> 07:51.490
in conjunction with temp tables is a very strong option.

07:52.240 --> 07:55.420
And this isn't the only value that update brings us.

07:56.040 --> 08:01.740
As you'll see later on, it can also play a key role in optimizing our queries, especially when they

08:01.740 --> 08:04.770
involve joining extremely large data sets together.

08:05.490 --> 08:07.560
But we'll get to that just a bit later.

08:08.010 --> 08:13.350
Up next, we'll briefly discuss the delete statement and how we can use it to purge targeted records

08:13.350 --> 08:14.190
from our data.

08:14.280 --> 08:15.390
I'll see you then.

Welcome back.

00:02.020 --> 00:09.160
This time we're going to discuss the Delete command in SQL, which allows us to selectively remove rows

00:09.160 --> 00:10.030
from our data.

00:10.330 --> 00:16.420
Now, contrast this with Truncate, which we saw earlier, which clears out all the rows from a table

00:16.420 --> 00:17.620
in one fell swoop.

00:17.650 --> 00:22.150
Delete allows us to do this more surgically by applying criteria.

00:23.040 --> 00:28.980
Now it's important to note that delete just isn't as useful for data analysts, at least in my opinion,

00:28.980 --> 00:31.410
as many of the other techniques we've discussed.

00:31.410 --> 00:34.560
And it can be a little dangerous as we'll see later.

00:34.560 --> 00:37.260
But it's something that you will encounter in the real world.

00:37.260 --> 00:38.970
So I wanted to at least touch on it.

00:39.560 --> 00:41.480
Let's dive right into a code example.

00:42.630 --> 00:49.170
Here we see what should be a pretty familiar example by now where we're pulling the top ten sales orders

00:49.170 --> 00:51.990
by month from our sales order header table.

00:52.350 --> 00:58.200
So we're currently establishing a ranking field in our select query that inserts into the sales temp

00:58.230 --> 00:58.860
table.

00:59.160 --> 01:05.730
And then in our final query, we're selecting from the sales temp table where the value in that ranking

01:05.730 --> 01:07.510
field is less than or equal to ten.

01:07.530 --> 01:10.470
That's what gets us to the top ten by month.

01:11.060 --> 01:17.750
So an alternative to this approach would actually be to simply clip out all the records from our sales

01:17.750 --> 01:24.800
temp table that have an order rank greater than ten and then just select everything from the sales table.

01:24.830 --> 01:26.900
Now we can accomplish this with delete.

01:26.900 --> 01:29.510
So let's take a look at how that would work.

01:30.560 --> 01:38.390
So below our temp table definition and insert, we'll just type the delete keyword.

01:39.150 --> 01:44.250
And then from and then just the name of our table.

01:45.360 --> 01:47.040
Now, this next part is key.

01:47.070 --> 01:53.190
You definitely want to add a where clause below delete unless you want to clear out all records, as

01:53.190 --> 01:54.120
we'll see in a minute.

01:54.920 --> 02:01.370
So the criteria we're going to apply is basically the inverse of what we're doing in our select query

02:01.400 --> 02:02.270
down here.

02:02.510 --> 02:06.890
Instead of saying Select everything, we're order rank is less than ten.

02:06.890 --> 02:11.380
We're saying delete everything where order rank is greater than ten.

02:11.390 --> 02:17.180
So we'll just say where order rank is greater than ten.

02:17.630 --> 02:23.480
So now let's first run our create table and insert statements.

02:25.160 --> 02:30.140
And then I'll run my select statement down here just so you can see how that works.

02:30.740 --> 02:35.300
And as you see, it's accurately pulling in our top ten orders per month.

02:35.630 --> 02:38.240
But now I'll run this delete statement.

02:39.860 --> 02:45.500
And now if I just run my select query again without the criteria.

02:47.280 --> 02:49.860
It looks like I'm still getting my top ten records.

02:49.950 --> 02:55.980
That's because Delete went into my sales temporary table and just got rid of every record where order

02:55.980 --> 02:57.310
rank was greater than ten.

02:57.330 --> 03:01.940
So now we don't even need our criteria in our select query anymore.

03:01.950 --> 03:06.810
We can just do a simple select star from sales and we get the same output.

03:07.080 --> 03:10.650
But now I want to point out how delete can be very dangerous.

03:11.230 --> 03:17.380
So throughout these videos, you've seen me do a lot of highlighting individual pieces of code to just

03:17.380 --> 03:21.190
run them without running everything else in the editor window.

03:21.400 --> 03:26.860
Well, sometimes you'll mistakenly highlight one line, but not two that you want to run and then run

03:26.860 --> 03:27.340
that.

03:27.900 --> 03:33.060
What would happen if I just highlighted delete from sales without highlighting that second line with

03:33.060 --> 03:33.990
their criteria?

03:35.050 --> 03:38.860
Well, now let's see what happens when I select Star from sales.

03:40.180 --> 03:40.960
Ouch.

03:40.990 --> 03:42.340
Everything's gone.

03:42.700 --> 03:47.520
So if you're only playing around with temp tables, this isn't the end of the world.

03:47.530 --> 03:54.970
But if you have access to actually manipulate real permanent tables in your database, delete can be

03:54.970 --> 03:56.200
very, very dangerous.

03:56.200 --> 04:03.130
So the best advice I can offer you here is proceed with caution when using delete and honestly, while

04:03.130 --> 04:09.880
delete can have a place in your toolbox, in my opinion, it just isn't an obviously superior technique

04:09.880 --> 04:14.110
for doing any one type of analytical task than anything else.

04:14.750 --> 04:21.370
If you're actually managing a database as a DBA, it can be an essential tool for table maintenance.

04:21.380 --> 04:26.930
But as a data analyst, it's really more something to just be aware of as opposed to something that

04:26.930 --> 04:28.130
you'll really use a lot.

04:29.180 --> 04:29.870
All right.

04:29.900 --> 04:37.580
Up next, we're going to go back to update and this time look at how it can be used to optimize queries

04:37.640 --> 04:44.960
against huge tables and in particular, joining those massive tables, as we will so often have to do

04:44.960 --> 04:45.980
in the real world.

04:46.010 --> 04:46.970
I'll see you then.
