00:00.310 --> 00:01.450
Welcome back.

00:02.180 --> 00:08.840
In this one, we're going to talk about how to optimize our queries, in particular using update statements.

00:09.140 --> 00:14.180
So that begs the question, what really slows down queries the most?

00:14.790 --> 00:22.140
While it is not always just one thing, the number one factor is usually joins between large tables.

00:22.560 --> 00:27.750
And by large I typically mean millions or even hundreds of millions of records.

00:28.860 --> 00:33.270
Joins between tables of this size are very expensive to use.

00:33.270 --> 00:37.380
Database speak and anything we can do to limit them will be beneficial.

00:37.990 --> 00:41.800
So what are some approaches we can take to make our joins less costly?

00:42.010 --> 00:49.850
Well, first, we can define a filtered data set as early as we can in our data transformation processes.

00:49.870 --> 00:55.090
That way we can join additional tables to a smaller core population.

00:55.090 --> 01:00.070
So if you know you have some kind of limiting criteria that limits the scope of the data that you care

01:00.070 --> 01:06.340
about, establish a temp table with just those records as early in your process as you can.

01:06.340 --> 01:10.840
And that way when you're joining in one of those mega tables with hundreds of millions of records,

01:10.840 --> 01:13.270
you're at least joining it to a small data set.

01:13.930 --> 01:20.740
Another rule of thumb is to avoid having a lot of joins in a single select query, especially when those

01:20.740 --> 01:23.350
joins are bringing in large tables.

01:23.380 --> 01:29.290
Later on in this video, we're going to look at an alternative approach that allows you to bring in

01:29.290 --> 01:35.020
fields from many different tables without having all of these joins in a single select query, and that

01:35.020 --> 01:41.590
will be to use update statements to populate fields in a temp table one source table at a time.

01:42.260 --> 01:48.050
So these update statements will actually update our target table based on values in another table.

01:48.350 --> 01:53.150
This is a technique we haven't seen before, but we'll walk through it in detail in this video.

01:53.420 --> 02:00.440
Now, you might be wondering why is updating a table based on values in another table faster than simply

02:00.440 --> 02:02.540
joining the two tables together directly?

02:03.200 --> 02:09.290
The simple answer is that the update statement will just grab the first matching value it finds from

02:09.290 --> 02:13.970
the secondary table and then populate the corresponding record in our target table.

02:14.300 --> 02:20.240
By contrast, direct joins between tables can require the secondary table to be fully scanned by the

02:20.240 --> 02:26.060
database even after a match has been found, because the possibility of additional matches theoretically

02:26.060 --> 02:26.930
exists.

02:27.140 --> 02:30.770
This can make such joins require more time and processing power.

02:31.550 --> 02:38.540
Now, I will again caution that query optimization is not necessarily an exact science and no one technique

02:38.540 --> 02:39.800
works every time.

02:40.130 --> 02:44.420
But the approaches we will walk through in this video will help more often than not.

02:44.870 --> 02:49.460
Now, one other optimization technique that we won't touch on in this video, but we will review in

02:49.460 --> 02:58.250
a later one, is indexes, which are basically just a construct in SQL that makes looking up data in

02:58.250 --> 03:04.910
a table faster by applying indexes to fields in our temp tables that will later be used in joins, we

03:04.910 --> 03:08.780
can often speed those joins up, but again, that's for a later video.

03:09.050 --> 03:15.440
For now, let's just begin our little journey towards using update statements as an alternative to joins.

03:16.110 --> 03:19.650
Now here we have our starter code, which looks simple enough.

03:20.160 --> 03:28.790
We join our sales order detail table here to our sales order header table and then join in the product

03:28.800 --> 03:36.180
product subcategory and product category fields on their respective primary and foreign keys to pull

03:36.180 --> 03:40.380
in product name, product subcategory and product category.

03:40.970 --> 03:44.510
Further, we filter the output based on an order date.

03:44.750 --> 03:46.010
In 2012.

03:47.070 --> 03:51.690
Now, you may be thinking that there's nothing wrong with this query and you would be generally right.

03:52.280 --> 03:57.740
And with tables as comparatively small as those in our Adventureworks sample database.

03:57.770 --> 04:02.030
A query written like this is totally fine and won't really cause any problems.

04:02.860 --> 04:09.310
However, if we were trying to join together, say, five massive tables with hundreds of millions of

04:09.310 --> 04:14.140
records, each having so many joins in, a single query might start to be an issue.

04:14.560 --> 04:19.930
So for the rest of this lecture, I'm going to ask you to play along with me and pretend like our little

04:19.930 --> 04:25.750
Adventureworks database is actually an enormous enterprise data warehouse and that every little bit

04:25.750 --> 04:28.630
of performance we can squeeze out of our query matters.

04:28.870 --> 04:32.200
So to that end, how can we optimize this code?

04:32.530 --> 04:39.760
Well, the best first step is often to leverage whatever criteria we intend to apply in our overall

04:39.760 --> 04:46.120
query to create a kind of base population of records that will allow us to join the other tables that

04:46.120 --> 04:48.430
we need to a smaller data set.

04:48.730 --> 04:54.140
Now, in our case, the limiting condition is order dates in the year 2012.

04:54.160 --> 04:59.680
So let's go ahead and create a temp table that we will populate with just those records as opposed to

04:59.680 --> 05:01.060
all sales orders.

05:01.270 --> 05:05.240
To save you the pain of watching me type, as you can see, I've written this out already.

05:05.510 --> 05:07.100
So let's just run it.

05:10.120 --> 05:13.300
And you'll see that 3900 records were affected.

05:13.300 --> 05:19.930
And if you compare that to the count of records in the sales order header table table overall.

05:28.490 --> 05:34.220
You'll see we've reduced the scope of our population by a factor of roughly ten.

05:34.550 --> 05:39.620
Now, when you start joining in tables down the line, this can have a pretty big performance impact.

05:39.950 --> 05:46.100
Next, we will create our master temp table that's going to house all of the fields we will need in

05:46.100 --> 05:47.300
our final output.

05:48.020 --> 05:51.500
Now, I've already written this one as well, so let's just take a quick look.

05:52.140 --> 05:58.350
As you can see, the our table basically has fields that line up with the output of our original query

05:58.350 --> 05:59.970
that we're trying to optimize.

06:00.090 --> 06:02.070
So after we run this.

06:03.890 --> 06:05.860
Our table is still going to be empty.

06:05.870 --> 06:11.330
So our next step is to populate it with the records that we're interested in via an insert statement.

06:11.540 --> 06:13.730
So let's roll down and take a look at that.

06:13.760 --> 06:21.350
Now our insert statement here leverages our sales 2012 temp table that we just created to limit the

06:21.350 --> 06:27.410
cost of our join to the sales order detail table, which is a pretty big table, at least by the standards

06:27.410 --> 06:28.790
of our sample database.

06:29.330 --> 06:35.690
The select query we are using to drive this insert is less expensive, so to speak, than if we had

06:35.690 --> 06:39.890
joined the entire sales order header table to the entire sales order detail table.

06:40.550 --> 06:45.530
So now let's run the insert and take a quick peek at our brand new products.

06:45.530 --> 06:47.570
Sold 2012 Temp table.

06:49.920 --> 06:52.590
And then just take a quick look at the data.

06:53.220 --> 06:58.400
Now, as you can see, we've inserted data to four of the nine fields in our table.

06:58.410 --> 07:02.880
So the others will be populated via update statements that we're going to write shortly.

07:03.510 --> 07:10.170
Also note that our table has more records than our original base population in the sales 2012 temp table.

07:10.840 --> 07:15.760
That's because sales orders have a one to many relationship with sales order details.

07:15.760 --> 07:20.590
So when we joined in the sales order detail table, we ended up with more total records.

07:21.160 --> 07:22.000
All right.

07:22.030 --> 07:29.350
Up next, we're going to look at populating our remaining null fields with values from other tables

07:29.350 --> 07:33.820
besides the one we're updating a little bit of a new technique, but I'll walk you through it step by

07:33.820 --> 07:34.450
step.

07:34.460 --> 07:35.320
I'll see you then.

Welcome back.

00:01.710 --> 00:03.900
Now is where we get into the new stuff.

00:04.260 --> 00:10.260
Next, we're going to try and update the product name and our products sold 2012 table.

00:10.470 --> 00:12.960
The new table we just created and inserted to.

00:13.500 --> 00:17.790
Based on the product name and the production product table.

00:18.210 --> 00:24.150
Now, thus far, our updates have always been based on values in the same table that we are applying

00:24.150 --> 00:25.230
the update to.

00:25.380 --> 00:31.200
So how does it work when we need to update Table A based on values in table B?

00:31.530 --> 00:33.600
Well, let's take a look at the syntax.

00:33.780 --> 00:38.520
First, we'll write a little skeleton of an update statement that will look like the updates we've done

00:38.520 --> 00:39.000
thus far.

00:39.000 --> 00:44.040
So we'll just say update our product sold 2012 table.

00:44.520 --> 00:53.010
And then we want to set the product name equal to something.

00:53.130 --> 00:58.560
So again, this something we're going to set it to is actually going to be value from a different table.

00:59.260 --> 01:04.330
So what we'll need to do next is add a from clause to our update.

01:05.860 --> 01:12.430
Now, the first table in the from will just be our products sold 2012 temp table and we'll alias that

01:12.430 --> 01:13.090
as a.

01:14.080 --> 01:19.990
But next we're actually going to need to connect this table to our production dot products table so

01:19.990 --> 01:23.480
we can grab that value from production dot products.

01:23.500 --> 01:27.880
And if when you heard Connect, you thought join you would be correct.

01:28.060 --> 01:34.660
So what we just need to do is say join and then I'll go grab our production dot product table from our

01:34.660 --> 01:35.650
other query.

01:38.590 --> 01:42.850
We'll alias that as B and we'll just join them on.

01:45.490 --> 01:55.660
A product ID equals B dot product ID and now we just need to actually set the value of our product name

01:55.660 --> 02:00.670
in our temp table to the name field and the production dot product table.

02:00.670 --> 02:07.030
So we'll just say product name equals B dot name.

02:07.360 --> 02:14.710
And then one last piece of kind of syntactic sugar I can layer on top of this is instead of saying update

02:14.710 --> 02:21.970
product sold 2012, I can actually just shorten that to a since we've already aliased our product sold

02:21.970 --> 02:25.330
2012 temp table as a down here in the from clause.

02:25.330 --> 02:28.000
So let's run this and see what happens.

02:29.350 --> 02:32.560
It looks like it affected all the rows in our temp table.

02:32.800 --> 02:38.080
So let's take a peek inside and see what happened.

02:38.080 --> 02:38.560
All right.

02:38.560 --> 02:46.390
So now it looks like we have values for all of our records in our product sold table in the product

02:46.420 --> 02:47.110
name field.

02:47.110 --> 02:51.220
So it looks like our update from a secondary table worked just fine.

02:51.950 --> 02:57.770
So the next one of our fields I'll need to update is this product subcategory ID right here.

02:57.800 --> 03:04.280
Now, if we go back to our original example query that we're trying to rewrite, you may note that I

03:04.280 --> 03:11.750
wasn't pulling in product subcategory ID, and in fact, this is not a field that we technically need

03:11.750 --> 03:13.220
in our final output.

03:13.520 --> 03:21.680
However, since we are going to be joining in our product subcategory table, whose primary key is subcategory

03:21.680 --> 03:28.400
ID, we're going to need that field to be updated in this table so we can join this table out to the

03:28.400 --> 03:29.600
subcategory field.

03:30.180 --> 03:35.580
So when you're populating fields in a temp table with updates like this, this is a consideration you'll

03:35.580 --> 03:36.810
have to keep in mind.

03:36.840 --> 03:44.610
What fields do I have to have in my temp table so that I can join my temp table out to some other table

03:44.640 --> 03:46.450
to grab that secondary value.

03:46.500 --> 03:50.850
So product subcategory ID is also in production product.

03:50.850 --> 03:54.660
So we can actually just add this to our update statement here.

03:54.930 --> 04:01.740
So we'll say product subcategory ID equals B dot.

04:04.030 --> 04:05.350
Product subcategory ID.

04:05.890 --> 04:13.060
Now, unlike an insert where if you run it twice, you end up with every record in the original insert

04:13.060 --> 04:17.650
being duplicated with an update, you can really run it as many times as you want.

04:17.680 --> 04:18.790
No harm done.

04:19.000 --> 04:20.680
So I can run this again.

04:23.130 --> 04:28.290
And then if we select from the table, we'll see that nothing bad happened to the data in our product

04:28.320 --> 04:29.280
name field.

04:29.310 --> 04:33.440
All of those records just got re updated to the same values they already were.

04:33.450 --> 04:37.200
But now we also have values in our product subcategory field.

04:38.020 --> 04:38.500
All right.

04:38.530 --> 04:45.970
Up next, we need to update our product subcategory field and our product category ID field, both of

04:45.970 --> 04:50.950
which we can source from the production dot product subcategory table.

04:51.100 --> 04:56.140
And that's going to work very similarly to our last update, so much so that I'm just going to copy

04:56.140 --> 04:57.730
this this update statement.

04:57.880 --> 05:05.740
Now I'm still going to have product sold 2012 in my from, but now I'm going to change the secondary

05:05.740 --> 05:07.510
table to.

05:08.160 --> 05:09.270
Production.

05:09.690 --> 05:11.200
Product subcategory.

05:11.250 --> 05:15.390
And I'll just copy and paste that from our starter code to save a lot of typing.

05:17.820 --> 05:24.330
And then for the join, we're going to use that product subcategory ID field that we added in the last

05:24.330 --> 05:25.020
update.

05:25.660 --> 05:28.180
To tie in to this product subcategory table.

05:30.070 --> 05:32.920
So I'll join on a product subcategory ID.

05:35.050 --> 05:35.800
To be.

05:36.040 --> 05:37.210
Product Subcategory ID.

05:37.690 --> 05:47.560
And now I will be setting the value of product subcategory in my temp table to the name field again

05:47.560 --> 05:50.350
in my product subcategory table.

05:50.350 --> 05:56.260
And then I'll also need to update product category ID in my temp table.

05:57.840 --> 05:58.730
Two.

05:59.370 --> 06:05.040
Product category ID in my product subcategory table.

06:05.460 --> 06:07.110
So now let's run this.

06:08.700 --> 06:12.090
Looks like that successfully updated all the records of my table.

06:12.090 --> 06:14.520
And then we'll take one more peek into our data.

06:15.270 --> 06:18.780
And it looks like these two fields populated successfully as well.

06:19.080 --> 06:24.110
Now we have product subcategory and product category ID for all of our records.

06:24.120 --> 06:27.600
So the final missing piece is just product category.

06:28.200 --> 06:31.980
So again, we'll just copy and paste our previous update.

06:33.690 --> 06:36.450
We'll keep product sold 2012 in the from.

06:37.950 --> 06:42.900
But instead of updating from the product subcategory table, we're just updating from the product category

06:42.900 --> 06:43.500
table.

06:44.550 --> 06:50.880
And instead of joining on product subcategory ID, you might have guessed we're updating on product

06:50.880 --> 06:51.600
category ID.

06:54.930 --> 07:00.960
And then instead of updating the value of product subcategory in our temp table, we're just updating

07:00.960 --> 07:02.850
the value of product category.

07:03.120 --> 07:08.250
And we don't have a need to tie in any more tables, so there's no more ID fields to update.

07:08.250 --> 07:10.470
We're just updating that product category.

07:10.830 --> 07:12.540
So I think this is good.

07:12.540 --> 07:20.190
We'll run this now and see how that affects our table and hopefully all of our fields and all of our

07:20.190 --> 07:22.770
records will now be populated with data.

07:23.340 --> 07:25.400
And it looks like that is the case.

07:25.470 --> 07:32.820
So now we have successfully rewritten our starter query over here using a series of update statements

07:32.850 --> 07:35.940
in which we never join more than one table at a time.

07:36.180 --> 07:42.810
Now, again, I imagine this might look like a lot of extra work for no obvious performance gains versus

07:42.840 --> 07:43.920
a single query.

07:44.450 --> 07:48.770
And on smaller datasets like this, that may very well be the case.

07:48.770 --> 07:54.320
And you might not necessarily try to write your queries like this from the get go every single time.

07:54.680 --> 08:01.040
Personally, I tend to only use updates to add fields from one table at a time, like we did here.

08:01.190 --> 08:04.910
Only when a select query is taking a long time to run.

08:05.240 --> 08:13.310
I would consider this a tool to break out once a query or a bit of code has proven that it needs some

08:13.310 --> 08:14.960
help to run faster.

08:15.230 --> 08:20.270
So I wouldn't blame you if you're sick and tired of update by now, but we have one more video about

08:20.270 --> 08:22.140
update to get through before you're done with it.

08:22.160 --> 08:28.190
In that one, we're going to take a look at how update can be used as an alternative to exists and not

08:28.190 --> 08:32.990
exists, if you remember those guys, but an alternative that gives us the added ability to pull in

08:32.990 --> 08:36.530
an actual matching value, something that exists can't do.

08:36.860 --> 08:37.790
I'll see you then.

Now that we've leveled up our updating skills, let's take a look at how we can use update to replicate

00:08.000 --> 00:11.660
the functionality of exists and not exists.

00:11.690 --> 00:17.810
Remember those, but with the ability to actually return data which exists cannot do.

00:18.380 --> 00:25.010
So just as a refresher, let's quickly review what exists, does and does not do so exists.

00:25.010 --> 00:32.330
Basically lets you check for matches from a table on the many side of a relationship without duplicating

00:32.330 --> 00:34.010
data from the one side.

00:34.620 --> 00:42.420
By contrast, joining directly to a table on the many side of the relationship will result in records

00:42.420 --> 00:46.320
from the one side potentially being duplicated in the output.

00:47.160 --> 00:50.170
Now exists works just fine in this scenario.

00:50.190 --> 00:56.520
If you don't need any additional information about the match other than it exists or in the case of

00:56.520 --> 00:58.830
not exists, it doesn't exist.

00:59.610 --> 01:05.670
But if you actually need to see any data points pertaining to the match, any actual data or information

01:05.670 --> 01:11.580
from that secondary table on the mini side, other than just the record is there or not update can be

01:11.580 --> 01:13.740
a superior alternative to exists.

01:14.680 --> 01:21.610
So to clarify why we might or might not want to use an update to grab a value from a table on the many

01:21.610 --> 01:27.370
side of a relationship, let's take a look at an example of how update can work differently than just

01:27.370 --> 01:28.330
a simple join.

01:29.530 --> 01:37.270
So here I've created a simple temp table with four fields and then inserted data into two of those fields

01:37.270 --> 01:41.800
from the sales order header table, including only orders from 2012.

01:42.550 --> 01:51.610
Now, if I select from this temp table, you'll see we return around 3900 records and that we have two

01:51.610 --> 01:53.470
null fields in the table.

01:54.110 --> 01:59.870
That I included in the table definition in my create table statement but haven't yet inserted data to.

02:02.630 --> 02:08.090
So now let's try updating the two null fields in our temp table from the sales order detail table.

02:08.910 --> 02:14.970
Keep in mind there is a one to many relationship between the sales order data and our temp table and

02:14.970 --> 02:22.080
the line level data in our sales order detail table in which each orders constituent items are listed.

02:22.960 --> 02:24.970
So first, let's run our update.

02:27.580 --> 02:30.250
And it says 3915 rows affected.

02:30.250 --> 02:32.630
So it affected all the rows in our temp table.

02:32.650 --> 02:38.680
And then let's run a query against our temp table again to see if it changed the number of rows.

02:38.920 --> 02:43.030
So as you can see, the number of records in our table is unchanged.

02:43.300 --> 02:49.270
So what happened when there were multiple line items in the sales order detail table for a single sales

02:49.270 --> 02:50.620
order in our temp table?

02:51.230 --> 02:57.890
Well, in that case, the update simply grabbed one matching record from the mini side and updated our

02:57.890 --> 02:59.030
temp table with that.

02:59.590 --> 03:05.080
Now, if you needed to see every line item tied to a given sales order, this probably isn't the right

03:05.080 --> 03:05.890
approach.

03:06.070 --> 03:12.160
However, if you only want to see a single match and aren't particular about which match is chosen,

03:12.160 --> 03:14.350
this can be a very useful strategy.

03:15.170 --> 03:21.560
Contrast this with what happens if we simply write a select query that joins our temp table here directly

03:21.560 --> 03:23.450
to the sales order detail table?

03:23.480 --> 03:25.120
So I've already written that.

03:25.130 --> 03:27.170
So let's roll down and run this.

03:27.170 --> 03:32.990
And again, we're joining the same product sold 2012 temp table that we just created and inserted to

03:32.990 --> 03:39.530
that has 3915 rows, but we're joining it directly to that sales order detail table now.

03:39.530 --> 03:40.790
So let's run this.

03:41.770 --> 03:49.990
So as you can see, this query resulted in around 22,000 records, which is close to six times our original

03:49.990 --> 03:50.650
output.

03:51.690 --> 03:58.080
This is because the output represents all of the matches from the many side of the relationship, meaning

03:58.080 --> 04:03.030
that information about each given sales order is potentially duplicated many times.

04:03.810 --> 04:07.140
Again, this may or may not be what you want.

04:08.270 --> 04:11.840
But you may ask, how does all this tie into exists?

04:12.760 --> 04:20.560
Well exists also solves this very same problem by testing for the existence of a match or conversely,

04:20.560 --> 04:26.800
no match from the many side of a relationship without introducing duplication that we may not want.

04:27.500 --> 04:34.250
And if all you're testing for is existence or non-existence and don't need to see any data associated

04:34.250 --> 04:38.450
with matching records from the many side exists can work just fine.

04:38.810 --> 04:45.890
However, update gives us the ability to replicate the functionality of exists, but also return data

04:45.890 --> 04:48.110
points from the many side of the relationship.

04:48.760 --> 04:53.530
So let's take a crack at rewriting a query that was written using exists with update.

04:54.640 --> 05:00.880
So here we have a query that selects all sales orders where there is at least a single associated line

05:00.880 --> 05:06.100
item from the sales order detail table with a line total greater than $10,000.

05:06.630 --> 05:12.960
Using exists, we are able to connect to the sales order detail table without duplicating records from

05:12.960 --> 05:14.370
our sales order header table.

05:15.390 --> 05:21.510
I've already created a temp table here and inserted a few fields from our sales order data to it just

05:21.510 --> 05:22.660
to see what we're working with.

05:22.680 --> 05:30.150
Let's take a quick peek at this data as it stands, So I'll just run a quick select star against our

05:30.150 --> 05:31.200
sales temp table.

05:32.050 --> 05:38.830
So basically we have all records and three fields from the sales order header table and an additional

05:38.830 --> 05:40.990
empty column called Line Total.

05:41.350 --> 05:47.050
We're going to populate this empty column with an update statement based on values from the sales order

05:47.050 --> 05:47.980
detail table.

05:48.010 --> 05:49.720
So let's dive right into that.

05:50.050 --> 05:56.440
So I'll just type update and then I'll alias our temp table sales as just a.

05:57.930 --> 06:04.530
And I'm going to set the line total to something

06:07.350 --> 06:15.900
and then I'll add a from clause from our sales temp table, which again we're aliasing is a and then

06:15.900 --> 06:21.090
we're going to join in our sales order detail table.

06:22.380 --> 06:28.560
And we'll alias that as B, and we're going to join them on sales order ID.

06:31.710 --> 06:39.120
And finally, we're going to set line total equal to the line total field from our secondary table,

06:39.120 --> 06:40.710
our sales order detail table.

06:42.840 --> 06:48.450
Now, thus far, this really isn't any different than the other update statements we've already seen

06:48.450 --> 06:50.940
that fetch values from secondary tables.

06:51.550 --> 06:55.750
But remember, we actually need to apply criteria to our update.

06:55.990 --> 07:00.200
We're only interested in checking for line totals greater than $10,000.

07:00.220 --> 07:04.120
So let's add a where clause to our code that includes that logic.

07:04.660 --> 07:06.130
So I'll just add.

07:09.550 --> 07:17.260
Where the line total from our secondary table is greater than $10,000.

07:17.890 --> 07:24.220
Now, if we run this only sales orders that have an associated line item with a line total greater than

07:24.220 --> 07:26.740
$10,000 should be updated.

07:27.240 --> 07:33.150
But because we're using an update, there is no possibility of our sales order data being duplicated.

07:33.480 --> 07:39.450
A single order will be updated with at most information from a single line item.

07:39.780 --> 07:43.500
So let's run this and take a look at how it changed our temp table.

07:44.280 --> 07:50.250
So we'll run this guy and then we'll just do another select star from our sales temp table.

07:51.420 --> 07:53.580
Now if we scroll down through our output.

07:54.130 --> 08:00.010
We'll see that our line total field and our temp table has been updated with values for a few, but

08:00.010 --> 08:01.240
not all records.

08:02.260 --> 08:10.030
Again, all the sales orders that have any line totals greater than $10,000 have been updated with one

08:10.030 --> 08:12.520
and only one of those line totals.

08:13.190 --> 08:18.350
And that means at this point, we've actually got everything in place to replicate the output of our

08:18.350 --> 08:24.590
original exists query, but including these line total values that we see in this last column.

08:25.010 --> 08:32.090
All we have to do is select all the records from our sales temp table where line total is not null.

08:32.750 --> 08:38.810
Null values in the line total field indicate that there wasn't a single match in the sales order detail

08:38.810 --> 08:39.110
table.

08:39.140 --> 08:44.540
Based on our criteria, which specified that there must be a line total greater than $10,000.

08:45.170 --> 08:51.290
If no such matches were found, that necessarily means that such a match does not exist.

08:51.910 --> 08:57.700
So let's just select all records from our sales temp table where line total is not null and compare

08:57.700 --> 08:59.980
the output to our original exist query.

09:00.340 --> 09:11.110
So here where we say select star from sales, we'll just add where line total is not null.

09:12.250 --> 09:18.150
We'll run that and it looks like we've got 416 records.

09:18.160 --> 09:23.830
So if we go back to our exists example, there we are, 416 records.

09:25.300 --> 09:31.450
But even better, we now have information about those matches from the sales order detail table that

09:31.450 --> 09:33.100
we couldn't get with exists.

09:33.670 --> 09:39.940
And recreating not exists is as simple as inverting our criteria to now select all records from the

09:39.940 --> 09:42.880
sales temp table where line total is null.

09:43.540 --> 09:50.170
Again since a null line total means no matches were found, the output should be equivalent to not exists,

09:50.170 --> 09:51.760
but let's verify that.

09:51.850 --> 09:55.960
So now we'll just say where line total is null.

09:57.270 --> 10:00.720
And if we run that, we get 31,049 rows.

10:01.410 --> 10:09.960
And then if we go back to our exists example and convert it to not exists and rerun it, we get 31,049

10:09.960 --> 10:11.490
rows the same output.

10:12.520 --> 10:18.190
So now that we've seen different approaches for handling one to many relationships, when should we

10:18.190 --> 10:19.390
use what technique?

10:19.720 --> 10:25.510
So if you need to see all the matches from the many side of a relationship between two tables, use

10:25.510 --> 10:26.230
a join.

10:26.320 --> 10:31.930
If for a given sales order, you want to see every single line item in that order.

10:31.960 --> 10:33.350
A join is the way to go.

10:33.370 --> 10:36.830
An update is just going to give you that one match.

10:36.850 --> 10:43.690
If your anchor table, the table you're updating just has one row per sales order and exists works the

10:43.690 --> 10:44.440
same way.

10:44.890 --> 10:49.720
Now, if you don't want to see all matches from the mini side, you just want to see one match.

10:49.990 --> 10:55.990
But you also don't really care about any information about those matches other than just their existence

10:56.020 --> 10:56.830
exists.

10:56.830 --> 10:57.910
Works just fine.

10:58.480 --> 11:04.090
If you again, don't want to see all the matches from the mini side, but you would like some information

11:04.090 --> 11:09.220
about a match, any match that was returned, that's where you use update.

11:10.450 --> 11:11.170
All right.

11:11.200 --> 11:17.530
Up next, we're going to look at one more optimization technique indexes before we dive into actually

11:17.530 --> 11:20.170
creating permanent objects in your database.

11:20.440 --> 11:23.920
There's some exciting stuff coming up, and I can't wait to get to it.

11:23.950 --> 11:25.480
I'll see you in the next video.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.110 --> 00:01.100
Welcome back.

00:01.400 --> 00:07.130
In this one, we're going to talk all about indexes, which are another optimization technique we can

00:07.130 --> 00:10.580
bring to bear on our queries as we try to make them run faster.

00:10.940 --> 00:17.390
They're also one of the main advantages of temp tables versus CTEs and subqueries since temp tables

00:17.390 --> 00:20.930
can be indexed and CTEs and subqueries cannot.

00:21.600 --> 00:23.250
But what are index?

00:23.460 --> 00:29.760
In short, indexes are basically database objects that can make queries against your tables faster.

00:29.760 --> 00:36.270
So there's something that you put on your table to make a query that's written against that table faster.

00:36.480 --> 00:43.830
Indexes do this by sorting the data in the fields that you apply them to, either in the table itself,

00:43.830 --> 00:47.310
the physical data of the table or in a separate data structure.

00:47.340 --> 00:51.930
These basically define two different types of indexes and we'll talk about both of those in a minute.

00:52.110 --> 00:59.490
So this sorting, this sorting of the data allows the database engine to find records within a table

00:59.490 --> 01:02.520
without having to go through that table row by row.

01:02.550 --> 01:05.100
That's what makes the data retrieval faster.

01:05.400 --> 01:11.220
Now, those two types of indexes I alluded to are called clustered and non-clustered indexes, and we're

01:11.220 --> 01:13.290
going to go through both of those individually.

01:13.840 --> 01:17.880
So first up are clustered indexes with clustered indexes.

01:17.890 --> 01:24.250
The rows of a table are physically sorted based on the field or fields the index is applied to.

01:24.460 --> 01:32.410
So if you have a clustered index on, for example, sales order ID, the rows of data in that table

01:32.440 --> 01:36.850
are going to be sorted based on that that field sales order ID.

01:38.080 --> 01:45.490
Now a table with a primary key is actually given a clustered index by default based on the primary key

01:45.490 --> 01:46.120
field.

01:46.570 --> 01:51.370
And before we move on with the conceptual stuff here, I actually want to take a look at a table in

01:51.370 --> 01:57.490
our database to see how the primary key and the indexes on that table align.

01:58.640 --> 02:05.690
So if we look at the columns under our sales order detail table over an object Explorer, we'll see

02:05.690 --> 02:12.500
the abbreviation PK After both the sales order ID field and the sales order detail ID field.

02:12.950 --> 02:20.240
This means that this table has a compound primary key, which is to say there are multiple fields in

02:20.240 --> 02:26.600
this case, two that when combined uniquely identify a row of data within that table.

02:26.600 --> 02:32.840
So sales order ID plus sales order detail ID comprise the primary key of the table.

02:33.350 --> 02:35.660
But if you go down and look under.

02:36.340 --> 02:37.480
Indexes.

02:37.840 --> 02:45.820
You'll see this little key icon next to something called PK Sales Order detail underscore sales order

02:45.820 --> 02:49.510
ID, underscore sales order detail ID That's quite a mouthful.

02:49.510 --> 02:51.160
And it says clustered.

02:51.160 --> 02:59.200
So basically that primary key comprised of sales order detail ID and sales order ID is also a clustered

02:59.200 --> 03:01.000
index on that table.

03:01.120 --> 03:05.020
Now you can see there are also a couple of other non-clustered indexes on that table.

03:05.020 --> 03:07.960
And we're going to talk about Non-clustered indexes in just a moment.

03:09.490 --> 03:16.300
So now that we know generally what a clustered index is and we've seen an example of how one is applied

03:16.300 --> 03:18.310
to one of the tables in our database.

03:18.580 --> 03:22.360
When should you use clustered indexes on your temp tables?

03:23.110 --> 03:28.990
Well, generally, most tables should have at least a clustered index, since queries against tables

03:28.990 --> 03:32.020
with a clustered index generally tend to be faster.

03:32.050 --> 03:38.680
That's because the data in a table with a clustered index has that physical sorting order, which just

03:38.680 --> 03:42.280
makes it easier for the database engine to grab a particular record.

03:42.610 --> 03:44.650
Now, one caveat worth noting.

03:44.800 --> 03:48.310
A table may only have one clustered index.

03:48.610 --> 03:54.130
If you want more than one index on your table, you'll have to resort to adding non-clustered indexes,

03:54.130 --> 03:55.900
which is something we'll get to in a minute.

03:56.720 --> 04:02.600
But first, let's take a look at a few strategies for applying clustered indexes to a table.

04:03.710 --> 04:10.580
First, you'll want to apply a clustered index to whatever field or fields are most likely to be used

04:10.580 --> 04:12.380
in a join against the table.

04:12.470 --> 04:20.330
I can't emphasize enough that you want to let how your table is going to be joined to other tables after

04:20.330 --> 04:21.290
you've built it.

04:21.320 --> 04:27.470
Kind of drive the design of your indexes, drive your decisions as to whether to index a field, what

04:27.500 --> 04:29.150
field to index and so forth.

04:29.800 --> 04:36.130
Now, ideally this field or combination of fields you chose for your clustered index should also be

04:36.130 --> 04:40.990
the one that most uniquely identifies or defines a record in the table.

04:41.630 --> 04:47.750
And as we saw when we looked at the index on the sales order detail table in our Adventureworks database,

04:47.750 --> 04:53.270
the primary key of a table is usually a pretty good candidate for a clustered index.

04:53.660 --> 04:56.480
So what about non-clustered indexes?

04:57.520 --> 05:04.300
Well, one of the big advantages of Non-clustered indexes is that a table may have many non-clustered

05:04.300 --> 05:07.540
indexes, whereas it may only have one clustered index.

05:08.650 --> 05:14.830
Now Non-clustered indexes do not physically sort the data in a table like clustered indexes do.

05:14.860 --> 05:17.140
This is how you're able to have more than one.

05:17.140 --> 05:20.890
You can't sort a table by five different indexes.

05:20.890 --> 05:24.550
You really have to you have to pick one way to physically sort the data in the table.

05:25.180 --> 05:33.340
Instead, the sorted order of whatever fields you applied non-clustered indexes to is stored in an external

05:33.340 --> 05:36.530
data structure which works kind of sort of like a phone book.

05:36.550 --> 05:41.830
And I realize I'm dating myself with that reference, but it was the best analogy I could come up with.

05:42.250 --> 05:47.470
So let's look at some strategies for applying Non-clustered indexes to our tables.

05:47.860 --> 05:54.260
If you will be joining your table on fields besides the one that is covered by your clustered index.

05:54.280 --> 05:58.750
Then you're going to want to consider non-clustered indexes on those fields.

05:58.930 --> 06:06.430
So let's say you pick your clustered index on, say, sales order ID, but you're going to be joining

06:06.430 --> 06:09.850
that table on some other field down the road.

06:10.030 --> 06:15.010
In that case, you may want to put a non-clustered index on that other field.

06:16.680 --> 06:22.590
Now you can add as many non-clustered indexes as you as you want, but you should be judicious when

06:22.590 --> 06:23.280
you're doing this.

06:23.280 --> 06:29.220
You shouldn't just go go crazy in your database and add a non-clustered index to every field or every

06:29.220 --> 06:31.740
combination combination of fields just because you can.

06:31.740 --> 06:34.320
And we'll see a few reasons for that in just a moment.

06:35.640 --> 06:42.120
Now fields covered by a non-clustered index should still have a high level of uniqueness, even if they're

06:42.120 --> 06:44.190
not a primary key per se.

06:44.220 --> 06:50.760
So something like, you know, first name would probably be a really bad candidate for any kind of index,

06:50.760 --> 06:54.660
clustered or non-clustered because it doesn't have a high level of uniqueness.

06:54.660 --> 07:00.000
There are certain values, you know, John, Tom, Mary that would be repeated over and over and over

07:00.000 --> 07:05.820
again, and that just makes a field much less effective as an index field.

07:06.480 --> 07:14.610
So big picture, how should we integrate indexes into our overall optimization strategy?

07:15.120 --> 07:21.390
Well, as I said before, it's really how our table is going to be utilized and joins that should drive

07:21.390 --> 07:23.730
your use and your design of indexes.

07:23.760 --> 07:29.070
If you've got a temp table and you're going to be joining it to several different tables later on as

07:29.070 --> 07:34.590
part of your data transformation process, look at how that table is going to be joined, what fields

07:34.590 --> 07:39.750
it's going to be joined on, and that will help you decide, Oh, this is the field that I want to put

07:39.750 --> 07:41.130
a clustered index on.

07:41.130 --> 07:43.620
And then I have these other couple fields I'm going to be joining on that.

07:43.620 --> 07:45.570
I'll put non-clustered indexes on.

07:46.540 --> 07:53.890
So the bottom line is you should generally add a clustered index first and then layer in non-clustered

07:53.890 --> 07:59.230
indexes as needed to cover additional fields used in joins against our table.

08:00.490 --> 08:06.190
Now indexes take up memory in the database, so you should only add them if they're actually needed.

08:06.220 --> 08:10.390
It's not a trivial or consequence free thing to add an index.

08:10.390 --> 08:14.260
As with almost everything in SQL or probably any programming language there.

08:14.290 --> 08:20.110
There are trade offs to any approach you take that has a one type of benefit.

08:20.110 --> 08:24.010
And with indexes, one of the downsides is they do take up memory.

08:24.610 --> 08:28.240
But if you apply them intelligently, they will be a net positive.

08:29.310 --> 08:32.610
Now, indexes also make inserts to the tables.

08:32.610 --> 08:34.680
They are applied to take longer.

08:34.770 --> 08:39.690
So you should generally add indexes after data has been inserted to the table.

08:39.690 --> 08:44.280
And this is yet another reason why you shouldn't put an index on a table unless you really think it's

08:44.280 --> 08:47.520
going to help your queries against that table run faster.

08:48.270 --> 08:53.460
Now I know that was a lot of slides and that's because we're presenting a brand new concept here.

08:53.460 --> 08:58.770
But now it's time to dive into a code example so we can see how indexes work in the real world.

08:59.460 --> 09:00.870
That's coming up next.

09:00.900 --> 09:01.890
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.330 --> 00:01.410
Welcome back.

00:02.040 --> 00:07.890
Now that you have a conceptual understanding of indexes, let's walk through a scenario where you can

00:07.890 --> 00:10.920
use them to optimize a SQL script.

00:11.190 --> 00:18.630
For our motivating code example, I'm actually going to use the code from our last video that dealt

00:18.630 --> 00:25.170
with optimization, and that's the one where we rewrote a query that utilized several, joins in a single

00:25.170 --> 00:33.750
select into a temp table that we subsequently updated with a series of update statements that pulled

00:33.750 --> 00:36.630
in values from secondary tables.

00:36.750 --> 00:43.560
So now what we're going to do is take a look at how indexes could potentially speed up a process like

00:43.560 --> 00:49.620
this, especially if the tables that you're doing those updates against have a lot of records.

00:49.890 --> 00:57.750
So first, by way of review, you'll see we created our sales 2012 temp table here and then we inserted

00:57.750 --> 01:04.180
data from our sales order header table to that temp table where the order date was 2012.

01:04.710 --> 01:10.590
Now, if we're thinking about how we might try to apply indexes to this table to help queries against

01:10.590 --> 01:18.540
it run faster, we first want to look at how our sales 2012 temp table here is actually used and joined

01:18.540 --> 01:21.610
to in subsequent steps of our process.

01:21.630 --> 01:29.010
So if we scroll down, we'll see that our sales 2012 temp table is being joined to our sales order detail

01:29.010 --> 01:31.080
table on sales order ID.

01:31.800 --> 01:38.550
So at this point you might have guessed what we need to do is create a clustered index on our sales

01:38.550 --> 01:42.990
2012 temp table, and that index should be on sales order ID.

01:44.420 --> 01:49.100
Now, remember, as I mentioned, you generally want to put the index on after you've inserted data

01:49.100 --> 01:49.880
to the table.

01:50.180 --> 01:54.770
So right below our insert to the sales 2012 temp table, I'll just type.

01:56.160 --> 02:03.390
Create clustered if I can spell clustered index.

02:03.660 --> 02:09.570
And now you just have to specify the name of the index, which could be anything you want.

02:09.600 --> 02:16.470
I'll just generally try to make my index name somewhat meaningful so it's easier for me to identify

02:16.470 --> 02:18.480
what it pertains to what I'm going through my code.

02:18.480 --> 02:28.650
So I'll just call it sales 2012, underscore ID, and then you have to say what table and field the

02:28.650 --> 02:29.910
index is on.

02:30.180 --> 02:37.080
So first you type the keyword on and then you include the name of the table that the index is going

02:37.080 --> 02:37.800
to be on.

02:38.550 --> 02:43.200
So that is our sales 2012 temp table.

02:43.890 --> 02:49.530
And then in parentheses, after the table name, you list the field or fields that the index is going

02:49.530 --> 02:56.070
to be on, and we're actually going to be indexing the sales order ID field.

02:56.850 --> 02:57.660
And that's it.

02:57.660 --> 03:05.850
At this point, we have a complete create clustered index statement, and if we run it, it completes

03:05.850 --> 03:06.420
successfully.

03:06.420 --> 03:09.570
But we don't see any other obvious magic happen.

03:09.570 --> 03:11.010
It doesn't return any data.

03:11.010 --> 03:15.840
And if you select from the table, you wouldn't see anything different there either, except that it

03:15.840 --> 03:21.540
would be sorted by sales order ID because we put a clustered index on that field.

03:22.300 --> 03:22.690
All right.

03:22.690 --> 03:27.060
So we've added our first index to our very first temp table.

03:27.070 --> 03:32.110
But down here we create a second table called Products Sold 2012.

03:32.290 --> 03:38.770
And as we've discussed, your first step should generally be to apply a clustered index to a table.

03:38.890 --> 03:47.560
So what field or fields would best define uniqueness in our product sold 2012 temp table and thus be

03:47.560 --> 03:50.170
the best candidates for a clustered index?

03:50.350 --> 03:56.320
Well, we've got our sales order ID field here, but if we look down at the query that populates this

03:56.320 --> 04:03.670
table, you'll see that we're joining to the sales order detail table, and that table has line level

04:03.670 --> 04:04.240
data.

04:04.240 --> 04:11.530
So our output of this query that we're inserting into our product sold 2012 temp table is not going

04:11.530 --> 04:18.130
to be unique by sales order ID, Sales order IDs might be repeated many times if there are many items

04:18.130 --> 04:20.560
within a given order.

04:20.680 --> 04:27.560
So in order to define uniqueness in our table, we probably want to pull in the sales order detail ID

04:27.560 --> 04:30.590
field from our sales order detail table.

04:31.160 --> 04:38.780
And then we can mirror the clustered index we saw on the sales order detail table previously that was

04:38.780 --> 04:42.950
applied to both the sales order ID field and the sales order detail field.

04:43.310 --> 04:47.420
So let's go ahead and add sales order detail ID up here.

04:55.370 --> 04:58.850
And then we'll also add that to our select and our insert.

05:11.620 --> 05:17.140
And then let's go ahead and run our create table statement and our insert.

05:21.510 --> 05:21.960
All right.

05:21.960 --> 05:29.010
So now that we have the two fields that uniquely identify each row in our temp table, we can go ahead

05:29.010 --> 05:30.060
and add our index.

05:30.390 --> 05:41.160
So after our insert statement that inserted data to our table, I'll just type create clustered index

05:41.310 --> 05:57.870
and I'll call this one products sold 2012, underscore ID and it will be on our products sold 2012 temp

05:57.900 --> 05:58.500
table.

05:59.520 --> 06:11.490
And within that table it will be on sales order ID and sales order detail ID.

06:12.600 --> 06:14.040
So now let's run that.

06:15.220 --> 06:15.700
All right.

06:15.730 --> 06:19.870
Now we have a clustered index on our main temp table.

06:20.200 --> 06:27.430
So before we add any more indexes, let's take a look at the rest of our data transformation process

06:27.430 --> 06:30.910
to see what other tables we are joining into our temp table.

06:32.030 --> 06:39.350
So the in the next step we are updating our product name and our product subcategory ID fields based

06:39.350 --> 06:42.590
on a join to our production product table.

06:43.090 --> 06:44.980
And we're joining on product ID.

06:45.550 --> 06:52.420
So we are using the product ID field in our temp table to join out to the products table.

06:53.350 --> 06:57.310
So that product ID field is another candidate for an index.

06:57.670 --> 07:02.050
So let's take a look at adding another index to our table.

07:02.260 --> 07:04.060
This one based on product ID.

07:04.990 --> 07:06.970
So we'll just copy and paste this code.

07:06.970 --> 07:14.740
And instead of calling our index product sold 2012 ID, I'll just call it product sold 2012 ID two for

07:14.740 --> 07:21.340
lack of imagination, and I'll put the index on the product ID field.

07:24.040 --> 07:26.830
So now let's run this and see what happens.

07:27.850 --> 07:29.260
Oops, we got an error.

07:29.410 --> 07:34.600
It says cannot create more than one clustered index on our table.

07:34.690 --> 07:36.610
So this is what we talked about before.

07:36.640 --> 07:42.730
If you want to index multiple fields, you can put a clustered index on one, but then you have to resort

07:42.730 --> 07:47.770
to non-clustered indexes for any subsequent fields that you want to index.

07:48.300 --> 07:51.090
So instead, let's just change this.

07:52.010 --> 07:58.790
Code to say create non-clustered index and you'll see our red Squigglies went away right away.

07:59.800 --> 08:01.630
Now let's highlight this again and run it.

08:02.410 --> 08:04.180
And it completed successfully.

08:04.890 --> 08:05.280
All right.

08:05.280 --> 08:12.690
So we've indexed the field we used in this particular update, and we see that in this update we populated

08:12.690 --> 08:15.120
a product subcategory ID field.

08:15.120 --> 08:23.040
So that data is now available at this step of the process for us to query against, join to or potentially

08:23.040 --> 08:24.180
apply an index to.

08:25.140 --> 08:32.100
So if you look at the next update, we're now pulling in product subcategory and product category ID

08:32.580 --> 08:39.720
from the product subcategory table, and we're doing that based on a join on the product subcategory

08:39.720 --> 08:40.590
ID field.

08:40.920 --> 08:48.000
So before that join, we probably want to add another index, this time on our product subcategory ID

08:48.000 --> 08:48.630
field.

08:49.480 --> 08:52.630
So let's go ahead and again, copy and paste that code.

08:54.280 --> 08:59.560
But again, it has to be a non-clustered index because we've already taken up our one clustered index

08:59.860 --> 09:01.480
and we'll name it.

09:02.160 --> 09:03.480
Products sold 2012.

09:04.470 --> 09:05.370
Three.

09:06.360 --> 09:11.190
And this time the index is going to be on product subcategory ID.

09:12.270 --> 09:13.650
So now let's run that.

09:15.050 --> 09:17.480
And then we can run our update.

09:18.470 --> 09:24.470
And now we'll take a look at our last update statement that pulls in the product category from the product

09:24.470 --> 09:25.520
category table.

09:26.160 --> 09:31.380
Now this one makes use of the product category ID field in our temp table.

09:31.560 --> 09:36.750
And if we roll back and look at our update statement, we'll see that that product category ID field

09:36.780 --> 09:42.930
has already been updated based on the join to the product subcategory table.

09:43.080 --> 09:50.940
So again, we'll probably want to index that product category ID field after this update, after the

09:50.940 --> 09:57.780
the update where it was populated in our table, but before it is actually being used in a join by our

09:57.780 --> 09:58.770
final update.

09:58.980 --> 10:06.570
So once again, I'll just reuse our previous syntax and I'll call this index ID for this time.

10:07.050 --> 10:14.640
And instead of indexing the product subcategory ID field, I'll just index the product category ID field.

10:15.390 --> 10:16.770
And we'll run this.

10:18.340 --> 10:20.590
And once again, it completed successfully.

10:20.890 --> 10:24.070
So finally, we'll run our last update statement here.

10:25.090 --> 10:28.510
And then we'll just take a quick peek at our data to make sure nothing went haywire.

10:28.510 --> 10:30.820
And it looks like everything worked just like before.

10:32.060 --> 10:38.420
So after watching this video, I hope you have not just an understanding of what indexes are and how

10:38.420 --> 10:45.890
they work syntax wise, but also an appreciation of when you would apply indexes and the general strategy

10:45.890 --> 10:52.430
and approach you should take when deciding when to use an index, what table it should go on, what

10:52.460 --> 10:54.710
fields should be indexed and so forth.

10:54.980 --> 11:01.940
It's really those decisions more so than just the syntax of indexes that will make them effective.

11:02.670 --> 11:03.090
All right.

11:03.090 --> 11:08.760
So at this point, we have explored the power and possibilities of temp tables to the nth degree.

11:09.060 --> 11:16.230
But up next, we're actually going to start diving into how you can create permanent objects that live

11:16.230 --> 11:18.900
on the database server that don't go away.

11:18.900 --> 11:22.500
Just when you close your session by closing out your editor window.

11:22.500 --> 11:25.770
And that will open up a whole new realm of possibilities.

11:26.040 --> 11:27.990
So let's start exploring those next.

11:28.020 --> 11:28.980
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.200 --> 00:01.250
Welcome back.

00:01.890 --> 00:09.450
So now that we're experts on temporary tables, let's take a look at how and why we might want to create

00:09.450 --> 00:12.000
permanent objects on our database server.

00:13.080 --> 00:19.650
The temporary tables we have created so far have only served to support intermediate steps in a single

00:19.650 --> 00:23.550
process of some sort that usually culminated in a query output.

00:24.090 --> 00:29.370
But by creating permanent tables and other types of database objects that will get into a little bit

00:29.370 --> 00:36.060
later, we can support an arbitrary number of queries and processes, including ones run by people other

00:36.060 --> 00:36.990
than ourselves.

00:37.470 --> 00:43.500
In fact, as a senior analyst, and if you've made it this far in the course and done all the exercises

00:43.500 --> 00:47.550
and understood all the concepts, you might well be able to call yourself that.

00:48.130 --> 00:54.430
It's quite likely that you'll graduate from just extracting data for your own needs to creating database

00:54.430 --> 00:58.840
objects that make the lives of other more junior analysts easier.

00:59.170 --> 01:02.680
That's going to be our focus in this video and the videos to come.

01:03.570 --> 01:06.900
The most obvious place to start is simply tables.

01:07.290 --> 01:12.810
And the great news here is that all the things we've learned about creating, dropping and manipulating

01:12.810 --> 01:17.760
the data in temporary tables applies equally to permanent tables in the database.

01:18.150 --> 01:24.750
If you understand how to create and manipulate temp tables, then you're 99.9% of the way to being able

01:24.750 --> 01:27.330
to create useful, permanent tables as well.

01:27.540 --> 01:32.760
Now, it's worth noting before we move on, that the commands we have already learned to define and

01:32.760 --> 01:39.870
manipulate temporary tables are broadly classified into two groups data definition language commands

01:39.870 --> 01:46.500
or DDL for short and data manipulation commands or DML for short.

01:47.260 --> 01:52.360
DDL commands pertain to the definition and structure of our database objects.

01:52.360 --> 01:55.870
So these include create, drop and truncate.

01:56.750 --> 02:01.850
DML commands, on the other hand, involve manipulating data in existing objects.

02:01.850 --> 02:05.690
So these include insert, update and delete.

02:06.440 --> 02:09.890
Now, how useful is knowledge of all these acronyms, really?

02:10.440 --> 02:15.060
Not very, in my opinion, but it's something that you may be asked in an interview, so it's probably

02:15.060 --> 02:16.560
worth having in the back of your head.

02:17.320 --> 02:23.560
Anyway, now that you're armed with both the syntax and the jargon to be comfortable with tables, let's

02:23.560 --> 02:28.240
consider a scenario in which it might be beneficial to create our own permanent table.

02:28.960 --> 02:34.150
One type of table, which is a common fixture in many analytics teams, is a calendar table.

02:34.480 --> 02:40.690
Such a table will have one row for every day in a given time period, which usually encompasses all

02:40.690 --> 02:46.180
the days that might possibly be in scope for the reporting and analytics that team produces.

02:46.730 --> 02:53.930
More importantly, the table will also have a wide range of attributes that parse, describe, categorize

02:53.930 --> 02:58.430
and otherwise provide useful information about each date in the table.

02:58.640 --> 03:04.580
For example, whether a date is a weekend, a holiday, what day of the month it is, the list goes

03:04.580 --> 03:05.240
on and on.

03:05.850 --> 03:11.820
Now, to be sure, all of these things can be defined using functions in a select query, but many of

03:11.820 --> 03:17.490
them are used over and over again, and many people's queries requiring analysts to redefine the same

03:17.490 --> 03:19.200
values over and over again.

03:19.380 --> 03:25.920
The calendar table offers a huge convenience boost by allowing analysts to join to it and get all of

03:25.920 --> 03:29.790
these various date related attributes for free, so to speak.

03:30.540 --> 03:37.080
And even more important, having all these things defined in a central location provides a single version

03:37.080 --> 03:42.810
of the truth, which is extremely important for the integrity and accuracy of the reporting and analytics

03:42.810 --> 03:44.010
your team produces.

03:44.840 --> 03:50.180
So without further ado, let's take a look at the steps required to create a permanent calendar table

03:50.180 --> 03:51.140
in our database.

03:52.080 --> 03:57.540
As I mentioned, the syntax for creating a permanent table is nearly identical to that, for creating

03:57.540 --> 03:58.680
a temporary table.

03:59.010 --> 04:04.320
The only practical difference is that instead of including a pound sign before the name of our table,

04:04.320 --> 04:10.560
we instead need to specify the database and the schema that we will be creating the table on since that

04:10.560 --> 04:13.350
database and schema will be its permanent home.

04:13.900 --> 04:19.030
In this case, we will obviously want to create our table in the Adventureworks database and for now

04:19.030 --> 04:21.730
we'll just leave it in the default DBO schema.

04:22.320 --> 04:26.970
So we can go ahead and put together the skeleton of our create table statement and we'll just call our

04:26.970 --> 04:28.320
table calendar.

04:28.620 --> 04:30.240
So now we'll just type.

04:30.840 --> 04:32.700
Just like with a temp table.

04:32.700 --> 04:34.650
Create table.

04:34.890 --> 04:46.500
But now we'll specify the name of our database Adventureworks 2019 dot and then the schema within that

04:46.500 --> 04:50.430
database that our table is going to live in and DBO is the default schema.

04:50.760 --> 04:54.690
And then finally, just the name of our table, which we'll just call calendar.

04:57.590 --> 04:58.510
And that's it.

04:58.520 --> 05:03.230
Other than this, everything else about defining the permanent table is just like a temp table.

05:03.230 --> 05:06.140
We'll include our pair of parentheses afterwards.

05:06.990 --> 05:08.940
So now we can define our fields.

05:09.480 --> 05:14.760
As I mentioned, the list of date related attributes that you could add to a calendar table can go on

05:14.760 --> 05:15.640
for miles.

05:15.660 --> 05:19.080
So for example, sake, I'm just going to limit it to a few.

05:19.230 --> 05:24.120
And to save you from watching me type for the next couple hours, I'm going to go ahead and just paste

05:24.120 --> 05:30.090
those in and we'll just briefly review the fields, their data types and why they might be useful.

05:30.300 --> 05:34.400
The first field here is kind of the unique identifier for the table.

05:34.410 --> 05:39.870
It is the actual date that all the other fields in the table will be describing.

05:39.870 --> 05:44.640
Every row in the table should have a different date, and all those dates together should just kind

05:44.640 --> 05:48.780
of be the date range that's in scope for our data.

05:49.320 --> 05:52.770
And now the next five fields are pretty self-explanatory.

05:52.770 --> 05:59.280
They're really just various attributes of a date parsed out of it, whether it's the day of the week,

05:59.310 --> 06:03.540
the month of the year, the year itself, etcetera.

06:03.870 --> 06:06.690
Now, the last two fields are a little more interesting.

06:07.620 --> 06:11.130
Weekend flag will be A10 indicator.

06:11.130 --> 06:12.300
One meaning yes.

06:12.300 --> 06:13.470
Zero meaning no.

06:13.500 --> 06:16.470
That says whether a given date is on a weekend.

06:17.200 --> 06:19.600
And then holiday flag will work very similarly.

06:19.600 --> 06:24.190
Just an indicator that says, is this particular date on a holiday or not?

06:24.670 --> 06:25.180
All right.

06:25.180 --> 06:29.320
So now that we have our table defined, the next step is to get some data into it.

06:29.910 --> 06:36.940
Now, let's say we consider the scope of our analytics to range from January 1st, 2011 to December

06:36.940 --> 06:38.730
31st, 2030.

06:39.410 --> 06:43.190
How the heck are we going to get all these dates inserted to a table?

06:44.070 --> 06:50.130
Well, now we could take a look at a technique we haven't reviewed yet, which involves manually inserting

06:50.130 --> 06:52.890
rows of data to a table one at a time.

06:53.280 --> 06:57.840
Let's actually take at least a quick look at what the syntax for that approach is.

06:58.290 --> 07:04.620
So here I've pre-written the boilerplate for an insert statement to our calendar table.

07:04.980 --> 07:12.210
And if we wanted to manually insert a row of data into this table, we'd follow that field list with

07:12.210 --> 07:17.310
the keyword values and then another set of parentheses.

07:17.580 --> 07:25.830
And then we would simply list out the values in these parentheses that correspond to all the values

07:25.830 --> 07:30.000
in our field list up here, separated by commas.

07:30.030 --> 07:31.620
So let's take a crack at that.

07:31.650 --> 07:36.540
Let's say we're just going to start with January 1st, 2011.

07:36.690 --> 07:45.190
So we'll just say cast A1A1 2011 as date.

07:45.190 --> 07:46.690
So that's our first value.

07:47.110 --> 07:53.560
And then the day of the week for that day is a seven, which is a Saturday.

07:53.740 --> 07:56.020
So that will be our day name.

07:58.600 --> 08:05.260
And then the day of the month is obviously the first the month number is also the first month of the

08:05.260 --> 08:07.330
year, so that that field gets a one as well.

08:07.990 --> 08:11.110
The year number is 2011.

08:12.880 --> 08:15.010
Now we see that the day is on a Saturday.

08:15.010 --> 08:16.570
So it is in fact a weekend.

08:16.570 --> 08:18.160
So that field gets a one.

08:19.010 --> 08:22.280
And then in many places, January 1st is celebrated as a holiday.

08:22.280 --> 08:24.750
So I'll go ahead and say, yes, that is a holiday.

08:24.770 --> 08:26.960
So I'll add the number one to the last field.

08:27.920 --> 08:33.680
So let's roll back up and run our create table statement and then we can try and insert this row of

08:33.680 --> 08:34.790
data into the table.

08:35.900 --> 08:42.440
So we'll just run our create table and then we can run our insert.

08:43.220 --> 08:44.870
It says one row affected.

08:45.050 --> 08:50.630
So now let's do a quick select star from our newly created calendar table

08:53.540 --> 08:55.220
and we'll see what's in it.

08:57.140 --> 08:57.590
All right.

08:57.590 --> 09:00.140
We do have one row of data in the table.

09:00.140 --> 09:04.820
And just taking a quick peek at the values in these fields, they appear pretty consistent with what

09:04.820 --> 09:05.690
we'd expect.

09:06.550 --> 09:13.030
Now, if we wanted to insert multiple rows at a time using this manual method, you certainly can.

09:13.060 --> 09:21.160
All you have to do is add more comma separated lists of values in between parentheses and then separate

09:21.160 --> 09:22.610
those lists with commas.

09:22.630 --> 09:28.930
So if I wanted to add another row at the same time, I would just put a comma after my first list of

09:28.930 --> 09:34.690
values and then include another list again inside of parentheses below that.

09:34.690 --> 09:36.840
And then I could keep doing that over and over again.

09:36.850 --> 09:43.810
The second list of values would just be January 2nd and Sunday and the second day of the month and so

09:43.810 --> 09:44.680
on and so forth.

09:45.320 --> 09:46.690
That's a little better.

09:46.700 --> 09:51.290
But inserting over 7000 days this way just doesn't seem very practical.

09:51.560 --> 09:57.290
In fact, as an analyst, you probably won't insert values manually like this very often.

09:57.650 --> 10:04.910
It's much more common for applications connected to databases to insert individual records of data like

10:04.910 --> 10:05.540
this.

10:05.690 --> 10:10.370
Think maybe a restaurant app recording someone's order to a table.

10:11.220 --> 10:17.070
As an analyst, you're much more likely to insert data into a temp table that you queried from another

10:17.070 --> 10:17.640
table.

10:18.360 --> 10:22.650
But in this particular case, we are trying to create a bunch of dates from thin air.

10:23.440 --> 10:28.420
Now, if you've been paying attention in the course, and I hope that you have, you might remember

10:28.420 --> 10:35.740
that we learned a technique previously for generating series of dates using recursive common table expressions

10:35.740 --> 10:37.120
or CTEs.

10:37.450 --> 10:42.280
Since that's a topic in and of itself and one that we've already covered, I'm not going to delve into

10:42.280 --> 10:48.550
the mechanics of how it works, but let's go ahead and use a recursive CTE like this to populate our

10:48.550 --> 10:50.140
lookup table with dates.

10:50.680 --> 10:55.270
So first I'm going to go ahead and truncate our table here to get rid of that record of data that we

10:55.270 --> 10:55.920
inserted.

10:55.930 --> 11:05.710
So I'll just type truncate table if I can spell table and then I'll run that.

11:07.690 --> 11:11.800
So now our table is cleared out and ready to insert a bunch of dates to.

11:12.750 --> 11:20.430
So here we have a recursive CTE that I've set up to generate a list of dates ranging from January 1st,

11:20.430 --> 11:24.720
2011 to December 31st, 2030.

11:24.990 --> 11:29.790
Now, before we move on, I'm just going to highlight this and run it to make sure it's generating the

11:29.790 --> 11:31.290
dates that I hope it does.

11:31.800 --> 11:39.840
And it looks like we start at one one, 2011 and if we scroll down, it looks like the series ends on

11:39.840 --> 11:41.520
December 31st, 2030.

11:41.550 --> 11:42.780
So far, so good.

11:43.350 --> 11:46.230
But how about getting these dates into our table?

11:46.530 --> 11:53.460
Well, it turns out that you can actually insert the results of the select query at the very end of

11:53.460 --> 11:55.920
your CTE into a table.

11:56.130 --> 12:03.060
So all we have to do is say insert into and then we'll just type out the name of our new table.

12:04.290 --> 12:09.930
Adventureworks dot dbo dot calendar.

12:13.950 --> 12:20.580
And then we're just going to be inserting into the date value field.

12:21.090 --> 12:22.990
And that should be all we need to do.

12:23.010 --> 12:25.830
So let's rerun this as an insert.

12:26.190 --> 12:31.480
And it looks like 7300 records were affected, which is what we'd expect.

12:31.500 --> 12:37.410
But just to make sure this worked, let's actually query our Adventureworks calendar table one more

12:37.410 --> 12:40.650
time to see if we see those dates in there.

12:43.800 --> 12:45.390
Now we'll run this.

12:46.980 --> 12:48.060
And there we are.

12:48.090 --> 12:55.980
We have our date value field populated for all the rows of the table, which now number 7305.

12:56.010 --> 13:01.680
The number of days from January 1st, 2011 to December 31st, 2030.

13:02.250 --> 13:07.680
But now we've got to get busy populating all of these other fields in the table that are going to make

13:07.680 --> 13:14.910
it so useful for yourself and maybe other analysts to join out to and pull in rather than having to

13:14.910 --> 13:16.860
define and derive themselves.

13:17.130 --> 13:21.930
But this one's already gone a little bit long, so we'll actually tackle that in the next video.

13:21.960 --> 13:22.890
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.310 --> 00:01.420
Welcome back.

00:01.660 --> 00:08.230
In this one, we're going to work on populating all of these null fields in our calendar table so we

00:08.230 --> 00:15.700
can start with our day of week number, day of week, name, day of month, number, month number and

00:15.700 --> 00:17.050
year number columns.

00:17.260 --> 00:22.990
Now, again, these are certainly things that we could define an individual queries, but the value

00:22.990 --> 00:28.180
of this lookup table is that now anyone with access to it will never have to perform these types of

00:28.180 --> 00:29.980
calculations against dates in their data.

00:30.010 --> 00:33.910
Again, a simple join to this table will do all the work for them.

00:35.160 --> 00:40.650
So the update statements we're going to use to populate these five date fields aren't anything cutting

00:40.650 --> 00:41.580
edge or revolutionary.

00:41.610 --> 00:43.230
Nothing we really haven't seen already.

00:43.230 --> 00:45.330
So I'm not going to go too deep into this.

00:45.360 --> 00:50.490
I've already typed the code out, but basically we're just using various date functions available to

00:50.490 --> 00:54.460
us in SQL to populate these fields with a simple update.

00:54.480 --> 00:57.420
So let me just go ahead and run this.

00:58.620 --> 01:03.480
And again, we'll take a peek inside of our table to see how we're progressing.

01:04.380 --> 01:04.890
All right.

01:04.890 --> 01:09.540
And now all but two of the fields in our table have been fully populated.

01:09.540 --> 01:16.890
And you can see how for every date in our table, we have all these nice, useful attributes that otherwise

01:16.920 --> 01:20.430
an analyst might have to calculate themselves in their queries.

01:20.430 --> 01:25.200
And now they can just join out on a date and grab all these attributes for free.

01:26.060 --> 01:31.310
So this looks great so far, but how are we going to populate our weekend flag field?

01:31.490 --> 01:38.390
So there's no obvious out of the box SQL function to tell us whether or not a date is a weekend.

01:38.600 --> 01:43.790
Well, the good thing is we already have a field in our table that tells us the day of the week so we

01:43.790 --> 01:48.800
can actually run a simple update statement on our table that checks if the value in that field is Saturday

01:48.800 --> 01:49.520
or Sunday.

01:49.550 --> 01:52.030
If so, we'll flag the day as a weekend.

01:52.040 --> 01:53.900
So let's code that up really quick.

01:54.230 --> 02:07.730
So I'll just type update our table and then I'll set our weekend flag field equal to the output of a

02:07.730 --> 02:08.780
case statement.

02:09.860 --> 02:29.270
And the case statement is going to say when day of week name in Saturday or Sunday, then one

02:31.640 --> 02:34.460
else zero.

02:36.440 --> 02:41.540
So let's run that update and take another look at our table.

02:44.270 --> 02:50.690
And now you see that our weekend flag is appropriately populating with ones or zeros, depending on

02:50.690 --> 02:51.560
the day of the week.

02:51.560 --> 02:58.430
So here we have a Saturday and a Sunday that are both populated as one and then Monday through Friday,

02:58.430 --> 02:59.510
all as zeros.

03:00.310 --> 03:02.110
So this looks like it's working fine.

03:02.530 --> 03:08.320
But last, we have our holiday flag field, which is going to be a little trickier to populate.

03:08.920 --> 03:12.970
Holidays vary by country and sometimes even by company.

03:13.000 --> 03:18.460
Since companies can observe different holidays, while this makes it a little more difficult to update

03:18.460 --> 03:23.980
our table, it also illustrates even more the value of lookup tables such as this.

03:24.610 --> 03:30.400
So let's say your particular company observes Veterans Day in the US but doesn't observe Presidents

03:30.400 --> 03:30.880
Day.

03:31.240 --> 03:34.790
There's no built in function in any language that's going to know this.

03:34.810 --> 03:40.210
So if analysts on your team have to do any holiday based reporting or analysis, they're going to have

03:40.210 --> 03:43.060
to spin up this logic individually each time.

03:43.330 --> 03:49.630
That is, unless we do all the heavy lifting for them in one centralized place, our little calendar

03:49.630 --> 03:50.170
table.

03:50.900 --> 03:53.390
And this isn't just a matter of convenience.

03:53.510 --> 03:59.180
If you have ten different people trying to define what is and is not a holiday in ten different queries,

03:59.180 --> 04:03.020
I can just about guarantee you that there's going to be a discrepancy somewhere.

04:03.380 --> 04:09.470
So lookup tables aren't just valuable for convenience, but also consistency and data integrity.

04:10.290 --> 04:14.940
With all of that said, I'm not going to bore you by coming up with a list of holidays that are celebrated

04:14.940 --> 04:17.670
in my country or observed by my company.

04:18.240 --> 04:19.860
Just for example sake.

04:19.890 --> 04:26.040
I'll merely update our holiday flag with with a one for January 1st of every year, which is a pretty

04:26.040 --> 04:27.570
widely celebrated holiday.

04:27.840 --> 04:32.940
So since our update statement is going to be fairly similar, I'll just copy and paste our previous

04:32.940 --> 04:33.450
one.

04:33.570 --> 04:43.830
And I'll say to set holiday flag equal to a case statement that checks when day of month number

04:47.160 --> 04:55.260
equals one and month number equals one.

04:55.620 --> 05:03.780
So the first day of the first month, if a date is those things, we'll say a one, otherwise zero.

05:04.110 --> 05:05.520
So let's run that.

05:05.920 --> 05:10.170
And now if we look at our calendar table one more time, we'll see.

05:10.170 --> 05:15.030
We do have a holiday flag for January 1st, but none of the other dates in our table.

05:16.110 --> 05:16.470
Okay.

05:16.470 --> 05:19.630
So at this point, our lookup table is pretty much complete.

05:20.200 --> 05:25.660
Now that we've got it working, let's take a look at an example of how it might save us some work in

05:25.660 --> 05:26.770
an actual query.

05:27.040 --> 05:31.810
So let's say we want to pull a list of all sales orders that were made on a weekend.

05:32.440 --> 05:37.450
Now, we could certainly use some date functions to determine this, but now that we have our handy

05:37.450 --> 05:43.600
calendar table, we can simply join to it on order, date to date value and then let our weekend flag

05:43.600 --> 05:44.860
do the rest of the work.

05:45.280 --> 05:47.080
So let's see what that looks like.

05:47.200 --> 05:57.730
So below our update statement here, I'll just write a simple select star from our Adventureworks sales

05:57.970 --> 05:59.470
Sales Order header table.

06:00.220 --> 06:07.160
But since I'm going to join in our calendar table, I'll alias it and I'll say a dot star.

06:07.180 --> 06:10.870
So we're just pulling in all fields from our sales order header table.

06:11.600 --> 06:20.720
And now I'll join in our calendar table and I'll join after aliasing.

06:20.720 --> 06:33.230
That is B, I'll join on a dot order date equals B dot date value.

06:33.350 --> 06:39.020
So now for every order date in our sales order header table, I'm going to pull in the corresponding

06:39.020 --> 06:46.640
row from our calendar table, which makes all of the attributes in that table for that particular date

06:46.640 --> 06:47.750
available to us.

06:48.170 --> 06:54.290
Now, lastly, since our goal is to pull in all orders that took place on a weekend, I'll add a where

06:54.320 --> 07:04.880
clause and I can just say where B dot weekend flag equals one.

07:05.690 --> 07:07.130
So let's run that.

07:07.460 --> 07:08.570
And there we are.

07:08.600 --> 07:09.950
Looks like it's working.

07:09.950 --> 07:15.630
If you look at the sequence of dates, there's a fourth and a fifth and then it skips ahead to the 11th

07:15.630 --> 07:19.770
and the 12th and then it skips ahead to the 18th and the 19th and so on and so forth.

07:19.770 --> 07:27.180
So it looks like we have with a very quick and easy query, limited our output to just orders that took

07:27.180 --> 07:28.230
place on the weekend.

07:28.230 --> 07:29.100
Very cool.

07:29.990 --> 07:36.950
So now we've seen how lookup tables can save analysts a lot of work by eliminating redundant code while

07:36.950 --> 07:43.460
at the same time encouraging consistency and integrity in our data by providing a single source of truth

07:43.460 --> 07:46.130
regarding whatever data is stored in the table.

07:46.880 --> 07:52.280
More generally, we're seeing how senior analysts can make the lives of their more junior counterparts

07:52.280 --> 07:59.030
easier by creating objects that simplify their work and lookup tables are just one example.

07:59.390 --> 08:04.970
