Coming up, we're going to start looking at other permanent objects you can create on a database server

08:04.970 --> 08:11.810
to streamline processes, eliminate redundant work, make people's lives easier, and most importantly,

08:11.810 --> 08:13.400
make you look like a rock star.

08:13.670 --> 08:16.610
We'll take the first step down that road in the next video.

08:16.640 --> 08:17.660
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.200 --> 00:01.280
Welcome back.

00:02.050 --> 00:10.150
So as your skills and responsibilities as an analyst continue to progress, you'll often find yourself

00:10.150 --> 00:16.540
building database features or objects for more junior analysts on your team.

00:17.430 --> 00:24.720
Objects that make their lives easier by hiding or to use the technical term, encapsulating.

00:24.840 --> 00:29.970
Complex logic behind a friendly intuitive interface.

00:30.760 --> 00:35.170
Now, one such object is something called a view.

00:36.040 --> 00:43.690
So in SQL, a view is essentially a virtual table based on the result set of a SQL query.

00:44.400 --> 00:48.240
It contains rows and columns just like a real table.

00:48.770 --> 00:55.670
And that's because the fields, in a view, are just fields from one or more real tables in the database,

00:55.670 --> 01:03.020
possibly combined with derived columns, just like the derived columns you might include in a SQL query.

01:03.970 --> 01:05.230
With views.

01:05.230 --> 01:08.860
You can incorporate all the SQL tricks in your toolkit.

01:09.040 --> 01:17.200
Built in functions joins case statements, window functions and so on into a query, but then make the

01:17.200 --> 01:22.840
query results available to other analysts as if the data was coming from a single table.

01:23.460 --> 01:28.530
So let's drill down a little deeper into exactly why views are so useful.

01:29.820 --> 01:32.640
For one thing, they offer simplification.

01:33.340 --> 01:41.260
Views can simplify the use of a database, especially from an analyst's perspective, by joining multiple

01:41.260 --> 01:48.160
tables and combining different fields from those tables, then presenting them as a single table.

01:48.860 --> 01:55.700
This can be particularly useful for users who might not know how to write complex queries or who might

01:55.700 --> 02:02.000
not be intimately familiar with how the tables in that particular database are related and thus not

02:02.000 --> 02:03.410
know how to join them together.

02:05.060 --> 02:08.960
A second benefit to views is consistent logic.

02:09.900 --> 02:15.660
If there's a specific calculation or transformation you're doing on your data regularly, you can embed

02:15.660 --> 02:17.250
that logic in a view.

02:17.860 --> 02:23.770
This ensures consistency as you don't have to rewrite that logic every time you need it.

02:25.300 --> 02:28.030
Finally, there's query abstraction.

02:28.770 --> 02:35.190
So if changes are made to your database, like, for example, changing the structure of various tables,

02:35.550 --> 02:42.690
you can modify the queries underlying your views to make sure they keep the same structure, which means

02:42.690 --> 02:48.180
that any applications or reports that rely on those views might not need to change.

02:49.190 --> 02:56.660
So generally speaking, the queries that we encapsulate with views tend to be on the complicated side.

02:57.380 --> 03:02.870
That's why we're creating the view to begin with, to spare other analysts from having to know how to

03:02.870 --> 03:06.020
put together an especially involved query.

03:06.860 --> 03:08.840
So for our example in this one.

03:09.980 --> 03:16.760
We'll create a view based on this query from our earlier video about the rows between clause.

03:17.030 --> 03:23.510
Certainly a very powerful and interesting feature of SQL Server, but not one that a lot of junior analysts

03:23.510 --> 03:25.100
are likely to be familiar with.

03:25.820 --> 03:32.960
Now, as you may recall, the query we're looking at here returns a rolling three day total of sales

03:32.960 --> 03:36.560
for each ordered date in the sales order header table.

03:37.540 --> 03:44.350
Now creating a view based on this query and creating views in general is pretty amazingly easy.

03:44.710 --> 03:50.830
The hard part is just putting together whatever query you're trying to encapsulate in that view.

03:52.090 --> 03:58.360
So our first step here is to make sure that what we're doing is in the context of the Adventureworks

03:58.360 --> 04:05.410
2019 sample database and not any of the other databases available to us in SQL Server Management Studio.

04:05.410 --> 04:07.150
And we've confirmed that.

04:07.780 --> 04:13.840
Obviously, if I had selected the master database up here, our view would be created inside of that

04:13.840 --> 04:17.260
database and not Adventureworks, which is not what we want.

04:18.550 --> 04:26.470
Now our next step is right above our query to type out the keywords create view.

04:28.600 --> 04:32.770
Next, we have to specify a schema for that view.

04:33.490 --> 04:37.840
Now expanding our list of tables over in our object Explorer.

04:37.840 --> 04:46.240
You can see that most of the tables in our database are assigned to a schema that organizes related

04:46.270 --> 04:51.190
tables in the database in a kind of virtual database folder.

04:52.030 --> 04:58.960
So given that our query here pertains to sales, I think I'll assign our view to the sales schema.

04:59.230 --> 05:02.710
So I'll say sales dot.

05:03.760 --> 05:10.000
And now that I've specified our views schema, we can simply give the view a name.

05:10.960 --> 05:16.480
Now you can really name the view whatever you want within the general guidelines for naming things within

05:16.480 --> 05:17.410
SQL Server.

05:18.000 --> 05:23.850
But it's conventional to prefix a view name with VW underscore.

05:24.560 --> 05:26.030
So we'll do that.

05:26.660 --> 05:31.040
And then I'll call our view sales rolling three days.

05:34.520 --> 05:42.470
Then finally, after the name of the View, we type the keyword as and then I'll just enter down once

05:42.470 --> 05:48.890
to create some space from our line of code that creates the view from the query that will actually define

05:48.890 --> 05:51.200
the data that that populates the view.

05:51.870 --> 05:56.580
And at this point, we should be ready to go ahead and execute this and try to create our view.

05:56.610 --> 05:57.990
So I'll do that.

05:59.090 --> 06:01.280
And our first attempt errors out.

06:01.830 --> 06:07.680
And it turns out that that's because we can't have order by statements in views.

06:07.710 --> 06:12.720
And our query that we are using to define the view includes an order by statement.

06:12.930 --> 06:19.170
It's actually up to the user to decide how the result set returned by the view should be sorted.

06:19.560 --> 06:25.230
So let's go ahead and remove this order by and then rerun our statement here.

06:26.810 --> 06:29.180
And it looks like it was created successfully.

06:29.510 --> 06:35.720
So how can we verify that the view was, in fact created successfully and that it works like we hope

06:35.720 --> 06:36.470
it should?

06:37.070 --> 06:45.440
Well, going over to Object Explorer, let's collapse this table section and then expand this views

06:45.440 --> 06:46.280
section.

06:47.360 --> 06:51.590
Now rolling down to the views that are prefixed with sales.

06:51.680 --> 06:54.530
That is views belonging to the sales schema.

06:54.710 --> 07:00.860
I don't see our new view, but that may mean I just need to refresh the object Explorer.

07:00.980 --> 07:03.080
So let me go ahead and hit that button.

07:05.000 --> 07:09.260
And sure enough, there's our sales rolling three days view.

07:09.830 --> 07:14.210
So how can we test whether this view is doing what it's supposed to do?

07:15.040 --> 07:15.880
Simple.

07:16.460 --> 07:20.960
Just the same way we would verify that a table contains the data we expect.

07:21.520 --> 07:26.380
So I'll just right click The View and say, select top 1000 rows.

07:28.640 --> 07:36.380
And sure enough, there's the exact same output we got from this significantly more complicated query

07:36.380 --> 07:38.930
that we're now rolling up into this view.

07:39.650 --> 07:46.850
So now, in order for an analyst on our team to benefit from this view of the data, they don't need

07:46.850 --> 07:52.610
to know how to write all of this complex code, including window functions and sub queries.

07:53.060 --> 07:58.310
They just need to be able to write a simple select fields from table type query.

07:59.150 --> 08:06.080
Now, just to emphasize how querying a view works, just like querying a table, I'm actually going

08:06.080 --> 08:10.610
to add a derived field to our query here against The View.

08:11.090 --> 08:16.250
So I'll call our derived field percent rolling three day sales.

08:23.830 --> 08:31.240
And in this column I'm going to calculate the percentage of the total due amount for a given order date

08:31.390 --> 08:36.370
compared to the sales for the last three days relative to that order date.

08:36.980 --> 08:45.050
So for January 3rd, 2014, I'll see what percent the total due on that day was of the combined totals

08:45.050 --> 08:47.240
due for the last three days.

08:47.960 --> 08:52.130
So to do that, I'll simply divide total due.

08:53.320 --> 09:01.960
By our sales last three Days column, which remember was something we derived with some level of difficulty

09:01.960 --> 09:05.380
in that query that's being encapsulated by this view.

09:06.160 --> 09:11.710
Now, to make this output a little bit prettier, I'll actually wrap this expression in a format function.

09:13.490 --> 09:16.670
And I'll format this result as a percent.

09:19.460 --> 09:25.370
Then I'll remove our top 1000 here because our view only returns 181 records.

09:27.050 --> 09:28.730
And now let's try running this.

09:29.900 --> 09:31.130
And look at that.

09:31.340 --> 09:38.630
We were able to create a derived column in this query based on the fields in the view, just like we'd

09:38.660 --> 09:42.890
be able to create a derived column based on fields in any old table.

09:43.190 --> 09:47.230
And you can also add criteria to queries against views.

09:47.240 --> 09:53.030
You can sort the output of queries against views and even join to other tables and so on.

09:53.510 --> 09:57.350
Again, just like with a quote unquote real table.

09:59.140 --> 09:59.830
Okay.

10:00.660 --> 10:06.690
So as programming languages go, SQL can be considered a bit of an odd bird.

10:07.300 --> 10:14.470
It's what's known as a set based language, which basically means it's optimized for the kinds of operations

10:14.470 --> 10:16.930
we perform on tables in a database.

10:17.970 --> 10:24.600
However, it does have some features that resemble what you'd see in a more traditional programming

10:24.600 --> 10:26.850
language like Python or JavaScript.

10:27.760 --> 10:35.440
We'll explore some of those and how they can take your game to another level coming up in the next section.

10:36.010 --> 10:37.000
See you there.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.140 --> 00:01.220
Welcome back.

00:01.610 --> 00:04.190
This is an advanced course.

00:04.190 --> 00:10.880
And part of what that means is that we are going to push past traditional SQL querying and introduce

00:10.880 --> 00:16.850
some programming techniques more commonly associated with programming languages like Python and JavaScript.

00:16.910 --> 00:22.130
Our first step in that direction will be to learn about variables and how they can help us streamline

00:22.130 --> 00:22.850
our code.

00:23.590 --> 00:29.290
Now a variable is simply a named placeholder for a value or set of values.

00:29.620 --> 00:35.410
One of the main advantages of variables is that while we only have to define them once, we can reuse

00:35.410 --> 00:36.940
them as many times as we want.

00:37.240 --> 00:42.100
So if we have a particularly complex piece of logic that we end up repeating in multiple parts of our

00:42.100 --> 00:47.950
code, we can roll that up into a single variable and then simply refer to the variable going forward.

00:48.160 --> 00:52.900
Let's start with a basic example of how to define a variable in SQL.

00:53.760 --> 01:00.300
First we have to declare the variable along with a name for the variable using the declare keyword.

01:01.050 --> 01:06.140
Local variables in SQL, which are the most common type and what we'll be covering here.

01:06.150 --> 01:11.400
Begin with an at sign, kind of like at gmail.com or at hotmail.com.

01:11.790 --> 01:14.730
So we'll make sure to include that in our variable name.

01:15.280 --> 01:21.010
We also need to define a data type, much like when we set the data type of a field in a create table

01:21.010 --> 01:21.670
statement.

01:21.850 --> 01:27.400
So let's start out just by defining a variable called myvar with a data type of int.

01:27.400 --> 01:32.650
So I'll just type declare at.

01:32.650 --> 01:35.650
Remember, the variable name has to start with an at sign.

01:35.680 --> 01:42.490
My var and then after the name of the variable, you just specify the data type which is int.

01:43.060 --> 01:51.760
Next, we can set the value of that variable to just as an example the number 11 using the set keyword.

01:51.940 --> 02:01.180
So on another line I'll say set at myvar equals 11.

02:02.170 --> 02:06.880
Finally we can show the output of our variable just by selecting it.

02:07.030 --> 02:12.940
So I can say select at myvar.

02:13.210 --> 02:18.860
Now, real quick, I want to show you what happens if I just try to run this without highlighting the

02:18.860 --> 02:21.260
declaration of the variable itself.

02:22.010 --> 02:22.430
All right.

02:22.430 --> 02:26.480
So SQL says must declare the scalar variable Myvar.

02:26.880 --> 02:32.550
So this doesn't exactly work like a temp table where you can define the variable somewhere else in your

02:32.550 --> 02:37.920
code and then refer to it in an independent statement where you're highlighting the select, but you're

02:37.920 --> 02:41.430
not highlighting where the temp table was created with variables.

02:41.430 --> 02:46.770
You actually have to highlight everything in order to run code that selects from that variable.

02:46.770 --> 02:53.310
So you have to include the declaration of the variable and where the variable is set to a value if you're

02:53.310 --> 02:54.570
also going to select the variable.

02:54.570 --> 02:59.340
So we have to actually select all of this or alternatively, don't select anything and just run everything

02:59.340 --> 03:00.180
in the editor.

03:00.930 --> 03:04.260
And there we are, we're able to select the value of that variable.

03:04.780 --> 03:11.830
There is also an alternative condensed syntax to accomplish the same thing that declares and sets the

03:11.830 --> 03:14.000
variable value on a single line.

03:14.020 --> 03:15.520
So here's what that looks like.

03:15.790 --> 03:23.650
So instead of having this set statement down here, we can actually just copy the value that we're setting

03:23.650 --> 03:24.910
the variable to.

03:25.300 --> 03:31.510
And then in our very first line, after we declare the variable in the data type, we can just say equal

03:31.510 --> 03:32.260
to 11.

03:32.760 --> 03:37.350
And then if we run these two lines, we get the same result.

03:37.950 --> 03:38.610
Okay.

03:38.790 --> 03:44.490
So now that we understand the basic mechanics of setting up a variable, let's take a look at a simple

03:44.490 --> 03:46.740
scenario in which one might be useful.

03:47.500 --> 03:53.080
Let's say we have a query in which we intend to pull all products above a certain minimum price.

03:53.620 --> 03:56.350
Right now that minimum price is $1,000.

03:56.350 --> 03:59.200
But these sorts of thresholds tend to be fickle.

03:59.200 --> 04:04.630
And it wouldn't be a major surprise if that price changes to 500 or $5000 next month.

04:05.590 --> 04:14.500
So I'll write a quick query against our production product table in which I select all records where

04:14.500 --> 04:19.210
the list price is greater than or equal to $1,000.

04:20.650 --> 04:23.560
And then we'll just run that to see what the output looks like.

04:24.130 --> 04:30.220
So we currently have that $1,000 number embedded in the where clause of our query.

04:30.750 --> 04:33.090
And there's nothing technically wrong with that.

04:33.090 --> 04:38.070
But since the number really is the most crucial component of our logic, it would be nice if we could

04:38.070 --> 04:43.110
declare it before our query so it's easy to locate and convenient to change.

04:43.350 --> 04:48.660
So let's refactor this query to use a variable as the price threshold of our criteria.

04:49.290 --> 04:54.840
So up top I'll declare a variable called at min price

04:58.740 --> 05:04.530
and I'll give it a data type of money, and then I'll just set that variable

05:07.950 --> 05:11.040
equal to $1,000.

05:11.670 --> 05:18.660
And lastly, down here in our query, I'll replace that hardcoded value to the value of our variable.

05:19.320 --> 05:23.910
And if we run this, you'll see we get the same output as before.

05:24.640 --> 05:31.690
Now a more powerful example of how variables can make our lives easier is as an alternative to embedded

05:31.690 --> 05:33.430
scalar subqueries.

05:33.820 --> 05:39.910
You might recall that we covered such subqueries previously largely as a way to embed the output of

05:39.910 --> 05:47.530
aggregate queries like the sum or count of a value in some field in our select or where clauses.

05:47.890 --> 05:51.610
And again, there's nothing technically wrong with that approach.

05:51.610 --> 05:57.550
But embedded subqueries can quickly become unwieldy to understand and maintain, especially if the same

05:57.550 --> 05:59.650
logic is repeated in multiple places.

06:00.310 --> 06:05.590
So let's take a look at an example of a query that incorporates the average list price of a product

06:05.590 --> 06:10.120
in our products table in both the select and where clauses of the query.

06:11.180 --> 06:19.010
So looking at this query, we are computing the average list price from our production dot product table

06:19.010 --> 06:25.250
in an embedded sub query and then using that in our where clause to compare to the list price for each

06:25.280 --> 06:26.480
individual record.

06:26.630 --> 06:31.670
So we're only returning records where the list price is greater than that average.

06:32.090 --> 06:39.020
And then we're repeating this exact same embedded sub query in two different locations in our select.

06:39.050 --> 06:44.060
We're including it just as a value in the average list price field.

06:44.300 --> 06:50.990
And then we're even doing a calculation based on the same value in our average list price diff column.

06:51.260 --> 06:56.510
And you can see from our average list price field, the average list price is 438.

06:57.050 --> 07:02.330
So this all works fine, but you can see that we're repeating the same sub query in three different

07:02.330 --> 07:08.540
places, which doesn't just result in ugly code, but also code that is difficult to maintain.

07:09.250 --> 07:15.550
If, for example, we wanted to change the average to a sum or we wanted to add some criteria to the

07:15.550 --> 07:19.270
subquery or apply it to a different field, et cetera.

07:19.450 --> 07:22.580
We would have to make those changes in three different places.

07:22.600 --> 07:27.070
And if you've been programming for any time at all, you know that's definitely not a good thing.

07:28.260 --> 07:33.630
It's not something we talk a lot about in regards to SQL, but there is a principle in other programming

07:33.630 --> 07:37.770
languages called DRI, which stands for Don't Repeat Yourself.

07:38.390 --> 07:43.430
It's a great rule of thumb to follow, and using variables makes doing so a lot easier.

07:44.100 --> 07:48.960
So let's go ahead and try this code up by pulling that subquery out into a variable.

07:50.100 --> 07:52.870
Declaring the variable will work just like before.

07:52.890 --> 07:58.200
But since we're populating the variable with the output of a query as opposed to a hard coded value,

07:58.230 --> 08:00.780
the syntax is going to be a little different.

08:01.050 --> 08:07.290
We will select a value into the variable as opposed to setting it, and our select query will need to

08:07.290 --> 08:08.720
be wrapped in parentheses.

08:08.730 --> 08:10.350
So let's see what that looks like.

08:11.040 --> 08:15.030
I'll start by declaring a variable called average price.

08:19.800 --> 08:22.590
And I'll set the data type of that to money.

08:24.780 --> 08:28.890
And then I'm going to select a value into that variable.

08:28.980 --> 08:40.320
So I'll type select average price equal to and I'm going to populate it with our little subquery here

08:40.320 --> 08:42.120
that gets the average list price.

08:43.560 --> 08:48.600
But I actually need to wrap this query in parentheses for this to work.

08:49.530 --> 08:55.020
Now, just to make sure this average price variable is populating with what we expect, I'll select

08:55.020 --> 08:56.100
it really quick.

08:57.840 --> 09:00.180
And then let's run these three lines.

09:01.050 --> 09:07.170
And it looks like my average price variable is populated with that same $438 average value.

09:07.920 --> 09:15.960
So our last step is just to refactor our query down here by substituting all of these ugly embedded

09:15.960 --> 09:18.810
subqueries with that clean little variable.

09:19.420 --> 09:27.040
So we'll overwrite this embedded subquery and this one and.

09:27.720 --> 09:28.560
This one.

09:29.250 --> 09:35.040
So now we'll just run all of this and it looks like we get the exact same result.

09:35.670 --> 09:41.550
I think we can all agree that this is just a much cleaner query that would be far easier for another

09:41.550 --> 09:44.640
analyst to understand and for us to maintain.

09:45.480 --> 09:46.200
All right.

09:46.410 --> 09:51.690
Up next, we'll take a look at another application of variables that can really help us streamline our

09:51.690 --> 09:52.260
code.

09:52.410 --> 09:53.460
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
