00:00.400 --> 00:01.450
Welcome back.

00:02.050 --> 00:07.360
Before we move on from variables, let's look at one more scenario in which variables can be extremely

00:07.360 --> 00:08.050
useful.

00:08.320 --> 00:12.000
That is when you need to build layers of logic upon each other.

00:12.010 --> 00:17.110
But using scalar values like single dates instead of values in a table.

00:18.200 --> 00:24.050
Let's say we want to compute the first and last days of the previous month to use as parameters in a

00:24.050 --> 00:27.380
query that will return all values from the previous month.

00:27.740 --> 00:33.950
In the real world, this is a very common scenario as it's very typical to have reporting that is concerned

00:33.950 --> 00:37.940
with the previous month's activity, the previous month's sales, etcetera.

00:38.120 --> 00:43.790
There isn't an off the shelf function in SQL that can accomplish this, but we can build the logic step

00:43.790 --> 00:47.270
by step with a series of variables that refer to each other.

00:47.660 --> 00:53.720
We'll begin by defining a variable for today's date since previous month is relative to the current

00:53.720 --> 00:54.140
date.

00:54.140 --> 00:55.820
That's a logical starting point.

00:56.600 --> 01:02.360
So down below our current example, I'll declare a variable called at today

01:06.710 --> 01:15.290
and I'll give it a data type of date, and then I'll set the value equal to the current date, which

01:15.290 --> 01:16.910
will retrieve with get date.

01:17.030 --> 01:28.020
But I will cast the value of that get date function which returns a date time to just a date and I actually

01:28.020 --> 01:33.480
forgot to include my variable name after set and it works a little better if you tell set what it's

01:33.480 --> 01:34.350
supposed to set.

01:34.990 --> 01:41.890
And then just to make sure this is doing what we think, I'll go ahead and select that variable and

01:41.890 --> 01:45.610
we'll run it and it's returning the current date.

01:45.640 --> 01:47.590
Where am when am.

01:48.350 --> 01:48.680
Now.

01:48.680 --> 01:55.100
Next, we'll calculate the first day of the current month based on the value of our today variable.

01:55.620 --> 02:00.540
Now we'll do this using the SQL function date from parts.

02:00.750 --> 02:04.800
So we'll declare another variable called Bom for beginning of month

02:08.040 --> 02:09.660
and that will also be a date.

02:10.710 --> 02:12.990
And we'll set that variable

02:17.160 --> 02:21.480
to be the output of the date from parts.

02:21.480 --> 02:28.800
Function and date from parts basically creates a date based on a year, a month and a day that you provide

02:28.800 --> 02:29.210
it.

02:29.220 --> 02:38.610
So the year will just be the year of our current date and month will work exactly the same, except

02:38.610 --> 02:40.140
we're just using the month function.

02:40.530 --> 02:45.900
And then the trick is for day, we're just going to hardcode day to the number one.

02:46.140 --> 02:51.510
So what this is going to do for us is give us a date that is the same year and month as the current

02:51.510 --> 02:54.570
date, but it is the first day of that month.

02:54.930 --> 03:02.170
So just to make sure that's working, we'll again select our variable and run all of this because we're

03:02.170 --> 03:08.530
referring to that today variable in our logic that populates the Bom variable.

03:09.340 --> 03:10.180
And there we are.

03:10.210 --> 03:12.640
We have the first day of the current month.

03:13.120 --> 03:19.210
So with our beginning of month date in hand, calculating the first and last days of the previous month

03:19.210 --> 03:23.260
is actually going to be pretty straightforward using the date add function.

03:23.740 --> 03:28.480
So I'll start by declaring a variable for our previous beginning of month.

03:34.590 --> 03:36.720
And that will also be a date type.

03:37.260 --> 03:43.310
And then we're going to set that to be the output of the function.

03:43.320 --> 03:49.980
And again, I forgot to include my variable name, but we'll set it to be the output of the function

03:50.220 --> 03:52.800
date Add.

03:53.850 --> 04:00.930
And we want to add a month actually, because we want to go back one month from our current beginning

04:00.930 --> 04:01.590
of month.

04:01.980 --> 04:07.830
And then we'll the second argument will be a minus one because again, we're going back one month and

04:07.830 --> 04:13.800
then the final argument will just be the date that we're referring to, which is our beginning of month

04:13.800 --> 04:14.220
date.

04:15.570 --> 04:24.030
And then just to make sure this is working, I'll again select this guy and we'll highlight all of this

04:24.030 --> 04:24.660
and run.

04:26.230 --> 04:32.920
And now we've got the first day of the previous month stored in our previous beginning of month variable.

04:33.450 --> 04:38.400
And then the last piece is just the previous end of month, which will be a very similar process to

04:38.400 --> 04:39.000
get to.

04:39.360 --> 04:42.720
I'll just copy and paste my previous code since it's quite similar.

04:44.190 --> 04:48.600
And here I'll say previous Eom for end of month.

04:49.190 --> 04:54.470
And I'll set the previous end of month equal to the output of the function date Add.

04:54.470 --> 05:01.130
But instead of subtracting a month from our current beginning of month, I'll subtract just a day.

05:01.130 --> 05:06.620
Because if you subtract one day from the beginning of the current month, you end up with the last day

05:06.620 --> 05:07.640
of the previous month.

05:08.250 --> 05:12.990
And then lastly, I'll just select our new previous end of month variable.

05:13.590 --> 05:15.450
So let's highlight all of this.

05:15.480 --> 05:16.470
Run it.

05:17.210 --> 05:18.320
And there we have it.

05:18.440 --> 05:23.480
Now we have the last day of the previous month stored in our previous end of month variable.

05:24.040 --> 05:30.520
Now, we could actually accomplish all of this by nesting our beginning of current month logic inside

05:30.520 --> 05:35.740
of our beginning of previous month logic and then nesting our today logic inside of that.

05:35.740 --> 05:38.850
But you might not want to go down that path.

05:38.860 --> 05:41.440
So here's what that would actually look like.

05:42.620 --> 05:45.230
But good luck figuring out what's going on here.

05:45.230 --> 05:49.160
If you're not the person who wrote the code, or maybe even if you were.

05:49.970 --> 05:57.560
Variables allow us to break up this somewhat complicated operation into discrete and descriptively named

05:57.560 --> 06:01.280
steps that make it easy for someone to follow what's going on?

06:02.120 --> 06:08.600
Now, finally, let's use our date variables to simply select all records from our new calendar table

06:08.600 --> 06:11.510
where the date is within our previous month date range.

06:11.660 --> 06:25.130
So in place of this mess, I'll just type select star from our calendar table where the date value field

06:25.610 --> 06:30.080
is between our.

06:32.140 --> 06:34.270
Previous beginning of month variable.

06:37.280 --> 06:40.520
And our previous end of month variable.

06:40.850 --> 06:46.610
And remember, we have to highlight our variables in addition to any code that fed into those variables

06:46.610 --> 06:47.940
in order for this to work.

06:47.960 --> 06:50.120
So we'll highlight all of this.

06:52.630 --> 06:53.890
And then run it.

06:54.100 --> 06:59.930
And now we see we're getting 30 rows from the previous month, April 2021.

06:59.950 --> 07:06.100
And just like that, we have yet another tool in our toolbox that can make our code cleaner and more

07:06.100 --> 07:06.730
elegant.

07:07.030 --> 07:12.400
But variables have a role beyond simply being placeholders for values in our select queries.

07:13.040 --> 07:18.860
There are certain types of database objects, two of which we'll be discussing very soon, which make

07:18.890 --> 07:24.380
extensive use of variables along with other programming structures more commonly found in languages

07:24.380 --> 07:26.210
used for application development.

07:26.570 --> 07:30.110
Now that we've mastered variables, we're ready to dive into that.

07:30.320 --> 07:31.770
Can't wait to get started.

07:31.790 --> 07:32.750
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.140 --> 00:01.160
Welcome back.

00:01.960 --> 00:07.990
We've already learned about how we can create permanent tables on our database server that make life

00:07.990 --> 00:10.360
easier for our teammates and ourselves.

00:10.880 --> 00:12.650
But what if it didn't end there?

00:13.040 --> 00:17.840
What if we could actually hack into the SQL language and create our own functions?

00:17.840 --> 00:21.650
If we can't find an existing SQL function that does what we want?

00:22.340 --> 00:29.720
Well, it turns out that we can with user defined functions, we can define blocks of logic that live

00:29.720 --> 00:34.490
on our database server and work just like many other functions we've already used.

00:35.330 --> 00:40.790
Let's say, for example, you'd like a function that returns the current date but truncated so as not

00:40.790 --> 00:42.110
to include a timestamp.

00:42.500 --> 00:46.310
SQL has the get date function, but that includes a timestamp.

00:46.760 --> 00:50.480
Sounds like a good opportunity for us to roll our own function.

00:51.430 --> 00:54.910
To do this, we'll have to consider a few things in advance.

00:55.210 --> 00:59.260
First, what is the data type of the value that will be returned?

00:59.590 --> 01:02.830
This will need to be specified in the function definition.

01:03.670 --> 01:07.930
Second, we need to decide whether the function will take any arguments.

01:08.510 --> 01:15.440
Think of just as an example, how the date add function requires us to pass in pieces of data that feed

01:15.440 --> 01:16.970
into the logic of the function.

01:17.630 --> 01:18.350
In this case.

01:18.350 --> 01:22.790
However, since we're just returning today's date, arguments won't be necessary.

01:23.620 --> 01:28.000
Our function definition begins with the keywords create function.

01:30.940 --> 01:37.120
Then, as when we created lookup tables, we need to specify the database and the schema.

01:37.150 --> 01:40.390
The function will live on just like a permanent table.

01:40.420 --> 01:45.400
Our user defined function will take up permanent residence on our database server, which is how it

01:45.400 --> 01:48.070
will be available for us and others to use.

01:48.220 --> 01:55.300
But the tricky part here is we're actually not permitted to specify the database in our function definition

01:55.300 --> 02:03.580
itself, so we can't say create function Adventureworks 2019 DBO like we did when we created tables.

02:03.730 --> 02:11.800
Instead, we have to make sure that our session here understands that any code we write in it applies

02:11.800 --> 02:12.640
to the database.

02:12.640 --> 02:14.350
We want that function to live on.

02:14.350 --> 02:19.570
And the easiest way to do that, and I'll go away from full screen mode here, is to just go up to this

02:19.570 --> 02:24.920
little window right here and make sure that the selected database is the one that you're interested

02:24.920 --> 02:26.180
in operating against.

02:26.210 --> 02:31.520
Now we have Adventureworks 2019 selected, which means we don't need to worry about spelling it out

02:31.520 --> 02:32.840
in this editor window.

02:32.840 --> 02:39.170
But if it was not selected, if, for example, the master database was selected instead when we created

02:39.170 --> 02:44.330
this function, the function would actually live in the master database and not adventureworks, which

02:44.360 --> 02:45.300
isn't what we want.

02:45.320 --> 02:52.400
So just double check to make sure that your database of choice is chosen here before you actually execute

02:52.400 --> 02:54.500
any code that creates a user defined function.

02:55.230 --> 02:59.160
Alternately, you can also use this syntax.

02:59.400 --> 03:07.530
Use Adventureworks 2019 and then below that the go keyword.

03:08.190 --> 03:10.590
That essentially accomplishes the same thing.

03:11.670 --> 03:17.070
Now, next, we'll just specify the schema within Adventureworks that we want the function to live on.

03:17.070 --> 03:21.690
And just like with our calendar table, we'll use the default DBO schema.

03:22.740 --> 03:32.820
And then we're going to name our function u n short for user defined function current date.

03:33.540 --> 03:38.850
After that, we'll have to include a pair of parentheses even though we're not passing any arguments

03:38.850 --> 03:40.600
to this particular function.

03:40.620 --> 03:46.290
All functions have to have a pair of parentheses after the name in the function definition.

03:46.290 --> 03:52.110
And if we did want to pass any arguments to our function in between these parentheses is where we would

03:52.140 --> 03:52.920
handle that.

03:53.490 --> 03:58.530
Next, we specify the data type of the value that the function will return.

03:58.920 --> 04:04.680
Since our function is returning today's date, that data type will be, not surprisingly, date.

04:04.830 --> 04:10.410
So I'll just say returns date.

04:11.400 --> 04:17.670
This is followed by some unusual syntax that I will strongly encourage you not to think too deeply about

04:17.670 --> 04:18.360
for now.

04:19.000 --> 04:24.970
Rather just consider it as a kind of template that you plug the main logic of your function definition

04:24.970 --> 04:25.570
into.

04:26.750 --> 04:32.540
First there is the as keyword and that is followed by the keywords.

04:32.630 --> 04:35.600
Begin and end.

04:36.650 --> 04:38.300
Begin and end here.

04:38.300 --> 04:41.180
Define what's called a block of code.

04:41.970 --> 04:47.940
The main thing you need to understand about that is that the beating heart of your function, the logic

04:47.940 --> 04:53.220
that takes whatever input you supply it, if any, and translates that into an output.

04:53.250 --> 04:57.150
Lives between these begin and end keywords.

04:57.510 --> 05:05.100
Finally, whatever value our function will ultimately return must be preceded by the return keyword.

05:05.740 --> 05:09.440
In the case of our little function, there's not a tremendous amount of logic.

05:09.460 --> 05:14.290
We're really just casting the output of the getdate function as a date and returning that.

05:14.500 --> 05:18.130
So we'll just have that cast of Getdate as the return value.

05:18.460 --> 05:29.230
So I'll just tab over and type return cast, get date as date.

05:29.560 --> 05:31.930
So this should be all we need to create the function.

05:31.930 --> 05:33.610
So I'll go ahead and run the code.

05:34.580 --> 05:36.620
And it looks like it was created successfully.

05:36.830 --> 05:42.920
But where can we find it in Object Explorer if it really is something that lives on our database?

05:42.920 --> 05:45.230
And then how can we use it in a query?

05:45.500 --> 05:49.820
Well, if we go over to Object Explorer under Programmability.

05:50.500 --> 05:53.080
And then functions.

05:54.410 --> 06:01.040
And then just to make sure that we have the latest and greatest available after we've after we've selected

06:01.040 --> 06:06.230
scalar valued functions here under functions, we'll click this little refresh button up here.

06:06.920 --> 06:10.040
And then we'll expand scalar valued functions.

06:10.460 --> 06:13.490
And there is our guy Ufn current date.

06:13.490 --> 06:20.510
So it now lives in our database permanently alongside all of these other user defined functions that

06:20.510 --> 06:21.350
were built in.

06:21.880 --> 06:28.060
Now, you may be wondering about these other flavors of functions that are listed in the function section

06:28.090 --> 06:30.910
of programmability in Object Explorer.

06:31.210 --> 06:37.450
Well, the bottom line is of these function types are scalar valued functions are just going to be used

06:37.480 --> 06:43.480
much more often and have more use cases than, for example, table valued functions.

06:43.480 --> 06:48.610
So we're really just going to concern ourselves with scalar valued functions when it comes to functions

06:48.610 --> 06:50.260
that we define ourselves.

06:50.650 --> 06:54.190
Now scalar, if you recall, means single value.

06:54.520 --> 07:00.490
Our particular function here is a scalar function because it returns a single value every time it is

07:00.490 --> 07:01.270
executed.

07:01.270 --> 07:07.660
And if you think about it, most of the functions we use in SQL date functions, text functions, etcetera

07:07.780 --> 07:13.960
are scalar functions too, because if you pass values into those functions, they return a single value.

07:14.880 --> 07:18.900
So now let's try using our scalar function in a simple query.

07:19.740 --> 07:25.350
Here we have some code that pulls all sales orders from the sales order header table that took place

07:25.350 --> 07:26.580
in 2011.

07:26.670 --> 07:32.700
And we just want to add a column in our output that shows today's date, but minus a timestamp.

07:33.680 --> 07:37.550
All we have to do is add a new column, which we will call today,

07:40.760 --> 07:45.050
and then set that column equal to the output of our new function.

07:45.170 --> 07:54.890
So we'll just say DBO, dot ufn current date, and then we do need to include the parentheses after

07:54.890 --> 07:55.700
the function call.

07:55.730 --> 08:00.260
But because we are not passing any arguments into it, we can leave the space between those parentheses

08:00.260 --> 08:00.830
empty.

08:01.190 --> 08:03.380
So let's run this and see what we get.

08:04.190 --> 08:10.010
And if you're seeing the current date, at whatever point in the future you're watching this, congratulations.

08:10.010 --> 08:12.380
You just created your own SQL function.

08:13.100 --> 08:14.850
And while this is pretty cool.

08:14.870 --> 08:21.020
User defined functions are capable of so much more, especially when we can pass arguments into them.

08:21.260 --> 08:24.320
We'll take a look at an example of that in the next video.

08:24.410 --> 08:25.370
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.240 --> 00:01.320
Welcome back.

00:02.110 --> 00:08.260
Now we're going to walk through an example that will demonstrate how adding parameters to our user defined

00:08.290 --> 00:11.980
functions can make them much more flexible and powerful.

00:12.930 --> 00:19.110
Here you can see a query that takes advantage of our newly created calendar table to show the number

00:19.110 --> 00:25.440
of business days elapsed between the order, date and ship date in our sales order header table.

00:25.770 --> 00:30.990
Now, this code is a little bit hairy, but if you recall our section on correlated subqueries, it

00:30.990 --> 00:33.180
shouldn't be too daunting for you to understand.

00:33.930 --> 00:40.740
Essentially for every sales order in our sales order header table, the order date and ship date of

00:40.770 --> 00:44.700
that order are passed into this correlated subquery.

00:45.620 --> 00:50.840
Those dates are then used as parameters to return the count of business days.

00:51.520 --> 00:58.120
That is to say, days that are not either holidays or weekends between those two dates.

00:58.300 --> 01:01.480
Order, date and ship date in our calendar table.

01:02.290 --> 01:07.870
Now, again, while you could write this query if you really needed to, it's a fairly tricky little

01:07.870 --> 01:13.630
piece of logic to implement and one that a more junior analyst is probably going to struggle to understand.

01:13.930 --> 01:18.700
And the worst part is you could certainly imagine this logic needing to be used frequently.

01:18.940 --> 01:24.850
It is a very common need to measure timeframes based on business days elapsed since many businesses

01:24.850 --> 01:26.920
are not open on weekends or holidays.

01:27.710 --> 01:33.770
When you find complicated logic like this that is being used repeatedly in different queries by different

01:33.770 --> 01:38.450
analysts, you have probably found yourself a good candidate for a user defined function.

01:39.130 --> 01:45.490
So let's take a crack at wrapping all of this nasty logic up into a nice, clean, user defined function

01:45.490 --> 01:50.590
that anybody can use without having to think about what's going on under the hood, so to speak.

01:50.860 --> 01:56.000
So this is going to work very much like our previous function, but with one big exception.

01:56.020 --> 02:01.810
We will now need to make use of parameters to tell the function what date range it should apply to our

02:01.810 --> 02:06.190
calendar table to give us a count of business days between those dates.

02:06.970 --> 02:11.470
These parameters are kind of sort of the same thing as arguments.

02:11.620 --> 02:13.810
The difference is in where they're found.

02:14.370 --> 02:21.510
Parameters are part of the function definition itself and operate as kind of placeholders that accept

02:21.510 --> 02:25.320
user input that is then used in the logic of the function.

02:26.200 --> 02:31.900
Arguments, on the other hand, are the actual values supplied to these parameters when someone calls

02:31.900 --> 02:32.650
the function.

02:33.340 --> 02:38.050
The parameters are implemented in our function as variables, something we learned about in the last

02:38.050 --> 02:38.710
video.

02:38.950 --> 02:41.410
So let's go ahead and see how all this works.

02:42.460 --> 02:45.880
So I'll go ahead and write our function out in a new editor window.

02:46.090 --> 02:49.540
And first I'll make sure we're using adventureworks.

02:54.490 --> 02:58.940
And then I'll write create function.

02:59.320 --> 03:04.840
DBO, Dot and I'll call our function UDF an elapsed

03:07.120 --> 03:09.580
business days.

03:10.450 --> 03:14.140
And for now, I'll leave the parentheses after the function definition.

03:14.930 --> 03:15.710
Blank.

03:15.710 --> 03:17.810
And we'll get back to those in just a moment.

03:18.320 --> 03:23.490
If we think about the value that our function needs to return, it's actually not a date.

03:23.540 --> 03:30.080
It's a whole number representing the number of business days between some start date and some end date.

03:30.110 --> 03:33.770
So our function will need to return an INT data type.

03:33.770 --> 03:46.550
So we'll just say returns int and then we'll add our as keyword and our block defined by begin and End.

03:47.090 --> 03:53.750
So again, this space between begin and end is where the heart of our function logic lives.

03:53.750 --> 04:01.070
And so in there I'm actually just going to drop our entire correlated subquery because that has 90%

04:01.070 --> 04:02.990
of what we need to implement the function.

04:03.320 --> 04:10.100
But what is not available to us in this function is the specific date values that were being passed

04:10.100 --> 04:16.760
in from the sales order header, table order date and ship date to our correlated subquery.

04:17.320 --> 04:22.180
So without those values being passed in from an outer query, where are we going to get them?

04:22.540 --> 04:26.050
Well, that's where our function parameters come in.

04:26.740 --> 04:29.380
We are actually going to define a pair of parameters.

04:29.410 --> 04:36.550
We'll call them start date and end date that a user will have to supply as arguments whenever they call

04:36.550 --> 04:37.390
the function.

04:37.630 --> 04:45.190
We will then replace the references to order, date and ship date down here in our code with these variables.

04:45.490 --> 04:50.710
So going back up to the top of the function definition, we'll add a start date variable inside of the

04:50.710 --> 04:53.290
parentheses and give it a date data type.

04:53.740 --> 04:58.930
And since we're dealing with a variable, we have to start it with an at symbol.

05:00.550 --> 05:04.000
And again, we're going to call this start date and give it a data type of date.

05:05.200 --> 05:12.310
Note that the variables that we define between the parentheses of a user defined function do not have

05:12.310 --> 05:16.480
to be declared, nor does their value have to be explicitly set.

05:16.510 --> 05:18.460
Like the other variables we've seen.

05:19.200 --> 05:23.580
Instead, these variables are passed in by whatever code calls the function.

05:24.390 --> 05:28.770
Our second argument will be end date, which will also be a date data type.

05:28.770 --> 05:38.040
So we can actually just copy and paste our start date here and just change start to end.

05:38.460 --> 05:43.710
So now that we have a start date and an end date value to work with, we can swap those into our query

05:43.710 --> 05:44.310
logic.

05:45.030 --> 05:46.950
So down here in the.

05:46.980 --> 05:49.140
And what was our correlated subquery?

05:49.170 --> 05:54.030
I'm going to replace a dot order date, which was the beginning of the interval.

05:54.030 --> 05:59.280
If you think about it, our event of interest starts when something is ordered and then ends when that

05:59.280 --> 06:00.240
something is shipped.

06:00.240 --> 06:02.640
So our order date is our start date.

06:03.250 --> 06:07.780
And our ship date is our end date because again, that's the interval we are trying to measure.

06:08.260 --> 06:13.690
And since this is no longer a correlated subquery that we're trying to connect and join to some outer

06:13.690 --> 06:21.250
query, we no longer need to alias our calendar table so we can get rid of all of these b dot references

06:21.430 --> 06:23.140
and the table alias.

06:23.830 --> 06:25.630
But we're still missing something.

06:25.630 --> 06:28.000
We're missing the return keyword.

06:28.000 --> 06:34.060
We actually have to tell the function what we want it to return every time it's called now we want it

06:34.060 --> 06:39.700
to return this, but we have to tell the function that by using the return keyword.

06:41.290 --> 06:48.490
But since we're returning a complex statement that spans multiple lines of code, we actually have to

06:48.490 --> 06:50.200
wrap it in parentheses.

06:50.200 --> 06:56.860
So we'll just put an opening parentheses before and a closing one after our little query here.

06:57.730 --> 06:59.920
So at this point, we should be good to go.

07:00.340 --> 07:05.800
Let's go ahead and run our Create function statement here and then refresh object Explorer to make sure

07:05.800 --> 07:06.430
it's there.

07:07.620 --> 07:09.990
So it looks like our function created successfully.

07:10.170 --> 07:15.300
So now I'll click scalar valued functions over an object explorer.

07:15.450 --> 07:17.130
Hit our little refresh button.

07:17.790 --> 07:19.940
And there it is.

07:19.950 --> 07:23.160
There is our elapsed business days function that we just created.

07:23.820 --> 07:29.430
Now that we have our user defined function written, let's see how much easier it makes Calculating

07:29.430 --> 07:33.840
elapsed business days versus our original correlated subquery example.

07:34.880 --> 07:40.190
So going back to that query, I can wipe out the entire correlated subquery here.

07:40.220 --> 07:45.560
All of this mess and replace it with a simple call to our user defined function.

07:45.680 --> 07:51.890
So let's go ahead and actually copy in our function from Object Explorer and we'll get rid of these

07:51.890 --> 07:54.560
unsightly brackets just because they're kind of annoying me.

07:55.070 --> 07:57.920
And then we'll add our parentheses after the function call.

07:58.070 --> 08:05.120
And then inside these parentheses, I'm now going to pass in order date as the first argument and ship

08:05.120 --> 08:06.820
date as the second argument.

08:06.830 --> 08:12.500
So those arguments are what are going to be passed in to those parameters.

08:12.500 --> 08:17.600
In the function definition, the start order date will be mapped to start date.

08:18.130 --> 08:21.100
And ship date will be mapped.

08:22.250 --> 08:23.090
To end date.

08:23.420 --> 08:30.170
But keep in mind, we could also pass in due date as the end date or due date as the start date or any

08:30.170 --> 08:35.720
other combination of dates that we would want to pass in to this function really in any order we want.

08:36.570 --> 08:36.900
All right.

08:36.900 --> 08:39.300
So without further ado, let's go ahead and run this.

08:40.740 --> 08:41.990
And there we go.

08:42.000 --> 08:45.570
It looks like our elapsed business day function is working.

08:45.570 --> 08:53.010
We're now getting a different number of elapsed business days between order, date and ship date, depending

08:53.010 --> 08:59.940
on whether the range of dates in between these two dates contains a holiday or a weekend.

08:59.940 --> 09:04.050
Some intervals are five days, some intervals are six.

09:04.610 --> 09:12.980
So behind the scenes, our function is being run once for each row of this data set and the sales order

09:12.980 --> 09:13.550
date.

09:14.240 --> 09:15.060
Like this.

09:15.080 --> 09:16.310
And the ship date.

09:16.900 --> 09:23.020
For a given row are passed in to the start date and end date parameters of the function respectively.

09:23.290 --> 09:28.180
The output of the function for those two dates is then returned on that row.

09:28.750 --> 09:34.480
So you can see that we were able to get the same output as with our correlated subquery, but with much

09:34.480 --> 09:36.910
cleaner, easier to understand code.

09:37.210 --> 09:43.270
And the more this logic is used by yourself or other analysts, the more of a positive impact this function

09:43.270 --> 09:43.960
can have.

09:44.320 --> 09:49.420
Imagine if some tweak needed to be made regarding how a lapsed business days are calculated.

09:49.720 --> 09:55.570
If that logic was being defined separately in dozens of different analysts queries, that update would

09:55.570 --> 09:58.120
have to be made in every one of those places.

09:58.480 --> 10:04.750
Instead, with our user defined function, we can make the change in one place and it will automatically

10:04.750 --> 10:09.250
propagate to whatever code uses or calls the function.

10:10.110 --> 10:16.110
As with any programming construct, you should employ user defined functions conservatively only as

10:16.110 --> 10:16.710
needed.

10:17.320 --> 10:22.510
Sometimes when somebody gives you a shiny new hammer, suddenly every problem looks like a nail.

10:22.980 --> 10:25.680
But most of the time you want to use a function for something.

10:25.710 --> 10:28.290
SQL already has what you need built in.

10:28.860 --> 10:34.200
But in those cases where SQL is built in toolbox is empty and it's likely that other people will need

10:34.200 --> 10:36.270
to solve the same problem we are dealing with.

10:36.660 --> 10:39.030
A user defined function can be the way to go.

10:40.280 --> 10:47.360
And speaking of which, one common scenario where user defined functions tend to prove helpful, doesn't

10:47.360 --> 10:53.420
involve returning individual values like a conventional SQL function at all.

10:54.180 --> 11:00.510
Instead, there's another flavor of ETFs that return entire tables.

11:01.050 --> 11:07.320
We'll see how to leverage these table valued functions to add even more value for other analysts on

11:07.320 --> 11:09.360
our team in the next video.

11:09.600 --> 11:10.590
See you there.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.290 --> 00:01.610
Hey, welcome back.

00:02.340 --> 00:10.470
So one of the lesser known yet immensely powerful tools within SQL Servers repertoire is something called

00:10.470 --> 00:15.000
the table valued function or TVF for short.

00:16.030 --> 00:24.010
So at a high level, a table valued function is a user defined function that returns a table.

00:24.880 --> 00:32.260
Instead of returning a single value like the scalar user defined functions we've already seen, it returns

00:32.260 --> 00:33.520
a set of rows.

00:34.170 --> 00:42.030
This is similar to how the views we recently learned about operate with the major added advantage that

00:42.030 --> 00:45.300
TVs also accept parameters.

00:46.150 --> 00:52.960
Because of this, TVs are sometimes referred to as parameterized views.

00:53.950 --> 00:57.460
So why are table valued functions so useful?

00:58.710 --> 01:05.010
First, they encourage modularity and reusability inside of your database.

01:05.740 --> 01:11.860
Just like functions in traditional programming, TVs encapsulate logic.

01:12.420 --> 01:18.540
So if there is a complex piece of SQL code you find yourself using repeatedly, you can wrap it in a

01:18.540 --> 01:21.540
TVF and then call that function instead.

01:23.040 --> 01:27.420
Another thing to consider is how TVs enhance ease of maintenance.

01:28.010 --> 01:35.180
Like with any modular approach, if a particular piece of logic encapsulated in a TVF needs to change,

01:35.180 --> 01:38.000
you only have to change it in one place.

01:38.810 --> 01:46.010
This is as opposed to the nightmare of having 50 different analyst queries, all deriving some piece

01:46.010 --> 01:53.420
of logic, and then all of those queries needing to be changed when that business logic inevitably changes.

01:54.440 --> 01:58.640
Now finally there's parameterization and this is the big one.

01:59.350 --> 02:06.640
So views which again we've already seen are fantastic for saving a static query that you can treat as

02:06.640 --> 02:08.800
a table elsewhere in your SQL code.

02:09.410 --> 02:12.020
However, they are static.

02:12.700 --> 02:18.700
But TVs add a dynamic element to this concept by allowing parameters.

02:19.330 --> 02:27.400
So if you need a view that can alter its output based on user input, table valued functions are the

02:27.400 --> 02:28.120
way to go.

02:29.280 --> 02:36.870
So in this video, we'll dive deep into the world of TVs by creating one that allows us to fetch products

02:36.870 --> 02:38.070
based on their color.

02:38.790 --> 02:42.390
A color that we specify when we run the query.

02:43.000 --> 02:44.260
Let's get started.

02:45.610 --> 02:52.900
So as we've already seen, whenever you want to create a new function in SQL, you start with the create

02:52.900 --> 02:54.220
function keywords.

02:54.610 --> 02:58.330
This basically just tells SQL Server we're about to define a new function.

02:58.690 --> 03:00.610
So I'll go ahead and add that.

03:02.890 --> 03:06.670
Next up, we'll need to provide a name for our function.

03:07.250 --> 03:12.620
That name starts with us specifying the schema that this function should belong to.

03:13.310 --> 03:20.510
Now, since the function pertains to our products data, I think I'll assign the function to the production

03:20.510 --> 03:24.080
schema, which is where most of our product data lives.

03:24.350 --> 03:26.960
So I'll say production dot.

03:30.050 --> 03:38.070
Then I'll name the function products by color, but I'll also prefix that name with the letters u f

03:38.120 --> 03:41.600
n, which stands for user function.

03:42.260 --> 03:48.080
This is a common but completely optional prefix to the names of these user defined functions.

03:48.640 --> 03:53.140
So I'll say use an underscore products by color.

03:55.480 --> 04:00.340
Now, next up, we need to define the parameters that our function will take.

04:00.960 --> 04:06.000
After all, this is what separates a table valued function from a simple view.

04:06.610 --> 04:12.790
Just like scalar user defined functions, TVs can accept parameters to influence their behavior.

04:13.520 --> 04:19.370
And these parameters are similarly defined within parentheses following the function name.

04:20.430 --> 04:24.540
Now, in our case, we want to fetch products based on a specific color.

04:24.660 --> 04:29.100
So we need a parameter that will accept that desired color as an input.

04:29.880 --> 04:36.720
Let's name this parameter at color and give it a data type of N varchar 15.

04:37.500 --> 04:44.280
So after our function name, I'll add a pair of parentheses and then the name of our parameter at color,

04:45.450 --> 04:49.050
and then the data type of n varchar 15.

04:53.260 --> 05:00.310
Okay, now that we've successfully defined the starting point of our TVF, the next step will be to

05:00.310 --> 05:05.680
describe what the function should return and what logic it should execute.

05:06.660 --> 05:13.020
So when working with functions in SQL, it's essential to specify what type of data the function will

05:13.020 --> 05:13.710
return.

05:14.570 --> 05:19.820
Now, in the case of TVs, the function will always return a table.

05:20.430 --> 05:22.500
But how do we tell SQL Server that?

05:23.650 --> 05:31.660
Well, just like with scalar user defined functions, we'll start with the returns keyword.

05:33.550 --> 05:40.900
And now since our function is going to return a set of rows, essentially a table, we use the keyword

05:40.930 --> 05:43.210
table after returns.

05:44.680 --> 05:51.460
This tells SQL Server that the output of this function will be a table which can then be used just like

05:51.460 --> 05:53.950
any other table in subsequent queries.

05:55.290 --> 05:56.100
All right.

05:56.100 --> 06:03.120
So with that, all that's left is to specify the exact logic the function should use to produce that

06:03.120 --> 06:07.590
table, which is where the main query of the function comes into play.

06:08.440 --> 06:15.550
Now for a TVF this typically revolves around a select statement that generates the table to be returned.

06:16.480 --> 06:19.780
Now, just like with a scalar user defined function.

06:19.780 --> 06:22.030
We'll start with the as keyword.

06:23.500 --> 06:31.150
Then immediately after as we'll add the return keyword followed by a pair of parentheses.

06:31.630 --> 06:34.330
Our actual select query will go inside of those.

06:37.440 --> 06:44.580
So in the context of our function, the return keyword here is basically saying, here's the query that's

06:44.580 --> 06:47.970
going to produce the table that the function is supposed to return.

06:48.850 --> 06:51.220
And that brings us to the heart of our function.

06:51.780 --> 06:57.180
The select statement that's going to generate that data that a user is going to see when they run our

06:57.180 --> 06:57.870
function.

06:58.500 --> 07:04.680
So the whole idea behind our function is, again, to retrieve products of a specific color.

07:05.350 --> 07:09.080
A color that will be specified by whomever runs the query.

07:09.100 --> 07:10.240
When they run it.

07:11.210 --> 07:18.760
In other words, our query will be dynamic, allowing users to choose their own adventure, so to speak,

07:18.770 --> 07:22.160
rather than predefining the query criteria.

07:23.110 --> 07:30.790
To accomplish this, we'll need to make use of that acolor parameter which will capture the color value

07:30.790 --> 07:33.700
the user passes to the function when they run it.

07:35.090 --> 07:42.290
But before we get to all that fun parameter stuff, we first need to decide what actual data should

07:42.290 --> 07:43.850
be returned by our function.

07:44.930 --> 07:53.840
So what I want our function to return is a table consisting of the name, product number and color fields

07:53.840 --> 07:56.300
from the production product table.

07:57.390 --> 08:03.600
Now because a simple data poll like that should be light work for an advanced analyst like you.

08:03.630 --> 08:07.340
I'm not going to waste your time by making you watch me type it out.

08:07.350 --> 08:11.580
So instead I'll just go ahead and paste that query in in between the parentheses here.

08:12.720 --> 08:18.840
And now we can get to the fun part, which is making this query dynamic based on user input.

08:19.590 --> 08:26.790
And that basically means that instead of setting our criteria to look at a specific hard coded color,

08:27.030 --> 08:30.030
for example, where color

08:32.250 --> 08:34.140
equals green.

08:36.510 --> 08:44.190
Will instead allow our query to return all records from that production product table where the color

08:44.190 --> 08:47.520
is whatever color our user specifies.

08:48.120 --> 08:54.510
And we can do that by referencing that at color parameter in our where clause here.

08:55.470 --> 09:03.810
So now if a user passes in red when they call this function, this query here that defines the function

09:03.810 --> 09:10.650
output is going to return all records from the production dot product table where the color equals red.

09:11.880 --> 09:18.630
Now to make our solution a little bit more robust, given that users aren't always the most conscientious

09:18.630 --> 09:22.620
when it comes to entering data in a consistent way.

09:22.890 --> 09:29.370
Let's make sure that our function can handle color names, whether they're uppercase, lowercase or

09:29.370 --> 09:30.420
anything in between.

09:31.280 --> 09:38.030
So to create a common denominator between the values and the color field and the color values being

09:38.030 --> 09:44.600
passed into that parameter by our users, we'll lowercase both of those with the lower function.

09:51.030 --> 09:58.560
So now our function should be able to handle user input that's in all caps, all lowercase, or any

09:58.560 --> 10:03.990
combination of uppercase and lowercase, just as long as the color names are spelled correctly.

10:05.570 --> 10:11.540
Okay, So at this point, we should be good to go ahead and run this statement to try and create our

10:11.540 --> 10:12.820
table valued function.

10:12.830 --> 10:14.180
So let's do that.

10:16.240 --> 10:18.460
And it looks like that ran successfully.

10:18.580 --> 10:24.910
So now let's see if we can locate our brand new table valued function over here in the Object Explorer.

10:25.770 --> 10:28.380
So first I'll collapse the tables section.

10:29.510 --> 10:31.850
And then I'll go under programmability.

10:32.430 --> 10:34.290
And then functions.

10:35.210 --> 10:41.120
And then I'll hit refresh just to make sure that we can see anything that was recently created like

10:41.120 --> 10:41.930
our function.

10:43.810 --> 10:47.170
And then I'll expand this table valued function section.

10:48.110 --> 10:51.920
And sure enough, there's our production stuff.

10:52.310 --> 10:54.110
Dot products by color function.

10:54.810 --> 11:00.510
So now the real question is, does this thing actually work and how do we use it?

11:01.170 --> 11:02.940
Well, let's just see.

11:03.510 --> 11:14.820
So in a new query window, I'll type select star from and then I'll just reference the name of our new

11:14.850 --> 11:15.900
TVF.

11:17.010 --> 11:24.180
And now you're going to see that the only way that selecting data from a table valued function differs

11:24.180 --> 11:31.500
from selecting data from a view or even a table is that table valued functions can be parameterized,

11:31.530 --> 11:38.400
which means we need to pass a parameter to that function in order for it to return data for us.

11:38.880 --> 11:45.120
So after the name of the function here, I'll add a pair of parentheses, just like you would include

11:45.120 --> 11:49.590
after the name of any function, whether it's a user defined function or a built in function.

11:50.220 --> 11:54.760
And then we'll pass in the name of whatever product color we're interested in.

11:55.210 --> 11:57.280
I'll say blue.

11:58.750 --> 12:00.370
And now running this.

12:01.840 --> 12:02.890
Look at that.

12:03.430 --> 12:10.600
We get a list of the 26 products in the production dot products table that have the color blue.

12:11.410 --> 12:18.010
And note that even though I typed in blue in all lowercase, while the actual color values and the color

12:18.010 --> 12:20.410
column all start with capital letters.

12:21.010 --> 12:28.000
Our TVF still returns the data we expect because of the handling we included in the where clause of

12:28.000 --> 12:30.340
the select statement in our TVF.

12:31.090 --> 12:39.340
And just to prove that I'll now fetch all red products except I'll enter red in all caps.

12:40.640 --> 12:46.580
And just like that, there are all the products in our products table with the color red.

12:47.840 --> 12:51.980
Now, as cool as this example is, at least I think it's cool.

12:52.600 --> 12:58.030
It's barely scratching the surface of the kinds of things you can do with table valued functions.

12:58.950 --> 13:03.810
Obviously the queries that you're encapsulating within those functions can be a lot more complicated

13:03.810 --> 13:05.070
than what we saw here.

13:05.070 --> 13:09.750
And you can also pass as many parameters to those functions as you want.

13:10.050 --> 13:16.530
And of course, multiple parameters would give your users that much more control over the output of

13:16.530 --> 13:17.670
the query they're seeing.

13:19.270 --> 13:19.960
All right.

13:20.440 --> 13:27.460
So up next, we're going to look at another kind of object in SQL that lets us return dynamic output

13:27.460 --> 13:28.960
based on user input.

13:29.580 --> 13:33.780
And it's one that might be even more powerful than user defined functions.

13:34.610 --> 13:41.390
That's stored procedures which are one of the most important things to understand for serious database

13:41.390 --> 13:42.170
development.

13:42.950 --> 13:45.440
We'll learn how those work in the next video.

13:45.650 --> 13:46.760
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.140 --> 00:01.100
Welcome back.

00:01.750 --> 00:08.500
We've now seen how user defined functions can give an advanced developer the power to roll up complex

00:08.500 --> 00:14.710
logic in a convenient little package that someone else can use, even if they don't necessarily understand

00:14.710 --> 00:16.180
the code behind the scenes.

00:16.990 --> 00:23.710
And while user defined functions are limited to returning values in individual select queries, stored

00:23.710 --> 00:26.620
procedures have a scope that is much broader.

00:27.620 --> 00:34.100
Stored procedures are database objects that provide almost unlimited flexibility in allowing us to execute

00:34.100 --> 00:41.330
single or multiple blocks of code that do anything from manipulating tables in our database to returning

00:41.330 --> 00:44.300
the output of whole select queries or both.

00:44.540 --> 00:51.320
At their most basic stored procedures essentially allow us to save queries to our database server and

00:51.320 --> 00:55.190
then execute them on demand by invoking the stored procedure.

00:55.610 --> 00:59.150
In this sense, they can work as a kind of canned report.

00:59.800 --> 01:06.250
But when we include parameters, much as with user defined functions, a whole new world of possibilities

01:06.250 --> 01:07.030
is opened.

01:07.330 --> 01:13.870
Parameterized stored procedures give us a practically infinite range of options when it comes to customizing

01:13.870 --> 01:17.320
a data set or in the realm of database administration.

01:17.350 --> 01:20.590
A database process based on user input.

01:21.370 --> 01:26.200
Such storage procedures in addition to having great utility for data analysts.

01:26.230 --> 01:33.430
Are also common interfaces between applications and databases rather than directly interacting with

01:33.430 --> 01:38.890
database tables, an application can instead call on stored procedures to handle the heavy lifting on

01:38.890 --> 01:45.340
the database side and then simply return whatever data the application needs from the stored procedure.

01:45.670 --> 01:51.850
But for this course, I'm going to focus more on using stored procedures as a way to generate dynamic,

01:51.880 --> 01:54.850
user driven data extracts and reports.

01:55.680 --> 02:01.440
To get started, let's take a look at a basic example of a stored procedure that essentially just takes

02:01.440 --> 02:06.150
a query and allows us to run it on demand when we execute the stored procedure.

02:07.490 --> 02:12.980
Our starter query here, which may look fairly familiar to you since we've used variations of it in

02:12.980 --> 02:14.210
previous videos.

02:14.630 --> 02:21.590
Aggregates line totals from the sales order detail table by product and then selects the top ten products

02:21.590 --> 02:23.480
by this aggregated line total.

02:23.810 --> 02:29.990
Now, if we consider the output of this query to be a useful report in and of itself, we can simply

02:29.990 --> 02:32.630
roll this code up into a stored procedure.

02:32.930 --> 02:38.840
At that point, anyone with access to our database could view the output of this query without having

02:38.840 --> 02:43.100
to worry about finding the code file somewhere, opening it and running it.

02:43.250 --> 02:45.200
Let's take a look at how that works.

02:45.500 --> 02:51.740
So the syntax for creating a stored procedure is very similar to that of creating a user defined function.

02:52.440 --> 02:55.740
We start with the keywords create procedure.

02:55.860 --> 03:02.220
We'll specify the schema for our stored procedure to live in and then we'll name it orders report.

03:02.950 --> 03:09.940
So I'll go ahead and widen my editor out a little bit and then I'll type create.

03:11.380 --> 03:18.580
Procedure DBO, dot orders report.

03:19.150 --> 03:25.900
Then since a stored procedure doesn't necessarily return a value like a user defined function, we don't

03:25.900 --> 03:29.170
need to worry with a returns data type statement.

03:29.410 --> 03:34.600
Instead, we can move right along to the as keyword and the begin end block.

03:34.930 --> 03:44.110
So I'll roll down a couple of lines and type as and then begin and then follow that with an end, as

03:44.140 --> 03:45.710
with user defined functions.

03:45.730 --> 03:51.520
The code within our begin end block constitutes the heart of our stored procedure.

03:52.120 --> 03:57.850
In this case, that heart will simply be the query we are looking to convert into a stored procedure.

03:58.210 --> 04:03.790
We can actually just paste that directly between our begin end, and that's really all we need to do

04:03.790 --> 04:05.560
to have a functioning, stored procedure.

04:05.560 --> 04:12.790
So all I have to do is just take this query, cut it and drop it right in between our begin and end

04:12.820 --> 04:13.570
keywords.

04:14.020 --> 04:21.490
Now basically what's happening here is any code between begin and end will be executed when we call

04:21.490 --> 04:22.690
this stored procedure.

04:23.240 --> 04:28.400
In this case, that's simply a select query whose output will be returned to our editor, just like

04:28.400 --> 04:30.290
any other select query we might run.

04:30.290 --> 04:37.190
But the code block could also contain code that executes multiple, quote unquote side effects that

04:37.190 --> 04:39.590
execute physical changes in our database.

04:40.130 --> 04:46.430
This flexibility is why you will see stored procedures used everywhere from analytics to IT and database

04:46.430 --> 04:47.480
development teams.

04:48.060 --> 04:49.560
But back to our example.

04:49.560 --> 04:52.290
We can now run our Create Procedure statement.

04:52.290 --> 04:53.910
So let's go ahead and do that.

04:54.480 --> 04:56.730
And it looks like it was created successfully.

04:57.630 --> 04:58.320
Next.

04:58.320 --> 05:01.230
Let's see what calling our stored procedure looks like.

05:01.790 --> 05:09.740
It turns out that all we have to do is type the exec keyword exec, followed by the name of the stored

05:09.740 --> 05:12.350
procedure and then followed by any arguments.

05:12.350 --> 05:16.430
The stored procedure takes like a user defined function.

05:16.460 --> 05:22.040
A stored procedure can accept arguments passed into it by a user, but our basic little proc here does

05:22.040 --> 05:22.310
not.

05:22.310 --> 05:23.930
So we won't worry about that for now.

05:24.470 --> 05:32.600
So let's go ahead and execute our stored procedure by typing exec and then the name of our proc.

05:32.810 --> 05:40.760
So I'll type exec and then just the name of our stored procedure and then we'll run that.

05:41.960 --> 05:47.450
And we see the exact same output that we got from running our query before.

05:47.570 --> 05:54.950
So now anyone with access to our database can get this report, this data extract on demand anytime

05:54.950 --> 06:01.340
without having to know how to write this query or where to find this query on some shared drive somewhere.

06:01.950 --> 06:03.270
So this is great.

06:03.270 --> 06:10.140
But what if someone calling the stored procedure wanted to customize the output to include the top 15

06:10.140 --> 06:12.570
orders or the top five or the top 20?

06:13.480 --> 06:14.890
With parameters.

06:14.890 --> 06:17.200
That is actually an easy feature to add.

06:17.790 --> 06:24.060
So let's go back up to the top of our stored procedure definition and add a top end parameter that will

06:24.060 --> 06:28.920
let users of the stored procedure customize the number of top products returned.

06:29.040 --> 06:36.540
To do that, we can simply replace the create keyword up here in our Create Procedure statement with

06:36.540 --> 06:38.850
the keyword alter.

06:39.240 --> 06:46.110
We haven't reviewed this keyword before, but it is another data definition language command that allows

06:46.110 --> 06:51.540
us to alter the definition of a database object like a table, or in this case, a stored procedure.

06:52.290 --> 06:57.660
But the whole point of a stored procedure is that the logic is saved to our database server so you don't

06:57.660 --> 06:59.160
have to dig it up in a file.

06:59.160 --> 07:01.980
Saved ten folders deep on a shared drive somewhere.

07:02.100 --> 07:05.520
So how do we get to where the logic is stored on the server?

07:06.090 --> 07:15.270
So all we actually have to do is go to our object Explorer and then under programmability, we go under

07:15.270 --> 07:16.680
stored procedures.

07:16.800 --> 07:22.470
And then just to make sure we're seeing the most up to date list of stored procedures, we click that

07:22.470 --> 07:26.250
stored procedures header and then go up to our little refresh key up here.

07:26.860 --> 07:27.970
And there we are.

07:28.000 --> 07:32.140
Now we see our borders report stored, procedure listed.

07:32.470 --> 07:37.570
But how could we get to the code inside of that stored procedure to modify it if we wanted?

07:37.870 --> 07:42.010
Well, all we have to do is right click the name of that stored procedure.

07:42.530 --> 07:46.310
And then roll down to where it says script stored procedure.

07:46.310 --> 07:48.710
S And then you're given a few options.

07:48.830 --> 07:54.320
If you want to change the stored procedure, go to alter to.

07:54.880 --> 07:57.610
And then new query editor window.

07:57.670 --> 07:59.230
Now if you click that.

08:01.730 --> 08:08.090
SQL Server Management Studio is automatically going to give you a template, a script that will allow

08:08.090 --> 08:13.490
you to alter the stored procedure to alter the definition of it, which basically means just change

08:13.490 --> 08:14.600
the code inside of it.

08:14.720 --> 08:20.660
You can see that the basic structure of our stored procedure is here, along with some boilerplate code

08:20.660 --> 08:22.850
that management studio throws in.

08:23.120 --> 08:29.690
So if we change this code in our begin end block and then run this script, the definition of our stored

08:29.690 --> 08:31.310
procedure will be changed.

08:31.610 --> 08:36.950
So let's go ahead and take this alter procedure script and modify it to give our stored procedure a

08:36.950 --> 08:38.810
top end parameter.

08:39.200 --> 08:45.650
So first, after the name of our stored procedure, we'll add a pair of parentheses and then we'll name

08:45.650 --> 08:52.310
our parameter top end and it will have a data type of int.

08:53.450 --> 09:02.640
And then all we actually have to do is just take that that variable and swap it in for that hardcoded

09:02.640 --> 09:06.960
number ten value down in the criteria of our query.

09:07.170 --> 09:08.790
And it's really just that simple.

09:08.790 --> 09:13.140
That's all we need to make this stored procedure a parameterized stored procedure.

09:13.140 --> 09:20.280
And how it will work is when a user calls the procedure, they'll pass in an argument specifying what

09:20.280 --> 09:22.290
the top end they're interested in is.

09:22.290 --> 09:25.320
Do they want to see the top five, the top ten, the top 15?

09:25.470 --> 09:33.180
And then that value will be passed in to the core of our stored procedure, the query that's executed.

09:33.360 --> 09:39.150
And it will determine down here in the where statement how many top products are actually returned.

09:39.300 --> 09:42.540
So let's go ahead and execute this alter procedure statement.

09:42.870 --> 09:44.850
And that was completed successfully.

09:45.340 --> 09:49.090
So now let's take a crack at executing our orders.

09:49.090 --> 09:52.450
Report stored procedure with various different arguments.

09:53.000 --> 09:57.650
Now, one difference you're going to note here between calling a stored procedure and calling a user

09:57.650 --> 10:02.510
defined function is the lack of parentheses after the name of the procedure.

10:02.540 --> 10:07.970
If this were a function, we would have had to call it with parentheses, even with even passing in

10:07.970 --> 10:10.100
no arguments, which we didn't before.

10:10.310 --> 10:16.760
And similarly, if we pass arguments to the stored procedure, we just list the arguments after the

10:16.760 --> 10:19.900
name of the procedure without putting them in parentheses.

10:19.910 --> 10:26.180
And even if we were passing in, say, 2 or 3 arguments, we would just separate those by commas, but

10:26.180 --> 10:29.270
we still wouldn't nest them inside of parentheses.

10:29.450 --> 10:32.810
But in this case, our procedure only takes one parameter.

10:33.170 --> 10:35.750
So we'll start with the number five.

10:36.020 --> 10:40.730
So let's run our orders report proc with an argument of five.

10:42.050 --> 10:43.160
And there we have it.

10:43.160 --> 10:45.550
There are the top five products.

10:45.560 --> 10:48.200
And then if I run it with 15.

10:51.000 --> 10:56.250
Looks like we are in fact pulling in the top 15 products based on the value we passed into the stored

10:56.250 --> 10:56.940
procedure.

10:57.730 --> 11:03.940
Now, if we stopped at using stored procedures as a way to save pre-written queries to our server while

11:03.940 --> 11:09.700
allowing users to pass parameters to them to customize their output, they would still be an extremely

11:09.700 --> 11:10.660
powerful tool.

11:11.220 --> 11:15.540
But we have actually only scratched the surface of what stored procedures are capable of.

11:15.870 --> 11:21.540
Taking them to the next level will involve borrowing another programming tool from the world of application

11:21.540 --> 11:22.320
development.

11:22.350 --> 11:23.880
The If statement.

11:24.000 --> 11:26.110
We'll dive into that in the next video.

11:26.130 --> 11:27.090
I'll see you then.

course_name: The Advanced SQL Server Masterclass For Data Analysis
transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.230 --> 00:01.220
Welcome back.

00:01.860 --> 00:08.070
In this one, we're going to explore the if statement, a foundational construct in most programming

00:08.070 --> 00:11.130
languages, but a bit of an exotic feature in SQL.

00:12.170 --> 00:19.040
If statements allow us to introduce what's called control flow to our SQL Scripts functions and stored

00:19.040 --> 00:19.850
procedures.

00:20.890 --> 00:27.520
This means that based on a given logical condition being true or false, our code can branch off in

00:27.520 --> 00:30.190
one direction or an entirely different one.

00:30.520 --> 00:37.060
We can run entirely different queries or blocks of code depending on this logical condition.

00:37.600 --> 00:44.140
Most often, especially in stored procedures, the logical condition will be based on some kind of user

00:44.140 --> 00:48.010
input being passed in to one of our stored procedure parameters.

00:48.370 --> 00:51.670
The same can also apply to user defined functions.

00:52.190 --> 00:53.510
But enough theory.

00:53.550 --> 00:57.200
Let's dive right into a basic example so I can show you what I mean.

00:58.340 --> 01:00.050
And I do mean basic.

01:00.290 --> 01:04.070
Since we're dealing with a traditional programming language construct.

01:04.070 --> 01:09.140
I'm actually going to start off with the most traditional programming language intro exercise, the

01:09.140 --> 01:11.030
classic Hello World.

01:11.680 --> 01:16.990
So we're going to write an if statement that will select Hello World if a certain logical condition

01:16.990 --> 01:20.770
is true and farewell for now, if it is false.

01:20.920 --> 01:26.140
So let's start by declaring a variable called my input with an int data type.

01:26.560 --> 01:28.990
So I'll just go ahead and declare that variable.

01:33.820 --> 01:38.650
Next, we'll write the keyword if followed by our logical condition.

01:39.280 --> 01:44.170
This logical condition works very similar to those in case statements that you've written.

01:44.710 --> 01:50.740
In fact, if statements in general are quite similar to case statements, with the main difference being

01:50.740 --> 01:56.770
that case statements can only return values in a select query, while if statements can actually execute

01:56.800 --> 02:00.850
whole query outputs and execute side effects on the database as well.

02:01.490 --> 02:06.470
So for now, our logical test will be if our variable is greater than one.

02:06.590 --> 02:09.980
If it is, we will simply select Hello World.

02:10.400 --> 02:22.310
So I'll enter down a couple times and type if my input is greater than one.

02:22.970 --> 02:24.350
Select.

02:28.450 --> 02:30.190
Hello, world.

02:31.150 --> 02:37.960
Now, before we add our alternate flow in which we'll select farewell for now, if my input is not greater

02:37.960 --> 02:42.760
than one, let's actually set our variable value to two so it's greater than one.

02:42.760 --> 02:46.090
And then run this to make sure it does what we think it should.

02:46.720 --> 02:56.890
So above our if statement, I'll just set my input equal to two and then let's run this and see if it

02:56.890 --> 02:58.120
does what we think it will.

02:59.110 --> 02:59.910
And it does.

02:59.920 --> 03:06.190
We get Hello world back, but let's try changing our variable value to one and then see what happens.

03:06.220 --> 03:12.340
Keep in mind that one is not greater than one, so in theory, nothing will happen.

03:13.090 --> 03:16.810
Well, nothing happens, which is exactly what we would expect.

03:16.840 --> 03:22.180
The logical condition was not met, hence the code in the if statement was not executed.

03:23.060 --> 03:29.210
It's worth pointing out that most if statements have a begin end block directly beneath them, much

03:29.210 --> 03:32.570
like our user defined function and stored procedure definitions.

03:32.930 --> 03:38.660
If the code to be executed is simple enough to be kept on one line, you can technically exclude the

03:38.660 --> 03:40.190
begin end keywords.

03:40.890 --> 03:46.140
This is rare enough, however, that I would recommend always throwing in your begin end block below

03:46.140 --> 03:50.700
the if statement just so you don't have to remember when and when not to use them.

03:50.820 --> 03:54.000
They don't hurt anything and they're often necessary.

03:54.590 --> 03:57.500
So let's go ahead and add our begin and end.

04:02.460 --> 04:06.270
And then we'll tab over just to get everything in line.

04:07.020 --> 04:07.800
Okay.

04:07.920 --> 04:13.530
So now what about our alternate condition if our variable is not greater than one?

04:14.310 --> 04:17.880
Well, this is where the else keyword comes in.

04:18.840 --> 04:24.450
Else allows us to branch off to a second block of code that can be totally different or unrelated to

04:24.450 --> 04:25.230
the first.

04:25.260 --> 04:29.100
If our logical condition after the if statement is not met.

04:29.820 --> 04:36.450
Think of else as default logic that ensures that some code will be executed even if our if criteria

04:36.450 --> 04:37.350
is not met.

04:37.940 --> 04:45.170
So in this case, inside of a begin end block after the else keyword, we'll select the phrase farewell

04:45.170 --> 04:45.830
for now.

04:46.400 --> 04:58.130
So basically, after our little if block, we'll type else and then another begin and end block And

04:58.130 --> 05:06.260
then between that, instead of selecting Hello World, we'll just select farewell

05:09.710 --> 05:15.020
for now and we'll tab everything over just to keep things nicely aligned.

05:15.530 --> 05:23.360
So with our my input variable set to one and our logical condition stipulating that my input should

05:23.360 --> 05:29.150
be greater than one, what should happen is that the code after else will be executed.

05:29.180 --> 05:31.340
So let's run this and verify.

05:31.340 --> 05:32.420
That's what happens.

05:32.810 --> 05:33.830
And it is.

05:34.160 --> 05:40.410
And then if I change my input to four and rerun, we get Hello world.

05:41.070 --> 05:41.670
All right.

05:41.670 --> 05:43.410
It looks like this is working.

05:43.740 --> 05:47.620
But that said, this doesn't seem to be a terribly useful example.

05:47.640 --> 05:48.510
I'll admit it.

05:48.690 --> 05:53.280
So how can we apply this type of if then logic in the real world?

05:54.250 --> 05:59.770
Well, for a great example, we can look back to our stored procedure from the previous video.

06:00.250 --> 06:06.580
So let's go over to Object Explorer and crack open that stored procedure using the alter proc template

06:06.580 --> 06:08.290
so we can change it as needed.

06:08.800 --> 06:11.920
So I'll just view my object Explorer.

06:12.600 --> 06:14.850
And then I've already got my orders.

06:14.850 --> 06:18.240
Report stored procedure selected over here, conveniently enough.

06:18.240 --> 06:18.960
So I'll just.

06:18.960 --> 06:19.890
Right click.

06:19.890 --> 06:25.170
Script stored procedure as alter to new query editor window.

06:26.570 --> 06:31.010
And now we can change the definition of the stored procedure and just run this script.

06:31.190 --> 06:34.790
And that updated definition will be saved over here on the server.

06:35.720 --> 06:43.250
Okay, so right now the stored procedure just cares about the top end products for sales orders in our

06:43.250 --> 06:44.720
Adventureworks database.

06:45.020 --> 06:48.610
But what if we wanted to look at purchase orders instead?

06:48.620 --> 06:50.030
Or maybe both?

06:50.620 --> 06:54.520
With a little bit of if then logic, it's actually not as hard as it seems.

06:54.820 --> 07:01.090
First, let's consider the type of logical condition we would want to put into place to determine which

07:01.090 --> 07:02.830
direction our code takes.

07:03.040 --> 07:07.690
Do we want to pull the top sales orders or the top purchase orders?

07:08.430 --> 07:14.100
Most commonly, this sort of conditional logic will be based on an input that is passed into one of

07:14.100 --> 07:17.070
our stored procedure parameters by an end user.

07:17.280 --> 07:22.500
So let's create a new parameter in our stored procedure called order type, which we will give a data

07:22.500 --> 07:23.550
type of int.

07:23.970 --> 07:33.000
So after our top end parameter here, I'll add another parameter called order type with a data type

07:33.000 --> 07:36.490
event with our order type parameter in place.

07:36.510 --> 07:43.500
We can now create a logical condition in our stored procedure that says if the order type is one, return

07:43.500 --> 07:44.550
sales orders.

07:44.580 --> 07:47.010
Otherwise return purchase orders.

07:47.610 --> 07:53.070
With this parameter in place, it would just be up to users of our stored procedure to know to enter

07:53.070 --> 07:55.440
a one as the argument to the stored procedure.

07:55.440 --> 08:02.160
If they want to see sales orders or two or really technically anything else if they want to see purchase

08:02.160 --> 08:02.820
orders.

08:03.500 --> 08:09.740
So to create that logical condition right below our as keyword, we'll type an if statement that says

08:09.740 --> 08:15.380
if order type equals one and then we'll start our begin end block right after that.

08:16.330 --> 08:24.520
So to create that logical condition inside of the begin end block in our stored procedure, we'll type

08:24.520 --> 08:31.510
an if statement that says if order type equals one and then below that we'll start our begin end block.

08:31.780 --> 08:46.390
So right below begin here I'll type if order type equals one and then we'll add our begin end block.

08:47.230 --> 08:54.220
Now we can cut and paste our existing query right in between the begin end keywords because our existing

08:54.220 --> 08:55.630
query returns sales data.

08:55.630 --> 08:59.950
And that's actually what we want to return if the order type parameter is one.

09:00.460 --> 09:06.430
So we'll just take all of this, this select query that we were returning and we'll drop that right

09:06.430 --> 09:08.440
between Begin and End.

09:08.740 --> 09:12.340
And then just to make things neat, I'll tab over a few times.

09:13.090 --> 09:20.390
Okay, next we can create an else block below the if statement along with another begin end block.

09:20.390 --> 09:27.230
Beneath that, then we'll just copy and paste our top end sales products query right within that begin

09:27.230 --> 09:33.200
end block and then just tweak the query so it pulls purchase information instead of sales information.

09:33.440 --> 09:44.930
So below our if begin end block, I'll type else and then another begin end and then between the begin

09:44.930 --> 09:45.710
and end.

09:46.950 --> 09:51.420
We'll just copy and paste our sales query because the query against our purchase date is going to be

09:51.420 --> 09:52.410
very similar.

09:53.050 --> 10:01.720
And here where we are referencing the sales schema, we'll instead reference the purchasing schema and

10:01.720 --> 10:08.140
instead of the sales order detail table, we'll use the purchase order detail table.

10:08.470 --> 10:14.260
And lastly, I'll just tab over this whole beginning block once just to make things nice and neat.

10:14.500 --> 10:16.120
And that just about does it.

10:16.390 --> 10:23.290
Now, based on user input, we should be able to dynamically pull either a top end sales report or a

10:23.290 --> 10:24.940
top end purchase report.

10:24.970 --> 10:26.050
Pretty cool.

10:26.350 --> 10:32.290
So now let's run our alter procedure statement here and try executing our proc with different combinations

10:32.290 --> 10:33.280
of parameters.

10:33.670 --> 10:36.700
So let's go ahead and run our alter procedure.

10:36.940 --> 10:43.750
And then I'll just copy the name of our orders report proc, and then we'll try executing our orders

10:43.750 --> 10:44.830
report proc

10:47.200 --> 10:49.870
with a few different combinations of arguments.

10:50.170 --> 10:56.330
So we previously accepted one parameter that specifies how many top products we want to see.

10:56.360 --> 11:02.240
But now we have this second parameter that determines whether we return sales or purchase data.

11:02.570 --> 11:12.590
So let's try top 15 products and let's see top 15 products from purchase orders and not sales orders.

11:13.310 --> 11:14.720
So let's run this.

11:15.890 --> 11:16.250
All right.

11:16.250 --> 11:19.190
And we see we have a certain list of products here.

11:19.310 --> 11:25.280
But how do we know that these are different from the products that would represent our top products

11:25.280 --> 11:26.390
by sales order?

11:26.420 --> 11:29.030
Well, let's just change that second argument.

11:29.030 --> 11:35.570
We're passing to the orders report proc to a one and see if we have a different list of products.

11:36.390 --> 11:37.020
And we do.

11:37.050 --> 11:39.120
We have a totally different list of products.

11:39.710 --> 11:41.510
So it looks like we're in business.

11:41.780 --> 11:48.170
But before we go, I'm going to throw another scenario at you that will make things a little more complicated,

11:48.170 --> 11:53.480
but also give us even more power and flexibility when it comes to controlling the flow of our logic.

11:53.990 --> 11:56.000
We'll tackle that in the next video.

11:56.030 --> 11:56.990
I'll see you then.
