00:00.310 --> 00:01.300
Welcome back.

00:01.920 --> 00:08.160
So you might have already been wondering, What if we want to account for more than just two conditions?

00:08.160 --> 00:08.850
If.

00:08.850 --> 00:09.900
Or else.

00:10.630 --> 00:15.460
If you have a background in other programming languages at this point, you might be pining for the

00:15.460 --> 00:16.690
else if statement.

00:17.260 --> 00:20.740
Unfortunately, SQL does not have an if else if statement.

00:20.740 --> 00:24.820
So we have to resort to other somewhat less elegant options.

00:25.580 --> 00:33.350
We could use a nested if block which is an if block nested inside of another if block But these, as

00:33.350 --> 00:37.630
you might imagine, can get messy and hard to reason about pretty fast.

00:37.640 --> 00:44.780
So as an alternative, we're going to convert our if else structure to multiple distinct if statements.

00:45.720 --> 00:52.620
At this point, it's important to understand that an if else statement will always do something, since

00:52.620 --> 00:58.050
the logical condition is either true, in which case the block of code under the if statement will execute

00:58.050 --> 01:03.000
or false, in which case the block of code under the Else is executed.

01:03.580 --> 01:08.710
However, a simple if statement without an else does not necessarily have to run.

01:08.950 --> 01:14.530
If the logical condition isn't true, the block is simply skipped over and our proc moves on to the

01:14.530 --> 01:15.640
next piece of code.

01:16.360 --> 01:22.360
That will be the key to unlocking our ability to branch our code out in more than just two directions

01:22.360 --> 01:25.000
without resorting to messy nested ifs.

01:25.950 --> 01:27.590
So back to our scenario.

01:27.600 --> 01:33.090
Let's consider a third option that a user might want to see from our little top end stored procedure.

01:33.670 --> 01:39.430
What if they want to see the top ten products by combined sales and purchase orders?

01:39.760 --> 01:46.240
Well, this is going to require a third distinct block of code since the query will need to be written

01:46.240 --> 01:49.630
somewhat differently than our individual sales and purchase queries.

01:50.080 --> 01:56.050
Now, to save you from watching me type code that you would already understand easily, I've pre-written

01:56.050 --> 02:01.780
a short little query that unions together our purchase and sales data and then takes the top ten products

02:01.780 --> 02:03.610
from that combined dataset.

02:03.640 --> 02:08.290
And in case you're curious, I'll just show you that standalone query here.

02:09.500 --> 02:17.840
Basically I select the product ID and line total fields from the sales order detail table into a temp

02:17.870 --> 02:25.910
table, and then I insert into that temp table again those same fields from the purchase order detail

02:25.910 --> 02:26.570
table.

02:26.660 --> 02:29.330
And then I pretty much just execute the same query.

02:29.330 --> 02:36.650
We've been running for our top end stored procedure against that temp table that combines the purchase

02:36.650 --> 02:38.720
and sales order detail data.

02:39.110 --> 02:42.200
So our plan is to execute this logic.

02:42.230 --> 02:46.340
If a user passes in a value of three to our stored procedure.

02:46.860 --> 02:50.700
So going back to our alter procedure statement.

02:51.490 --> 03:00.070
Our first step here is to convert our else block right here to another if statement and make sure that

03:00.070 --> 03:04.540
the if criteria for our two blocks are mutually exclusive.

03:04.570 --> 03:07.690
That is to say, they cannot both be true.

03:08.290 --> 03:14.800
If we did have overlapping criteria in our two if statements, then both blocks of code would be executed.

03:14.950 --> 03:16.690
This wouldn't be the end of the world.

03:16.690 --> 03:18.220
But it is not what we want.

03:18.580 --> 03:29.440
So let's go ahead and say instead of else, we'll be more explicit and say if my order type variable

03:29.470 --> 03:30.850
equals two.

03:31.120 --> 03:39.190
So now what will happen is if a user passes in a one in our order type parameter, then this block of

03:39.190 --> 03:40.140
code will run.

03:40.150 --> 03:44.740
If they pass in a two, then this block of code will run.

03:45.070 --> 03:48.100
So at this point you can probably see where this is going.

03:48.720 --> 03:55.290
Now that we have our else block converted to an if block, all we have to do is add a third if block.

03:55.530 --> 04:01.440
This one will specify that if a user enters a value of three in that order type parameter, we will

04:01.440 --> 04:03.630
run another distinct type of query.

04:03.630 --> 04:06.240
That being that query I just showed you a moment ago.

04:06.540 --> 04:10.470
So let's go ahead and add our third if block.

04:10.680 --> 04:18.240
So we'll say if order type equals three and then we'll add our.

04:19.610 --> 04:27.140
Begin and end and then we'll just paste in our new logic.

04:28.930 --> 04:32.560
And it looks like that's already pretty well aligned with our begin and end.

04:33.310 --> 04:40.900
And in the query that I pre wrote, I already have this line total sum rank criteria down here referring

04:40.930 --> 04:42.510
to our top end variable.

04:42.520 --> 04:49.420
So at this point we should have everything we need to conditionally run our query for all three conditions

04:49.420 --> 04:53.680
sales orders, purchase orders or sales and purchase orders combined.

04:54.270 --> 04:59.430
So let's execute our alter proc statement one more time and then put it to the test.

05:00.450 --> 05:07.350
So let's go back over to our other query editor window and then roll back up to where we had previously

05:07.350 --> 05:09.900
called our orders report stored procedure.

05:10.140 --> 05:15.240
Now, keep in mind before that, the second argument really only had two options.

05:15.330 --> 05:22.200
We could either pass in a one to get top products by sales orders or a two for top products by purchase

05:22.200 --> 05:22.650
orders.

05:22.650 --> 05:24.420
But now we have a third option.

05:24.720 --> 05:32.370
So let's try pulling the top ten products for first sales.

05:34.870 --> 05:40.660
And I'll expand our little data window so we have a clearer idea of what's going on.

05:40.990 --> 05:47.350
So we can see that the top six are all just variations of that mountain 200 bike.

05:48.180 --> 05:52.860
So now let's change that to purchase orders.

05:55.390 --> 05:58.150
And now we see we have a totally different list of products.

05:58.150 --> 06:01.690
And the number one is the crank arm.

06:02.510 --> 06:05.960
But now let's see what happens if we run it with the parameter three.

06:09.790 --> 06:15.370
Okay, so the top five products are still those mountain 200 bikes.

06:16.080 --> 06:19.380
But the sixth product is now that crank arm.

06:19.380 --> 06:26.430
So one of our top products is now a product that was featured in our purchase list and not our sales

06:26.430 --> 06:26.880
list.

06:26.880 --> 06:33.720
So it looks like our combined purchase and sales product roll up is working just like we want.

06:34.570 --> 06:38.540
So now that you've seen, we can add as many if blocks as we want.

06:38.560 --> 06:44.650
I hope you appreciate the nearly unlimited flexibility that if statements when combined with stored

06:44.650 --> 06:46.270
procedures give us.

06:46.900 --> 06:53.230
Your ability to customize output based on user input is really only limited by your imagination.

06:53.590 --> 06:59.860
When using multiple independent if blocks as we did in our last example, you'll definitely want to

06:59.860 --> 07:06.370
take great care to make sure that your criteria for each if statement do not overlap unless you want

07:06.400 --> 07:09.640
multiple blocks of code to potentially run in the same procedure.

07:10.100 --> 07:15.560
But if you take care to avoid unexpected outcomes like this, if statements can take what you already

07:15.560 --> 07:20.270
know about SQL and allow you to apply it in tons of creative and interesting ways.

07:21.120 --> 07:26.100
Now, speaking of creative and interesting, our next technique really ramps up the flexibility of our

07:26.100 --> 07:32.400
stored procedures by allowing them to write their own SQL code at runtime every time a user runs the

07:32.400 --> 07:33.840
procedure with different input.

07:34.350 --> 07:40.230
So wait, am I saying that we can write a stored procedure that will in turn write its own SQL?

07:40.500 --> 07:42.330
Well, kind of.

07:42.630 --> 07:47.190
We're not talking, you know, Siri level artificial intelligence here, but it's still pretty darn

07:47.190 --> 07:47.790
cool.

07:47.910 --> 07:49.920
Let's take a look at that in the next video.

00:00.140 --> 00:01.160
Welcome back.

00:01.840 --> 00:08.710
In the last video we saw how we can conditionally execute different chunks of code based on criteria

00:08.740 --> 00:10.150
using If statements.

00:10.790 --> 00:15.770
And while this technique is powerful, it can also get a little unwieldy if we're dealing with more

00:15.770 --> 00:17.420
than 2 or 3 conditions.

00:18.030 --> 00:23.880
While there's nothing technically wrong with a long series of if blocks, you definitely run the risk

00:23.880 --> 00:30.060
of repeating similar code, especially if each block of code is only slightly different than the others.

00:30.180 --> 00:35.820
Now, in our example here from the previous video, we only have three if blocks.

00:35.940 --> 00:43.440
But imagine if we needed to account for 5 or 10 or more scenarios, all of which involved slight variations

00:43.440 --> 00:44.760
of the same logic.

00:45.000 --> 00:51.660
We would now be essentially repeating ourselves that number of times, which violates the don't repeat

00:51.660 --> 00:54.030
yourself or dry principle.

00:54.760 --> 01:00.970
So if at some point we wanted to change the structure of our output here in some fundamental way, we'd

01:00.970 --> 01:06.940
probably end up having to make a similar change in most, if not all, of the if blocks.

01:07.180 --> 01:11.380
This kind of repetitiveness makes our code harder to maintain in the long run.

01:11.650 --> 01:13.150
So what's an alternative?

01:14.390 --> 01:18.800
One approach is to use what's called dynamic SQL.

01:19.340 --> 01:25.410
This technique, which is probably going to sound a little wacky to you at first, involves our SQL

01:25.490 --> 01:33.680
code, actually constructing more SQL code at runtime, which is to say when the code is actually run.

01:34.320 --> 01:40.500
In other words, the code that is actually executed on the server isn't fully assembled until the query

01:40.500 --> 01:41.250
is run.

01:42.160 --> 01:49.300
Now, how this can work for us is we can take user inputs, typically parameters passed to a stored

01:49.300 --> 01:56.230
procedure or function and use them to dynamically construct a single SQL query that incorporates that

01:56.230 --> 01:56.920
input.

01:57.010 --> 02:04.000
This is in contrast to our previous approach of running different predefined blocks of code in response

02:04.000 --> 02:05.620
to different user inputs.

02:06.200 --> 02:10.490
Now, this is one of those things that just sounds crazy until you see it in practice.

02:10.490 --> 02:15.170
So I'm not going to waste your time trying to explain it further without showing you an example.

02:16.440 --> 02:23.910
So the central concept behind dynamic SQL is that we can take a text string no different than any other

02:23.910 --> 02:29.940
text string in a database such as a person's name or a product description, and run that string as

02:29.940 --> 02:35.100
a SQL query as long as the string itself represents valid SQL.

02:35.890 --> 02:37.780
To see how this works in action.

02:37.810 --> 02:44.140
Let's declare a variable called dynamic SQL and give it a data type of varchar max.

02:44.260 --> 02:49.540
We'll need to give it the biggest possible varchar data type because a text string that encompasses

02:49.570 --> 02:54.280
a SQL query is likely to get pretty long relative to normal text strings.

02:54.940 --> 02:57.460
So let's go ahead and declare our variable.

03:02.910 --> 03:10.350
Next, we'll set the value of our dynamic variable to a text string that just happens to be a valid

03:10.350 --> 03:13.050
SQL statement that will run on our database.

03:13.050 --> 03:19.140
And that's actually the query whose output we see here that just selects the top 100 records from the

03:19.140 --> 03:20.010
products table.

03:20.760 --> 03:27.540
So we'll go ahead and copy this query in its entirety here and then below our variable declaration,

03:27.540 --> 03:39.480
we'll type, set, and then we'll set our dynamic SQL variable to a string which includes this query.

03:39.720 --> 03:46.890
And then just because it's bugging me, I'm actually going to capitalize the L in our variable declaration

03:46.890 --> 03:48.000
and where we're setting it.

03:48.390 --> 03:55.950
Then what brings this whole process together is passing this text string in our variable into the exec

03:55.950 --> 03:56.710
function.

03:56.730 --> 03:57.960
The Exec.

03:58.860 --> 04:04.200
Now, you may have remembered that when we called stored procedures with the exec keyword, we don't

04:04.200 --> 04:05.910
include parentheses after them.

04:06.480 --> 04:13.410
However, to execute a text string as a SQL query using exec, we will need to wrap that string inside

04:13.410 --> 04:15.720
of parentheses after our exec call.

04:16.390 --> 04:21.100
So we'll just type exec and then drop our variable inside of the parentheses.

04:21.580 --> 04:30.160
So we'll type exec and then we'll just grab our variable value and drop that in here.

04:31.120 --> 04:33.520
And now let's highlight all this and run it.

04:35.200 --> 04:42.760
And you can see we get the exact same query output as we did from just running the query itself up here.

04:43.430 --> 04:47.060
Now, at this point, you might be wondering, how is this helping us?

04:47.150 --> 04:53.180
We literally just took an extra step to run a query that we could have quite simply run by itself without

04:53.180 --> 04:56.150
the need for fancy variables and exec calls.

04:56.720 --> 05:04.070
Well, if you think about what we just proved, that we can run a simple text string as a SQL query

05:04.070 --> 05:06.830
as long as that text represents valid SQL.

05:07.100 --> 05:13.130
And then if you consider that using string concatenation, we can glue different strings together in

05:13.130 --> 05:14.290
creative ways.

05:14.300 --> 05:17.240
You might start to see the potential of this approach.

05:18.000 --> 05:24.450
Now, instead of needing to write out several different blocks of similar code, which may or may not

05:24.450 --> 05:30.900
need to be executed based on some condition, we can instead take the one piece of code that changes

05:30.900 --> 05:35.490
based on each condition and just incorporate that into a text string.

05:35.490 --> 05:37.980
That will ultimately be our SQL statement.

05:38.760 --> 05:43.230
Let's take, for example, once again our top ten products query.

05:43.350 --> 05:48.870
Right now, it defines top products based on the sum of line totals.

05:49.260 --> 05:55.530
But what if we wanted to incorporate this logic in this query into a stored procedure that allows the

05:55.530 --> 06:01.100
user to define top ten products by other different aggregate functions?

06:01.110 --> 06:04.980
Perhaps Max or maybe Min, maybe average?

06:04.980 --> 06:05.700
ET cetera.

06:06.280 --> 06:11.140
Now, we could certainly take the if statement approach here and have a long series of if statements

06:11.140 --> 06:17.140
with variations of this same query where the only difference from one query to the other is which aggregate

06:17.140 --> 06:18.100
function they use.

06:18.690 --> 06:24.270
But again, this involves a lot of code duplication and it's only going to get messier and messier the

06:24.270 --> 06:25.650
more variations we have.

06:26.470 --> 06:33.340
Using dynamic SQL, we can instead piece together a single text string that incorporates the name of

06:33.340 --> 06:39.790
whatever aggregate function the user specifies and then executes that SQL string at the end of the procedure.

06:40.410 --> 06:46.290
In this way, we are avoiding all of that code repetition and only swapping in the single aspect of

06:46.290 --> 06:49.410
the code that changes based on user input.

06:50.140 --> 06:51.940
Let's see how that would work in action.

06:52.700 --> 06:58.010
Now, before we go, wrapping this into a stored procedure for ease of testing, I'm actually going

06:58.010 --> 07:00.080
to just develop it as a standalone query.

07:00.780 --> 07:07.830
One downside of dynamic SQL is that it is somewhat difficult to debug and it makes life easier to take

07:07.830 --> 07:13.970
what will ultimately be the parameters of our stored procedure and instead just declare them as variables.

07:13.980 --> 07:19.350
We can then set those variables to example values that will help us test our code as we go.

07:20.080 --> 07:25.840
Since we ultimately want our query to accept user input for the top end products that will be displayed

07:25.840 --> 07:32.620
as well as for the aggregate function that will be used as the basis of the top end calculation.

07:32.830 --> 07:37.390
We'll just declare variables for those two items and set them to example values.

07:37.630 --> 07:42.070
Then we can continually test our work based on those values as we go.

07:42.900 --> 07:47.130
We'll start by declaring our top end variable, which I'll set to ten.

07:47.580 --> 07:51.270
So above our query here, I'll declare

07:54.930 --> 07:58.170
at top n int equals ten.

07:58.620 --> 08:05.100
Then I'll declare a variable called ag function, which will allow us to dynamically specify which aggregate

08:05.100 --> 08:07.050
function we want the query to use.

08:07.350 --> 08:18.810
So I'll just copy and paste my previous variable declaration and I'll call this guy ag function and

08:18.810 --> 08:21.750
I'll make the data type A varchar 50.

08:25.980 --> 08:33.060
And we'll set the value equal to AVG for the average function.

08:33.690 --> 08:39.930
Finally, I'll add a declaration for our dynamic SQL variable, which will house the string that is

08:39.930 --> 08:45.420
constructed, then executed as SQL when someone calls our procedure.

08:46.050 --> 08:52.260
So again, I'll just copy and paste another of our variable declarations, and I'm going to call this

08:52.260 --> 08:54.480
variable dynamic SQL

08:57.420 --> 09:00.270
and I'll give it a varchar max.

09:01.890 --> 09:06.450
And right now we don't even need to set the value of that because we'll be building it as we go.

09:07.080 --> 09:14.790
Now the next step is to take our query and break it into string fragments sandwiched around the variable

09:14.790 --> 09:16.710
input that users pass in.

09:17.410 --> 09:23.890
The general idea is that we take the parts of the query that won't change based on user input, say

09:23.890 --> 09:30.730
the fields in the select list or the tables in the from clause, and use those as a kind of template

09:30.850 --> 09:38.080
that we will then concatenate our variable values to ultimately resulting in a string that changes based

09:38.080 --> 09:39.760
on the provided user input.

09:40.030 --> 09:45.070
Now, getting this done is going to require a non-trivial amount of work, so I'm actually going to

09:45.070 --> 09:46.630
save it for the next video.

09:46.660 --> 09:47.710
I'll see you then.

00:00.260 --> 00:01.370
Welcome back.

00:02.180 --> 00:04.700
Picking up where we left off in the last video.

00:04.850 --> 00:12.320
We're going to start breaking up our query here into a series of text strings that we can later execute

00:12.320 --> 00:13.640
as dynamic SQL.

00:14.210 --> 00:15.320
To get started.

00:15.320 --> 00:20.830
We'll copy everything before the first instance of an aggregate function in our query.

00:20.840 --> 00:28.910
So basically everything before this first sum here, and then we'll initialize our dynamic SQL variable

00:28.940 --> 00:29.660
to that.

00:29.840 --> 00:34.970
So below our dynamic SQL declaration, I'll type set.

00:35.600 --> 00:41.750
And then I'll just grab the name of our variable there and I'll set that equal to.

00:42.530 --> 00:49.280
All of the code from this query up to that first instance of an aggregate function.

00:50.690 --> 00:56.420
So I'll just type a couple of single quotes to, to hold our string and I'll paste that code right in

00:56.420 --> 00:57.740
between those single quotes.

00:58.400 --> 01:05.450
Next, we can take advantage of string concatenation along with the fact that you can reset a variable's

01:05.450 --> 01:09.470
value to tack on the value in our function variable.

01:09.860 --> 01:17.030
So we'll set our dynamic variables value to its current value plus the function variable.

01:17.450 --> 01:24.260
So we've already set dynamic SQL here, but what we're going to do next is set it again, but we're

01:24.260 --> 01:29.270
going to set it to its own value itself basically.

01:31.030 --> 01:35.860
Plus whatever value is in our agg function variable.

01:36.430 --> 01:42.070
Now, to be sure, we could have achieved this concatenation in our in our original set statement for

01:42.070 --> 01:43.600
the dynamic variable.

01:43.960 --> 01:51.580
But as you'll see, building out dynamic strings tends to involve many layers of concatenation and trying

01:51.580 --> 01:58.240
to do all of them in a single giant statement makes a prosthetic process that's already kind of challenging,

01:58.240 --> 02:00.430
much more difficult to understand.

04:41.200 --> 04:47.140
